## 1 Introduction

Biodiversity is crucial for a healthy biosphere in view of the different functional roles’ species perform and the ecosystem stability they can attain (IPBES [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR71 "IPBES (2019) Global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services of the intergovernmental science-Policy platform on biodiversity and ecosystem services. 
                  https://zenodo.org/records/6417333
                  
                . IPBES secretariat")). However, biosphere integrity is one of the six planetary boundaries that had been transgressed in the Anthropocene (Richardson et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR108 "Richardson K, Steffen W, Lucht W, Bendtsen J, Cornell SE, Donges JF, Drüke M, Fetzer I, Bala G, Von Bloh W, Feulner G, Fiedler S, Gerten D, Gleeson T, Hofmann M, Huiskamp W, Kummu M, Mohan C, Nogués-Bravo D, … Rockström J (2023) Earth beyond six of nine planetary boundaries. Sci Adv 9(37)")). In this context, the current extinction rate has been estimated to be 100–1,000 times the natural background rate (Cowie et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR32 "Cowie RH, Bouchet P, Fontaine B (2022) The sixth Mass extinction: fact, fiction or speculation? Biol Rev 97(2):640–663")), with the number of threatened species reaching 46,337 in 2024 (IUCN [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR74 "IUCN (2024) Summary statistics. The IUCN red list of threatened species. 
                  https://www.iucnredlist.org/resources/summary-statistics
                  
                . Retrieved January 30, 2025, from")).

Food systems, through their production, distribution and consumption patterns, are considered the main cause of this biodiversity decline given the chemicals, energy, land and water use, and unsustainable practices employed (Benton et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR11 "Benton T, Bieg C, Harwatt H, Pudasaini R, Wellesley L (2021) Food system impacts on biodiversity loss: three levers for food system transformation in support of nature. In Chatham House. 
                  https://www.chathamhouse.org/2021/02/food-system-impacts-biodiversity-loss
                  
                ")). Among these systems, seafood is attracting attention as its nutritional profile can be exploited to improve food security and because it contributes to local and national economies, especially in coastal regions. Seafood value chains rely on wild capture fisheries and aquaculture. In 2022, global captures amounted to 91 million tonnes, and, for the first time, these were surpassed by aquaculture production, 94 million tonnes (FAO [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR47 "FAO (2024) The state of world fisheries and aquaculture. Blue Transformation in action")), revealing the importance of inputs such as fishmeal and fish oil (FMFO) to meet the requirements of this growing sector. Despite this transition in seafood production, over 37% of the 442 stocks analyzed remain unsustainably exploited (FAO [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR47 "FAO (2024) The state of world fisheries and aquaculture. Blue Transformation in action")). These factors, along with the fact that many coastal communities rely on small-scale fisheries and that aquafeed mainly arrive from the ocean (Farmery et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR48 "Farmery AK, Alexander K, Anderson K, Blanchard JL, Carter CG, Evans K, Fischer M, Fleming A, Frusher S, Fulton EA, Haas B, Ck M, Murray L, Nash KL, Pecl GT, Rousseau Y, Trebilco R, Van Putten IE, Mauli S, … Nowak B (2022) Food for all: designing sustainable and secure future seafood systems. Rev Fish Biol Fish 32(1):101–121")) indicate that fisheries biodiversity impacts cannot be disregarded and require urgent attention, particularly in prominent fishing nations like Peru (Deville et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR39 "Deville A, Vázquez-Rowe I, Avadí A, Miranda F, Kahhat R (2025) Identifying current trends in the environmental impacts linked to fishmeal and fish oil production in Peru. Aquaculture 600:742239")).

### 1.1 Peruvian fisheries: challenges regarding biotic resource depletion

Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally (Majluf et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR88 "Majluf P, Matthews K, Pauly D, Skerritt DJ, Palomares MLD (2024) A review of the global use of fishmeal and fish oil and the fish in. Fish Out Metr. Sci Adv 10(42)")), with important fisheries within its exclusive economic zone (EEZ), especially Peruvian anchoveta(_Engraulis ringens_), which is the largest fishery worldwide by volume (Gozzer-Wuest et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR57 "Gozzer-Wuest R, Alonso-Población E, Tingley GA (2021) Identifying priority areas for improvement in Peruvian fisheries. Mar Policy 129:104545")). Industrial and artisanal fleets target this species, and landings are almost exclusively reduced to produce FMFO, an important ingredient for aquafeed (PRODUCE [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR101 "PRODUCE (2024) Anuario Estadístico Pesquero y Acuícola 2023. 
                  https://www.producempresarial.pe/anuario-estadistico-pesquero-y-acuicola-2023/
                  
                . Retrieved February 11, 2025, from")), with only a minor fraction of catch directed to direct human consumption – DHC (De La Puente et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR37 "De La Puente S, De La Lama RL, Benavente S, Sueiro JC, Pauly D (2020) Growing into poverty: reconstructing Peruvian small-scale fishing effort between 1950 and 2018. Front Mar Sci 7")). In recent decades, _ca._ 95% of landed anchoveta has been directed to FMFO production (PRODUCE [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR101 "PRODUCE (2024) Anuario Estadístico Pesquero y Acuícola 2023. 
                  https://www.producempresarial.pe/anuario-estadistico-pesquero-y-acuicola-2023/
                  
                . Retrieved February 11, 2025, from")), consistently supplying 15–20% of global FMFO (EUMOFA [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR45 "EUMOFA (2021) Fishmeal and fish oil - production and trade flows in the EU. European Union")). Peruvian fishmeal (FM) is mainly exported to Asia (Coayla et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR28 "Coayla E, Bedón Y, Rosales T, Jiménez L (2023) Industrial marine fishing in the face of climate change in Peru. J Mar Sci 1–10")), whereas much of the fish oil (FO) is exported to countries such as China, United States, Chile, or Norway (PRODUCE [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR101 "PRODUCE (2024) Anuario Estadístico Pesquero y Acuícola 2023. 
                  https://www.producempresarial.pe/anuario-estadistico-pesquero-y-acuicola-2023/
                  
                . Retrieved February 11, 2025, from")).

Despite the prominence of the anchoveta fishery, other species are exploited in the Peruvian EEZ and destined mainly for DHC, contributing to _ca_. 20% of annual landings and yielding 2600 million US$ in exports revenue in 2023 alone (PRODUCE [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR101 "PRODUCE (2024) Anuario Estadístico Pesquero y Acuícola 2023. 
                  https://www.producempresarial.pe/anuario-estadistico-pesquero-y-acuicola-2023/
                  
                . Retrieved February 11, 2025, from")). These species include several pelagic species, such as jack mackerel (_Trachurus murphyi_), bonito (_Sarda chiliensis_) or chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_), hake (_Merluccius gayi_), which is an important demersal species caught by midwater trawling (PRODUCE [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR101 "PRODUCE (2024) Anuario Estadístico Pesquero y Acuícola 2023. 
                  https://www.producempresarial.pe/anuario-estadistico-pesquero-y-acuicola-2023/
                  
                . Retrieved February 11, 2025, from")), jumbo squid (_Dosidicus gigas_), and calico scallop (_Argopecten purpuratus_) (Sánchez Durand and Gallo Seminario [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR111 "Sánchez Durand, Gallo Seminario M (2009) Status of and trends in the use of small pelagic fish species for reduction fisheries and for human consumption in Peru. In: Hasan MR, Halwart M (eds) Fish as feed inputs for aquaculture, vol 518. FAO, pp 325–370. 
                  https://www.fao.org/4/i1140e/i1140e00.htm
                  
                ")). These species represent an important fraction of the economic revenue of the Peruvian fishing industry, with the contribution of jumbo squid in a similar range to that of anchoveta (Christensen et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR26 "Christensen DLP V, Sueiro S, Steenbeek JC, Majluf J, P (2014) Valuing seafood: the Peruvian fisheries sector. Mar Policy 44:302–311")).

Species population is a key variable to measure when aiming to systematically assess biological diversity loss in a given environmental compartment (Jetz et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR77 "Jetz W, McGeoch MA, Guralnick R, Ferrier S, Beck J, Costello MJ, Fernandez M, Geller GN, Keil P, Merow C, Meyer C, Muller-Karger FE, Pereira HM, Regan EC, Schmeller DS, Turak E (2019) Essential biodiversity variables for mapping and monitoring species populations. Nat Ecol Evol 3(4):539–551")). The seasonal fluctuation of climatic conditions in the Peruvian marine system, the growing fishing pressure by industrial and artisanal fleets, and the regulation through quota systems are critical factors that affect stock abundance in the Peruvian EEZ. Although Peruvian upwelling supports high productivity (Mogollón & Callil [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR91 "Mogollón R, Calil PH (2017) On the effects of ENSO on ocean biogeochemistry in the northern Humboldt Current System (NHCS): a modeling study. J Mar Syst 172:137–159")), positive temperature shifts caused by El Niño phenomena trigger fluctuations in abundance of Peruvian anchoveta, and other commercial stock populations (Alheit and Niquen [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR1 "Alheit J, Niquen M (2004) Regime shifts in the Humboldt Current ecosystem. Prog Oceanogr 60(2–4):201–222"); Chavez et al. [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR25 "Chavez FP, Ryan J, Lluch-Cota SE, Ñiquen CM (2003) From anchovies to sardines and back: multidecadal change in the Pacific Ocean. Science 299(5604):217–221")), as illustrated in Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#Fig1). The effect El Niño has on stock abundance and landed catch depends on its conditions and types (Bertrand et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR13 "Bertrand A, Lengaigne M, Takahashi K, Avadí A, Poulain F, Harrod C (2020) El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) effects on fisheries and aquaculture. FAO eBooks")). Extreme and Eastern Pacific El Niño events drive pelagic species to evade warm currents typical of northern Peruvian by moving closer to the shore, delaying their biomass recovery (Bertrand et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR13 "Bertrand A, Lengaigne M, Takahashi K, Avadí A, Poulain F, Harrod C (2020) El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) effects on fisheries and aquaculture. FAO eBooks")). Under Central Pacific and moderate El Niño conditions, negative effects on most pelagic species biology are observed, except for sardine (Cárdenas [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR19 "Cárdenas G (2009) Análisis de series de tiempo de los indicadores biológicos, pesqueros y poblacionales de la sardina, Sardinops sagax sagax (Jenyns, 1842), en función de la variabilidad ambiental y la pesca [PhD Thesis, Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos")). Demersal species like hake are drawn closer to the coast but driven by higher oxygen concentrations (Chavez et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR24 "Chavez FP, Bertrand A, Guevara-Carrasco R, Soler P, Csirke J (2008) The northern Humboldt Current System: brief history, present status and a view towards the future. Prog Oceanogr 79(2–4):95–105")). Regarding invertebrates, the abundance of jumbo squid is negatively affected by prey availability rather than the sea surface temperature typical of El Niño and La Niña events (Argüelles et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR2 "Argüelles J, Tafur R, Taipe A, Villegas P, Keyl F, Dominguez N, Salazar M (2008) Size increment of jumbo flying squid Dosidicus gigas mature females in Peruvian waters, 1989-2004. Prog Oceanogr 79(2–4):308–312"); Waluda et al. [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR124 "Waluda CM, Yamashiro C, Rodhouse PG (2006) Influence of the ENSO cycle on the light-fishery for Dosidicus gigas in the Peru Current: an analysis of remotely sensed data. Fish Res 79(1–2):56–63")).

Front Mar Sci 7"))

Growing fishing pressure in Peru’s EEZ can be illustrated by two historic episodes of biodiversity decline in the anchoveta stock. The Peruvian FMFO industry started in the 1950s and expanded rapidly, contributing to economic growth (Wintersteen [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR128 "Wintersteen KA (2021) The fishmeal revolution. In University of California Press eBooks")). Therefore, El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), together with unregulated overfishing, led the industry to collapse in 1972 (Alheit and Niquen [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR1 "Alheit J, Niquen M (2004) Regime shifts in the Humboldt Current ecosystem. Prog Oceanogr 60(2–4):201–222")), taking decades for the stock to recover a healthy state. While a similar event occurred in 1998, new enforced quota systems based not only on economic yield but in real stock status have allowed the anchoveta stock to remain relatively healthy (Wintersteen [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR128 "Wintersteen KA (2021) The fishmeal revolution. In University of California Press eBooks")). In fact, the amount of anchoveta that can be captured seasonally is dictated by the government, following the advice of the Peruvian Marine Institute (IMARPE). An individual quota system has been established for the industrial fleet since 2009 ([2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR35 "D. S. N° 021-2008-PRODUCE (2008) Ley sobre límites máximos de captura por embarcación. Gobierno del Perú. 
                  https://www.gob.pe/institucion/produce/normas-legales/6526341-21-2008-produce
                  
                ")). Thereafter, in 2017, a total allowable catch limit was also set for the artisanal fleet ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR34 "D. S. N° 005-2017-PRODUCE (2017) Reglamento de Ordenamiento Pesquero del Recurso Anchoveta para Consumo Humano Directo. Diario Oficial El Peruano. 
                  https://busquedas.elperuano.pe/dispositivo/NL/1509249-2
                  
                ")). An important feature stated in this latter document is linked with the allowed redirection of discards from the artisanal fleet that do not comply with human consumption standards towards FMFO production. Strategies to attain sustainability in the management of Peruvian fisheries include IMARPE scientific advice, regulatory frameworks addressing fishing quotas, total allowable catch and fishing gears (Arias-Schreiber [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR3 "Arias-Schreiber M (2012) The evolution of legal instruments and the sustainability of the Peruvian anchovy fishery. Mar Policy 36(1):78–89")). Regardless negative repercussions of overexploitation on marine biodiversity (Jaureguiberry et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR75 "Jaureguiberry P, Titeux N, Wiemers M, Bowler DE, Coscieme L, Golden AS, Guerra CA, Jacob U, Takahashi Y, Settele J, Díaz S, Molnár Z, Purvis A (2022) The direct drivers of recent global anthropogenic biodiversity loss. Sci Adv 8(45)")), sustainability of the anchoveta stock has been maintained over time thanks to precautionary and adaptive fishing management (Castillo et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR23 "Castillo PR, Xu H, Cuadros G, Grados D, Valdez C, Cornejo R, Pozada-Herrera M (2025) Spatial structure and decadal spatiotemporal distribution of the anchoveta (Engraulis ringens) in the marine ecosystem of the Peruvian Current between 1985 and 2024. Fish Oceanogr 34(6):70–88")).

This evidence demonstrates that the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, along with other nationally managed commercial fish species (e.g., giant squid or chub mackerel), is highly influenced by fishing pressure, management policies and the climatic fluctuations related to the pseudo-cyclical behavior of the ENSO phenomenon (Bertrand et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR13 "Bertrand A, Lengaigne M, Takahashi K, Avadí A, Poulain F, Harrod C (2020) El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) effects on fisheries and aquaculture. FAO eBooks")). This behavior implies that far from showing a dichotomous pattern, ENSO effects are highly variable in terms of intensity and length, and, therefore, the effects on marine biota and, more specifically, commercial fishing species, are highly variable across historical time series. Therefore, we argue that these considerations highlight the need under certain circumstances of computing EEZ-oriented approaches to develop a time series of CFs accounting for fish stock depletion within a comprehensive impact assessment framework.

### 1.2 Life cycle assessment: a comprehensive approach to measure biodiversity loss from marine biotic resources depletion

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) has emerged as a standardized approach to evaluate the environmental footprint along the life cycle of products or goods (ISO [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR72 "ISO (2006) Environmental management - life cycle assessment - principles and framework (ISO Standard No. 14040: 2006). 
                  https://www.iso.org/standard/37456.html
                  
                ")) through the aggregation of elementary flows in impact categories (Valente et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR120 "Valente A, Vadenbo C, Fazio S, Shobatake K, Edelen A, Sonderegger T, … Ingwersen WW (2024) Elementary flow mapping across life cycle inventory data systems: a case study for data interoperability under the global Life cycle assessment data access (GLAD) initiative. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 29(5):789–802")), including, among others, biodiversity impacts (Hellweg et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR63 "Hellweg S, Benetto E, MaJ H, Verones F, Wood R (2023) Life-cycle assessment to guide solutions for the triple planetary crisis. Nat Rev Earth Environ 4(7):471–486"); Marques et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR89 "Marques A, Verones F, Kok MT, Huijbregts MA, Pereira HM (2017) How to quantify biodiversity footprints of consumption? A review of multi-regional input-output analysis and life cycle assessment. Curr Opin Environ Sustain 29:75–81")).

A detailed review of recent LCA indicators for biodiversity loss revealed that a limited number of life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods incorporates sufficient marine ecosystem metrics as impact categories (Bergman et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR12 "Bergman K, Gröndahl F, Hasselström L, Strand Å, Thomas JBE, Hornborg S (2025) Integrating biodiversity impacts into seafood life cycle assessments: pathways for improvement. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 30(3):477–490")), and even fewer account for exploitation of marine resources (Damiani et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR36 "Damiani M, Sinkko T, Caldeira C, Tosches D, Robuchon M, Sala S (2023) Critical review of methods and models for biodiversity impact assessment and their applicability in the LCA context. Environ Impact Assess Rev 101:107134")). For instance, ReCiPe (Huijbregts et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR65 "Huijbregts MA, Steinmann ZJ, Elshout PM, Stam G, Verones F, Vieira M, … Van Zelm R (2017) ReCiPe2016: a harmonised life cycle impact assessment method at midpoint and endpoint level. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 22:138–147")) only includes two impact categories within the ecosystem quality area of protection (AoP) that represent an impact pathway related to the marine environment (i.e., marine eutrophication and marine ecotoxicity), denoting a problem when aiming at identifying the direct impacts and damages on marine biodiversity (Bergman et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR12 "Bergman K, Gröndahl F, Hasselström L, Strand Å, Thomas JBE, Hornborg S (2025) Integrating biodiversity impacts into seafood life cycle assessments: pathways for improvement. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 30(3):477–490")). The past few years, however, have been relatively prolific in terms of new models to characterize marine-related environmental impacts (Bergman et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR12 "Bergman K, Gröndahl F, Hasselström L, Strand Å, Thomas JBE, Hornborg S (2025) Integrating biodiversity impacts into seafood life cycle assessments: pathways for improvement. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 30(3):477–490")), although their use in LCA case studies or their availability in broader assessment methods is still limited. Methods in these categories aim at refining the assessment of biodiversity loss in the marine environment, such as biotic resource depletion (Hélias et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR62 "Hélias A, Stanford-Clark C, Bach V (2023) A new impact pathway towards ecosystem quality in life cycle assessment: characterisation factors for fisheries. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 28(4):367–379"); Bach et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR7 "Bach H V, Muhl A, M et al (2022) Assessing overfishing based on the distance-to-target approach. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 27:573–586")), seabed damage (Woods & Verones [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR130 "Woods JS, Verones F (2019) Ecosystem damage from anthropogenic seabed disturbance: a life cycle impact assessment characterisation model. Sci Total Environ 649:1481–1490"); Préat et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR100 "Préat N, Lefaible N, Alvarenga RA, Taelman SE, Dewulf J (2021) Development of a life cycle impact assessment framework accounting for biodiversity in deep seafloor ecosystems: a case study on the clarion clipperton fracture Zone. Sci Total Environ 770:144747")), invasive species (Verones et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR121 "Verones F, Gjedde P, Koslowski M, Woods JS, Lonka R, Stadler K (2023) MarINvaders: a web toolkit of marine species for use in environmental assessments. Ecosphere 14(11)")) and plastic emissions to the ocean (Corella-Puertas et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR30 "Corella-Puertas E, Hajjar C, Lavoie J, Boulay A (2023) MarILCA characterization factors for microplastic impacts in life cycle assessment: physical effects on biota from emissions to aquatic environments. J. Clean. Prod 418:138197"); Hajjar et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR59 "Hajjar C, Bulle C, Boulay A (2024) Life cycle impact assessment framework for assessing physical effects on biota of marine microplastics emissions. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 29(1):25–45") ).

The extraction of biotic resources from the ocean through fishing activities is the fishery-specific category that has evolved the most in recent years, as overfishing has been considered the major driver of biodiversity loss in aquatic ecosystems (Hald-Mortensen [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR60 "Hald-Mortensen C (2023) The main drivers of biodiversity loss: a brief overview. J Ecol Nat Resour 7(3):000346")). Most of the models in this category are based on stock assessments (see Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#Tab1)), which require parameters such as catch, biomass, intrinsic population growth, carrying capacity, or maximum sustainable yield - MSY (Brown et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR16 "Brown E, Vázquez-Rowe I, Ulrich C, Asselin A-C, Casonato C, Ferrara N, Ardente F, Garcia-Herrero L (2025) Exploring environmental impact methodologies to quantify fish stock exploitation and seabed impacts of fishing: evaluating LCA and Non-LCA approaches. Publications Office of the European Union. 
                  https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC142085
                  
                ")). These data are commonly obtained from the stock status assessments conducted by regional or national fishing authorities to monitor the sustainable management of specific fisheries (Costello et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR31 "Costello C, Ovando D, Clavelle T, Strauss CK, Hilborn R, Melnychuk MC, … Leland A (2016) Global fishery prospects under contrasting management regimes. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 113(18):5125–5129")). Other models estimate free net primary production that represent the amount of carbon equivalents removed that will not be available to the biochemical processes in the ecosystem (Langlois et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR83 "Langlois J, Fréon P, Delgenes J, Steyer J, Hélias A (2014) New methods for impact assessment of biotic-resource depletion in life cycle assessment of fisheries: theory and application. J. Clean. Prod 73:63–71"), [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR84 "Langlois J, Fréon P, Steyer J, Delgenès J, Hélias A (2015) Sea use impact category in life cycle assessment: characterization factors for life support functions. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 20(7):970–981")). Models based on distance-to-target (Bach et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR7 "Bach H V, Muhl A, M et al (2022) Assessing overfishing based on the distance-to-target approach. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 27:573–586")) and distance-to-nature (Farmery et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR49 "Farmery AK, Jennings S, Gardner C, Watson RA, Green BS (2017) Naturalness as a basis for incorporating marine biodiversity into life cycle assessment of seafood. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 22:1571–1587")) assess proximity to specific science- or policy-related targets and pristine conditions.

**Table 1 Fishery-specific Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) models within biotic resource use impact category. CF= characterization factor.**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z/tables/1)

Among the models shown in Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#Tab1), the Fisheries Impact Pathway (FIP) can be considered as one of the most advanced within the metrics relying on stock assessments(Brown et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR16 "Brown E, Vázquez-Rowe I, Ulrich C, Asselin A-C, Casonato C, Ferrara N, Ardente F, Garcia-Herrero L (2025) Exploring environmental impact methodologies to quantify fish stock exploitation and seabed impacts of fishing: evaluating LCA and Non-LCA approaches. Publications Office of the European Union. 
                  https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC142085
                  
                ")), given its ability to account for fish stock population dynamics, its global applicability and stock-level granularity, and the use of the broadly accepted potentially disappeared fraction of species (PDF) of species as an endpoint unit (Stanford-Clark et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR117 "Stanford-Clark C, Loiseau E, Helias A (2024) Fisheries impact pathway: making global and regionalised impacts on marine ecosystem quality accessible in Life cycle impact assessment. Sustainability 16(9):3870")). With endpoint CFs for more than 5000 stocks distributed in FAO major fishing areas worldwide, it represents one of the most recent refinements of a series of studies (Hélias et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR61 "Hélias A, Langlois J, Fréon P (2018) Fisheries in life cycle assessment: operational factors for biotic resources depletion. Fish Fish 19(6):951–963"), [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR62 "Hélias A, Stanford-Clark C, Bach V (2023) A new impact pathway towards ecosystem quality in life cycle assessment: characterisation factors for fisheries. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 28(4):367–379")). These CFs are available at regional and global scales, accounting for the effects of discarding unwanted by-catch. The authors used the open-source algorithm CMSY+, an updated version of the code presented by Froese et al. ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR53 "Froese R, Demirel N, Coro G, Kleisner KM, Winker H (2017) Estimating fisheries reference points from catch and resilience. Fish Fish 18(3):506–526")), to overcome lack of data in stocks from fisheries with limited available information. As of late 2024, and for the first time, an indicator that quantifies impacts of fish extraction from wild-capture fisheries (i.e., Stanford-Clark et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR117 "Stanford-Clark C, Loiseau E, Helias A (2024) Fisheries impact pathway: making global and regionalised impacts on marine ecosystem quality accessible in Life cycle impact assessment. Sustainability 16(9):3870")) was included in a holistic multi-impact category assessment method, Impact World+ v2.1 (CIRAIG [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR27 "CIRAIG (2023) IMPACT world report changes. 
                  https://github.com/CIRAIG/IWP_Reborn/tree/master/Report_changes
                  
                . Retrieved June 4, 2025")).

### 1.3 Current research needs addressing temporal dynamics in fisheries impact pathway (FIP) LCA method

Despite the step forward in aligning LCA impact pathways for the overexploitation of wild-capture fisheries provided by the series of publications that led to a final method by Stanford-Clark and colleagues (2024), we have identified a series of methodological aspects that could be included within the framework to account for temporal, geographical and statistical considerations in fisheries management. Firstly, the original FIP method does not reflect in-depth time-dependent variability of fish stocks, although it does recommend the use of a moving average based on several years and regular updates (Stanford-Clark et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR117 "Stanford-Clark C, Loiseau E, Helias A (2024) Fisheries impact pathway: making global and regionalised impacts on marine ecosystem quality accessible in Life cycle impact assessment. Sustainability 16(9):3870")). Peruvian stocks are driven by climatic temporal fluctuations linked to the pseudo-cyclical ENSO phenomenon (Bertrand et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR13 "Bertrand A, Lengaigne M, Takahashi K, Avadí A, Poulain F, Harrod C (2020) El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) effects on fisheries and aquaculture. FAO eBooks")), suggesting that static CFs may significantly misrepresent LCA impacts on marine biota. Even though dynamic CFs (here denoting time differentiated CFs or annual CFs) for other impact categories exist (Beloin-Saint-Pierre et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR10 "Beloin-Saint-Pierre D, Levasseur A, Margni M, Blanc I (2016) Implementing a dynamic Life cycle assessment methodology with a case study on domestic hot water production. J Ind Ecol 21(5):1128–1138"); Levasseur et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR85 "Levasseur A, Cavalett O, Fuglestvedt JS, Gasser T, Johansson DJ, Jørgensen SV, Raugei M, Reisinger A, Schivley G, Strømman A, Tanaka K, Cherubini F (2016) Enhancing life cycle impact assessment from climate science: review of recent findings and recommendations for application to LCA. Ecol Indic 71:163–174")), fisheries currently lack robust dynamic CFs for assessing impacts on marine biodiversity (Emanuelsson et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR42 "Emanuelsson A, Ziegler F, Pihl L, Sköld M, Sonesson U (2014) Accounting for overfishing in life cycle assessment: new impact categories for biotic resource use. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 19(5):1156–1168"); Langlois et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR83 "Langlois J, Fréon P, Delgenes J, Steyer J, Hélias A (2014) New methods for impact assessment of biotic-resource depletion in life cycle assessment of fisheries: theory and application. J. Clean. Prod 73:63–71")).

Secondly, the original FIP method employs large FAO fishing areas suitable for global consistent assessment, neglecting national management regimes (Stanford-Clark et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR117 "Stanford-Clark C, Loiseau E, Helias A (2024) Fisheries impact pathway: making global and regionalised impacts on marine ecosystem quality accessible in Life cycle impact assessment. Sustainability 16(9):3870")). Analysis at an EEZ level would better capture distinct fishery policies, particularly for transboundary stocks where competitive access compromise stock populations (Liu and Molina [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR86 "Liu OR, Molina R (2021) The persistent transboundary problem in marine natural resource management. Front Mar Sci 8"); Østhagen et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR94 "Østhagen A, Spijkers J, Totland OA (2020) Collapse of cooperation? The North-Atlantic mackerel dispute and lessons for international cooperation on transboundary fish stocks. MAST 19(2):155–165")). This spatial resolution refinement could be interpreted as regionalization within the marine environment, which remains a challenge for the LCA community (Pfister et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR98 "Pfister S, Oberschelp C, Sonderegger T (2020) Regionalized LCA in practice: the need for a universal shapefile to match LCI and LCIA. The Int J Life Cycle Assess 25:1867–1871")).

Thirdly, while the statistical analysis of the CMSY++ algorithm addresses convergence, residual and prior-to-posterior analyses, model performance can be further explored to include a wider number of criteria to provide more reliable estimates, therefore improving CF certainty. These include retrospective pattern analysis, which reveals differences between catch-only and data-rich models (Wang et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR125 "Wang K, Li Q, Zhang C, Xu B, Ren Y (2025) Enhancing catch-based stock assessment in data-limited fisheries with proxy CPUE indicators in the Yellow Sea. Sci Rep 15(1):11043")); hindcasting analysis, that enables examination of model consistency relative to observed abundance data (Derhy et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR38 "Derhy G, Elkalay K, Rincón MM, Khalil K (2024) Stochastic surplus production and length-based assessment models to compare maximum sustainable yield advice for the Moroccan Atlantic chub mackerel. Front Mar Sci 11")); biological plausibility analysis, which uses biological knowledge to judge final model estimations credibility (Bouch et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR15 "Bouch P, Minto C, Reid DG (2021) Comparative performance of data-poor CMSY and data-moderate SPiCT stock assessment methods when applied to data-rich, real-world stocks. ICES J Mar Sci 78(1):264–276")); and jittering analysis, detecting optimal input parameter combinations (Cai et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR18 "Cai K, Kindong R, Ma Q, Tian S (2023) Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Northwest Pacific using a multi-model approach. Fishes 8(2):80")). In addition, optimized model performance can be achieved when abundance indices are included in modeling (Zhai et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR132 "Zhai L, Liang C, Pauly D (2020) Assessments of 16 exploited fish stocks in Chinese waters using the CMSY and BSM methods. Front Mar Sci 7")), a procedure not implemented in Stanford-Clark et al. ([2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z#ref-CR117 "Stanford-Clark C, Loiseau E, Helias A (2024) Fisheries impact pathway: making global and regionalised impacts on marine ecosystem quality accessible in Life cycle impact assessment. Sustainability 16(9):3870")).

Therefore, in this study we revisit the FIP method on overexploitation of wild-capture fisheries with the aim of providing enhanced endpoint level CF temporal series for relevant Peruvian fishing stocks, including anchoveta, within the national EEZ. args.summary:
This article, published in The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment (Volume 31, article 69, 2026) as open access, presents the development of characterization factors (CFs) for 10 Peruvian fishing stocks within the Fisheries Impact Pathway (FIP) framework for Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The authors (Rubén Manrique-Muñante, Alejandro Deville, Ramzy Kahhat, and Ian Vázquez-Rowe, all from the same institution) address the gap that biodiversity impacts of Peruvian fisheries—strongly influenced by El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)—are not fully covered by current LCIA models.

Key methodological aspects include: (1) optimization of CMSY++ stock assessment model performance using exhaustive statistical analysis (including retrospective, hindcasting, biological plausibility, and jittering analyses); (2) calculation of CF time series (2007–2023) under an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) approach for anchoveta, jack mackerel, chub mackerel, bonito, hake, common dolphinfish, skipjack tuna, jumbo squid and calico scallop; (3) statistical evaluation of enhanced CFs including uncertainty, sensitivity analyses, and correlation with ENSO indices; and (4) application of CFs in case studies for direct and indirect human consumption fisheries.

Key findings:
- Enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values, usually showing lower values
- CFs exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with typical ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship
- Case studies in the Peruvian EEZ confirmed significant differences in fishing impacts for stocks destined to direct human consumption during El Niño and La Niña years, with additional LCIA impacts ranging from 0.1% to 61% in fishmeal and fish oil production among plants of a major producer during 2019 and 2021

Background context: Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally, with Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens) being the largest fishery worldwide by volume. Approximately 95% of landed anchoveta goes to fishmeal and fish oil (FMFO) production, supplying 15–20% of global FMFO. Other species (jack mackerel, bonito, chub mackerel, hake, jumbo squid, calico scallop) contribute to about 20% of annual landings and generated 2600 million US$ in export revenue in 2023. The historical context includes the fishery collapse in 1972 driven by ENSO and overfishing, after which quota systems (individual quotas for industrial fleet since 2009, artisanal fleet TAC since 2017) have helped maintain stock health.

The authors argue that the enhanced CF time series more accurately represents stock population dynamics under fluctuating climatic stressors and management regimes than the original FIP method, responding to international LCA guidelines calling for regionalized and temporally explicit impact assessment. The study recommends using these CFs for assessing biotic resource depletion in Peruvian seafood and aquaculture systems, and extending the methodology to other EEZs affected by similar ecosystem dynamics and fishing pressure.

# Moving beyond controversy: is the chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) stock recovering?

Dong-Jin Kwak 1†

Do-Hoon Kim 1\*

Kyounghoon Lee 2

1. Department of Marine & Fisheries Business and Economics, Pukyong National University, Busan, Republic of Korea

2. Division of Marine Production System Management, Pukyong National University, Busan, Republic of Korea

Article metrics

## Abstract

Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is a commercially significant and highly migratory species in the Northwest Pacific. Despite various management efforts, previous stock assessments have yielded inconsistent results, leading to ongoing debates regarding its stock status. To provide a robust assessment, this study employed two complementary models: CMSY++, which utilizes an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to objectively estimate prior biomass ranges, and a Bayesian State-Space (BSS) model. Crucially, the BSS model incorporated a correction for technical creep to address biases in Catch Per Unit Effort (CPUE) data—a factor frequently overlooked in previous research. The results from both models were consistent. In 2024, the relative biomass (*B*/*B**MSY*) was estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), indicating that the stock remains overfished and below the Biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (*BMSY*). Kobe plot analysis further revealed that sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s has impeded recovery. This study demonstrates CMSY++ as an effective tool for reconciling discrepancies in data-limited assessments and underscores the necessity of correcting for technical creep to ensure accurate management decisions. Enhanced scientific surveys and the systematic collection of high-quality fisheries data are essential for the sustainable management of this transboundary stock.

## 1 Introduction

Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is a representative migratory species of considerable commercial and geopolitical significance, particularly the stock component in Korean waters of the Northwest Pacific. Since its designation as a target species for the Total Allowable Catch (TAC) system in 1999, Korea has implemented various management measures. These include its inclusion in the Fishery Resources Recovery Plan in 2012 and the establishment of closed seasons and minimum size limits (NIFS, 2025a; FIRA, 2023). Neighboring countries have also initiated comparable management actions. Notably, Japan has operated an autonomous catch allocation system since 1996, managed by the Federation of North Pacific District Purse Seine Fisheries Cooperative Association of Japan (FNPD-PSFCA) in conjunction with its TAC system (Tsujita et al., 2022). Furthermore, the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC) has designated chub mackerel as a priority species for management since 2015 (NPFC, 2017).

Despite extensive management efforts, the absence of consistent stock assessment conclusions in Korea presents a significant challenge for policymakers in determining whether to tighten or relax current TAC quotas. Some studies report the stock as recovered and well-managed (Kim et al., 2020; Lee, 2021), while others suggest it remains overfished, necessitating more stringent management measures (Park and Kwon, 2019; Hong and Kim, 2021; Jung et al., 2021). For instance, Kim et al. (2020) reported that the Spawning-Stock Biomass (SSB) of chub mackerel in Korean waters increased from 76,000 tons in 2000 to 190,000 tons in 2019. In contrast, Hong and Kim (2021) estimated the ratio of 2020 biomass to the Biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (*BMSY*) (*B2020*/*BMSY*) to be 0.40 (via CMSY) and 0.61 (via BSS), indicating an overfished state.

Conflicting assessment results are prevalent not only in Korea but also in neighboring countries such as China and Japan (Hiyama et al., 2002; Ju et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; [Wang et al., 2020](#B73); Shi et al., 2022; [Yin et al., 2023](#B78); [Zhao et al., 2025](#B81)). For instance, [Wang et al. (2020)](#B73) evaluated the *B*/*BMSY* of chub mackerel in the East China Sea as 0.091 (Collapsed), whereas Ju et al. (2020) reported it as 1.13 (Healthy). The migratory nature of the stock further contributes to divergent assessment outcomes for the North Pacific stock (Liang et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2023). Specifically, Hong et al. (2022) estimated *B*/*BMSY* at 0.60, while Cai et al. (2023) reported *B*/*BMSY* values ranging from 0.81 to 2.30 across various model scenarios. These discrepancies, mirroring those observed in Korean assessments, are primarily attributable to the subjective configuration of biomass prior ranges and the omission of technical efficiency gains in CPUE data. Such methodological inconsistencies hinder the development of a domestic consensus on stock status, thereby complicating both the optimization of the Korean TAC system and the implementation of more stringent technical regulations for the stock within Korean waters.

Prior research has largely utilized the Monte Carlo-based CMSY model to establish management reference points, such as Maximum Sustainable Yield (*MSY*), primarily relying on catch data (Ju et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Hong and Kim, 2021; Hong et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2023; [Yin et al., 2023](#B78)). Although the CMSY model offers efficient stock assessment in data-limited contexts (Froese et al., 2017), it possesses notable limitations. Chief among these is its considerable sensitivity to the specification of biomass prior ranges, which introduces substantial uncertainty into the assessment outcomes (Falsone et al., 2021; Bouch et al., 2021; Geng et al., 2025). Therefore, a novel approach is necessary to mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the reliability of stock assessment results for chub mackerel.

The CMSY++ model is a recently developed catch-based assessment model engineered to address the shortcomings of the original CMSY. It accomplishes this by estimating biomass within a state-space framework rooted in Bayesian inference (Froese et al., 2023). A key advantage of CMSY++ is its ability to establish more robust biomass prior ranges through the integration of an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) (Froese et al., 2023). Recent applications of CMSY++ to data-limited stocks have demonstrated its broad utility across various species, including elasmobranchs and crustaceans (Kindong et al., 2022; Ferragut-Perello et al., 2023; Harby-Rashed et al., 2024).

In the application of catch-based models, validating the reliability of results through comparative analysis with models incorporating more comprehensive data is essential (Sharma et al., 2021). Consequently, this study evaluates and compares the stock status of mackerel using the Bayesian State-Space (BSS) model, a widely accepted approach. The BSS model, which employs both catch and CPUE data, offers a Bayesian state-space framework that can simultaneously account for observation error in the data and process error within the assessment model (Meyer and Millar, 1999; Thorson et al., 2014).

While CPUE serves as a critical indicator of biomass fluctuations (Hilborn and Walters, 1992), enhancements in fishing efficiency stemming from technical creep can obscure actual fishing effort and amplify uncertainties in stock assessments (Munro and Sumaila, 2002; Pauly et al., 2002; Marchal et al., 2006; Palomares and Pauly, 2019). For example, Kleiven et al. (2022) demonstrated that the nominal CPUE for the European lobster (*Homarus gammarus*) fishery indicated an 8% increase in biomass, whereas the technical creep-corrected CPUE estimated a substantial 57% decline. This underscores how unaddressed technological advancements can lead to a significant underestimation of stock depletion. Previous studies utilizing BSS models for mackerel have frequently neglected the influence of technical creep (Ju et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2023; [Yin et al., 2023](#B78)). For instance, when estimating the biomass ratio (*B2017*/*BMSY*), Ju et al. (2020) reported a value of 1.13, whereas Liang et al. (2020) found it to be 0.70. Consequently, an approach that incorporates technical creep is imperative for improving the accuracy of stock assessment outcomes (Thurstan et al., 2010).

This study aims to provide a robust assessment of the chub mackerel stock in Korean waters utilizing both CMSY++ and BSS models. To address the inherent limitations of catch-based models and enhance objectivity, rational biomass prior ranges are estimated using ANN within the CMSY++ model. Concurrently, a parallel BSS analysis is conducted, explicitly accounting for technical creep. Notably, this integration of fishing effort, adjusted for technical creep, into the BSS model analysis represents a significant advancement, largely overlooked in previous research. Specifically, CPUE data are corrected based on annual technical creep rates reported in the existing literature to minimize potential bias (Palomares and Pauly, 2019; Froese et al., 2023). This approach aims to provide objective and scientifically sound management reference points for the sustainable management of mackerel resources.

## 2 Materials and methods

### 2.1 Trends in the catch of *Scomber japonicus*

Although this study primarily focuses on the chub mackerel stock in Korean waters, annual catch data from neighboring countries (China and Japan) spanning 1970 to 2024 were also compiled to account for the species’ migratory behavior ([**Figure 1**](#f1)). Korean catch data were sourced from the Korean Statistical Information Service (KOSIS), while China’s data were obtained from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) FishStatJ database. Japanese data were extracted from the stock assessment report by Muko et al. (2025). Although Northwest Pacific mackerel are classified as either the Tsushima Current stock or the Pacific stock (Murayama et al., 1995; [Watanabe et al., 1999](#B74)), this study exclusively focused on Japanese catch data from the Tsushima Current stock to ensure spatial and biological consistency with the stock occurring in Korean waters.

Historical catch trajectories revealed distinct regional fluctuations. In Korea, the catch increased from 38,256 tons in 1970, peaking at 415,003 tons in 1996, before a gradual decline to an average of 130,000 tons in the 2000s, and reached a historical low of 77,603 tons in 2020. As of 2024, the Korean catch was recorded at 124,928 tons (KOSIS, 2025a). China’s catch, commencing at 173,100 tons in 1970, expanded rapidly after 2000, peaking at 592,637 tons in 2008 before declining to 405,541 tons in 2024 (FAO, 2025). For Japan’s Tsushima Current stock, production peaked in 1996 (411,000 tons) but subsequently declined sharply to approximately 100,000 tons during the 2000s, with a reported catch of 135,000 tons in 2024 (Muko et al., 2025).

The observed disparities in regional catch levels are attributable to multifaceted factors, including ecological distribution, management regimes, and socioeconomic demand. While variations in primary fishing methods (predominantly purse seine) are marginal, the spatial distribution of the two stocks significantly influences fishing ground productivity. The Tsushima Current stock is predominantly concentrated in the East China Sea and the western waters of Japan and Korea, whereas the Pacific stock undertakes migratory movements along Japan’s eastern pacific coast (Murayama et al., 1995; Hiyama et al., 2002). Notably, the high productivity of the Kuroshio-Oyashio transition zone in northeastern Japan facilitates large-scale harvesting of the Pacific stock, which constitutes the majority of Japan’s total mackerel production (Tsujita et al., 2022).

Differential management policies also significantly influence catch levels. Japan and Korea implemented TAC systems in 1997 and 1999, respectively. Japan also instituted autonomous catch limits through the FNPD-PSFCA. Conversely, while China introduced a summer fishing moratorium in 1995 and a “Zero-growth” policy in 1999 (Huang and He, 2019), their effectiveness has been constrained by intensified fishing effort immediately following moratorium periods (Kang et al., 2022). Furthermore, market dynamics exert considerable influence on fishing pressure. In Korea, competitiveness has diminished due to the prevalence of smaller-sized fish and an increasing preference for imported Norwegian chub mackerel (Jang et al., 2024). In China, a substantial increase in seafood demand across various demographic groups has been observed ([Zhang et al., 2021](#B80)). Japan, conversely, has exhibited a declining trend, influenced by dietary shifts toward meat-centric and convenience-oriented products (USDA, 2023). Collectively, these factors, coupled with environmental variability such as rising sea temperatures and El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events, underpin the observed interannual fluctuations in mackerel catch ([Yu et al., 2018](#B79)).

### 2.3 Dataset for analysis

The stock assessment of chub mackerel, utilizing the CMSY++ and BSS models, necessitated time-series catch and CPUE data, alongside a resilience value for estimating the intrinsic rate (*r*). The resilience value was derived from FishBase (Froese and Pauly, 2015). While FishBase represents global life-history averages and may not fully capture local ecological specificities (e.g., distinct growth and maturity patterns in Korean waters), its application is justified by the current scarcity of empirical resilience data for the regional stock. Furthermore, adopting the FishBase resilience value for this species aligns with established practice in several regional assessments conducted in Korea and China (Park and Kwon, 2019; Ju et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Hong and Kim, 2021; Hong et al., 2022). Consistent with this practice, chub mackerel resilience was categorized as “Medium,” reflecting a median *r* value of 0.48 (95% credible interval (CI): 0.32–0.73).

Stock assessments conducted under data-deficient conditions are subject to considerable uncertainties, underscoring the need for optimal utilization of available data to accurately reflect long-term population dynamics. A comprehensive understanding of a fishery’s historical context provides crucial insights into stock responses to previous management measures, thereby facilitating the establishment of more robust management reference points (Melnychuk et al., 2021). Furthermore, in catch-based models, the use of an extended time series is essential, as it mitigates estimation uncertainty and reduces retrospective bias in analytical results (Li et al., 2023).

Consequently, to enhance the precision of the chub mackerel stock assessment and mitigate inherent uncertainties, this study incorporated all available long-term data. Specifically, a 55-year time series of catch data (1970–2024) and 27 years of CPUE data (1997–2023) was compiled, primarily sourced from the KOSIS ([**Table 2**](#T2)). To derive a reliable CPUE series for the large purse seine mackerel fishery, three candidate fishing effort variables—number of vessels, gross tonnage (GT), and engine horsepower (EHP)—were subsequently evaluated using these compiled records. Adopting the methodology of Hong and Kim (2021), a correlation analysis was conducted to identify the most representative effort variable exhibiting the highest explanatory power.

### 2.4 Analysis method

Both the CMSY++ and Bayesian State-Space (BSS) models utilize a state-space framework and Bayesian inference. The state-space model is beneficial for stock assessment as it accounts for both process errors, which arise during biological transitions, and observation errors inherent in the data (Aanes et al., 2007; Aeberhard et al., 2018). Bayesian inference, a statistical method grounded in Bayes’ Theorem, derives posterior distributions by integrating prior information with new evidence (Bayes, 1763). In stock assessments employing Bayesian inference, prior distributions must be assigned to key parameters, including the *r*, carrying capacity (*k*), and *MSY*. To avoid negative estimates, a log-normal prior distribution is applied to each parameter (Froese et al., 2023).

Prior to estimating the distributions, both the CMSY++ and BSS models assume the Schaefer production model, which posits that stock biomass increases over time in a density-dependent manner. Consequently, the biomass at time *t + 1* can be expressed as shown in [Equation 1](#eq1) (Schaefer, 1954, 1957; Froese et al., 2023). However, when the stock is reduced to a level below 0.25 of *k*, the dynamics are represented as indicated in [Equation 2](#eq2).

In this context, *Bt* signifies biomass in year *t*, *r* refers to the intrinsic growth rate, *k* represents the carrying capacity, and *Ct* indicates the catch in year *t*. The observation error () and process error () are denoted separately. The prior distribution for *r* is derived from the “Resilience” value obtained from Fishbase ([www.fishbase.se](http://www.fishbase.se)) (Froese et al., 2017). Specifically, the *r* prior is classified into four categories as proposed by Froese et al. (2017): High (0.6–1.5), Medium (0.2–0.8), Low (0.05–0.5), and Very Low (0.015–0.4).

The prior for *k* is subsequently estimated using [Equation 3](#eq3). In this context, *kprior*, *MSYprior*, and *rprior* denote the priors for *k*, *MSY*, and *r*, respectively. The boundaries for *kprior*—*klow* and *khigh*—are determined based on the maximum catch, max(C), and the range of *r*, as indicated in [Equation 4](#eq4). In instances where the prior biomass level is elevated, [Equation 5](#eq5) is applied.

The prior distribution for *MSY* is established based on the empirical relationship between maximum catch and *MSY*, categorized by catch trends. First, if the catch trend is stable or increasing, it is assumed that the catch has not exceeded the *MSY* level; consequently, the *MSY* prior is defined as the average catch of the top three years. Second, if the catch trend declines following a peak—indicating that the peak catch may have surpassed *MSY*—the *MSY* prior is set to 75% (3/4) of the average catch from the top five years (Froese et al., 2023).

An ANN was applied to estimate the *B/k* prior distributions, following the methodology of Froese et al. (2023). The ANN was trained on catch time-series data from 400 global stocks to predict biomass status relative to *BMSY* at the initial, intermediate, and final time points within each series. Input features for the network consisted of 14 distinct characteristics derived from the catch data and classified into two categories: (1) scalar statistics, such as the ratio between minimum and maximum catch, catch ratios during the initial and final decades, relative catch levels at the start (1970) and end (2024), temporal markers of catch extremes, and total time-series length; and (2) six representative catch trajectory shapes (Flat, LH, LHL, HL, HLH, and OTH).

The network architecture was optimized based on the growing strategy proposed by Bishop (1995). To ensure model robustness and mitigate potential over-fitting, a 20-fold cross-validation was conducted with a random 95:5 split of the training and test datasets. The finalized topology comprised a single hidden layer with 71 neurons. The model generated a binary output (*At*), with +1 signifying biomass levels above *BMSY* and -1 indicating levels below *BMSY* (Froese et al., 2023).

The estimated *B/k* prior ranges were then integrated into the stock assessment framework as defined in [Equation 6](#eq6), with *At* serving as the primary decision variable. Acknowledging that catch-biomass relationships are frequently in non-equilibrium, the lower and upper bounds for these priors were subsequently determined using specific linear regression equations, as summarized in [**Table 4**](#T4), adapted from the reference values presented by Froese et al. (2023).

Specifically, when the relative catch is below the *MSY* (*Ct*≤*MSY*) and biomass exceeds the *BMSY* (*Bt* > *BMSY*), the lower bound of the biomass prior range is established as -0.8 - 0.45·(*Ct*/*MSYprior*), with the upper bound defined as 1.02 - 0.247·(*Ct*/*MSYprior*). If the biomass does not exceed *BMSY*, the lower bound is set to 0.01 + 0.203·(*Ct*/*MSYprior*), and the upper bound is -0.2 + 0.431·(*Ct*/*MSYprior*). Finally, in instances where *Ct* > *MSY*, and considering the limited reliability of linear regression in this interval, fixed lower (0.256*k*) and upper (0.721*k*) bounds relative to the *k* were applied.

In this study, the CMSY++ model employed a Multivariate Lognormal (MVLN) prior distribution that accounts for the correlation between *r* and *k* within a Bayesian state-space framework. Unlike the traditional CMSY approach, which filters ‘viable *r–k* pairs’ post hoc, this methodology integrates the *r–k* correlation a priori. Specifically, random samples (n = 10,000) were drawn from the log-prior distributions of *r* and *k*, as calculated using [Equation 7](#eq7).

Subsequently, the means and covariances of  and  were estimated to construct an *r–k* pair covariance matrix. This approach mitigates Borel’s Paradox, a phenomenon wherein the assessment model relies solely on prior information due to deterministic functional relationships, thereby facilitating a more nuanced representation of the uncertainties inherent in actual resource dynamics (Schweder and Hjort, 1996). Furthermore, to address the bias toward high *k* and low *r* regions, the optimal estimate was positioned in the lower-right quadrant of the elliptical estimation interval, where viable *r–k* pairs are concentrated. Confidence intervals were established based on the range where *r* values exceed the bottom 25% of the total distribution, thereby minimizing result distortion caused by unrealistically low *r* values (Froese et al., 2023).

To account for the increase in fishing effort attributed to potential technical creep, a CPUE correction process was implemented following the methodology of Palomares and Pauly (2019). Accordingly, the effective fishing effort, *E(t)*, is estimated as demonstrated in [Equation 8](#eq8):

Where *E(t)* represents the effective fishing effort at time *t*, and *E(t=0)* denotes the nominal fishing effort, *pd* refers to the percentage creep. For instance, if *pd* = 0.02, the effective fishing effort for the current year is assumed to have increased by a factor of 1.02 compared to the previous year due to technical creep. The fishing effort and corrected CPUE at time *t*, reflecting these advancements, can be estimated using [Equations 9](#eq9) and [10](#eq10) (Froese et al., 2023).

Here, *Corr(t)* denotes the technical advancement coefficient, and *CPUECorr(t)* represents the corrected CPUE. Palomares and Pauly (2019) estimated that the annual rate of technical creep (*pd*) typically ranges from 0.0049 to 0.201, implying that values below 0.0245 may underrepresent technological progress. However, in accordance with Froese et al. (2021) recommendations, this study adopted a conservative baseline of *pd* = 0.02. Consequently, the CPUE data used in the BSS model were cumulatively adjusted downward by 2% annually across the entire time series. This adjustment was implemented to mitigate potential biases in stock assessment outcomes stemming from technological changes and to enhance the overall reliability of the assessment.

Prior distributions for each parameter were updated to posterior distributions through Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. The MCMC method was implemented using the JAGS (Just Another Gibbs Sampler) software package (Plummer, 2003). MCMC generates samples that converge to a target distribution by performing Monte Carlo simulations within a Markov Chain designed to reach a stationary state (Annis et al., 2017). During these simulations, samples were drawn sequentially from conditional probability distributions using a Gibbs Sampler (Kéry and Schaub, 2011).

A total of 60,000 iterations were employed for sampling. The initial 30,000 samples were discarded as a burn-in period to mitigate the influence of starting values. Subsequently, a thinning interval of 10 was applied to reduce autocorrelation (Froese et al., 2023). The stock status of chub mackerel was then assessed based on the resulting posterior distributions. As detailed in [**Table 5**](#T5), the stock status was categorized into five levels based on the ratio of the terminal year’s biomass to *BMSY* (Froese et al., 2017).

## 3 Results

Before presenting the stock assessment results, the Posterior-to-Prior Variance Ratio (PPVR) was estimated to evaluate the efficacy of the input data in refining the prior information ([**Figure 3**](#f3)). According to [Winker et al. (2018)](#B76), a PPVR < 0.5 indicates that the data significantly updated the priors, thereby primarily determining the posterior distributions. The analysis revealed that the PPVR for the primary parameters (*r*, *k*, and *MSY*) ranged from 0.1 to 0.23 for the CMSY++ model and from 0.03 to 0.32 for the BSS model, with all values consistently well below the 0.5 threshold. The notably low PPVR for *MSY* (0.1 in CMSY++ and 0.03 in BSS) suggests that the posterior distributions were predominantly driven by catch or effort data rather than the prior information.

Summary of stock assessment results for chub mackerel estimated by the CMSY++ and BSS models.

[**Table 7**](#T7) details the 2024 chub mackerel biomass relative to *BMSY*. According to the CMSY++ model, the estimated 2024 biomass (*B2024*) was 779,191 tons, representing 63% of *BMSY* and consequently categorizing the stock as “Overfished.” The BSS model estimated *B2024* at 549,884 tons, representing 59% of *BMSY*, also indicating an “Overfished” status. Although the diagnostic results for *B/BMSY* were consistent across both models, numerical discrepancies were observed in the estimates for the *B2024* and *BMSY*. Specifically, the CMSY++ model estimated *B2024* at 779,191 tons, approximately 34% higher than the BSS model’s estimate of 549,884 tons. Additionally, a 10% difference was noted in their *BMSY* estimates. Nevertheless, despite these numerical variations, the 95% CIs for both *B2024* and *BMSY* exhibited significant overlap between the two models, suggesting statistical consistency within their respective uncertainties.

Furthermore, the average annual catch for the most recent five-year period (2020–2024) was 111,143 tons, which is below the estimated *MSY*. However, the current biomass levels, at 63% (CMSY++) and 59% (BSS) of *BMSY*, indicate an overfished state. Consequently, the prevailing level of fishing pressure is insufficient to ensure stock recovery. Therefore, given that the sustainable yield for a depleted stock is substantially lower than the *MSY*, more stringent catch limits and management measures are imperative to facilitate the recovery of the chub mackerel stock.

To assess the BSS model’s sensitivity to assumptions concerning technical evolution, a sensitivity analysis was conducted across varying technical creep rates: 0%, 1.3%, 1.79%, and the baseline 2% ([**Table 8**](#T8)). The 1.3% rate was derived from Palomares and Pauly (2019) global estimate, while the 1.79% rate was calculated by substituting the analysis period (Y = 55) into their empirical formula (C% = 13.8·Y-0.511).

The results indicated that while the primary parameters—*r*, *k*, and *MSY*—remained relatively robust across the scenarios, biomass estimates exhibited a pronounced downward trend as the assumed technical creep rate increased. Specifically, *B2024* was estimated at 824,168 tons under the 0% scenario (no correction), but decreased significantly to 549,884 tons with the application of the 2% rate. Similarly, the *BMSY* under the 2% scenario (901,191 tons) was approximately 15% lower than that of the 0% scenario (1,062,792 tons). While the current stock status was consistently diagnosed as “Overfished” across all scenarios, the numerical estimates for biomass varied by up to 34% depending on the inclusion of CPUE correction.

Notably, the results for the 1.79% scenario closely aligned with those of the 2.0% baseline utilized in this study. These findings underscore that a failure to account for increased fishing efficiency due to technological advancement leads to a substantial overestimation of biomass and induces significant bias in stock status assessments.

The chub mackerel stock status over time was visualized using a Kobe plot ([**Figure 5**](#f5)), illustrating the relationship between relative fishing mortality (*F/FMSY*) and *B/BMSY* (Maunder and Aires-da-Silva, 2011). The probability of the stock residing in each quadrant was determined directly from the density of the joint posterior distribution of MCMC samples. Quantitative diagnosis was performed by calculating the proportion of valid MCMC samples that simultaneously met the criteria for *B/BMSY* < 1 and *F/FMSY* > 1 (representing an overfished and overfishing state). The CMSY++ model indicated a stable stock status in 1970; however, intensified fishing pressure led to a transition to an “overfished and overfishing” state (red quadrant) by 1998. This overfished and overfishing state has persisted through 2024 with no significant evidence of recovery, with an 87.6% posterior probability of remaining in this quadrant ([**Figure 5A**](#f5)). Consistent with these findings, the BSS model indicated the stock’s entry into the red quadrant in 1998 and its maintenance of this status through 2024, with a posterior probability of 95.3% ([**Figure 5B**](#f5)).

The Kobe plots illustrate the trajectory of relative biomass (*B/BMSY*) and fishing mortality (*F/FMSY*). The background colors indicate the stock status: red (overfished and overfishing), orange (overfishing), yellow (overfished), and green (sustainable).

## 4 Discussion and conclusion

This study evaluated the stock status of chub mackerel using ANN-based CMSY++ and BSS models to address challenges related to inconsistent prior assessments and limited data availability. The analysis utilized a comprehensive 55-year time series of total catch data (1970–2024) and 27 years of CPUE (engine horsepower) data from Korea (1997–2023). Both models yielded consistent estimates, demonstrating the robustness and utility of CMSY++ for stock assessment in data-limited scenarios.

As of 2024, the CMSY++ model estimated chub mackerel biomass at 779,191 tons, whereas the BSS model estimated it at 549,884 tons. The corresponding relative biomass (*B/BMSY*) was 0.63 and 0.59 respectively, classifying the stock as “Overfished.” These findings align with previous studies reporting *B/BMSY* between 0.60 and 0.67 (Park and Kwon, 2019; Hong and Kim, 2021; Liang et al., 2020; [Wang et al., 2020](#B73); Hong et al., 2022; [Yin et al., 2023](#B78)). Although some researchers have reported relatively higher biomass estimates (Ju et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Lee, 2021; Cai et al., 2023), these discrepancies likely stem from variations in spatial boundaries, data sources, and assessment periods. Collectively, the evidence suggests that the chub mackerel stock is currently overexploited and remains below the *BMSY* threshold.

To further contextualize the stock assessment results, recent trends in domestic chub mackerel landings were examined as a biological indicator of stock health. Data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market (BCFM), which handles approximately 90% of domestic large purse seine chub mackerel landings, reveal a concerning and persistent increase in the proportion of small-sized individuals (weighing ≤ 250 g). This proportion rose from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024 (BCFM, 2025). Applying the length-weight relationship (W = 0.0025FL3.4696, *R2* = 0.9314) and the length-length relationships (LLRs) between fork length (FL) and total length (TL) (TL = 1.0827FL-0.3393, *R2* = 0.9886), as defined by Kim et al. (2021), the 250 g threshold was converted to an approximate TL of 29.7 cm. Notably, this derived length is below the length at 50% maturity (*L50* = 31.4 cm) for the species, indicating that a substantial proportion of the current catch comprises immature individuals that have not yet attained reproductive potential. While these landing statistics were not direct inputs for the assessment models, they provide critical indirect evidence that aligns with the quantitative findings of this study. The observed miniaturization trend in the fishing grounds serves as a tangible biological indicator of the overfished state and biomass depletion suggested by both the CMSY++ and BSS models, reinforcing the quantitative findings and underscoring the deterioration of the mackerel stock.

Kobe plots illustrate the temporal dynamics of biomass in relation to fishing mortality, as analyzed by the CMSY++ and BSS models, respectively ([**Figure 5**](#f5)). The assessment results indicate that the chub mackerel stock remains depleted due to sustained high fishing intensity, with a high probability of residing in the red zone (87.6% for CMSY++ and 95.3% for BSS). This signifies an overfished state subject to ongoing overfishing. Therefore, more stringent management measures are imperative to ensure the long-term sustainability of the stock. Specifically, a reduction in TAC quotas is essential to alleviate excessive fishing pressure. Alongside TAC adjustments, structural and technical regulations—including vessel buyback programs, extended closed seasons, and an upward revision of the minimum legal size—must be further strengthened to facilitate stock recovery.

Although the annual catch of chub mackerel exhibited a slight recovery between 2020 and 2024 ([**Figure 1**](#f1)), the analysis indicates that the *B2024* remains at approximately 60% of *BMSY*. This suggests that the stock has not yet recovered from its depleted state. Given this fragile recovery trend, the implementation of flexible management measures—such as temporarily suspending minimum size limits or potentially abolishing fishing regulations based on monitoring, as proposed in the ‘Recommendations for Innovation in Fishery Resources Management Policy (2022)’—raises significant concerns regarding the risk of further stock degradation.

The recovery of highly migratory species, such as chub mackerel, is often observed to be more limited than that of sedentary species (Caddy and Agnew, 2004). To mitigate the inherent uncertainties in fisheries management, a combined approach utilizing two or more regulatory measures is substantially more effective than relying on a single control method (Stefansson and Rosenberg, 2005). However, despite the implementation of the TAC in 1999, the chub mackerel in Korean waters has not exhibited a clear recovery over the past 25 years. Furthermore, the intensive harvesting of immature individuals has resulted in both a quantitative decline and qualitative deterioration of the stock. Therefore, the strict enforcement of minimum size limits for juveniles is essential to prevent stock depletion and enhance long-term yields (Prince and Hordyk, 2019; [Vahabnezhad et al., 2024](#B72)).

The consequences of neglecting this biological imperative are evident in Mediterranean fisheries, where technical measures were historically driven by market demand, specifically a preference for small fish, rather than by scientific evidence. For instance, the minimum size limit for European hake (*Merluccius merluccius*) was set at 20 cm, significantly below its *L50*. This discrepancy ultimately resulted in a severely truncated size structure, depleted of large reproductive individuals (Colloca et al., 2013).

In alignment with the ‘Fisheries Innovation 2030 Plan (2019)’ and subsequent policy recommendations, the Korean government aims to transition toward a TAC-centric management framework, with the goal of increasing the proportion of TAC-managed catch to 80% by 2030. As the TAC system constitutes a science-based output control, its effectiveness fundamentally relies on systematic and advanced stock assessments. Therefore, it is imperative to maintain continuous and rigorous evaluations of chub mackerel and other commercially important species utilizing diverse assessment models.

The CMSY++ model is expected to address the limitations of the original CMSY by establishing more rational biomass priors. While the biomass priors in the original CMSY are based on heuristic rules proposed by Froese et al. (2017), CMSY++ employs an ANN to define these ranges more logically.
