**Key Contribution:** This study indicated spawning grounds of chub mackerel will shift northward due to a warming ocean driven by a climate change scenario, resulting in a subsequent change in the distribution of exploitable mackerel. The results of this study are expected to contribute to the development of bio-physical coupled, individual-based models for predicting the recruitment and spatio-temporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel.

## 1. Introduction

Chub mackerel, Scomber japonicus, are forage fish that play a crucial role in the transfer of energy within marine food webs, serving as the primary food source for various marine predators and feeding on zooplankton and phytoplankton [[1](#B1-fishes-10-00020),[2](#B2-fishes-10-00020),[3](#B3-fishes-10-00020)]. This species is widely distributed in the western North Pacific with two stocks, namely the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock in the East China Sea (ECS), Yellow Sea (YS), and Japan/East Sea (JES), and the Pacific stock along the Pacific coast [[4](#B4-fishes-10-00020),[5](#B5-fishes-10-00020),[6](#B6-fishes-10-00020),[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020)]. The TWC stock is an economically valuable fishery that is exploited by various countries, including China, Korea, and Japan [[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020),[8](#B8-fishes-10-00020),[9](#B9-fishes-10-00020),[10](#B10-fishes-10-00020)]. From February to June, the TWC stock spawns mainly in the ECS and Korea Strait (KS), after which it migrates to its northern feeding grounds in the JES and YS through the KS [[6](#B6-fishes-10-00020),[11](#B11-fishes-10-00020),[12](#B12-fishes-10-00020),[13](#B13-fishes-10-00020),[14](#B14-fishes-10-00020)].

Variations in the environmental conditions of spawning grounds caused by climate change can cause changes in the physiochemistry of spawners and food availability during the early life stages of fish, and these alterations have implications for spawning behavior, growth, and survival rates, as well as for recruitment strength and fluctuations in the abundance of fish [[10](#B10-fishes-10-00020),[15](#B15-fishes-10-00020),[16](#B16-fishes-10-00020),[17](#B17-fishes-10-00020)]. Changes in the marine environment can result in shifts in spawning ground locations and conditions for chub mackerel, driving subsequent changes in the spatial distribution and survival of hatched eggs and larvae [[10](#B10-fishes-10-00020),[14](#B14-fishes-10-00020),[18](#B18-fishes-10-00020)]. Spawners of the TWC stock predominantly lay their eggs at water temperatures from 15 to 22 °C within 25 m of the seafloor [[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020),[19](#B19-fishes-10-00020),[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)]. The salinity associated with the highest hatching rate is 33 to 35 under laboratory conditions, and habitat suitability during early life stages requires salinity from 33 to 34.25 according to survey results [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[21](#B21-fishes-10-00020)]. The TWC stock is mostly distributed in the continental shelf region during the spawning season, and early-stage mackerel can be collected in this area [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[22](#B22-fishes-10-00020),[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020)].

Spawning ground locations may shift due to climate change and subsequent variations in the marine environment, as chub mackerel must spawn under conditions that are both environmentally and geographically suitable. However, few studies have aimed to project shifts in the spawning grounds of chub mackerel driven by climate change. As a case study, we evaluated and projected the effects of climate-driven changes in ocean circulation and water temperature on the potential spawning ground of the TWC stock of chub mackerel. For this purpose, we developed spawning ground indices for chub mackerel and tested whether potential spawning grounds will shift under a climate change scenario published by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) [[24](#B24-fishes-10-00020)]. The results will be useful for estimating and predicting distributions of chub mackerel during early life stages, as well as the subsequent exploitable abundance and fisheries production of chub mackerel.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Environmental Model

The TWC stock of chub mackerel is mainly distributed in the ECS, YS, and JES [[6](#B6-fishes-10-00020),[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020),[11](#B11-fishes-10-00020),[12](#B12-fishes-10-00020),[13](#B13-fishes-10-00020),[14](#B14-fishes-10-00020)]. Prior research has demonstrated that the optimal spawning temperature is 15 to 22 °C [[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020),[19](#B19-fishes-10-00020),[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)], with the highest hatching rate occurring at salinities of 33 to 35 [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[21](#B21-fishes-10-00020)]. This stock generally spawns within 25 m of the seafloor on the continental shelf [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[22](#B22-fishes-10-00020),[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020)]. The depth of habitat utilized by the TWC stock ranges from 50 to 300 m.

To identify potential spawning grounds, we estimated and projected water temperature and salinity at a depth of 10 m in the western North Pacific Ocean. We derived water temperature and salinity for the 2010s (2010–2019) and 2050s (2050–2059) with an ocean circulation model based on a scenario of the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (IPCC AR5) [[24](#B24-fishes-10-00020)].

To construct the regional ocean circulation model, we utilized the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS), which has its foundations in the Semi-spectral Primitive Equation Model (SPEM) and was adapted to include a terrain-following model structure, designated the S-coordinate Rutgers University Model (SCRUM). These elements, developed by Shchepetkin and McWilliams [[25](#B25-fishes-10-00020)] and Haidvogel et al. [[26](#B26-fishes-10-00020)], enabled us to simulate ocean dynamics with sufficient precision. Additionally, this model incorporates detailed governing equations that address momentum, continuity, temperature, and salinity transport, allowing for a comprehensive representation of oceanic processes. The model’s accuracy has been validated through comparisons with observational data, ensuring reliable simulations that capture both large-scale and finer oceanic features. Furthermore, the model domain used in this study has undergone accuracy verification through the work of Lee et al. [[27](#B27-fishes-10-00020)], supporting its robustness for simulating regional ocean circulation.

The grid structure we employed was the Arakawa C-grid, a staggered system that allows for differentiation between points when calculating sea surface elevation and current velocity. Vertically, we implemented a stretched terrain-following coordinate system that captures the complexity of seabed features, ensuring our model realistically mirrored the terrain beneath the ocean surface.

Our model domain spanned Korean waters and surrounding seas, encompassing the region of 118°00′–143°00′ E and 20°00′–52°00′ N ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_fishes-10-00020-f001)). We achieved horizontal resolution of 1/12°, with 30 sigma layers vertically, striking a balance between detail and computational efficiency. For bottom topography, we integrated data from the global ETOPO2 dataset with regional findings from Seo [[28](#B28-fishes-10-00020)] to enhance the accuracy of our simulation.

![Fishes 10 00020 g001](/fishes/fishes-10-00020/article_deploy/html/images/fishes-10-00020-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.**
Regional ocean modeling system (ROMS) of the study area and major currents (blue arrow: cold currents, red arrow: warm currents, solid: continuous currents, dashed: periodicity currents).

The model was designed to simulate ocean conditions from 2010 to 2059 under climate change conditions based on the projections of IPCC AR5. As the AR5 model does not directly provide appropriate boundary conditions for our regional ocean simulation, we took an additional step. We first ran a Pacific model spanning 104°00′ E to 104°00′ W and 20°00′ S to 65°00′ N with a horizontal resolution of 1° to 1/6° to generate the necessary initial and boundary conditions. This large-scale Pacific model, driven by atmospheric boundary conditions from the ECHAM6 RCP85 scenario provided by the Max Planck Institute, produced monthly average values of sea surface height, temperature, salinity, and velocity. These outputs were then fed into our regional model, ensuring consistency between large-scale Pacific dynamics and our focused regional study.

Atmospheric forcing data for the northwestern Pacific in the regional model mirrored the data used in the Pacific model to maintain alignment. Additionally, we incorporated river discharge data from the Changjiang (Yangtze River), sourced from the Datong station, to accurately simulate freshwater inflow. Tidal effects are another critical aspect of the model. To simulate tides, we extracted ten tidal harmonics from the global tide simulation of Egbert et al. [[29](#B29-fishes-10-00020)] and Egbert and Erofeeva [[30](#B30-fishes-10-00020)], and used them to develop surface height and depth-averaged velocity boundary conditions, as described by Chapman [[31](#B31-fishes-10-00020)] and Flather [[32](#B32-fishes-10-00020)].

In sum, this multi-layered approach combining global and regional data with atmospheric and tidal forces allowed us to simulate the complex oceanic conditions surrounding Korea with a high degree of precision, capturing both the broad effects of climate change and local ocean dynamics.

### 2.2. Spawning Ground Indices

We defined the potential spawning grounds of the TWC stock of chub mackerel in the western North Pacific using 4 parameters: water temperature, salinity, habitat area, and bottom topography. We set the range of suitable water temperatures to 15 to 22 °C [[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020),[19](#B19-fishes-10-00020),[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)]; suitable salinities to 33 to 35 [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[21](#B21-fishes-10-00020)]; habitat areas as the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, and Japan/East Sea; and assumed that chub mackerel can spawn at locations where the bottom depth ranges from 50 to 300 m. Bottom topography was extracted from a combined dataset consisting of ETOPO2 data and the results of Seo [[28](#B28-fishes-10-00020)].

### 2.3. Retrospective Comparison

To validate our regional circulation model, we compared its predicted water temperatures with observed water temperatures compiled bimonthly by the Korea Oceanographic Database Center (KODC) from 2010 to 2019 [[34](#B34-fishes-10-00020)]. We first matched the observed data with predicted data corresponding to the location and date of the observation, and then applied regression through the origin (RTO). As the purpose of this analysis was evaluation of model performance, we selected observations from February to June, which is the spawning period of chub mackerel, rather than including all observed data. Additionally, we assessed whether the same trends were present in the observed and predicted data. For this assessment, we averaged the water temperatures in the observed data and the predicted data at the observed locations on a bimonthly basis, employing Student’s t-test to compare the linear regression slopes of the two datasets.

To diagnose our SGI, we compared the model results with data collected in previous studies [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020),[35](#B35-fishes-10-00020)]. Early-stage chub mackerel were collected in the southern ECS in March of 2004 and 2005 [[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020)], along the coast of Jeju Island in April and May of 2013 as well as May and June of 2014, and in Korean waters in May and June of 2016 and 2017 [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)].

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Environmental Conditions

From the 2010s to the 2050s, our regional circulation model projected that temperatures will generally increase overall, while salinities will increase primarily in the YS ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_fishes-10-00020-f003)). We compared latitude-specific changes between the 2010s and 2050s in water temperature and salinity at a 10 m depth for the habitat area of the TWC stock ([Table 1](#table_body_display_fishes-10-00020-t001)). Water temperature exhibited a tendency to increase by 0.90–1.42 °C throughout the entire latitudinal range, while salinity similarly increased by 0.112–0.324, with the largest changes occurring between 35 and 40 degrees latitude.

### 3.2. Potential Spawning Grounds

We derived a daily SGI from February to June in the 2010s and 2050s based on the ROMS results and projected the monthly potential spawning ground area ([Figure 5](#fig_body_display_fishes-10-00020-f005)). In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (MSG), with a monthly average SGI greater than 0.7, was predominantly observed in the northern waters of Taiwan in February and subsequently shifted northward through the KS to the JES and then the YS in June. In the 2050s, the MSG showed a similar trend of shifting northward over this season. However, compared to the 2010s, the MSG was further north and covered a larger area in the 2050s. This difference was most notable in June, and the MSG spread more widely in the YS than in the JES.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1. Comparison with Previous Studies

The spawning ground of the TWC stock has been reported to extend from the southern part of the ECS to the southwestern part of the JES [[8](#B8-fishes-10-00020),[12](#B12-fishes-10-00020),[13](#B13-fishes-10-00020),[14](#B14-fishes-10-00020)]. Yukami et al. [[7](#B7-fishes-10-00020)] estimated the monthly position of the spawning ground as the central and southern part of the ECS from February through April, the central part of the ECS and the KS in May, and the KS and southwestern JES in June. Our potential spawning grounds were similar to previous reports, although our results also included the YS in June. The TWC stock has been caught in the YS [[36](#B36-fishes-10-00020)], and its larvae have been collected in the same region [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)], which lends support to the reliability of our findings. Moreover, Shelekhov et al. [[37](#B37-fishes-10-00020)] reported that chub mackerel eggs and larvae were collected in the northern JES, along the coast of Primorye and the Strait of Tartary from 23 July to 18 August, 2017. These findings, along with our own results, suggest that the spawning grounds extend northward from the southern ECS in February to the southern JES in June, with possible extension to the waters off Vladivostok and Hokkaido after June.

To determine the SGI, we compared our potential spawning grounds based on ROMS for the 2010s with survey data for the TWC stock during the early life stages, which were collected in the southern ECS in March of 2004 and 2005 [[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020)], along the coast of Jeju Island from April to May of 2013 and May to June of 2014, and in Korean waters from May to June of 2016 and 2017 [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020)]. In March, our MSG in the 2010s included 26.5–28° N and 123–126° E, and chub mackerel larvae were collected from 25.5 to 28.5° N and 122.5 to 126.5° E in 2004 and 2005 [[23](#B23-fishes-10-00020)]. Their eggs and larvae were collected from the coast of Jeju Island in April 2013 [[35](#B35-fishes-10-00020)], even though SGI values were less than 0.3. In May, eggs were collected along the northwestern coast of Jeju Island and in the KS, and larvae were collected in the KS [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[35](#B35-fishes-10-00020)]; our MSG included the KS but not the northwestern coast of Jeju Island. In June, our MSG shifted northward to include the KS, the southwestern part of the JES, and the eastern part of the YS, while eggs were collected in the KS and the southwestern part of the JES and larvae were collected in the KS, the southwestern part of the JES, and the southeastern part of the YS [[20](#B20-fishes-10-00020),[35](#B35-fishes-10-00020)]. These comparisons suggest that our SGI results are reliable.

### 4.2. Comparison Between the 2010s and 2050s

Our model was used to estimate and project potential spawning grounds from February to June for both the 2010s and 2050s. Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to 2050s, and these suggested that chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s compared to the 2010s, which means that spawning will become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current. This shift in spawning grounds will affect chub mackerel survival and growth during early life stages and in nursery grounds, as their weak swimming ability during the early life stages limits movement toward favorable habitat [[38](#B38-fishes-10-00020),[39](#B39-fishes-10-00020),[40](#B40-fishes-10-00020),[41](#B41-fishes-10-00020),[42](#B42-fishes-10-00020)]. Li et al. [[14](#B14-fishes-10-00020)] proposed that the main nursery ground of the TWC stock would shift longitudinally westward from the Pacific side of Japan and the JES to the waters off Jeju Island if the spawning grounds shifted and the influence of the Kuroshio Current weakened. Therefore, we expect that the spawning grounds of the TWC stock will shift northward in the 2050s relative to the 2010s, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of the nursery grounds. Driven by these changes, the ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production will increase in the KS and the YS relative to the JES.

### 4.3. Merits of This Study

Our SGI predicted spatio-temporal changes in the potential spawning ground of the TWC stock using the ROMS. Our model outcomes were generally compatible with previous observations and modeling studies in the region, and the differences were explainable. This compatibility suggests that our method can be applied to the estimation of potential spawning grounds for other stocks or species, provided that sufficient research is available on their spawning characteristics and the marine environment of the area. The results of this study are expected to contribute to the development of bio-physical coupled, individual-based models for predicting the recruitment and spatio-temporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel based on simulation of three-dimensional coordinates consisting of the location, size, and abundance of each super-individual, whose initial abundance, growth, and mortality vary with ambient oceanic conditions.

### 4.4. Limitations and Challenges of the Present Study and Future Research

We diagnosed our regional ocean circulation model for the western North Pacific using two methods and found that, while the model results did not align well with observations in the same space and time, the overall trends were significantly similar. To improve the model’s accuracy, data assimilation methods, such as the Ensemble Kalman Filter or four-dimensional data assimilation, should be applied in future studies.

Although we assumed that the spawning period would not change, the main spawning period may shift due to the environmental changes, even at the same spawning location. For example, past studies have reported that photoperiod influences gonad development [[43](#B43-fishes-10-00020),[44](#B44-fishes-10-00020)], suggesting that the spawning period may be influenced by changes in the annual photoperiod driven by climate change, and this possibility requires further exploration in the near future.

In the present study, we calculated the SGI under the assumption that the spawning area of the TWC stock is located within the continental shelf areas of the ECS, YS, and JES where depths are 50 to 300 m. However, Kume et al. [[45](#B45-fishes-10-00020)] collected chub mackerel larvae in Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait, which included shallow areas of <50 m, suggesting that chub mackerel may spawn in shallow coastal areas. Our results demonstrate that the spawning grounds of chub mackerel could extend into the YS and northern JES. To improve the reliability of the present study regarding chub mackerel spawning grounds, and migration from the southern ECS to the northern JES, international cooperative surveys and research are required in the region, which would comprehensively elucidate the distribution of mackerel eggs and adults. Although chub mackerel are reported to spawn generally within a 25 m depth, we considered only 10 m depth environmental conditions to estimate and project the potential spawning grounds. Moreover, we employed water temperature and salinity as ambient oceanographic variables to predict the spawning grounds of chub mackerel. Environmental conditions of other depths or other marine environmental conditions (such as turbulence, currents, and dissolved oxygen) may influence spawning conditions, and these factors require further research.

We projected changes in the distribution of catchable chub mackerel in the 2050s relative to the 2010s simply by using a climate change scenario and subsequent changes in potential spawning grounds. Further detailed projections, in particular, our ongoing development of individual-based models covering all life stages of chub mackerel, are expected to validate and extend the projections of the present study.

## 5. Conclusions

We estimated potential spawning grounds for chub mackerel in the western North Pacific Ocean using the newly developed spawning ground index. Our model projected that increased regional surface water temperatures in the 2050s due to global warming will cause a northward shift of the spawning grounds of the TWC stock of chub mackerel. The distribution of chub mackerel at early life stages observed in the ECS and the KS was consistent with our model outputs, except for the waters off Jeju Island, and the spawning grounds of chub mackerel suggested in previous studies were compatible with our model results. This study will enhance the reliability of stock assessment for fisheries management of chub mackerel and contribute to the development of individual-based models for exploitable chub mackerel as well as fisheries policies accounting for climate change in the region.

## Appendix A

To test whether our TSI curve and a normal distribution with a mean of 18.5 and a standard deviation of 1.75 were not significantly different, we compared the two distributions using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (K-S) test. The one-sample K-S test can be used to test whether a sample came from a given reference probability distribution. Therefore, we first randomly selected 1000 temperature samples from our TSI curve, and tested whether the 1000 samples came from the normal distribution using the one-sample K-S test, and the result showed that the two distributions did not differ significantly (p = 0.3781; [Figure A1](#fig_body_display_fishes-10-00020-f0A1)).

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Fishes* (2025, Volume 10, Issue 1, Article 20) by authors Seonggil Go (Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology), Joon-ho Lee (Underwater Survey Technology 21), and Sukgeun Jung (Jeju National University, corresponding author). The study projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the western North Pacific Ocean.

**Methodology:** The researchers developed a spawning ground index (SGI) based on a Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′ E, 20°00′–52°00′ N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers), driven by the IPCC AR5 RCP85 scenario. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010–2059. SGI was calculated using four parameters: water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m). The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001).

**Key Findings:**
- In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June.
- By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes).
- Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea.
- The study suggests biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea.

**Limitations noted:** The model results did not perfectly align with observations in the same space and time (though trends were similar); the assumed spawning period may shift due to photoperiod changes; only 10 m depth environmental conditions were considered; and chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m depth).

**Funding:** Supported by the Korea Institute of Marine Science and Technology (KIMST), Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries (RS-2023-00256330 and RS-2022-KS221566), and Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST grant PEA0306).
args.key_excerpts: "Despite some uncertainty, our model based on climate change scenarios projected that, by the 2050s, spawning grounds will shift northward due to warming of the ocean surface, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea."

## Highlights

*   •Our results indicated that the chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation. 
*   •Moreover, sea-surface height and mixed-layer depth exerted the most and least significant effects on chub mackerel distribution, respectively. 
*   •The chub mackerel catch rate peaked in the study area with a sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m3, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psμ, and SSH of 0.575 m. 

## Abstract

Changes in oceanographic conditions can affect species distribution in [marine habitats](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/marine-habitats). Global [climate change](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/climate-change) may negatively influence the oceanographic factor–species distribution relationship. Here, we assessed the influence of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel ([Scomber japonicus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/scomber-japonicus)) distribution in northeastern Taiwan by constructing and using a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery, climatic oscillation, and oceanography data. Our results indicated that the chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation. Moreover, sea-surface height and mixed-layer depth exerted the most and least significant effects on chub mackerel distribution, respectively. The chub mackerel catch rate peaked in the study area with a sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m 3, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psμ, and SSH of 0.575 m. Chub mackerel was the most widely distributed in the area between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E. Our findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in the northeastern waters of Taiwan. Considering changing climate conditions globally, the incorporation of this knowledge into managerial strategies may aid decision-makers in protecting not only other ocean fisheries but also individuals dependent on them.

## Introduction

Global climate change considerably affects marine ecosystems, biodiversity, and the livelihoods of communities dependent on ocean resources (Guo et al., 2023). Oceans absorb a significant portion of surplus heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions, which eventually leads to ocean warming. Ocean warming has numerous significant effects, including coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, sea-level rise, and reduced oxygen levels (Yashayaev et al., 2015). The cumulative impact of these alterations in oceanographic conditions engenders significant challenges for marine ecosystems and biodiversity. These alterations can also significantly impact fish stocks, affecting their productivity, catch rates, and financial sustainability. They can shift species distribution and migration patterns, making some species more vulnerable, affecting fishing patterns, and negatively affecting livelihoods and food security (Mordy et al., 2023). Numerous studies have forecasted a major habitat shift or loss due to changing oceanographic and climate conditions (Hollowed et al., 2019; Heck et al., 2023). For instance, under Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 [climate change scenario (extreme warming condition)], Lam et al. (2020) predicted that by the 2050s, alterations in oceanographic conditions would lead to a 40% decline in the tropical fish catch in some economic zones. Therefore, research on the impact of oceanographic conditions on fisheries is crucial for preserving biodiversity, sustainably managing fisheries, and supporting communities dependent on fisheries for their food security and livelihood.

Oceanographic conditions, including physical, chemical, and biological factors, significantly influence fishery distribution, affecting the availability and abundance of fish species. Thus, studying the relationship between these conditions and fish distribution is crucial and can represent an initial step in sustainable fishery management (Frawley et al., 2024). Oceanographic conditions include sea-surface temperature (SST), sea-surface salinity (SSS), sea-surface chlorophyll (SSC), mixed-layer depth (MLD), and ocean currents. These factors can influence distribution directly or indirectly. For instance, SST is a crucial oceanographic factor that regulates an organism's thermoregulation, affecting its distribution, ecology, behavior, and interactions with other organisms (Fredston et al., 2023). SSS is another crucial oceanographic factor that significantly influences fish distribution, migration patterns, physiology, spawning, and reproduction (Miah et al., 2023). MLD influences water column temperature and nutrient distribution, affecting plankton abundance and fish species reliant on these resources (Wang et al., 2023a, Wang et al., 2023b). However, numerous other factors affect fisheries (Molina-Valdivia et al., 2021). Moreover, climate oscillations can cause extreme ocean events, engendering changes in oceanographic conditions (Mondal et al., 2023a, Mondal et al., 2023b; Báez et al., 2021). These events are a part of a broader climate system, influencing SST variations and ocean currents, affecting ocean conditions, and altering fishery distribution.

Species distribution models (SDMs), also known as habitat models, ecological niche models, and bioclimatic envelopes, are widely used for assessing species–oceanography relationships (Rodrigues et al., 2023). SDMs are mathematical models that can predict the distribution of a species in its environment, and algorithmic representations are used to represent its environmental habitats accurately (Panzeri et al., 2024). Arithmetic and geometric mean models, which are based on the habitat suitability index (HSI) (Lee et al., 2020), have limitations such as outlier sensitivity, non-applicability to zero and negative numbers, and unsuitability for exponential growth modeling. With technological advancements, the potential of statistical regression models, artificial intelligence models, and classification and regression tree models has been significantly enhanced (Mondal et al., 2023a, Mondal et al., 2023b). New-generation models provide flexibility, prediction accuracy, and scalability for large datasets, surpassing previous approaches in terms of performance (Brodie et al., 2023). Recent years have seen multiple efforts to integrate ensemble learning with deep learning (Tasci et al., 2021). Most of these attempts utilize the average voting method employed by baseline deep learning models. The ensemble process utilizing average voting methods exhibits a bias towards weak baseline learners, rendering it an ineffective strategy for combining these learners. Although various strategies exist for combining baseline learners in ensemble deep learning, these approaches exhibit limitations related to generalization, training challenges, and other concerns (Tasci et al., 2021). Several review efforts in the literature have introduced the concept of deep ensemble learning (Dong et al., 2020). This effort is limited to the application of ensemble methods in specific domains, accompanied by reviews of traditional ensemble approaches. However, ensemble approaches, including core bagging, boosting, and stacking, have gained popularity because of their superior performance to that of single-algorithm models. These models reduce prediction error variance by considering bias; thus, they provide more robust and accurate predictions than individual models (Makki et al., 2023).

Chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_, Linnaeus, 1758) is a key coastal–pelagic fish found in warm and temperate waters, spanning the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans. It is harvested in the East China and Yellow Seas by lighting-purse seine fisheries operated by China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan (Han et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2023). Three commercial fishing grounds have been identified between 1998 and 2011 during the peak fishing seasons: the southern fishing ground in the summer in the south East China Sea, the central fishing ground in the autumn in the north East China Sea and the south Yellow Sea, and the northern fishing ground in the winter in the north Yellow Sea (Li et al. 2014). In Taiwan, chub mackerel fishery is economically crucial providing income, employment, and export earnings (Yu et al., 2018). However, sustainable management techniques are crucial for the long-term survival and health of the species.

Few studies have assessed the distribution of chub mackerel in the northeastern Pacific (Chen et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023). However, none of them have used more than one algorithm to confirm the significance of oceanographic conditions, examine the distribution patterns of chub mackerel, and then compare the results. Furthermore, research on the effects of climatic oscillations on chub mackerel catch has been scarce which posed a major research gap. Our study proposed a hypothesis that the catch rate of chub mackerel in northern Taiwan waters is greatly affected by climatic oscillation and oceanographic circumstances. Furthermore, ensemble modelling is more adept at accurately determining the distribution based on oceanographic conditions compared to models that rely on a single algorithm. The main objective of the current study was to determine climatic oscillations impact on chub mackerel catch rate and the distribution of chub mackerel in relation to the oceanographic conditions in the northern waters of Taiwan by using an ensemble modeling approach. We also assessed the effects of climatic oscillations on chub mackerel fisheries. We focused on chub mackerel fish captured using the Taiwanese purse-seine, as it is the predominant method used in Taiwan, accounting for 98.66% of all captures (Supplementary Fig. 1). The incorporation of current findings on the influence of changing climatic condition into management strategies may aid in making informed decisions to ensure the sustainable management of chub mackerel as well as other coastal fisheries of Taiwan and to ensure the well-being of the communities relying on them.

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in Marine Environmental Research (Volume 202, November 2024, Article 106803) as part of a special issue on "Climate Change and the Oceans," edited by Fangli QIAO of the First Institute of Oceanography. The study examines the effects of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) distribution in northeastern Taiwan.

**Authors:** Sandipan Mondal, Frank Muller-Karger, Aratrika Ray, Shin-Ichi Ito, Ming-An Lee, and Hsueh-Jung Lu.

**Methodology:** The researchers constructed a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery data, climatic oscillation data, and oceanography data. Fishery and oceanographic data were rescaled using MATLAB (2022a) to a consistent spatial and temporal grid, then standardized using a generalized linear model (GLM). Five single-algorithm models were used: GLM, generalized additive model (GAM), gradient boosting method (GBM), random forest (RF), and classification models, combined into an ensemble approach.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO), which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792).
- NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level.
- Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect.
- Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m.
- Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E.

**Background Context:** Global climate change is significantly affecting marine ecosystems, with ocean warming causing coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, and sea-level rise. Under RCP 8.5 scenario, a predicted 40% decline in tropical fish catch by the 2050s in some economic zones (Lam et al., 2020) highlights the urgency of this research. Chub mackerel is economically crucial to Taiwan, with Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries accounting for 98.66% of captures. The study addresses a research gap by using multiple algorithms to confirm oceanographic significance, unlike previous studies that relied on single models.

**Funding:** National Science & Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC) grant 112-2811-M-019-004 and Fisheries Agency, Council of Agriculture, Taiwan grant 112-FM-2.31-A-03.

**Applications:** Findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in northeastern Taiwan waters and may aid decision-makers in protecting other ocean fisheries and dependent communities under changing climate conditions. The article has been cited by 5 subsequent publications (as of the page retrieval date).

# Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (_Scomber Japonicus_) larvae in the East China Sea

Author links open overlay panel Yuesong Li a e, [Xinjun Chen a e](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/23491495500/xinjun-chen), [Changsheng Chen b a](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/35298445100/changsheng-chen), [Jianzhong Ge c](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/26638756300/jiangzhong-ge), [Rubao Ji d](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/15122175100/rubao-ji), Rucheng Tian b, [Pengfei Xue b](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/24081949800/pengfei-xue), [Liuxiong Xu a e](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/16204581100/liuxiong-xu)

## Abstract

An early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_) (IBM-CM) is developed and coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). Using this coupled physical-biological model, we examined the influences of regional physical processes on the dispersion and survival of chub mackerel larvae in the ECS under climatological spring–summer temperature and circulation conditions with and without the inclusion of short-time fluctuations of a typhoon. The model results show that the seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during the early life stages. Sensitivity experiments suggest that under the same physical environment, the larval dispersal distributions and survival rates can be significantly influenced by the location of [spawning ground](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/spawning-ground). The impact of a typhoon on the [larval transport](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/larval-transport) depends on its path, intensity, speed and timing since most typhoons swept the ECS over a time scale of a few days. The comparison of the cases with and without inclusion of Typhoon Alice indicates that cancelation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents in the ECS could limit the influence of the typhoon on the low-frequency flow and thus on larval dispersion in this region, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing could significantly increase larval mortality and thus decrease the abundance of surviving larvae in the nursery ground in the ECS.

## Introduction

It is well recognized that natural environmental variability has a pronounced influence on fish recruitment, particularly on their early larval stages (Bartsch and Coombs, 2001, Bartsch and Coombs, 2004). In addition to bottom-up (food availability) and top-down (predation pressure) mediation, ocean circulation, water temperature and stratification, and mixing can directly affect larval dispersion, growth, and mortality and thus larval survival rate. Chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_), a coastal pelagic species, is widely distributed on the continental shelf in the tropical and subtropical regions of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans (Tang, 2006). In the East China Sea (ECS) and the Japan/East Sea (JES), chub mackerel are classified into two regional stocks: (1) the Tsushima Current (TS) stock and (2) the ECS stock (Yamada et al., 1986). In the purse-seine fishery, the TS stock is more commercially valuable than the ECS stock (Hwang and Lee, 2005). As with many living marine resources, the chub mackerel fishery stocks are subject to fishing pressures, with yield and recruitment considerably influenced by natural environmental factors (Bartsch and Coombs, 2004, Daskalov, 1999).

The current research on chub mackerel is mainly focused on age and growth studies (Gluyas-Millan et al., 1998), resource and environmental dynamics (Hiyama et al., 2002, Watanabe and Yatsu, 2004) and stock assessments (Hill and Crone, 2006), with little consideration of the fluctuation driven by the temporal and spatial variability of the physical environment. In the ECS, the early life of chub mackerel is composed of five life stages: eggs, early larvae, larvae, early juvenile and juvenile (Hunter and Kimbrell, 1980). The early larvae grow slowly in the first 10–15 days until reaching about 6–7 mm, followed by rapid growth. When the larvae reach ∼15 mm over a period of 20 days, metamorphosis to the early juvenile stage occurs. The spawning grounds of the Tsushima Current stock are in the northern waters off Taiwan (Fig. 1), with a spawning period from February to June (Yukami et al., 2009). Spawning occurs in the upper 10 m of the water column (Fritzsche, 1978), with substantial influence of the local and regional circulation on dispersion and survival of mackerel larvae.

Circulation, stratification and mixing in the ECS are controlled by complex physical processes associated with the Kuroshio, the Changjiang River discharges, tides and air–sea interactions (Chen et al., 1994) (Fig. 1). The Kuroshio, a warm and saline current, enters the ECS east of Taiwan, flows northeastward along the edge of the continental slope, and then moves eastward into the interior of the Pacific Ocean off the Tokyo coast. The Taiwan Warm Current (TWC) originates from the Taiwan Strait, flows northeastward over the continental shelf, and then separates into two branches: one flowing toward the inner shelf off the Changjiang and the other toward the Tsushima/East Strait. The Changjiang Coastal Current (CCC) forms as a result of the Changjiang River discharge and flows southward along the Chinese coast. The ECS features a strong semidiurnal tide, particularly in the shallow region over the continental shelf (Choi, 1984). The air–sea interactions influence vertical stratification in the ECS, which is vertically well-mixed in the shallow coastal region due to surface cooling and wind mixing during winter, and re-stratified due to surface heating in the summer. Circulation in the ECS varies significantly from season to season as a result of the Changjiang River discharges, winds and cooling/heating. The Kuroshio acts as a retention mechanism to keep the mackerel larvae over the continental shelf of the ECS, while the combined CCC, TWC and monsoon winds tend to advect larvae eastward over the continental shelf to the Tsushima/East Strait. Since these physical processes vary significantly in space and time, they can have a direct impact on the recruitment of chub mackerel in the ECS. What level of influence do the regional circulation and stratification have on the survival rate, dispersion and abundance of mackerel larvae? In addition, the ECS is a subtropical region with frequent disturbance by typhoons, particularly during spring and summer (Chen and Qin, 1985). Typhoons cause strong cyclonic currents and vertical mixing along their pathways when sweeping the ECS. If a typhoon appears during spawning and early larvae stages, is it a hazard to the mackerel larvae? These questions, to our knowledge, have not been thoroughly examined yet.

Investigation of environmental impacts on mackerel recruitment can be approached by either observational field ecology with statistical correlation techniques (Hiyama et al., 2002) or fully coupled physical-fishery models (Werner et al., 1993, Miller et al., 1998). Built on the Lagrangian theory, the individual-based model (IBM) is a state-of-the-art traditional tool to incorporate the physical processes (such as advection and turbulent mixing) into the behavior of individual larvae in their early life stages (Bartsch and Coombs, 2004, Tian et al., 2009a). The IBM approach is appropriate for application to fisheries ecology when theoretical frameworks have been constructed on growth, mortality and energy flow (Bartsch et al., 2004, Sassa et al., 2008, Wang et al., 2013). To our knowledge, no IBM has been developed to study recruitment of the chub mackerel in the ECS.

The circulation model of the ECS has been continually refined (e.g. Choi, 1984, Yanagi and Takahashi, 1993, Chang and Isobe, 2003, Chen et al., 2008). An unstructured-grid, three-dimensional, primitive-equation, Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM) was applied to the ECS (hereafter referred to as ECS-FVCOM) by Chen et al. (2008). The non-overlapped triangular mesh provides increased resolution of complex irregular coastal geometry and steep bottom topography in the ECS. The volume-conservative, finite-volume algorithm makes this model suitable for biological applications in which mass conservation is prerequisite. Built on the success of ECS-FVCOM development, we have developed an IBM of chub mackerel (hereafter referred to as IBM-CM) and coupled it to ECS-FVCOM. Using this coupled physical-biological model, we examined the influence of the physical environment on the survival and distribution of chub larvae in the ECS.

This paper summarizes the development of the coupled high-resolution ECS-FVCOM and IBM-CM system and presents new findings from process-oriented experiments. It is the first study of this kind in the East China Sea with a focus on examining the impact of the regional-scale physical environment and typhoons on the early life of mackerel larvae. The remaining sections are organized as follows. In Section 2, the coupled model is introduced. In Section 3, the design of process-oriented numerical experiments is described. In Section 4, the model results for 1-D and 3-D experiments are presented, in which the experiments were made for the climatological physical conditions and a selected typhoon event. Discussion and conclusions are followed in Section 5.

As predicting CHAB intensity and spatial distribution is critical to Lake Erie ecosystem management, this study focuses on a comprehensive evaluation of Lagrangian and Eulerian transport models for Lake Erie CHAB forecasts, including 1) a Lagrangian particle model (LPM), 2) an Eulerian tracer model (ETM), and 3) a property-carrying particle model (PCPM) that utilizes the hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian approach. We evaluated the models' performance against the latest high-resolution satellite product from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-3 OLCI sensor over 24- to 240-h hindcasts for each CHAB occurrence in three consecutive CHAB seasons (2017–2019). We examined the relative contributions of horizontal transport, vertical turbulent mixing, and algal buoyancy on the CHAB inter- and intra-day variability. In the short-term forecast, we emphasize the highly dynamic reaction of currents to weather-scale wind events that are crucial to CHAB transport. While statistical skill assessments show that these three transport models attain comparable levels of hindcast accuracy, we explore the advantages and disadvantages of each model in the context of general biophysical modeling. In particular, the fact that the ETM and PCPM perform as well as or better than the LPM sets up a promising path to developing more biological realism in future operational forecast models using Eulerian or hybrid approaches.    
*   ### [Evaluating the influence of environmental factors on the early life history growth of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) using a growth and migration model](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0079661122000829)

2022, Progress in Oceanography Citation Excerpt : 
Models with bioenergetics modules have been applied to study many fish species, including the Atlantic mackerel (Boyd et al., 2020a, 2020b). In the Northwest Pacific, however, modeling studies of chub mackerel using bioenergetics are limited (Li et al., 2014). This study first developed an IBM for chub mackerel in the Northwest Pacific with a bioenergetics module.   Show abstract Chub mackerel is one of the most important fisheries target species worldwide. These fish have large fluctuations in biomass, the mechanism of which remains unclear. This study developed a bioenergetics individual-based model for chub mackerel distributed in the Northwest Pacific and evaluated the dominant environmental factors that affect their early life history. The parameters in the bioenergetics model were obtained or estimated from previous studies, and a migration model with a gradient area search algorithm was coupled. The growth rate of chub mackerel was calibrated to _in situ_ growth data by adjusting the half-saturation constant of consumption (_K_). During 2002–2016, the growth and migration of chub mackerel were reproduced using the model with satellite-derived forcing. The migration routes and growth were tightly coupled: individuals located to the north of the Kuroshio axis experienced a better prey environment, showed a relatively higher growth rate, and entered a better prey field by self-selected swimming. Years with more high-growth individuals in the model corresponded to observed higher recruitment (R) and recruitment per spawner (RPS). These results support the hypothesis that a higher growth rate in the early stage results in higher recruitment, because individuals with higher growth can migrate into a better prey environment. A negative correlation was found between R and the distance of the Kuroshio axis from the Boso Peninsula, indicating that when the Kuroshio axis was located closer to the Boso Peninsula, the water temperature of the coastal area increased, resulting in an increase in coastal-dominant zooplankton species, which positively affected the growth of chub mackerel in the early life stage. In addition, interannual variations in prey zooplankton species composition and the relative position of the Kuroshio to the spawning grounds partially influenced the early growth of chub mackerel. The results demonstrate the complex mechanisms of ocean currents and prey fields controlling the recruitment of small pelagic species.    
*   ### [Larval Dispersal Modeling Reveals Low Connectivity among National Marine Protected Areas in the Yellow and East China Seas](https://doi.org/10.3390/biology12030396)

2023, Biology  Show abstract In this study, a biophysical model was developed to assess the ecological connectivity of national marine protected areas in the Yellow and East China Seas. The results showed that ocean dynamics, pelagic larval duration, and distribution patterns had significant effects on larval dispersal. The existing national marine reserves in the Yellow and East China Seas did not form a well-connected network, and nearly 30% of them were isolated. The only connections were mostly from north to south. Four marine protected areas (all in coastal Zhejiang) emerged as key nodes for ensuring multi-generational connectivity. Due to the selection of study species with weak to strong potential dispersal, the results of this study can be applied to other organisms with similar life history characteristics, and can provide scientific reference for future reserve planning in coastal China. Marine protected areas (MPAs) are vital for protecting biodiversity, maintaining ecosystem integrity, and tackling future climate change. The effectiveness of MPA networks relies on connectivity, yet connectivity assessments are often skipped in the planning process. Here we employed a multi-species biophysical model to examine the connectivity patterns formed among the 21 national MPAs in the Yellow and East China Seas. We simulated the potential larval dispersal of 14 oviparous species of five classes. Larvae of non-migratory species with pelagic larval duration (PLD) were assumed to be passive floating particles with no explicit vertical migration. A total of 217,000 particles were released according to spawning period, living depth, and species distribution, and they were assumed to move with currents during the PLD. Most larvae were dispersed around the MPAs (0–60 m isobaths) and consistent with the currents. Larval export increased with PLD and current velocity, but if PLD was too long, few larvae survived due to high daily mortality during pelagic dispersal. The overall connectivity pattern exhibited a north-to-south dispersal trend corresponding to coastal currents. Our results indicated that the national MPAs in the Yellow and East China Seas did not form a well-connected network and nearly 30% of them were isolated. These MPAs formed three distinct groups, one in the Yellow Sea ecoregion and two in the East China Sea ecoregion. Four MPAs (all in coastal Zhejiang) emerged as key nodes for ensuring multi-generational connectivity. Under the pressure of future climate change, high self-recruitment and low connectivity present significant challenges for building well-connected MPA networks. We suggest adding new protected areas as stepping stones for bioecological corridors. Focused protection of the Yellow Sea ecoregion could have a good effect on the southern part of the population recruitment downstream. Conservation management should be adjusted according to the life cycles and distributions of vulnerable species, as well as seasonal changes in coastal currents. This study provides a scientific basis for improving ecological connectivity and conservation effectiveness of MPAs in the Yellow and East China Seas.

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in Ecological Modelling (Volume 283, 10 July 2014, Pages 70-84) titled "Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea" by Yuesong Li, Xinjun Chen, Changsheng Chen, Jianzhong Ge, Rubao Ji, Rucheng Tian, Pengfei Xue, and Liuxiong Xu. DOI: 10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2014.03.016.

The study developed an early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The researchers examined how regional physical processes affect larval dispersal and survival under climatological spring-summer conditions, both with and without short-time fluctuations from a typhoon.

Key findings include:
- Seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages.
- Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location.
- Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing. Comparison of cases with and without Typhoon Alice showed that cancellation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents limits typhoon influence on low-frequency flow and larval dispersion, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds.
- Temperature and food play significant roles in early larval development; water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March-July.
- Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June).
- Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion.

The article provides background on the ECS physical oceanography, including the Kuroshio Current (which acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf), the Taiwan Warm Current, and the Changjiang Coastal Current (which tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East Strait). Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. The study is the first IBM developed to examine chub mackerel recruitment in the ECS.

The paper has 41 references and has been cited 27 times. It was supported by multiple Chinese national research projects including the National 863 project, Shanghai Education Committee, and Shanghai Ocean University programs.

# Stock assessment of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the central East China Sea based on length data

Published online by Cambridge University Press: 
**30 October 2013**

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](/core/page-component/img/share-icon.cbcfad8.svg)
![](/core/page-component/img/close-icon.194b28a.svg)
![](/core/page-component/img/cite-icon.44eaaa4.svg)
![](/core/page-component/img/rights-icon.d4a677c.svg)

## Abstract

The chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) has been one of the important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea since the decline of traditional demersal economic species. Although chub mackerel resources are suffering over-exploitation with the increase of fishing effort, their response to fishing and changing trends have not been analysed because of a shortage of data. In this paper we separated sample catches of chub mackerel from the central East China Sea during 2009 and 2010 into three age groups based on the age–fork length key. We then estimated the maximum sustainable yield (MSY) and built a spawner–recruitment relationship based on the fishery statistics of purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. We predicted the biomass, spawning biomass, catches and the length compositions of catches when fishing at the current intensity (fishing mortality (*F*) = 0.7). The results showed that the MSY of chub mackerel is about 18.8 × 104t, and the fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (both the lighting purse seine vessels and deep-water purse seine vessels were standardized to purse seine vessels), which is equivalent to *F* = 0.4. If *F* remains at the current level, the biomass of chub mackerel will remain at 45.3 × 104t. At the same time, more than 40% in the catch will be the individuals smaller than 200 mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300 mm. Therefore, there is little potential for further exploitation of the chub mackerel resources in the central East China Sea, and it is better to reduce *F* to less than 0.4 for sustainable utilization.

args.summary: This webpage is a Cambridge University Press journal article (published online October 30, 2013, in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom) titled "Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data." The study addresses the chub mackerel, an important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea that rose to prominence after the decline of traditional demersal economic species. The research methodology involved separating sample catches from 2009-2010 into three age groups based on an age–fork length key, estimating maximum sustainable yield (MSY), and building a spawner–recruitment relationship using fishery statistics from purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels, and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. Key findings: (1) The MSY of chub mackerel is approximately 18.8 × 10⁴ tonnes; (2) The fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (with lighting and deep-water purse seine vessels standardized to purse seine vessels), equivalent to a fishing mortality rate (F) of 0.4; (3) If fishing mortality remains at the current level (F = 0.7), the biomass will remain at 45.3 × 10⁴ tonnes; (4) At current fishing intensity, more than 40% of catches will consist of individuals smaller than 200mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300mm. The study concludes there is little potential for further exploitation of chub mackerel resources in the central East China Sea, and recommends reducing fishing mortality (F) to less than 0.4 for sustainable utilization. The chub mackerel resources are suffering over-exploitation due to increased fishing effort, and this paper represents the first analysis of their response to fishing because of previous data shortages.

## Abstract

Spatio-temporal distribution of chub mackerel _Scomber japonicus_ is strongly susceptible to climate variability. In this study, a weighting-based habitat suitability index (HSI) model was established to assess the impacts of Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) on habitat range and distribution of _S. japonicus_ in the East China Sea (ECS) using vertical water temperature at depths of 2.5 m, 25 m and 50 m. Results showed that the optimal HSI model selected from ten weighting scenarios can yield reliable predictions. Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative relationship between the PDO index and water temperature anomaly at different depths. The water temperatures at three different layers on the fishing ground of _S. japonicus_ tended to be low in the warm PDO phase and high in the cold PDO phase, respectively. The range of suitable habitats and its spatial distribution exhibited large differences between the warm and cold PDO regimes. During a warm PDO phase, vertical water temperature became cool, and the monthly preferred water temperature at each depth for _S. japonicus_ shifted southeastward. Consequently, habitat quality dramatically decreased, and suitable habitat ranges also reduced and moved southeastward. Conversely, in a cool PDO phase, with the warmer vertical water temperature and northwestward shift of the preferred water temperature, the suitable habitats enlarged and migrated in the same direction. Our findings indicate that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of _S. japonicus_ in the East China Sea.

This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Ocean University of China (Volume 20, pages 1483–1494, 2021) titled "Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea." Published on November 21, 2021, the study was conducted by authors Wei Yu, Jian Wen, Xinjun Chen, Gang Li, Yuesong Li, and Zhong Zhang, affiliated with Shanghai Ocean University and the Qingdao National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology.

The study investigated how the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) impacts the habitat range and distribution of the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the East China Sea (ECS). A weighting-based Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) model was established using vertical water temperature data at depths of 2.5 m, 25 m, and 50 m. From ten weighting scenarios tested, the optimal HSI model yielded reliable predictions.

Key findings include:
- A significant negative relationship was found between the PDO index and water temperature anomaly at different depths.
- Water temperatures at three different layers on the fishing ground tended to be LOW during the warm PDO phase and HIGH during the cold PDO phase.
- During a warm PDO phase: vertical water temperature cooled, the monthly preferred water temperature shifted southeastward, habitat quality dramatically decreased, and suitable habitat ranges reduced and moved southeastward.
- During a cool PDO phase: warmer vertical water temperatures occurred, preferred water temperature shifted northwestward, and suitable habitats enlarged and migrated in the same direction.

The study concludes that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of S. japonicus in the East China Sea. The article received 279 accesses, 7 citations, and 1 Altmetric score. The research was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2018YFD0900906), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 41906073), the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (No. 19ZR1423000), and the Shanghai Universities First-Class Disciplines Project (Fisheries A).

# Climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index of chub mackerel in the spawning season and its effect on the abundance

Liangming Wang 1,2,3

Shuyang Ma 2

Yang Liu 2

Jianchao Li 2

Dianrong Sun 1,3

Yongjun Tian 2,4\*

1. Key Laboratory of Marine Ranching, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Guangzhou, China
