The Kuroshio Current is the west side of the clockwise North Pacific [ocean gyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_gyre "Ocean gyre").

The **Kuroshio Current** ([黒潮](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/黒潮 "wikt:黒潮"); "Black Stream"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) also known as the **Black Current** or **Japan Current** ([日本海流](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/日本海流 "wikt:日本海流"), *Nihon Kairyū*), is a north-flowing, warm [ocean current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_current "Ocean current") on the west side of the North [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") basin. It was named for the deep blue appearance of its waters. Similar to the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") in the North Atlantic, the Kuroshio is a powerful [western boundary current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_boundary_current "Western boundary current") that transports warm equatorial water poleward and forms the western limb of the [North Pacific Subtropical Gyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pacific_Gyre "North Pacific Gyre"). Off the East Coast of Japan, it merges with the [Oyashio Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyashio_Current "Oyashio Current") to form the [North Pacific Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pacific_Current "North Pacific Current").

The Kuroshio Current has significant effects on both physical and biological processes of the North Pacific Ocean, including nutrient and sediment transport, major Pacific storm tracks and regional climate, and Pacific mode water formation.[[2]](#cite_note-:253-2)[[3]](#cite_note-:103-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Terazaki2-4) Additionally, the current's significant nutrient transport results in a biologically rich [ecoregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecoregion "Ecoregion") supporting an important fishing industry as well as diverse marine food webs. The [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea") for example has relatively low nutrient concentrations in its upper waters, but experiences enhanced biological productivity due to the input from the [Kuroshio Current Intrusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuroshio_Current_Intrusion "Kuroshio Current Intrusion").[[5]](#cite_note-5) Ongoing research centered around the Kuroshio Current's response to [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") predicts a strengthening in surface flows of this western boundary current which contrasts the predicted changes in the Atlantic Ocean's Gulf Stream.[[6]](#cite_note-:323-6)

Since the early 20th century, anthropologists have debated the role of the current in Japanese culture.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Today, historians are reevaluating the role of the current as a factor in Japan's economic development.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Kuroshio current was discovered in 1565 by [Andrés de Urdaneta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrés_de_Urdaneta "Andrés de Urdaneta"), a native of Guipuzcoa, colonial administrator, supervisor of nautical expeditions, [Corregidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corregidor "Corregidor"), Augustinian monk and loyal navigator in the service of [King Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain"), when, aboard the [nao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nao_(ship) "Nao (ship)") *San Pedro*, he was the first to open the "tornaviaje" between Cebu ([Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines")) and the coasts of Old California ([New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain")). The secret of the tornaviaje gave Spain absolute hegemony over the Pacific Ocean for centuries, a hegemony that was embodied in the so-called "[Manila galleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon "Manila galleon")".

The existence of the Kuroshio Current was known to Europeans from as early as 1650. This was shown in a map drawn by [Bernhardus Varenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhardus_Varenius "Bernhardus Varenius"). As well as this, it was also noted by [Captain J. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_J._King?action=edit&redlink=1 "Captain J. King (page does not exist)") during a British expedition under [Captain James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook").[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Historians have debated the current’s role in structuring the economic geography of Japan, especially at the time before steam navigation. The current’s path influenced the development of fisheries and whaling businesses that grew in the early modern period in specific regions. Its movement was also a factor in the development of maritime routes for domestic shipping as well as international navigation along the shores of Japan. In the mid-19th century, the current became an object of oceanographic interest both in Japan and abroad. The ideological effect of scientific conquest and industrial appropriation of the Kuroshio by the Japanese Empire has been likened to a frontier incorporation.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Physical properties

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Physical properties")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Kuroshio_Temperature.png/250px-Kuroshio_Temperature.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kuroshio_Temperature.png)

Averaged winter sea surface temperatures in the western Pacific Ocean using satellite data. The Kuroshio current is warm, compared to cooler waters in the [Yellow Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Sea "Yellow Sea"), and Sea of Japan.

The Kuroshio is a relatively warm ocean current with an annual average [sea-surface temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature") of about 24 °C (75 °F), is approximately 100 kilometres (62 mi) wide, and produces frequent small to [meso-scale eddies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_(fluid_dynamics)#Mesoscale_ocean_eddies "Eddy (fluid dynamics)"). The Kuroshio originates from the Pacific [North Equatorial Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Equatorial_Current "North Equatorial Current"), which splits in two at the east coast of [Luzon, Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzon "Luzon"), to form the southward-flowing [Mindanao Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao_Current "Mindanao Current") and the more significant northward-flowing Kuroshio Current.[[10]](#cite_note-10) East of Taiwan, the Kuroshio enters the [East China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_China_Sea "East China Sea") through a deep break in the [Ryukyu island chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryukyu_Islands "Ryukyu Islands") known as the Yonaguni Depression. The Kuroshio then continues northwards and parallel to the Ryukyu islands, steered by the deepest part of the East China Sea, the [Okinawa Trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_Trough "Okinawa Trough"), before leaving the East China Sea and re-entering the Pacific through the Tokara Strait.[[11]](#cite_note-:022-11) It then flows along the southern margin of Japan but meanders significantly.[[12]](#cite_note-12) At the [Bōsō Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bōsō_Peninsula "Bōsō Peninsula"), the Kuroshio finally separates from the Japanese coast and travels eastward as the Kuroshio Extension.[[13]](#cite_note-13) The Kuroshio Current is the Pacific analogue of the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"),[[14]](#cite_note-EB1911-14) transporting warm, tropical water northward toward the [polar region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_region "Polar region").

The Kuroshio's counterparts associated with the North Pacific Gyre are the: east flowing North Pacific Current to the north, the south flowing [California Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Current "California Current") to the east, and the west flowing [North Equatorial Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Equatorial_Current "North Equatorial Current") to the south. The warm waters of the Kuroshio Current sustain the [coral reefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_reef "Coral reef") of Japan, the northernmost coral reefs in the world. The part of the Kuroshio that branches into the [Sea of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan "Sea of Japan") is called **Tsushima Current** (対馬海流, *Tsushima Kairyū*).

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Japan%27s_ocean_currents.PNG/250px-Japan%27s_ocean_currents.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Japan's_ocean_currents.PNG)

The ocean currents surrounding the Japanese archipelago: **1. Kuroshio** 2. Kuroshio extension 3. Kuroshio countercurrent 4. Tsushima Current 5. Tsugaru Current 6. Sōya Current 7. [Oyashio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyashio_Current "Oyashio Current") 8. Liman Current

Similar to the Atlantic Ocean's Gulf Stream, the Kuroshio Current creates warm ocean surface temperatures, and significant moisture in the atmosphere along the western Pacific basin, and thus produces and sustains [tropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone"). Tropical cyclones, also known as [typhoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon "Typhoon"), are formed when [atmospheric instability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_instability "Atmospheric instability"), warm ocean surface temperatures, and moist air are combined to fuel an atmospheric low-pressure system. The Western North Pacific Ocean experiences an average of 25 typhoons annually.[[15]](#cite_note-:62-15) The majority of typhoons occur from July through October during northern hemisphere summer,[[15]](#cite_note-:62-15) and typically form where the Kuroshio Current is the warmest near the equator. Typhoons tend to track along the current's warm water poleward until they dissipate in colder waters.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

The strength ([transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volumetric_flow_rate "Volumetric flow rate")) of the Kuroshio varies along its path and seasonally. Within the Sea of Japan, observations suggest that the Kuroshio transport is relatively steady at about 25[Sv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sverdrup "Sverdrup")[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) (25 million cubic metres per second). The Kuroshio strengthens significantly when it rejoins the Pacific Ocean, reaching 65[Sv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sverdrup "Sverdrup") (65 million cubic metres per second) southeast of Japan,[[11]](#cite_note-:022-11) although this transport has significant seasonal variability.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The Kuroshio Current splits into Kuroshio Current extension and the Tsushima Current, as the currents wrap around Japanese Island and reconnects, changes in flow will impact the flows of the other currents.

The path of the Kuroshio may have been different in the geologic past based on historical sea level and bathymetry, however there is currently[*[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] conflicting scientific evidence. It has been proposed that lower [sea-level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level_rise "Sea level rise") and [tectonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonics "Tectonics") may have prevented the Kuroshio from entering the Sea of Japan during the [last glacial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period"), approximately c. 115,000 – c. 11,700 years ago, and remained entirely within the Pacific basin.[[20]](#cite_note-20) However, other proxies and [ocean models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_general_circulation_model "Ocean general circulation model") have alternatively suggested that the Kuroshio path was relatively unaltered,[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22) possibly as far back as 700,000 years ago.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

### Sediment transport

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Sediment transport")]

The magnitude of the Kuroshio Current and seafloor bathymetry results in deep sea [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion "Erosion") and [sediment transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sediment_transport "Sediment transport") in multiple regions. Offshore of Southern Taiwan on the Kenting Plateau erosion is likely caused by the strong bottom currents which increase in velocity along the rise on this plateau.[[24]](#cite_note-:92-24) The bottom water accelerates as it travels from a depth of 3500 m to a depth around 400–700 m. The increase in current velocity exacerbates erosion revealing the Kuroshio Knoll, a 3 km × 7 km bean-shaped elevated flat area 60–70 m below surface levels in comparison to the rest of the Plateau which located at around 400–700 m.[[3]](#cite_note-:103-3) The Plateau is being uplifted and is balanced with erosion.[[3]](#cite_note-:103-3)

The [granulometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granulometry_(morphology) "Granulometry (morphology)") of the Kenting Plateau and surrounding area demonstrates the eroding qualities of the Kuroshio Current.[[24]](#cite_note-:92-24) The sediment grain size of the sand varies along the edge of the Plateau. The deeper down the edge, the larger the grains as smaller grains are swept away by the current. Some of these fine sand particles have settled into a dune field while the remaining sediment is transported and deposited throughout the region by the Kuroshio Current.[[3]](#cite_note-:103-3)

The Kuroshio Current also transports [Yangtze River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze "Yangtze") sediment. The amount of sediment transport is highly dependent on the relationship between the Kuroshio Current intrusion, the China Coastal Current, and the Taiwan Warm Current. The Yangtze River sediment is being deposited on the [East China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_China_Sea "East China Sea") inner shelf rather than the deep sea due to the interaction of the three currents.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Western_Boundary_Currents_-_The_Kuroshio_Current.jpg/250px-Western_Boundary_Currents_-_The_Kuroshio_Current.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Western_Boundary_Currents_-_The_Kuroshio_Current.jpg)

The Kuroshio Current, as idealized from space. The resulting circulation and eddying demonstrate the mixing caused by the input of warm equatorial water poleward. Image by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center.

Distinct elemental characteristics of sediments from differing sources permits tracking sources of sediments within the Kuroshio. Taiwanese sediment notably contains [illite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illite "Illite") and [chlorite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorite_group "Chlorite group"). These traceable compounds have been found all the way through the Kuroshio Current up into its branch through the Kuroshio Current Intrusion in the South China Sea.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The South China Sea branch of the Kuroshio and the cyclonic eddy west of [Luzon Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzon "Luzon") impact Luzon and [Pearl River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_River_Delta "Pearl River Delta") sediments. The Luzon sediment containing high levels of [smectite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clay_mineral "Clay mineral") is unable to travel northwestward. The Pearl River sediments contains high levels of [kaolinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite "Kaolinite") and [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium") (Ti) and is trapped above the abyssal basin between [Hainan Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hainan "Hainan") and the Pearl River mouth.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25) These compounds allow scientists to track sediment transport throughout the Kuroshio Current.

### Eddies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Eddies")]

There are indications that [eddies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_(fluid_dynamics) "Eddy (fluid dynamics)") contribute to the preservation and survival of fish larvae transported by the Kuroshio.[[27]](#cite_note-27) [Plankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plankton "Plankton") biomass fluctuates yearly and is typically highest in the eddy area of the Kuroshio's edge. Warm-core rings are not known for having high productivity. However, there is evidence of equal distribution of biological productivity throughout the warm-core rings from the Kuroshio Current, supported by the upwelling at the periphery and the [convective mixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection "Convection") caused by the cooling of surface water as the rings move north of the current. The [thermostad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermostad "Thermostad") is the deep [mixed layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_layer "Mixed layer") that has discrete boundaries and uniform temperature. Within this layer, nutrient-rich water is brought to the surface, which generates a burst of primary production. Given that the water in the core of a ring has a different temperature regime than the shelf waters, there are times when a warm-core ring is undergoing its [spring bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_bloom "Spring bloom") while the surrounding shelf waters are not.[[28]](#cite_note-:2-28)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Pacific_typhoon_tracks_1980-2005.jpg/250px-Pacific_typhoon_tracks_1980-2005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pacific_typhoon_tracks_1980-2005.jpg)

Western Pacific Ocean tropical cyclone tracks compiled from 1980 to 2005

There are many complex interactions within [warm-core rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warm_core_ring "Warm core ring") and thus, lifetime productivity is not very different from the surrounding shelf water. A study from 1998[[28]](#cite_note-:2-28) found that the primary productivity within a warm-core ring was almost the same as in the cold jet outside it, with evidence of upwelling of nutrients within the ring. In addition, there was discovery of dense populations of [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") at the nutricline within a ring, presumably supported by the upward mixing of nutrients.[[28]](#cite_note-:2-28) Furthermore, there have been [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustics "Acoustics") studies in the warm-core ring, which showed intense sound scattering from [zooplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zooplankton "Zooplankton") and fish populations in the ring and very sparse acoustic signals outside of it.

### Typhoons

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Typhoons")]

[Typhoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon "Typhoon") can produce intense winds which push on the surface layer of the ocean for brief periods of time. These winds induce the warmer surface layer of the ocean to mix with the deeper cooler layer of water that is situated below the [pycnocline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pycnocline "Pycnocline"). This mixing introduces nutrients from deeper cooler water to the warmer surface layer of the ocean.[[29]](#cite_note-29) Organisms such as [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") and [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae") use these newly introduced nutrients to grow. In 2003, two typhoons induced significant surface layer mixing as they passed through the region. This mixing directly produced two algal bloom events in the North Western Pacific Ocean that negatively affected Japan.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

## Nutrient transport

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Nutrient transport")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Nitrate_and_Phosphate_Pacific_Ocean.jpg/250px-Nitrate_and_Phosphate_Pacific_Ocean.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nitrate_and_Phosphate_Pacific_Ocean.jpg)

Annual average chlorophyll concentrations are shaded, and annual average surface (A) nitrate and (B) phosphate concentrations are contoured. The Kuroshio Current transports nitrate and phosphate from the South China Sea, increasing productivity.

The Kuroshio Current is considered a nutrient stream because of high nutrient flux from surrounding oligotrophic waters with [primary production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_production "Primary production") of 150 to 300 grams of carbon per square meter per year based on [SeaWiFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaWiFS "SeaWiFS") global primary productivity estimates. The current transports significant amounts of nutrients to support this primary production from the East China Sea continental shelf to the subarctic Pacific Ocean. The maximum [chlorophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorophyll "Chlorophyll") value is found around 100 metres (330 ft) depth.[[4]](#cite_note-Terazaki2-4) Its importance in nutrient transport is demonstrated by the nutrient rich water in the Kuroshio Current is surrounded by ambient water of the same density with lower relative nutrient levels. The downstream of the Kuroshio Current receives large amounts of nutrients at rates of 100–280 kmol N\*s-1.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Nutrients are brought to the surface water from deeper layers where the Kuroshio Current flows over shallow areas and seamounts. This process occurs over the [Okinawa Trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_Trough "Okinawa Trough") and the Tokara Strait.[[32]](#cite_note-:13-32) The Tokara Strait also has high cyclonic activity where the Kuroshio Current passes through. This in combination with the [Coriolis effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_Effect "Coriolis Effect") causes intense upwelling along the continental shelf.[[32]](#cite_note-:13-32) This upwelling and nutrient transport into surface layers is essential for primary production because these vital nutrients would otherwise be inaccessible to phytoplankton which need to remain in upper layers where sunlight is available for them to perform [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"). The constant transport of nutrient rich waters to regions with high levels of light therefore supports increased photosynthesis supporting the rest of the biologically diverse ecosystem associated with the Kuroshio current.

## Marine life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Marine life")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Spring_Bloom_Colors_the_Pacific_Near_Hokkaido.jpg/250px-Spring_Bloom_Colors_the_Pacific_Near_Hokkaido.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spring_Bloom_Colors_the_Pacific_Near_Hokkaido.jpg)

The [Oyashio Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyashio_Current "Oyashio Current") colliding with the Kuroshio Current near [Hokkaido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hokkaido "Hokkaido"). When two currents collide, they create [eddies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_(fluid_dynamics) "Eddy (fluid dynamics)"). [Phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") growing in the surface waters become concentrated along the boundaries of these eddies, tracing out the motions of the water.

The transportation of nutrients, heat and plankton by the Kuroshio Current and the current's transection of multiple different waterbodies gives way to high species richness in and adjacent to this current. In addition, the Kuroshio is classified as a [biodiversity hotspot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity_hotspot "Biodiversity hotspot"), meaning the waters circulating through the region are host to many different species, yet many of its resident organisms are at risk of becoming endangered or are already at the brink of extinction as a result of local and/or global human activity. Overfishing and overharvest are the primary risks for many of the [threatened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threatened_species "Threatened species") or [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered_species "Endangered species") species here.[[33]](#cite_note-:36-33)

### Photoautotrophs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Photoautotrophs")]

#### Phytoplankton

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Phytoplankton")]

[Phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") are responsible for the aforementioned high rates of primary productivity within the current. Warm sea surface temperatures and low turbidity in the region lead to clearer waters which allows for deeper penetration of sunlight and an extension of the epipelagic zone. These particular characteristics, along with lower nutrient availability within the current, correspond well with the requirements of two specific [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"): *[Prochlorococcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prochlorococcus "Prochlorococcus") and [Synechococcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synechococcus "Synechococcus")*.[[34]](#cite_note-:72-34) *Prochlorococcus* is the dominant species of picophytoplankton within the Kuroshio Current and these two species may be responsible for as much as half of the fixation of CO2 in the entire Kuroshio Current photic zone.[[34]](#cite_note-:72-34) Further, there are substantial dust deposition events in this region due to Asian Dust Storms from the Gobi desert.[[34]](#cite_note-:72-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35) During these events, dust clouds transport and deposit phosphate and trace metals which subsequently stimulate growth in both *Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus* as well as [diatoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatom "Diatom").[[34]](#cite_note-:72-34)

Diatoms and [Trichodesmium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichodesmium "Trichodesmium") are speculated to play an important role in the redistribution of nitrogen and carbon in and out of the euphotic zone. Trichodesmium is an abundant [diazotroph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diazotroph "Diazotroph") that directly correlates with overall nitrogen fixation within the current.[[36]](#cite_note-36) This nitrogen fixation supplies a limiting nutrient (nitrate), to other photoautotrophs for growth and reproduction. Meanwhile, in areas influenced by upwelling with higher nutrient and carbon concentrations, diatoms are important contributors to carbon and nitrogen out of the euphotic zone due to the weight of their "glass houses" made of silica and their tendencies to sink.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

#### Macro-flora

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Macro-flora")]

At least ten genera of seaweed reside in waters in and around the Kuroshio Current.[[33]](#cite_note-:36-33) *[Caulerpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caulerpa "Caulerpa")*, is a [green algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_algae "Green algae") that grows densely near shore on the periphery of the Kuroshio Current while [brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_algae "Brown algae") and [red algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_algae "Red algae") also flourish adjacent the current, and like other photosynthesizing organisms, benefit from the nutrient transport and low turbidity of the region.[[33]](#cite_note-:36-33)

### Invertebrates

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Invertebrates")]

#### Zooplankton

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Zooplankton")]

An increase in [zooplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zooplankton "Zooplankton") biomass occurs in the significantly lower water temperatures of the upwelling sites within the Kuroshio Current due to high phytoplankton concentrations which are nourished by upwelling northeast of Taiwan.[[38]](#cite_note-38) This upwelling event, the [Kuroshio Current intrusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuroshio_Current_Intrusion "Kuroshio Current Intrusion") through the Luzon Strait and [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"), and summer monsoons, represent the convergence of a multitude of oceanic waters of different origin.[[39]](#cite_note-39) These water convergence zones and subsequent circulation and mixing, have a major influence on the transport and distribution of many zooplankton species causing zooplankton communities to be more nutritious, unique and diverse.[[40]](#cite_note-40) High diversity in copepods in waters adjacent the Kuroshio Current have also been reported.[[41]](#cite_note-41) Two dominant copepod species of the current, *C. sinicus* and *E. concinna*, are transported northward in high concentrations by the current from the East China Sea in winter.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

Like copepods and diatoms, [tunicates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunicate "Tunicate"), specifically [salps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salp "Salp") and [doliolids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doliolida "Doliolida"), also play an important role on the biogeochemical cycle as well as on the food web in the Kuroshio.[[43]](#cite_note-:82-43) Salps transport carbon to the region's bottom water with their carbon-rich, fast-sinking fecal pellets and carcasses. [*Thaliaceans*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thaliacea "Thaliacea") (salps and doliolids) are known to feed a minimum of 202 marine species, however, these animal's blooms have been found to cause harmful feeding conditions for pelagic fishes in the region.[[43]](#cite_note-:82-43)

Many species of fish larvae are also found in zooplankton communities transported by the current. Fish larvae are important contributor to the Kuroshio Current system food chain. Baleen whales for instance, make use of the current's transport of Japanese sardine and jack mackerel larvae to their feeding grounds in the north pacific. Climate change is reported to alter endemic fish larvae distribution. A fish [species composition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_composition "Species composition") change analysis by Lu and Lee (2014) showed changes in fish larvae distribution have occurred during the region and suggest this altered clustering is associated with changes in the intensities and flow rates of the Kuroshio Current.[[44]](#cite_note-44) These changes impacts the food chain below and above this trophic level. This can influence fish migration, fish population's at large and major fisheries.

The Kuroshio Current has an influence of several species of [foraminifera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foraminifera "Foraminifera"), including species *G. ruber* and *P. obliquiloculate*. *G. ruber* is normally a surface dweller and was found at depths of 1000 meters along the Kuroshio Current. *P. obliquiloculate* normally resides between 25 and 100 m, yet was found deep in the abyssal basin (>1000 m).[[45]](#cite_note-:52-45) The distribution of these species in comparison to their standard dwelling depths observed by Gallagher (2015) demonstrates the ability of this intrusion and the overall Kuroshio Current's to redistribute nutrients vertically[[45]](#cite_note-:52-45) making nutrients available many different species with differing requirements for prosperity.

#### Coral

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Coral")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Acropora_hyacinthus%2C_NPS.jpg/250px-Acropora_hyacinthus%2C_NPS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Acropora_hyacinthus,_NPS.jpg)

*Acropora hyacinthus* is a reef-building coral native to coral reefs in the Kuroshio Current region.

The coral reefs within the Kuroshio Current reside at a higher latitude than any other tropical reef placement in the world (33.48°N).[[46]](#cite_note-46) An important reef-building coral to this area, [*Heliopora coerulea*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_coral "Blue coral"), has been listed as threatened due to anthropogenic stressors to its environment such as: warming sea surface temperatures from climate change, ocean acidification from anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and [dynamite fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast_fishing "Blast fishing").[[33]](#cite_note-:36-33) Studies confirming low genotypic diversity within the species further emphasizes this blue coral's threatened status.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

*[Acropora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropora "Acropora") japonica*, *[Acropora secale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropora_secale "Acropora secale")*, and *[Acropora hyacinthus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropora_hyacinthus "Acropora hyacinthus")* are 3 more reef-building corals in the region.[[48]](#cite_note-:17-48) These species utilize symbiotic relationships with zooxanthellae, [peridinin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peridinin "Peridinin") and pyrrhoxanthin, as a source of [carotenoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carotenoid "Carotenoid").[[48]](#cite_note-:17-48)

In addition to anthropogenic, threats, these corals also have predators in the region such as the [Crown-of-thorns starfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown-of-thorns_starfish "Crown-of-thorns starfish"), *Acanthaster planci*, and a regional sea snail, *[Drupella fragum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drupella_fragum "Drupella fragum")*.[[48]](#cite_note-:17-48) The Crown-of-thorns starfish feeds on corals. When conditions are favorable, the population of this native starfish can explode, resulting in significant damage on entire coral communities, as well as the ecosystems these coral reefs support. A Crown-of-thorns starfish outbreak in conjunction with anthropogenic stressors can cause irreversible reef-system damage.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)

The Kuroshio Current controls patterns of connectivity between coral reefs (as well as other marine organisms with a larval phase), transporting larvae from southerly coral reefs to downstream reefs along the Ryukyu Arc.[[51]](#cite_note-51)

#### Squid

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Squid")]

[Western boundary currents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_boundary_currents "Western boundary currents") are used by certain species of squid for rapid and easy transport, allowing mature squid to travel with minimum energy expenditure to exploit rich northern feeding grounds, while eggs and larvae develop in the warm current waters during winter. The [Japanese flying squid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_flying_squid "Japanese flying squid") (*Todarodes pacificus*), for example, has three populations that breed in winter, summer, and autumn. The winter spawning group is associated with the Kuroshio Current, because following spawning events in January to April in the [East China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_China_Sea "East China Sea") the larvae and juveniles travel north with the Kuroshio Current. They are turned inshore and are caught between the islands of [Honshu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honshu "Honshu") and [Hokkaido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hokkaido "Hokkaido") during the summer. The summer spawning is in another part of the East China Sea, from which the larvae are entrained into the [Tsushima current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsushima_Strait "Tsushima Strait") that flows north between the islands of Japan and the mainland. Afterward, the current meets a southward flowing cold coastal current, the Liman Current. The group of squid spawned in the summer are traditionally found around the boundary between the two currents, sustaining rich fisheries. In fact, studies have reported that annual catches in Japan have gradually increased since the late 1980s and it has been proposed that changing environmental conditions have caused the autumn and winter spawning areas in the Tsushima Strait and near the [Goto Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goto_Islands "Goto Islands") to overlap. In addition, winter spawning sites over the [continental shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_shelf "Continental shelf") and slope in the East China Sea are expanding.

### Vertebrates

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Vertebrates")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Darker_Colored_Parrot_Fish.jpg/250px-Darker_Colored_Parrot_Fish.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Darker_Colored_Parrot_Fish.jpg)

Parrotfish (*[Scarus frenatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarus_frenatus "Scarus frenatus")*) are reef fish commonly found in the Kuroshio Current reef systems.

#### Fish

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kuroshio_Current&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Fish")]

The Kuroshio Current is home to thousands of fish species occupying nutrient rich and diverse waters in this region. This expansive biomass is influenced by elevated rates of primary production leading to large biomass in the lower [trophic levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trophic_level "Trophic level"), facilitated by warmer local oceanic and atmospheric conditions. Resident fish of this area include reef fish like rabbitfish and parrotfish, pelagic fishes such as [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"), [anchovies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchovy "Anchovy"), [mackerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackerel "Mackerel"), and [sailfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sailfish "Sailfish"), and higher trophic predators such as [sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark").[[33]](#cite_note-:36-33)

Fisheries have a strong presence in this area and depend strongly on the changing oceanic conditions, largely dependent on the Kuroshio Current. To the north, the [Oyashio Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyashio_Current "Oyashio Current") contains [subarctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subarctic "Subarctic") water that is much colder and fresher than the resident water east of Honshu, and the intersection of these two currents is called the Kuroshio-Oyashio region. Here, local oceanographic conditions vary through the year and determine the species assemblage and thus the success of fisheries. For example, when the Oyashio current is well developed and protrudes southward, the cold waters are favorable for capturing sardines. The Wikipedia article on the Kuroshio Current (黒潮, "Black Stream"), also known as the Black Current or Japan Current, describes it as a north-flowing, warm ocean current on the west side of the North Pacific Ocean basin. Named for its deep blue waters, it is analogous to the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic and serves as the western boundary current of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre. Off the east coast of Japan, it merges with the Oyashio Current to form the North Pacific Current.

HISTORY: The current was discovered in 1565 by Andrés de Urdaneta during his voyage from Cebu (Philippines) to California, which opened the "tornaviaje" route and gave Spain hegemony over the Pacific via the Manila galleon trade. Europeans knew of it as early as 1650 from a map by Bernhardus Varenius, and Captain J. King noted it during Captain James Cook's expedition. Historians have debated its role in structuring Japan's economic geography, including fisheries, whaling, and maritime routes.

PHYSICAL PROPERTIES: The Kuroshio has an annual average sea-surface temperature of about 24°C (75°F), is approximately 100 km wide, and produces frequent small to meso-scale eddies. It originates from the Pacific North Equatorial Current, splits at Luzon (Philippines), enters the East China Sea via the Yonaguni Depression east of Taiwan, is steered by the Okinawa Trough, re-enters the Pacific through the Tokara Strait, flows along southern Japan, and separates at the Bōsō Peninsula as the Kuroshio Extension. Its branch into the Sea of Japan is the Tsushima Current. Transport is ~25 Sv in the Sea of Japan and reaches 65 Sv southeast of Japan, with significant seasonal variability. The warm waters sustain the northernmost coral reefs in the world (at 33.48°N). The current creates warm surface temperatures and moisture that fuel typhoons—the Western North Pacific averages about 25 typhoons annually, mostly July–October. Regarding the geologic past, there is conflicting evidence about whether lower sea levels prevented the Kuroshio from entering the Sea of Japan during the last glacial period.

SEDIMENT TRANSPORT: The current causes deep-sea erosion, notably on the Kenting Plateau offshore Southern Taiwan, where accelerating bottom currents (from 3500m to 400-700m depth) erode sediment and reveal the Kuroshio Knoll. Sediment grain sizes increase with depth as fine particles are swept away. The current also transports Yangtze River sediment, with deposition controlled by the interaction of the Kuroshio intrusion, China Coastal Current, and Taiwan Warm Current. Distinct elemental tracers (illite, chlorite from Taiwan; smectite from Luzon; kaolinite and titanium from the Pearl River) allow tracking of sediment sources.

EDDIES & TYPHOONS: Eddies contribute to fish larvae survival. Warm-core rings show productivity comparable to surrounding shelf waters, with nutrient upwelling at perimeters and deep convective mixing via thermostads. A 1998 study found primary productivity within a warm-core ring was nearly equal to the cold jet outside it. Typhoon-induced mixing brings nutrients to surface layers; two typhoons in 2003 produced two algal bloom events in the NW Pacific that negatively affected Japan.

NUTRIENT TRANSPORT: The Kuroshio is a "nutrient stream" with primary production of 150-300 grams of carbon per square meter per year. Maximum chlorophyll occurs around 100m depth. Downstream receives nutrients at rates of 100-280 kmol N·s⁻¹. Upwelling over the Okinawa Trough and Tokara Strait (with Coriolis-driven cyclonic activity) brings deep nutrients to surface layers, essential for phytoplankton photosynthesis.

MARINE LIFE: The region is a biodiversity hotspot but many species are threatened by overfishing/overharvest. Phytoplankton: Prochlorococcus dominates picophytoplankton; with Synechococcus, they may fix half of CO2 in the photic zone. Dust deposition from Gobi desert storms stimulates growth. Trichodesmium (a diazotroph) correlates with nitrogen fixation. Ten genera of seaweed reside in the region. Zooplankton: Copepod species C. sinicus and E. concinna are transported northward from the East China Sea. Tunicates (salps and doliolids) transport carbon to bottom waters and feed at least 202 marine species. Coral: Heliopora coerulea is threatened by warming, acidification, and dynamite fishing; Acropora japonica, A. secale, and A. hyacinthus are key reef-builders using zooxanthellae symbioses. Crown-of-thorns starfish and Drupella fragum prey on corals. The current connects coral reefs via larval transport along the Ryukyu Arc. Squid: Japanese flying squid (Todarodes pacificus) has winter-spawning populations associated with the Kuroshio; expanding spawning areas in the East China Sea have contributed to increased annual catches in Japan since the late 1980s. Fish: Thousands of species including reef fish (rabbitfish, parrotfish), pelagic fish (sardines, anchovies, mackerel, sailfish), and sharks. The Kuroshio-Oyashio intersection region supports major fisheries whose success depends on oceanographic conditions varying through the year.

# Projecting the shift of chub mackerel spawning grounds from climate change in the Western North Pacific Ocean

[![Responsible Seafood Advocate logo](https://www.globalseafood.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/RSA-logo.svg)](/advocate/)

Sukgeun Jung, Ph.D.

## Spawning grounds of chub mackerel shifting northward due to ocean warming driven by climate change

![mackerel](https://www.globalseafood.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/JUNG-mackerel_1500.png)

Study projected the shift of chub mackerel spawning grounds in the Western North Pacific Ocean. Results showed the spawning grounds of this fish species shifting northward due to ocean warming driven by climate change; the data will be useful for estimating and predicting distributions of chub mackerel during early life stages, and its subsequent exploitable abundance and fisheries production. Photo by Brian Gratwicke from DC, USA (CC BY 2.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) are forage fish that play a crucial role in the transfer of energy within marine food webs, serving as the primary food source for various marine predators and feeding on zooplankton and phytoplankton. This species is [**widely distributed**](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-008-0015-7) in the western North Pacific with two stocks, namely the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock in the East China Sea (ECS), Yellow Sea (YS), and Japan/East Sea (JES), and the Pacific stock along the Pacific coast.

The TWC stock is an [**economically valuable fishery**](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626) that is exploited by various countries, including China, Korea, and Japan. From February to June, the [**TWC stock spawns**](https://doi.org/10.1577/M07-063.1) mainly in the ECS and Korea Strait (KS), after which it migrates to its northern feeding grounds in the JES and YS through the KS [6,11,12,13,14].

Variations in the environmental conditions of spawning grounds caused by climate change can cause changes in the physiochemistry of spawners and food availability during the early life stages of fish, and these alterations have [**implications**](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps13037) for spawning behavior, growth, and survival rates, as well as for recruitment strength and fluctuations in the abundance of fish. Changes in the marine environment can result in shifts in spawning ground locations and conditions for chub mackerel, driving subsequent changes in the spatial distribution and survival of hatched eggs and larvae.

Spawning ground locations may shift due to climate change and subsequent variations in the marine environment, as chub mackerel must spawn under conditions that are both environmentally and geographically suitable. However, few studies have aimed to project shifts in the spawning grounds of chub mackerel driven by climate change.

[![Ad for [membership]](https://www.globalseafood.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/membership_web2025_1050x125.gif)](https://www.globalseafood.org/membership/)

This article – [**summarized**](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) from the [**original publication**](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes10010020) [Go, S. et al. 2025. Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean. *Fishes* 2025, 10(1), 20] – evaluated and projected the effects of climate-driven changes in ocean circulation and water temperature on the potential spawning ground of the TWC stock of chub mackerel.

> [‘They need a good reason to stay’: How one coalition may break a decade of deadlock in the North Atlantic mackerel fishery](https://www.globalseafood.org/advocate/they-need-a-good-reason-to-stay-how-one-coalition-may-break-a-decade-of-deadlock-in-the-north-atlantic-mackerel-fishery/)

## Study setup

We developed spawning ground indices for chub mackerel and tested whether potential spawning grounds will shift under a climate change scenario published by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). To identify potential spawning grounds, we estimated and projected water temperature and salinity at a depth of 10 m in the western North Pacific Ocean. We also derived water temperature and salinity for the 2010s (2010–2019) and 2050s (2050–2059) with an ocean circulation model based on a scenario of the [**IPCC Fifth Assessment Report**](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar5/wg2/) (IPCC AR5).

To construct the regional ocean circulation model, we utilized the [**Regional Ocean Modeling System**](https://www.myroms.org/) (ROMS). Additionally, this model incorporates detailed governing equations that address momentum, continuity, temperature, and salinity transport, allowing for a comprehensive representation of oceanic processes. The model’s accuracy has been validated through comparisons with observational data, ensuring reliable simulations that capture both large-scale and finer oceanic features.

The model was designed to simulate ocean conditions from 2010 to 2059 under climate change conditions based on the projections of IPCC AR5. In sum, this multi-layered approach combining global and regional data with atmospheric and tidal forces allowed us to simulate the complex oceanic conditions surrounding Korea with a high degree of precision, capturing both the broad effects of climate change and local ocean dynamics.

For detailed information on the data and modeling used, refer to the original publication.

## Results and discussion

The [**spawning ground of the TWC stock**](https://doi.org/10.1577/M07-063.1) has been reported to extend from the southern part of the ECS to the southwestern part of the JES. The spawning grounds previously reported by several researchers, along with our own results, suggest that the spawning grounds extend northward from the southern ECS in February to the southern JES in June, with possible extension to the waters off Vladivostok and Hokkaido after June.

Our model was used to estimate and project potential spawning grounds from February to June for both the 2010s and 2050s. Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to 2050s, and these suggested that chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s compared to the 2010s, which means that spawning will become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current. This shift in spawning grounds [**will affect chub mackerel survival and growth**](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12601-020-0004-z) during early life stages and in nursery grounds, as their weak swimming ability during the early life stages limits movement toward favorable habitat.

![mackerel](https://www.globalseafood.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/JUNG-Fig-1_1500.jpg)

Fig. 1: Predicted water temperature and salinity at 10 meters depth for (a) the 2010s and (b) 2050s, and (c) their differences. Adapted from the original.

[**Li et al.**](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chnaes.2013.06.001) proposed that the main nursery ground of the TWC stock would shift longitudinally westward from the Pacific side of Japan and the Japan/East Sea (JES) to the waters off Jeju Island if the spawning grounds shifted and the influence of the Kuroshio Current weakened. Therefore, we expect that the spawning grounds of the TWC stock will shift northward in the 2050s relative to the 2010s, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of the nursery grounds. Driven by these changes, the ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production will increase in the Korean Straits (KS) and the Yellow Sea (YS) relative to the JES.

Our spawning grounds data predicted spatiotemporal changes in the potential spawning ground of the TWC stock using the ROMS. Our model outcomes were generally compatible with previous observations and modeling studies in the region, and the differences were explainable. This compatibility suggests that our method can be applied to the estimation of potential spawning grounds for other stocks or species, provided that sufficient research is available on their spawning characteristics and the marine environment of the area.

![](https://www.globalseafood.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/JUNG-Fig-2_1500.png)

Fig. 2: Monthly potential spawning grounds of chub mackerel averaged for (a) the 2010s and (b) 2050s, as well as (c) differences between the two periods predicted using the spawning ground index based on the ocean circulation model. Adapted from the original.

Results diagnosed the regional ocean circulation model for the western North Pacific using two methods and found that, while the model results did not align well with observations in the same space and time, the overall trends were significantly similar. To improve the model’s accuracy, data assimilation methods should be applied in future studies.

Although it was assumed that the spawning period would not change, the main spawning period may shift due to the environmental changes, even at the same spawning location. For example, past studies have reported that [**photoperiod influences gonad development**](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes8020077), suggesting that the spawning period may be influenced by changes in the annual photoperiod driven by climate change, and this possibility requires further exploration in the near future.

In this study, we calculated spawning grounds under the assumption that the spawning area of the TWC stock is located within the continental shelf areas of the ECS, YS and JES where depths are 50 to 300 meters. However, other researchers reported collecting chub mackerel larvae in Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait, which included shallow areas of <50 meters, suggesting that chub mackerel may spawn in shallow coastal areas. Results of this study demonstrate that the spawning grounds of chub mackerel could extend into the YS and northern JES.

To improve the reliability of the present study regarding chub mackerel spawning grounds, and migration from the southern East China Sea (ECS) to the northern JES, international cooperative surveys and research are required in the region, which would comprehensively elucidate the distribution of mackerel eggs and adults. Although chub mackerel are reported to spawn generally within a 25 meters depth, this study considered only 10 meters depth environmental conditions to estimate and project the potential spawning grounds. And it used water temperature and salinity as ambient oceanographic variables to predict the spawning grounds of chub mackerel. Environmental conditions of other depths or other marine environmental conditions (such as turbulence, currents and dissolved oxygen) may influence spawning conditions, and these factors require further research.

Overall, results project changes in the distribution of catchable chub mackerel in the 2050s relative to the 2010s simply by using a climate change scenario and subsequent changes in potential spawning grounds. Further detailed projections, in particular ongoing development of individual-based models covering all life stages of chub mackerel, are expected to validate and extend the projections of the present study. The results of this study are expected to contribute to the development of bio-physical coupled, individual-based models for predicting the recruitment and spatiotemporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel based on simulation of three-dimensional coordinates consisting of the location, size, and abundance of each super-individual, whose initial abundance, growth, and mortality vary with ambient oceanic conditions.

## Perspectives

This research estimated potential spawning grounds for chub mackerel in the western North Pacific Ocean using the newly developed spawning ground index. Our model projected that increased regional surface water temperatures in the 2050s due to global warming will cause a northward shift of the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel. The distribution of chub mackerel at early-life stages observed in the East China Sea (ECS) and the Korea Strait (KS) was consistent with our model outputs, except for the waters off Jeju Island, and the spawning grounds of chub mackerel suggested in previous studies were compatible with our model results.

This study will enhance the reliability of stock assessment for fisheries management of chub mackerel and contribute to the development of individual-based models for exploitable chub mackerel as well as fisheries policies accounting for climate change in the region.

This article from the Global Seafood Alliance's Responsible Seafood Advocate, authored by Sukgeun Jung, Ph.D. (Jeju National University, Republic of Korea), summarizes a study published in Fishes (2025, 10(1), 20) by Go, S. et al. that projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Western North Pacific Ocean.

**Key background:** Chub mackerel are forage fish crucial to marine food webs, feeding on zooplankton/phytoplankton and serving as prey for larger marine predators. The Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock is an economically valuable fishery exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the East China Sea (ECS) and Korea Strait (KS) from February to June before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the Japan/East Sea (JES) and Yellow Sea (YS).

**Study methodology:** Researchers developed spawning ground indices and used the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to estimate and project water temperature and salinity at 10 meters depth in the western North Pacific. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010 to 2059 under an IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (IPCC AR5) climate change scenario, comparing the 2010s (2010–2019) and 2050s (2050–2059) periods.

**Key findings:**
- Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to the 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s and become less influenced by the Kuroshio Current.
- This northward shift is expected to cause a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds (from the Pacific side of Japan and JES toward waters off Jeju Island), consistent with earlier work by Li et al.
- Ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production are expected to increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the JES.
- Model outputs were generally compatible with previous observations, though the model did not perfectly align with observational data in the same space and time; data assimilation methods were suggested for future improvements.
- Spawning grounds were assumed to be limited to continental shelf areas (50–300 meters depth), though other research suggests chub mackerel may also spawn in shallower coastal areas (<50 meters), including Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait.
- The study only considered environmental conditions at 10 meters depth and used only temperature and salinity variables; other factors (turbulence, currents, dissolved oxygen) and photoperiod influences on spawning periods require further research.

**Conclusions:** The study enhances the reliability of stock assessment for fisheries management of chub mackerel and contributes to the development of individual-based bio-physical coupled models for predicting recruitment and spatiotemporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel. The results are expected to inform fisheries policies accounting for climate change in the region.

## Abstract

The Kuroshio south of Japan exhibits bimodal variations between large meander (LM) and non-LM paths. The Kuroshio LM drastically changes the distribution of currents and water temperature in the surface and subsurface layers, affecting atmospheric conditions, marine ecosystems, and fisheries resources. The most recent Kuroshio LM event occurred in August 2017 and is still continuing as of March 2025 (LM2017). Through studies of the long-lived LM2017, many new insights into the Kuroshio LM and its impact have been gained in recent years. This study aims to organize and share our current understanding of the Kuroshio LM and its impacts by reviewing past and present studies. Future directions for research on the Kuroshio LM and its impacts are also presented. This review advances the literature by covering not only the oceanic dynamics of the Kuroshio LM, but also its impacts on ocean conditions, atmospheric phenomena, lower ecosystems, and fisheries resources, thereby presenting the first attempt at such a comprehensive review of the Kuroshio LM.

## 1 Introduction

The Kuroshio, which is the western boundary current (WBC) of the wind-driven subtropical gyre in the North Pacific, transports large amounts of heat, salt, and biogeochemical materials to the north (Kida et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR36 "Kida S, Mitsudera H, Aoki S, Guo X, Ito SI, Kobashi F, Komori N, Kubokawa A, Miyama T, Morie R, Nakamura H (2015) Oceanic fronts and jets around Japan: a review. J Oceanogr 71:469–497. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-015-0283-7
                  
                "); Saito [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR84 "Saito H (2019) The Kuroshio: its recognition, scientific activities and emerging issues. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 1–11")). This transport has various impacts on oceanic conditions, atmosphere, marine ecosystems, and fisheries resources.

The Kuroshio originates from the northern branch of the North Equatorial Current of the Philippines, flows northward east of Taiwan, and proceeds northeastward along a steep continental slope in the East China Sea (Qiu [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR78 "Qiu B (2019) Kuroshio and Oyashio currents. In: Cochran JK, Bokuniewicz H, Yager P (eds) Encyclopedia of ocean sciences, 3rd edn. Academic Press, Cambridge, pp 384–394")). After passing through the Tokara Strait, south of Kyushu, it enters the deep Shikoku Basin. Around 140°E, the Kuroshio encounters the meridionally oriented Izu Ridge and exits the Shikoku Basin either through a deep channel around 34°N or through a relatively deep part south of Hachijojima Island (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig1)). After passing through the Izu Ridge, it enters the North Pacific Basin as a free jet called the Kuroshio Extension (KE).

**Fig.1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs10872-025-00753-z/MediaObjects/10872_2025_753_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z/figures/1)

Three typical paths of the Kuroshio south of Japan proposed by Kawabe ([1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR32 "Kawabe M (1995) Variations of current path, velocity, and volume transport of the Kuroshio in relation with the large meander. J Phys Oceanogr 25:3103–3117. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1995)025%3c3103:VOCPVA%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                ")): large meander (LM), offshore non-LM (oNLM), and nearshore NLM (nNLM) paths. Shading indicates ocean bathymetry based on the 2-min gridded elevation/bathymetry of the National Geophysical Data Center for the world (ETOPO2) (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR65 "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (2006) 2-minute Gridded Global Relief Data (ETOPO2) v2. NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. 
                  https://doi.org/10.7289/V5J1012Q
                  
                ")). Geographic names used in Sects.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec1)–[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec7) are also shown

Because of the topographic constraints in the Shikoku Basin, inflow and outflow locations are restricted to specific points in the Tokara Strait and the Izu Ridge, and the Kuroshio south of Japan is known to exhibit bimodal path fluctuations between the large meander (LM) and non-LM (NLM) paths (Masuda [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR51 "Masuda A (1982) An interpretation of the bimodal character of the stable Kuroshio path. Deep-Sea Res 29:471–484. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/0198-0149(82)90071-1
                  
                "); Kawabe [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR32 "Kawabe M (1995) Variations of current path, velocity, and volume transport of the Kuroshio in relation with the large meander. J Phys Oceanogr 25:3103–3117. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1995)025%3c3103:VOCPVA%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                ")); the NLM path can be further classified into two types: offshore NLM (oNLM) and nearshore NLM (nNLM). This bimodal feature, particularly the existence of the LM, is unique to the Kuroshio and is not observed in other WBCs. The LM and NLM paths can persist for a year to a decade (Kawabe [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR30 "Kawabe M (1987) Spectral properties of sea level and time scale of Kuroshio path variations. J Oceanogr Soc Jpn 43:111–123. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02111887
                  
                ")). In contrast, their path transition occurs on time scales of several months (Kawabe [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR32 "Kawabe M (1995) Variations of current path, velocity, and volume transport of the Kuroshio in relation with the large meander. J Phys Oceanogr 25:3103–3117. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1995)025%3c3103:VOCPVA%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                ")). The LM path forms because of a transition from the nNLM path. This is typically triggered by a small meander that first appears southeast of Kyushu (Shoji [1972](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR91 "Shoji D (1972) Time variation of the Kuroshio south of Japan. In: Stommel H, Yoshida K (eds) Kuroshio—its physical aspects. University of Tokyo Press, Tokyo, pp 217–234"); Yamashiro and Kawabe [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR117 "Yamashiro T, Kawabe M (1996) Monitoring of position of the Kuroshio axis in the Tokara Strait using sea level data. J Oceanogr 52:675–687. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02239459
                  
                "), [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR118 "Yamashiro T, Kawabe M (2002) Variations of the Kuroshio axis south of kyushu in relation to the large Meander of the Kuroshio. J Oceanogr 58:487–503. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1021265315858
                  
                ")). The meander grows while moving eastward, and develops into an LM path. According to the criteria for determining the LM path proposed by Yoshida et al. ([2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR125 "Yoshida T, Shimohira Y, Rinno H, Yokouchi K, Akiyama H (2006) Criteria for the determination of a large meander of the Kuroshio based on its path information. Oceanogr Jpn 15:499–507. 
                  https://kaiyo-gakkai.jp/jos/uminokenkyu/vol15/15-6/KJ00004389990.pdf
                  
                . Accessed 29 November 2024 (in Japanese with English abstract)")), the southernmost latitude of the Kuroshio axis off Enshu-nada is located south of 32°N, with a minor sea level difference and minimal variability between Kishimoto and Uragami; accordingly, six LMs have been observed since 1965 (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig2)). The most recent LM event began in August 2017 (LM2017), and is ongoing as of March 2025. The duration of LM2017 has exceeded seven years, which is the longest on record (Qiu et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR83 "Qiu B, Chen S, Oka E (2023) Why did the 2017 Kuroshio large meander become the longest in the past 70 years? Geophys Res Lett 50:e2023GL103548. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL103548
                  
                ")).

Owing to the unique features of the Kuroshio, its path variations have been extensively studied. Early modeling (e.g., Chao [1984](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR5 "Chao SY (1984) Bimodality of the Kuroshio. J Phys Oceanogr 14:92–103. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1984)014%3c0092:BOTK%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                "); Yasuda et al. [1985](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR120 "Yasuda I, Yoon JH, Suginohara N (1985) Dynamics of the Kuroshio large meander-barotropic model. J Oceanogr Soc Jpn 48:259–273. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02109275
                  
                "); Yoon and Yasuda [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR123 "Yoon JH, Yasuda I (1987) Dynamics of the Kuroshio large meander: two-layer model. J Phys Oceanogr 17:66–81. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1987)017%3c0066:DOTKLM%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                ")) and theoretical studies (e.g., Masuda [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR51 "Masuda A (1982) An interpretation of the bimodal character of the stable Kuroshio path. Deep-Sea Res 29:471–484. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/0198-0149(82)90071-1
                  
                ")) aimed to understand the bimodality of the Kuroshio path south of Japan. An important suggestion from these studies is that the LM path should be understood as a stationary Rossby wave with a wavelength scaled by the square root of the current velocity (White and McCreary [1976](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR113 "White WB, McCreary JP (1976) On the formation of the Kuroshio meander and its relationship to the large-scale ocean circulation. Deep-Sea Res 23:33–47. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/0011-7471(76)90806-8
                  
                ")). Accordingly, in addition to the above modeling studies, observational studies have investigated the relationship between bimodality and Kuroshio transport (e.g., Nitani [1975](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR69 "Nitani H (1975) Variation of the Kuroshio south of Japan. J Oceanogr Soc Jpn 31:154–173. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02107107
                  
                "); Kawabe [1980](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR29 "Kawabe M (1980) Sea level variations around the Nansei Islands and the large meander in the Kuroshio south of central Japan. J Oceanogr Soc Jpn 36:227–235. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02070336
                  
                "), [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR32 "Kawabe M (1995) Variations of current path, velocity, and volume transport of the Kuroshio in relation with the large meander. J Phys Oceanogr 25:3103–3117. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(1995)025%3c3103:VOCPVA%3e2.0.CO;2
                  
                ")). Since the launch of satellite altimetry in the early 1990s, the importance of mesoscale eddies in the Kuroshio path variations has been widely recognized. Modeling studies have also been directed toward the path transition mechanism, focusing on the eddy–Kuroshio interaction using high-resolution models. In the 2010s, advancements in high-resolution ocean models and supercomputing capabilities enabled long-term simulations at eddy-resolving resolutions, leading to a deeper understanding of the long-term variability of the Kuroshio and its relation to large-scale circulation variability. A comprehensive review of research on the Kuroshio path variability in the 2000s and the 2010s can be found in Usui ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR108 "Usui N (2019) Progress of studies on Kuroshio path variations south of Japan in the past decade. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 147–161")). In addition, new findings have been accumulated since the occurrence of the historically long-lived LM2017.

The impacts of Kuroshio path variations, especially the Kuroshio LM, on oceanic conditions, the atmosphere, marine ecosystems, and fisheries resources have also been studied extensively. The current velocity of the Kuroshio has a subsurface maximum (> 1 m s–1); its vertical structure extends down to approximately 1000 m (Kida et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR36 "Kida S, Mitsudera H, Aoki S, Guo X, Ito SI, Kobashi F, Komori N, Kubokawa A, Miyama T, Morie R, Nakamura H (2015) Oceanic fronts and jets around Japan: a review. J Oceanogr 71:469–497. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-015-0283-7
                  
                ")) and the net volume transport is approximately 42 Sv (Imawaki et al. [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR23 "Imawaki S, Uchida H, Ichikawa H, Fukasawa M, Umatani S, the ASUKA Group (2001) Satellite altimeter monitoring the Kuroshio transport south of Japan. Geophys Res Lett 28:17–20. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2000GL011796
                  
                ")). The Kuroshio is accompanied by a large horizontal sea surface height (SSH) gradient owing to its deep structure (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig3)a). Additionally, this is accompanied by a large horizontal temperature gradient in the ocean’s surface and subsurface layers (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig3)b). As such, the Kuroshio LM has various impacts on oceanic conditions, such as coastal sea level, coastal circulation, and water temperature and mass distributions.
