The Kuroshio region and its adjacent areas are known spawning and nursery grounds for various fish species; thus, the impacts of the Kuroshio on marine ecosystems and fisheries resources have also been an important target of Kuroshio studies. Although the surface waters south of the Kuroshio main stream are oligotrophic with low nutrient concentrations, phytoplankton biomass, and primary production (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig3)d), the Kuroshio transports nutrient-rich water below the euphotic zone (Guo et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR12 "Guo X, Zhu XH, Wu QS, Huang D (2012) The Kuroshio nutrient stream and its temporal variation in the East China Sea. J Geophys Res Oceans 117:C01026. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2011JC007292
                  
                "); Komatsu and Hiroe [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR40 "Komatsu K, Hiroe Y (2019) Structure and impact of the Kuroshio nutrient stream. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 85–104")). The nutrient transport by a WBC is known as the nutrient stream, which was originally identified in the Gulf Stream (Pelegrí and Csanady [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR77 "Pelegrí JL, Csanady GT (1991) Nutrient transport and mixing in the Gulf Stream. J Geophys Res Oceans 96:2577–2583. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/90JC02535
                  
                ")). Because only nutrients transported into the euphotic zone can be used for primary production, observational and modeling studies have been conducted to elucidate where and how nutrient-rich water is supplied to the euphotic zone (e.g., Nagai et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR55 "Nagai T, Tandon A, Yamazaki H, Doubell MJ (2009) Evidence of enhanced turbulent dissipation in the frontogenetic Kuroshio Front thermocline. Geophys Res Lett 36:L12609. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2009GL038832
                  
                "); Kaneko et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR27 "Kaneko H, Yasuda I, Komatsu K, Itoh S (2013) Observations of vertical turbulent nitrate flux across the Kuroshio. Geophys Res Lett 40:3123–3127. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/grl.50613
                  
                "); Uchiyama et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR107 "Uchiyama Y, Suzue Y, Yamazaki H (2017) Eddy-driven nutrient transport and associated upper-ocean primary production along the Kuroshio. J Geophys Res Oceans 122:5046–5062. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/2017JC012847
                  
                ")). Recent studies on the physical, chemical, and biological aspects of the Kuroshio nutrient stream have been summarized by Nagai et al. ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR56 "Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (2019) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken")). Therefore, this study focuses on studies on the impacts of the Kuroshio LM on lower trophic marine ecosystems and fisheries resources. The impact of LMs on fisheries resources has been extensively studied (e.g., Ogawa and Wakabayashi [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR72 "Ogawa Y, Wakabayashi K (1992) Changes in hydrographic conditions in relation to the Kuroshio meanders and their influence on fishery resources. Bull Natl Res Inst Fish Sci 4:71–89. 
                  https://agriknowledge.affrc.go.jp/RN/2010500439.pdf
                  
                . Accessed 29 November 2024 (in Japanese with English abstract)"); Kusaka et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR46 "Kusaka A et al (2021) Influence of Kuroshio large meander on the oceanographic conditions and fisheries in the coastal area off the Pacific coast of Honshu Island, Japan. Fish Biol Oceanogr Kuroshio 22:1–5. 
                  https://agriknowledge.affrc.go.jp/RN/2010937248.pdf
                  
                . Accessed 29 November 2024 (in Japanese)"); Kusaka and Setou [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR45 "Kusaka A, Setou T (2022) Influence of Kuroshio Large Meander on the oceanographic conditions and fisheries in the coastal area off the Kanto-Tokai, Japan. Kaiyo Mon 54:10–14. 
                  https://kaiyo-chikyu-s.com/gekkann-kaiyo/
                  
                 (in Japanese)")). Most previous studies have investigated the impact on specific fishery species owing to oceanic changes associated with specific LM events. Thus, the findings of previous studies should be summarized to provide integrated insight into the impacts of LM on fisheries resources.

The purpose of this review is to organize and share our current understanding of the Kuroshio LM and its various impacts by reviewing past and present studies. For the LM studies, we focus on the similarity and uniqueness of LM2017 to previous events. Given that the oceanic dynamics of the Kuroshio LM have been comprehensively reviewed by Usui ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR108 "Usui N (2019) Progress of studies on Kuroshio path variations south of Japan in the past decade. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 147–161")), this topic will not be discussed further in the present review. Moreover, we review the impacts of LMs on oceanic conditions, atmospheric phenomena, lower trophic marine ecosystems, and fisheries resources. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec2) presents the similarities and uniqueness of LM2017 with previous events. Section[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec3) reviews LM impact studies for ocean conditions, Sect.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec7) for atmospheric phenomena, and Sect.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec11) for lower trophic marine ecosystems and fisheries resources. Finally, Sect.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec16) presents a summary and the future research directions.

## 2 Overview of the most recent Kuroshio LM

As mentioned in Sect.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec1), the most recent Kuroshio LM event, LM2017, began in August 2017 and is ongoing. In this section, we present the similarity and uniqueness of LM2017 to previous events with reference to Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4), which shows the sequence of formation, development, and maintenance of LM2017.

**Fig.4**

LM2017 began as a small meander (also known as a trigger meander) of the Kuroshio that occurred southeast of Kyushu (marked A in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)a–c) (Usui [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR108 "Usui N (2019) Progress of studies on Kuroshio path variations south of Japan in the past decade. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR58 "Nagano A, Yamashita Y, Ariyoshi K, Hasegawa T, Matsumoto H, Shinohara M (2021) Seafloor pressure change excited at the northwest corner of the Shikoku Basin by the formation of the Kuroshio large-meander in September 2017. Thereafter, the small meander moved eastward and developed after passing through the Kii Peninsula, forming the Kuroshio LM (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)a–c). Nagano et al. ([2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR58 "Nagano A, Yamashita Y, Ariyoshi K, Hasegawa T, Matsumoto H, Shinohara M (2021) Seafloor pressure change excited at the northwest corner of the Shikoku Basin by the formation of the Kuroshio large-meander in September 2017. Usui et al. ([2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR110 "Usui N, Tsujino H, Nakano H, Matsumoto S (2013) Long-term variability of the Kuroshio path south of Japan. J Oceanogr 69:647–670. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-013-0197-1
                  
                ")) proposed three favorable factors for LM formation: (1) positive SSH anomalies (anticyclonic eddies) east of Taiwan, (2) the westward propagation of negative SSH anomalies (cyclonic eddies) in the Kuroshio region, and (3) a stable KE state. The first and second factors, which are related to the formation of the small meander of the Kuroshio southeast of Kyushu and its subsequent development, were fulfilled at the time of the occurrence of LM2017 (Usui [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR108 "Usui N (2019) Progress of studies on Kuroshio path variations south of Japan in the past decade. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 147–161"); Qiu et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR82 "Qiu B, Chen S, Schneider N, Oka E, Sugimoto S (2020) On reset of the wind-forced decadal Kuroshio Extension variability in late 2017. J Clim 33:10813–10828. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-20-0237.1
                  
                "); Qiu and Chen [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR81 "Qiu B, Chen S (2021) Revisit of the occurrence of the Kuroshio large meander south of Japan. J Phys Oceanogr 51:3679–3694. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO-D-21-0167.1
                  
                ")). The third factor is related to the position of the Kuroshio axis over the Izu Ridge. As outlined in the introduction, the LM path typically transitions from the nNLM path, with both the LM and nNLM paths passing through the deep channel of the Izu Ridge at approximately 34°N (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig1)). This implies that, for an LM to occur, the Kuroshio axis over the Izu Ridge must remain over the deep channel near 34°N prior to LM formation. This condition is generally achieved during the stable KE state (Qiu and Chen [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR79 "Qiu B, Chen S (2005) Variability of the Kuroshio Extension jet, recirculation gyre and mesoscale eddies on decadal timescales. J Phys Oceanogr 35:2090–2103. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO2807.1
                  
                "); Sugimoto and Hanawa [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR95 "Sugimoto S, Hanawa K (2012) Relationship between the path of the Kuroshio in the south of Japan and the path of the Kuroshio extension in the east. J Oceanogr 68:219–225. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-011-0089-1
                  
                "); Usui et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR110 "Usui N, Tsujino H, Nakano H, Matsumoto S (2013) Long-term variability of the Kuroshio path south of Japan. J Oceanogr 69:647–670. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-013-0197-1
                  
                ")). However, during the formation phase of LM2017, the KE was in an unstable state, and the Kuroshio followed the oNLM path (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)a, b) (Nagano et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR57 "Nagano A, Yamashita Y, Hasegawa T, Ariyoshi K, Matsumoto H, Shinohara M (2019) Characteristics of an atypical large-meander path of the Kuroshio current south of Japan formed in September 2017. Mar Geophys Res 40:525–539. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11001-018-9372-5
                  
                "); Usui [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR108 "Usui N (2019) Progress of studies on Kuroshio path variations south of Japan in the past decade. In: Nagai T, Saito H, Suzuki K, Takahashi M (eds) Kuroshio current: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem dynamics. Wiley, Hoboken, pp 147–161"); Qiu et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR82 "Qiu B, Chen S, Schneider N, Oka E, Sugimoto S (2020) On reset of the wind-forced decadal Kuroshio Extension variability in late 2017. J Clim 33:10813–10828. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-20-0237.1
                  
                ")). This means that LM2017 does not satisfy the third criterion.

A unique aspect of LM2017 is its long duration. Eight LM events have occurred since 1950, and LM2017 is the longest-recorded LM (Qiu et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR83 "Qiu B, Chen S, Oka E (2023) Why did the 2017 Kuroshio large meander become the longest in the past 70 years? Geophys Res Lett 50:e2023GL103548. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL103548
                  
                ")). Usui et al. ([2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR110 "Usui N, Tsujino H, Nakano H, Matsumoto S (2013) Long-term variability of the Kuroshio path south of Japan. J Oceanogr 69:647–670. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10872-013-0197-1
                  
                ")) pointed out that low Kuroshio transport can cause a long LM duration because the vorticity balance of the stationary Rossby wave between the eastward and westward tendencies due to advection and the planetary beta effect can be achieved under low Kuroshio transport south of Japan. In fact, Kuroshio transport has been low since 2017, which seems to be a reason for the long-lived LM2017 (Kawakami et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR35 "Kawakami Y, Kojima A, Murakami K, Nakano T, Sugimoto S (2022) Temporal variations of net Kuroshio transport based on a repeated hydrographic section along 137°E. Clim Dyn 59:1703–1713. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-021-06061-8
                  
                "); Qiu et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR83 "Qiu B, Chen S, Oka E (2023) Why did the 2017 Kuroshio large meander become the longest in the past 70 years? Geophys Res Lett 50:e2023GL103548. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL103548
                  
                ")). Qiu et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR83 "Qiu B, Chen S, Oka E (2023) Why did the 2017 Kuroshio large meander become the longest in the past 70 years? Geophys Res Lett 50:e2023GL103548. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL103548
                  
                ")) claimed that the wind-forced stability of the KE system east of Izu Ridge after 2018 also played an important role in the duration of LM2017. Specifically, the highly stable KE system not only minimized westward eddy perturbations that could disrupt the upstream Kuroshio path but also enhanced the southern recirculation gyre, further stabilizing the position of the Kuroshio across the Izu Ridge.

The flow pattern variations of LM2017 are also unique. In the early stages of LM2017 until 2018, the meander trough frequently shifted eastward and its eastern periphery crossed the Izu Ridge (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)d). These features are different from those of a typical LM path but similar to those of the LM from 1981 to 1984, which was also an unstable type of LM (Nagano et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR57 "Nagano A, Yamashita Y, Hasegawa T, Ariyoshi K, Matsumoto H, Shinohara M (2019) Characteristics of an atypical large-meander path of the Kuroshio current south of Japan formed in September 2017. Mar Geophys Res 40:525–539. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s11001-018-9372-5
                  
                ")). Therefore, the flow path was not stable during the early stages of LM2017, as reported by Qiu et al. ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR83 "Qiu B, Chen S, Oka E (2023) Why did the 2017 Kuroshio large meander become the longest in the past 70 years? Geophys Res Lett 50:e2023GL103548. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL103548
                  
                ")). Subsequently, the meander trough shifted westward and the flow path frequently exhibited an S-shaped curvature (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)e). During the S-shaped curvature, the Kuroshio approached the coastal region of the Kanto–Tokai area closer compared with the NLM periods, resulting in coastal warming (see Sect.[3.1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Sec4)).

The detachment of the cyclonic eddies is another unique feature of LM2017. Eddies are often detached from the S-shaped flow paths. The most significant eddy detachment occurred in 2020 (marked B in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)f). The brief northward retreat of the Kuroshio associated with the eddy detachment is also evident in the time series of the southernmost position of the Kuroshio (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig2)). Owing to this detachment, the meander amplitude was significantly reduced. However, a new small meander soon grew (marked C in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)f, g), and the detached eddy was subsequently reabsorbed by the Kuroshio to the southeast of Kyushu (marked B in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)g). Eventually, the two eddies merged, leading to the rapid recovery of the LM (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#Fig4)h). The detachment of an eddy and its attachment to the Kuroshio were also observed during the LM from 1975 to 1980 (Konaga and Nishiyama [1978](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10872-025-00753-z#ref-CR41 "Konaga S, Nishiyama K (1978) Behavior of a detached eddy “Harukaze” around the seamount of Daiiti- and Daini-Kinan Kaizan. Pap Meteorol Geophys 29:151–156. 
                  https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/mripapers1950/29/3/29_151/_pdf
                  
                . Accessed 29 November 2024 (in Japanese with English abstract)")). Since this case in the late 1970s, such a phenomenon has only been observed in LM2017.

This webpage is a peer-reviewed review article published in the Journal of Oceanography (Volume 81, pages 165–185, published March 29, 2025) titled "The Kuroshio large meander and its various impacts: a review." It is an open-access, Special Section review paper focused on "Midlatitude ocean-atmosphere interactions and extreme events," with 8,571 accesses, 28 citations, 93 Altmetric mentions, and 9 mentions.

AUTHORS: Hidetaka Hirata, Hatsumi Nishikawa, Norihisa Usui, Toru Miyama, Shusaku Sugimoto, Akira Kusaka, and Takashi Seto.

KEY TOPIC: The Kuroshio (the western boundary current of the North Pacific subtropical gyre) south of Japan exhibits bimodal path variations between large meander (LM) and non-LM (NLM) paths, which can be further classified as offshore NLM (oNLM) and nearshore NLM (nNLM). This bimodal feature is unique to the Kuroshio and not observed in other western boundary currents. LM and NLM paths can persist from a year to a decade, while transitions occur over several months. The LM path typically forms via transition from the nNLM path, triggered by a small meander that first appears southeast of Kyushu, grows eastward, and develops into an LM.

THE MOST RECENT EVENT (LM2017): The most recent LM event began in August 2017 and was still ongoing as of March 2025, exceeding seven years duration—the longest on record. Six LMs have been observed since 1965 according to Yoshida et al.'s criteria (southernmost latitude of the Kuroshio axis off Enshu-nada south of 32°N). LM2017 is unique in several ways: (1) it formed despite an unstable Kuroshio Extension (KE) state, not satisfying all three favorable formation conditions proposed by Usui et al. (2013)—positive SSH anomalies east of Taiwan, westward propagation of cyclonic eddies, and a stable KE state; (2) its exceptionally long duration is attributed to low Kuroshio transport since 2017 and wind-forced stability of the KE system east of the Izu Ridge after 2018; (3) it exhibited unstable flow patterns in its early stages (meander trough shifting eastward, S-shaped curvature) similar to the 1981–1984 LM; and (4) it featured significant cyclonic eddy detachment in 2020, followed by reabsorption and merging that led to rapid LM recovery—a phenomenon only previously observed during the 1975–1980 LM.

KUROSHIO CHARACTERISTICS: The Kuroshio transports large amounts of heat, salt, and biogeochemical materials northward. Its current velocity has a subsurface maximum (>1 m/s) extending to ~1000 m depth, with net volume transport of approximately 42 Sv. The Kuroshio exhibits large horizontal SSH and temperature gradients in surface and subsurface layers.

IMPACTS COVERED: The review covers LM impacts on (1) oceanic conditions (coastal sea level, coastal circulation, water temperature, and mass distributions), (2) atmospheric phenomena (via SST distribution changes that alter heat and moisture supply to the atmosphere; LM-associated SST anomalies have mesoscale horizontal scales of several hundred kilometers), (3) lower trophic marine ecosystems (Kuroshio carries a "nutrient stream"—nutrient-rich water below the euphotic zone—with studies on vertical turbulent nitrate flux and eddy-driven nutrient transport), and (4) fisheries resources (the Kuroshio region and adjacent areas are spawning and nursery grounds for various fish species, especially in the coastal Kanto-Tokai area where the Kuroshio approaches the coast during S-shaped curvature phases, causing coastal warming).

RESEARCH CONTEXT: The review notes significant contributions from the "Hotspots in the Climate System" (hotspot1; 2010–2014) and "Midlatitude ocean-atmosphere interaction hotspots under the changing climate" (hotspot2; 2019–2023) research projects. It positions itself as the first comprehensive review covering both oceanic dynamics and the broad impacts of the Kuroshio LM across ocean conditions, atmosphere, ecosystems, and fisheries, and emphasizes that 21st-century research has shown mid-latitude oceanic fronts and WBCs actively influence atmospheric variability (not merely passively responding).

The Kuroshio LM drastically changes the distribution of currents and water temperature in the surface and subsurface layers, affecting atmospheric conditions, marine ecosystems, and fisheries resources. The most recent Kuroshio LM event occurred in August 2017 and is still continuing as of March 2025 (LM2017)."

## Highlights

*   •16 orders and 78 families are identified for larval fish assemblage. 
*   •Larval fish abundance is comparable between the Kuroshio and coastal waters. 
*   •Larval fishes are classified into the Kuroshio and coastal communities. 
*   •Abundances of representative families are significantly correlated with salinity. 
*   •Mixture of advected fish larvae results in their high biodiversity. 

## Abstract

The Kuroshio has been long thought to be disadvantageous as nursery grounds for larval fishes due to the low plankton standing stocks under the oligotrophic conditions. Despite of the potential risk for survival and growth, early life stages of various fishes appear abundantly in the Kuroshio and its neighboring waters. Here, we report what kind of taxonomic groups establish community structure of larval fishes in the Continental shelf waters (CW) and the Kuroshio (KW). 16 orders and 78 families were classified in the present study. Mesopelagic fishes more abundantly appeared in the KW than in the CW, while larval fish abundance was not different between the two areas. Multivariate analysis demonstrated the regional difference of the taxonomic compositions, represented by Callionymidae, Bothidae, Labridae and Bregmacerotidae for the CW and Gonostomatidae, Myctophidae and Notosudidae for the KW. Abundance of fish larvae to ambient salinity exhibited significantly positive correlations for Gonostomatidae, _Sigmops gracilis_ and _Myctophum orientale_ predominated in the KW and negative correlations for Labridae appeared abundantly in the CW. These results suggest that mixture of advected specimens from the coastal and Kuroshio waters also contribute to larval fish community with high biodiversity and comparable abundance between the Kuroshio and its neighboring waters.

2026, Progress in Oceanography  Show abstract The Kuroshio Current and its neighboring waters are nursery grounds for the early life stages of migratory fish, despite poor food availability under oligotrophic conditions. Although recent findings suggest that standing stocks of mesozooplankton are not low and provide good prey availability for fish larvae, no information is available at their prey quality. Here, we investigated the spatial and temporal variations in the fatty acid content of mesozooplankton communities from transect lines across the Kuroshio to evaluate the nutritional quality of mesozooplankton as prey for fish larvae. We identified 5 saturated fatty acids (SFAs), 4 mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), and 13 poly-unsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) in the mesozooplankton community. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that fatty acid contents in mesozooplankton dry mass were more variable between the seasons than at the sites, with increasing SFA in summer. Long-chain PUFA (LC-PUFA) content, represented by arachidonic, eicosapentaenoic, and docosahexaenoic acids, was comparable between the Kuroshio and its neighboring waters. These LC-PUFA contents exhibited significant positive correlations with the relative abundance of Eucalanidae copepods and molluscans determined with metabarcoding analysis. These contents were also positively correlated with the fatty acid content of the haptophyte biomarker. Beaked sandfish larvae had higher LC-PUFA contents than those of Anguilliformes leptocephali. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that the fatty acid composition of omnivorous crustaceans, such as decapods and Eucalanidae copepods, was synchronized with that of beaked sandfish larvae. These findings suggest that the LC-PUFA contents of mesozooplankton communities accumulate in omnivorous crustaceans feeding on nano- to micro-sized phytoplankton and are transferred to planktivorous fish larvae.

This study focused on the impact of the KE on the structure and function of zooplankton communities in the open waters off eastern Japan. The results showed that the presence of the KE strongly hindered water exchange between its northern and southern sides, leading to significant differences in zooplankton community structure. Zooplankton in the Oyashio regions exhibited high abundance (3791.9 ind.·m−3) and low species richness (118 taxa), while the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG) regions had higher species richness (207 taxa) but lower abundance (134.5±112.0 ind.·m−3) compared to the Oyashio regions. The maximum species number of zooplankton occurred in the Kuroshio-Oyashio mixing water (KOMW) regions (327 taxa). Regarding zooplankton functional groups, small-bodied ambush–feeding, omnivore–herbivores and medium-bodied current–feeding, omnivore–herbivores, broadcast spawners were dominant in the Oyashio regions and the KOMW regions, whereas cruise–feeding, omnivore–herbivores, sac spawners prevailed in the oligotrophic NPSG regions. This is a scientific research article published in Progress in Oceanography (Volume 231, February 2025, Article 103386), examining the community structure of fish larvae associated with advections of the Kuroshio Current and its neighboring waters. The study is authored by Toru Kobari and colleagues (Gen Kume, Yusuke Manako, Airi Hara, Kaori Yamanoue, Takafumi Azuma, Ryuji Fukuda, Yi-Chen Wang, Masafumi Kodama) and is open access under a Creative Commons license.

KEY FINDINGS:
- A total of 16 orders and 78 families of fish larvae were identified in the study area, which covered Continental shelf waters (CW) and the Kuroshio waters (KW) in the western North Pacific.
- Mesopelagic fishes appeared more abundantly in the Kuroshio waters (KW) than in the continental shelf waters (CW), but overall larval fish abundance was comparable between the two areas.
- Multivariate analysis revealed regional differences in taxonomic composition: Callionymidae, Bothidae, Labridae, and Bregmacerotidae were representative of the CW, while Gonostomatidae, Myctophidae, and Notosudidae were representative of the KW.
- Significant positive correlations were found between larval fish abundance and ambient salinity for Gonostomatidae, Sigmops gracilis, and Myctophum orientale (predominant in KW), while negative correlations were found for Labridae (abundant in CW).
- The study concludes that the mixture of advected specimens from both coastal and Kuroshio waters contributes to larval fish community with high biodiversity and comparable abundance between the Kuroshio and its neighboring waters.

CONTEXT: The Kuroshio has traditionally been considered disadvantageous as a nursery ground for larval fishes due to low plankton standing stocks under oligotrophic conditions, yet early life stages of various fishes appear abundantly in these waters. The article includes 10 figures and 3 tables, and has been cited by 2 subsequent papers (one on fatty acid contents of mesozooplankton in the Kuroshio, and one on Kuroshio extension-driven variability in spring zooplankton community structure). Data availability: data will be made available on request.

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | A new modeling strategy for the predictive model of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) central fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific Ocean based on machine learning and operational characteristics of the light fishing vessels ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2024.1451104/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (14 October 2024, Volume 11) that presents a new modeling strategy for predicting chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) central fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific Ocean. The study used 70,147 fishing logbook records from Chinese commercial light purse seine fishing vessels (2014-2022, March-December) in the high seas of the northwest Pacific (35°-45°N, 145°-165°E), obtained from the East China Sea and Pelagic Seas Data Service Center Database.

Key methodological elements:
- Six marine environmental variables were used: Sea Surface Temperature (SST), Sea Surface Salinity (SSS), Chlorophyll-a (Chla), Current Velocity (CV), Sea Level Anomaly (SLA), and Dissolved Oxygen (DO), sourced from Copernicus Marine Service at 0.25°×0.25° spatial resolution with daily temporal resolution.
- Data were divided into three datasets: Dataset A (no moonlight days: lunar days 1-10 and 20-30), Dataset B (bright moonlight days: lunar days 11-19), and Dataset C (all days).
- Two modeling approaches were compared: Approach One (based on light fishing vessel operational characteristics, modeling datasets A and B separately) and Approach Two (no distinction between moonlight conditions, modeling dataset C as a whole).
- Two machine learning models were compared: Random Forest (RF) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), with tuning via grid search and 5-fold cross-validation, using 80%:20% training:test split.
- Central fishing grounds were defined as those with daily catches at or above the daily median (label 1), others labeled 0.

Key results:
1) Stronger moonlight intensity (especially full moon) limits fishing efficiency. Most years showed a higher percentage of fishing days on bright moonlight days than catch percentages, with bright moonlight days accounting for 26.95%-34.24% of catches and 28.9%-32.87% of fishing days. No-moonlight days yielded higher catches with fewer fishing days.
2) Under Approach One, the LightGBM model achieved the best prediction results on all three datasets. The optimal prediction performance on the complete dataset C improved from 65.02% (RF model, Approach Two) to 66.52% (LightGBM model, Approach One).
3) Variable importance was highly similar between datasets A and C, suggesting that Approach Two (not accounting for operational characteristics) could misguide fisheries during bright moonlight days.
4) Under the optimal model (LightGBM, Approach One), the most important environmental variables were CV, SLA, and SSS for dataset A, and CV, DO, and SLA for dataset B. Chla was the least important variable, and SST had weaker influence. Year and lunar phase were most important temporal variables; longitude was more important than latitude spatially. Environmental variables were overall more important than spatiotemporal variables.

The study compared favorably with prior work by Han et al. (2023) that used 3DCNN models at coarser scales (monthly, 1°×1°), noting that fine spatial-temporal scales (0.25°, daily) used here are closer to fishery production needs but still affected by data bias from factors like fishermen decision-making and vessel production capacity differences. The authors recommend future research combining spatiotemporal models like 3DCNN, ConvLSTM, and vision Transformer with the current approaches, while expanding spatial-temporal scales to balance prediction performance and production needs. The study concludes that considering light fishing vessel operational characteristics (lunar phase effects) is critical for improving model selection and prediction accuracy, and contributes to more accurate guidance for fishermen on operating area and time for the Scomber japonicus fishery, supporting balanced ecological and economic fisheries development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) is one of the most influential small pelagic fish in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, and accurate modeling approaches and model selection are critical points in predicting the Scomber japonicus fishing grounds."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: CATCH-ONLY STOCK ASSESSMENT OF ... ---
URL: https://www.pcouncil.org/documents/2025/05/catch-only-stock-assessment-of-pacific-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-for-u-s-management-in-the-2025-26-and-2026-27-fishing-years.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a NOAA Technical Memorandum (NMFS-SWFSC-718) published in March 2025 presenting a catch-only stock assessment of Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) for U.S. management in the 2025-26 and 2026-27 fishing years. Authors include Alexander J. Jensen, Caitlin Allen Akselrud, Peter T. Kuriyama, and Kevin T. Hill (NOAA Southwest Fisheries Science Center) and Juan P. Zwolinski (UC Santa Cruz, affiliated with NOAA SWFSC).

The assessment follows the Pacific Fishery Management Council's (PFMC) schedule of benchmark assessments every 4 years (2015, 2019, 2023) and catch-only projection assessments every 4 years (2017, 2021, and now 2025). It uses the same model structure as the 2023 benchmark assessment (Stock Synthesis v3.30.22.1) with updated catch values for model years 2008-2022, new catch values for 2023 and 2024, and forecasted landings for 2025 and 2026 based on average landings from 2021-2023.

Key findings include: The estimated stock biomass (age 1+) is 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26 and 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for fishing year 2026-27. Stock biomass generally declined between 2008 and 2022, with relatively high recruitment in model years 2011, 2016, and 2018. Estimates for 2023-onwards are informed primarily by the stock-recruitment relationship and are highly uncertain.

Harvest guidelines are 9,143 mt for 2025-26 and 10,448 mt for 2026-27, with the stock projected to remain above the 18,200 mt management threshold. The OFL is 12,965 mt (2025-26) and 14,270 mt (2026-27). The SSC-selected tier 2 sigma (σ = 2.0) was adopted by the Council at their April 2025 meeting, using the tier 3 default because tier 2 values exceeded it.

Exploitation rates ranged from roughly 1-27% annually from model years 2008-2023, with U.S. fisheries harvesting between 7 and 39% of the harvest guideline. The 2024-25 annual catch limit was 10,073 mt, and U.S. landings have remained below annual catch limits.

Sensitivity analyses all resulted in lower forecasted biomass than the base model, with the scenario fixing recruitment to average 2019-2021 values producing the largest reduction (age-1+ biomass = 56,390 mt by 2026-27). A model issue was identified where age-0 fish incorrectly contributed to spawning stock biomass during forecast years; this was flagged as a Stock Synthesis issue and structural modifications (e.g., two-season model) may be considered in future assessments.

Uncertainties include the lack of AT survey data for 2020 and 2022 (no survey conducted in 2020; 2022 survey data not recommended for use), inherent uncertainty in stock distribution between U.S. and Mexican waters (with 70% assumed U.S. distribution), and oceanographic variability affecting recruitment success. Research needs include exploring natural mortality estimates for similar CPS and improving spatial variability characterization of stock structure and distribution, including prioritized survey data collection in Mexican waters.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Animals (Basel) on September 27, 2025 (DOI: 10.3390/ani15192822), examining the relative abundance distribution and environmental differences between Blue Mackerel (Scomber australasicus) and Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean.

**Study Context and Problem:** These two economically important fish species look highly similar, leading to aggregated catch reporting in fishery logbooks that prevents accurate per-species stock assessments. Both species are priority stocks under the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC).

**Methods:**
- Integrated fishery logbook data from Chinese purse seine fleets (2014–2023) with field sampling data for species identification
- Introduced a Zero-One Inflated Beta Model (ZOIBM) built in a Bayesian framework (brms package in R) to quantify the proportional composition of the two co-occurring species in mixed catches—the first application of this model in marine fishery research
- Used a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to analyze environmental drivers of niche differentiation
- Seven candidate environmental variables were considered (SST, VO, UO, Chla, SSH, SSS, MLD); SSH was excluded due to high correlation with SSS (r=0.72), leaving six final variables
- ZOIBM used 4 MCMC chains × 4000 iterations, with adapt_delta=0.99 and max_treedepth=15, validated via 5-fold cross-validation
- Annual centroids were calculated to track distributional shifts

**Key Results:**
- ZOIBM performed excellently: R² = 0.63, RMSE = 0.305, MAE = 0.298; all Gelman-Rubin R-hat values (0.9996–1.0047) confirmed convergence; posterior predictive checks confirmed model adequacy
- Blue Mackerel high-abundance areas concentrated at 35–44°N, 145–160°E, with proportions decreasing at higher latitudes (below 10% north of 45°N)
- Chub Mackerel showed an opposite latitudinal pattern, with high-abundance areas spanning 35–47.5°N (a wider latitudinal range)
- Environmental driver analysis: SST was the most critical differentiating factor—Chub Mackerel showed a unimodal response peaking at 17–19°C (narrow optimal temperature, higher warm-water sensitivity), while Blue Mackerel increased monotonically with SST, tolerating temperatures up to ~23°C
- Chla and VO further amplified differences in resource utilization strategies
- Both species showed similar unimodal salinity responses (Chub peak ~33.9‰, Blue peak ~34.0‰); UO plays a weak role in niche differentiation; MLD positively correlated with both species
- From 2014–2023, both species shifted northward and eastward: Blue Mackerel centroid moved from 40.61°N to 43.46°N (0.3062°/year, R²=0.820) and from 150.82°E to 157.10°E (0.5736°/year); Chub Mackerel moved from 41.27°N to 43.72°N (0.2708°/year) and 151.45°E to 157.00°E (0.5125°/year)
- Spatial overlap between the two species has been continuously increasing as their distributions converge

**Conclusions:** Blue Mackerel prefer warmer southern waters while Chub Mackerel dominate cooler northern areas. The northward/eastward shifts likely reflect climate change responses. Increasing range overlap may lead to heightened interspecific competition. The ZOIBM provides a novel methodological reference for fine-scale assessment of co-occurring fish resources and supports sustainable management of the North Pacific mackerel fishery.

--- SOURCE 2: 豊洲市場の魚の価格はどう決まるのか？　マグロとサンマはまったく別…消費者が知らない裏側に迫る：時事ドットコム ---
URL: https://www.jiji.com/jc/v8?id=20220410toyosunews

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from Jiji Press (時事通信) published on April 15, 2022, explaining how fish prices are determined at the Toyosu Market in Tokyo, Japan's largest fish market. The article was written by Okayama Toshinori of Jiji Press's Fisheries Department.

**Three types of trading methods:**
1. **Auction (競り)** - The buyer offering the highest price wins. Used for tuna, sea urchin, and other premium items. Tuna auctions use finger signals ("teyari") as bids, taking only seconds per fish.
2. **Bidding (入札)** - Buyers submit written bids without knowing others' prices, a "one-shot gamble." Used for dried sardines and boiled-dried fish.
3. **Relative/negotiated trading (相対取引)** - Direct negotiations between sellers and buyers. Despite the market's auction image, nearly 90% of fish (by monetary value) at Toyosu are traded this way. Used for common fish like mackerel, sardines, saury, plus imported salmon and frozen shrimp/crab.

**Key price records:**
- January 2019: First New Year tuna auction at Toyosu after relocating from Tsukiji set a historic record - a bluefin tuna from Oma, Aomori Prefecture sold for ¥333.6 million (¥1.2 million/kg), the highest price ever.
- July 2020: First saury of the season sold for ¥125,000 per fish (¥100,000/kg), a record high during a period of poor catches. This unusually high price was partly motivated by a desire to liven up the market during COVID-19 restrictions.

**Price factors:**
- Supply (landing volume), origin, size, and quality determine prices.
- Poor catches have driven up prices for saury, squid (2-3x higher than a decade ago), and salmon roe (ikura). Meanwhile, abundant sardine harvests have prices below ¥50 per fish.
- Fishing methods matter: single-line fishing ("ippon-zuri") fetches premium prices (e.g., Oita's "Seki-aji" and Kanagawa's "Matsura saba" sell for 5x+ more than standard fish) due to better condition and freshness. Wild bluefin tuna caught by single-line or longline fishing is prized by sushi chefs, with large 100kg+ fish exceeding ¥10,000/kg (3x+ more than farmed tuna).
- Celebrity influence: Kei Nishikori's comment about wanting "nodoguro" (blackthroat sea perch) after his US Open performance boosted its popularity and price.
- Historical note: Fatty tuna (otoro), once discarded in the Edo period due to spoilage, became a luxury item with refrigeration and logistics advances.

**Market history:** During the Tsukiji era, almost all fish traded via auction. But "advance purchasing" (negotiating before auction times to secure supply) increased, causing auctions to become formalities for common fish. Law reforms led most fish to shift to relative trading. The article notes a decline in market-through distribution as direct producer-retailer trades increase, but Toyosu still serves as a national benchmark price-setting market.

**Consumer trends:** Ministry of Agriculture statistics show 40%+ of consumers cite "family prefers meat" and "fish is too expensive" as reasons for not buying fish more often - both ahead of "preparing fish is troublesome."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"取引手法は、最高値を提示した買い手が入手できる「競り」と「入札」、売り手と買い手が個別に交渉する「相対取引」の３種類。市場といえば競りのイメージが強いが、同市場では意外にも大半の魚が相対取引で、金額ベースで「全体の９割近く」（豊洲の卸会社）とされる。"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: 水産物流通のこれから～流通現場からのアプローチ～(6) - 水産物のサプライチェーン（その４）、漁獲量・流通・消費について（その１）／浦和栄助 | 水産振興コラム | 東京水産振興会 ---
URL: https://lib.suisan-shinkou.or.jp/column/ryutsu-korekara/vol06.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is the 6th installment in a column series titled "The Future of Seafood Distribution" (水産物流通のこれから), written by Urawa Eisuke, Executive Director of the Tokyo Seafood Wholesalers Association, published in March 2025 in the Suisan Shinko (Fisheries Promotion) online magazine.

**Toyosu Market vs. Global Markets:**
- Toyosu Market's seafood handling volume (quantity and value) surpasses major global markets including Paris' Rungis Market, Spain's Mercamadrid, and London's Billingsgate Fish Market (using 2022 data).
- Rungis is three times the size of Toyosu by area (1.2 million m² vs. 400,000 m²) but is primarily an agricultural/livestock market with only one small seafood building.

**Toyosu Market within Japan:**
- Combining all categories (seafood and produce), Ota Market leads in quantity (~1 million tons) but Toyosu leads in value (~450 billion yen) nationwide.
- Only Toyosu, Ota, and Osaka Main Market are large; most other markets fall below 50 billion yen / 200,000 tons.
- Total central wholesale market seafood handling fell from ~4.3 million tons (1988) to ~1.3 million tons (2020+), mirroring Japan's national catch decline from ~12 million tons (1988 peak) to ~4 million tons.
- Toyosu (Tsukiji) seafood volume declined from ~800,000 tons (1988) to ~330,000 tons recently, but Toyosu's share of the national market increased from under 20% to 26%, showing increasing concentration.

**Category-wise Volume Trends (Toyosu, 2000 vs. 2023):**
- Total volume halved: 638,000 tons → 295,000 tons.
- Tuna (大物): halved from 70,000 to 33,000 tons.
- Specialty items (特種): nearly halved from 76,000 to 40,000 tons (shellfish decline notable due to coastal development).
- Fresh fish (鮮魚): -30% (136,000 → 95,000 tons), holding steady until ~2018 but recent declines driven by reduced catches of saury and squid.

--- SOURCE 1: A Study on the Impact of Environmental Factors on Chub Mackerel Scomber japonicus Fishing Grounds Based on a Linear Mixed Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/9/8/323

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the journal Fishes (2024, Volume 9, Issue 8, Article 323; DOI: 10.3390/fishes9080323), examines how marine environmental factors affect Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific using a linear mixed model (LMM). Authors include Jiasheng Li, Fenghua Tang, Yumei Wu, Shengmao Zhang, Weifeng Zhou, and Xuesen Cui (corresponding author), affiliated with the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute (Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences) and Shanghai Ocean University. The study was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (grant 2023YFD2401303) and received on 14 June 2024, published 14 August 2024.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used fishery data from China's high-sea light-purse seine operations (2014–2020) covering fishing grounds between 140–165°E and 30–50°N, combined with monthly averaged sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL) data from Oregon State University's Ocean Productivity database. Data were aggregated at 0.5° × 0.5° spatial resolution. CPUE was calculated as catch per net-haul (t/net). Square-root transformation of CPUE and natural logarithm of CHL were applied to achieve normal distributions; VIF values of 1.990 confirmed no multicollinearity between SST and logCHL. The LMM included SST and logCHL as fixed effects, with Year, Month, and fishing Zone as random effects, using the lme4 package in R. Among 256 candidate models, the optimal model (scenario 5) was selected based on lowest AIC, BIC, and logLik values.

KEY RESULTS: (1) SST had a significant fixed effect on CPUE with a negative slope (p < 0.001), meaning CPUE increases as SST decreases. (2) logCHL had no fixed effect on CPUE but showed significant random effects by month. (3) logCHL was positively correlated with CPUE during spawning and wintering periods (April–May, November–December) and negatively correlated during the summer feeding period (June–October), consistent with patterns observed in neon flying squid. (4) Annual average CPUE decreased from 2014 to 2020, peaking at 15.501 t/net (2015) and 11.363 t/net (2018), with a low of 8.355 t/net in 2020; monthly CPUE peaked in November (14.426 t/net). (5) Low CPUE areas (<5 t/net) were south of 34°N, while high CPUE areas (>15 t/net) were between 148–159°E. (6) The random intercept for Year showed highest value (0.353) in 2015 and lowest (−0.480) in 2019; a high-random-intercept zone at 150–152°E, 39–41°N corresponded to high catch rates. Residuals approximated a normal distribution (skewness 0.031, kurtosis 3.532).

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS: The negative SST-CPUE relationship aligns with prior studies in the East China Sea and Japan coastal waters. Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019). The optimal SST range for fishing grounds is 14–18°C (~16°C ideal), and optimal chlorophyll-a range is 0.3–0.8 mg/m³. LIMITATIONS: Interpretation complexity with crossed random effects, high parameterization risks (overfitting), and incomplete spatial/temporal data coverage (no data from Japan/Russia EEZs, no January–March data).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SST had a significant fixed effect on the CPUE. In contrast, the natural logarithm of chlorophyll (logCHL) had no fixed effect on the CPUE. Based on the monthly analysis, random fluctuations were observed in the impact of logCHL on the CPUE. LogCHL and CPUE show a positive correlation during spawning and wintering periods and a negative correlation during the feeding period."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/10/1/20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Fishes* (2025, Volume 10, Issue 1, Article 20) by authors Seonggil Go (Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology), Joon-ho Lee (Underwater Survey Technology 21), and Sukgeun Jung (Jeju National University, corresponding author). The study projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the western North Pacific Ocean.

**Methodology:** The researchers developed a spawning ground index (SGI) based on a Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′ E, 20°00′–52°00′ N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers), driven by the IPCC AR5 RCP85 scenario. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010–2059. SGI was calculated using four parameters: water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m). The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001).

**Key Findings:**
- In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June.
- By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes).
- Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea.
- The study suggests biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea.

**Limitations noted:** The model results did not perfectly align with observations in the same space and time (though trends were similar); the assumed spawning period may shift due to photoperiod changes; only 10 m depth environmental conditions were considered; and chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m depth).

**Funding:** Supported by the Korea Institute of Marine Science and Technology (KIMST), Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries (RS-2023-00256330 and RS-2022-KS221566), and Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST grant PEA0306).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite some uncertainty, our model based on climate change scenarios projected that, by the 2050s, spawning grounds will shift northward due to warming of the ocean surface, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Effects of oceanographic conditions on fishery distribution: A case study of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in northeastern Taiwan ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0141113624004641

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Marine Environmental Research (Volume 202, November 2024, Article 106803) as part of a special issue on "Climate Change and the Oceans," edited by Fangli QIAO of the First Institute of Oceanography. The study examines the effects of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) distribution in northeastern Taiwan.

**Authors:** Sandipan Mondal, Frank Muller-Karger, Aratrika Ray, Shin-Ichi Ito, Ming-An Lee, and Hsueh-Jung Lu.

**Methodology:** The researchers constructed a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery data, climatic oscillation data, and oceanography data. Fishery and oceanographic data were rescaled using MATLAB (2022a) to a consistent spatial and temporal grid, then standardized using a generalized linear model (GLM). Five single-algorithm models were used: GLM, generalized additive model (GAM), gradient boosting method (GBM), random forest (RF), and classification models, combined into an ensemble approach.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO), which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792).
- NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level.
- Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect.
- Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m.
- Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E.

**Background Context:** Global climate change is significantly affecting marine ecosystems, with ocean warming causing coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, and sea-level rise. Under RCP 8.5 scenario, a predicted 40% decline in tropical fish catch by the 2050s in some economic zones (Lam et al., 2020) highlights the urgency of this research. Chub mackerel is economically crucial to Taiwan, with Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries accounting for 98.66% of captures. The study addresses a research gap by using multiple algorithms to confirm oceanographic significance, unlike previous studies that relied on single models.

**Funding:** National Science & Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC) grant 112-2811-M-019-004 and Fisheries Agency, Council of Agriculture, Taiwan grant 112-FM-2.31-A-03.

**Applications:** Findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in northeastern Taiwan waters and may aid decision-makers in protecting other ocean fisheries and dependent communities under changing climate conditions. The article has been cited by 5 subsequent publications (as of the page retrieval date).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our results indicated that the chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation. Moreover, sea-surface height and mixed-layer depth exerted the most and least significant effects on chub mackerel distribution, respectively."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304380014001604

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Ecological Modelling (Volume 283, 10 July 2014, Pages 70-84) titled "Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea" by Yuesong Li, Xinjun Chen, Changsheng Chen, Jianzhong Ge, Rubao Ji, Rucheng Tian, Pengfei Xue, and Liuxiong Xu. DOI: 10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2014.03.016.

The study developed an early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The researchers examined how regional physical processes affect larval dispersal and survival under climatological spring-summer conditions, both with and without short-time fluctuations from a typhoon.

Key findings include:
- Seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages.
- Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location.
- Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing. Comparison of cases with and without Typhoon Alice showed that cancellation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents limits typhoon influence on low-frequency flow and larval dispersion, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds.
- Temperature and food play significant roles in early larval development; water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March-July.
- Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June).
- Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion.

The article provides background on the ECS physical oceanography, including the Kuroshio Current (which acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf), the Taiwan Warm Current, and the Changjiang Coastal Current (which tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East Strait). Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. The study is the first IBM developed to examine chub mackerel recruitment in the ECS.

The paper has 41 references and has been cited 27 times. It was supported by multiple Chinese national research projects including the National 863 project, Shanghai Education Committee, and Shanghai Ocean University programs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The model results show that the seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during the early life stages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data | Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom | Cambridge Core ---
URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/stock-assessment-of-chub-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-in-the-central-east-china-sea-based-on-length-data/9AC92B324DD34E8BA019F5462A821E73

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Cambridge University Press journal article (published online October 30, 2013, in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom) titled "Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data." The study addresses the chub mackerel, an important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea that rose to prominence after the decline of traditional demersal economic species. The research methodology involved separating sample catches from 2009-2010 into three age groups based on an age–fork length key, estimating maximum sustainable yield (MSY), and building a spawner–recruitment relationship using fishery statistics from purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels, and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. Key findings: (1) The MSY of chub mackerel is approximately 18.8 × 10⁴ tonnes; (2) The fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (with lighting and deep-water purse seine vessels standardized to purse seine vessels), equivalent to a fishing mortality rate (F) of 0.4; (3) If fishing mortality remains at the current level (F = 0.7), the biomass will remain at 45.3 × 10⁴ tonnes; (4) At current fishing intensity, more than 40% of catches will consist of individuals smaller than 200mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300mm. The study concludes there is little potential for further exploitation of chub mackerel resources in the central East China Sea, and recommends reducing fishing mortality (F) to less than 0.4 for sustainable utilization. The chub mackerel resources are suffering over-exploitation due to increased fishing effort, and this paper represents the first analysis of their response to fishing because of previous data shortages.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results showed that the MSY of chub mackerel is about 18.8 × 10⁴t, and the fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (both the lighting purse seine vessels and deep-water purse seine vessels were standardized to purse seine vessels), which is equivalent to F = 0.4."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea | Journal of Ocean University of China | Springer Nature Link ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11802-021-4760-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Ocean University of China (Volume 20, pages 1483–1494, 2021) titled "Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea." Published on November 21, 2021, the study was conducted by authors Wei Yu, Jian Wen, Xinjun Chen, Gang Li, Yuesong Li, and Zhong Zhang, affiliated with Shanghai Ocean University and the Qingdao National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology.

The study investigated how the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) impacts the habitat range and distribution of the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the East China Sea (ECS). A weighting-based Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) model was established using vertical water temperature data at depths of 2.5 m, 25 m, and 50 m. From ten weighting scenarios tested, the optimal HSI model yielded reliable predictions.

Key findings include:
- A significant negative relationship was found between the PDO index and water temperature anomaly at different depths.
- Water temperatures at three different layers on the fishing ground tended to be LOW during the warm PDO phase and HIGH during the cold PDO phase.
- During a warm PDO phase: vertical water temperature cooled, the monthly preferred water temperature shifted southeastward, habitat quality dramatically decreased, and suitable habitat ranges reduced and moved southeastward.
- During a cool PDO phase: warmer vertical water temperatures occurred, preferred water temperature shifted northwestward, and suitable habitats enlarged and migrated in the same direction.

The study concludes that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of S. japonicus in the East China Sea. The article received 279 accesses, 7 citations, and 1 Altmetric score. The research was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2018YFD0900906), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 41906073), the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (No. 19ZR1423000), and the Shanghai Universities First-Class Disciplines Project (Fisheries A).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Spatio-temporal distribution of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus is strongly susceptible to climate variability."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index of chub mackerel in the spawning season and its effect on the abundance ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (25 November 2022) examining climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index (TSI) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and its effect on stock abundance.

**Study Context and Species:**
- Chub mackerel is widely distributed in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and is fished by China, Korea, and Japan in different seasons and areas.
- The species is divided into two stocks: the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock (distributed in the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and Sea of Japan) and the Pacific stock (inhabiting the Pacific coast of Japan and high seas of the northwestern Pacific).
- Main spawning period is March to June, with suitable spawning SST ranging from 15°C to 22°C and optimal at 18°C.

**Methods:**
- The authors estimated average TSI for chub mackerel in main spawning areas using the relationship between spawning probability and SST, assuming a Gaussian distribution with mean 18°C and variance 2.0°C.
- Data sources included FAO catch data (1950-2017), Japanese Fisheries Agency stock assessments (TWC and Pacific stock data, 1970-2017), and SST data from Japan Meteorological Agency (1970-2011), AVHRR (2012-2015), and GOES (2016-2017).
- Analytical techniques included Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis, sequential t-test analysis of regime shifts (STARS), Gradient Forest (GF) analysis, Generalized Additive Models (GAM), and Threshold GAMs (TGAM) to detect stationary vs. non-stationary relationships.
- Three main spawning areas were defined: coastal waters of China seas (24°N-36°N/118°E-124°E), southern Sea of Japan/Tsushima Strait (31°N-36°N/126°E-132°E), and Pacific coast of Japan (30°N-38°N/129°E-147°E).

**Key Results:**
- TSI in the shelf waters of China seas and Tsushima Strait showed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock.
- TSI on the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock.
- Chinese catch showed an increasing trend since the 1970s with step changes in 1986/1987, 1993/1994, and 2003/2004; TWC catch by Korea/Japan decreased in the late 1990s (step-change in 1998/1999).
- Pacific catch dramatically decreased in the late 1970s and 1980s but began recovering after the 2000s, with step changes in 1979/1980, 1988/1989, and 2014/2015.
- EOF analysis showed TSI had opposite loading on either side of the Kuroshio axis; first four EOFs explained 43.10% of total variance in TSI.
- TWC stock showed non-stationary relationships with TSI with threshold years in 1993/1994 and the late 1990s; Pacific stock showed non-stationary relationships with thresholds in the late 1970s to early 1980s.
- All relationships between chub mackerel abundance and TSI were better fitted by non-stationary TGAMs than stationary GAMs.
- Effects of spawning temperature suitability on abundance had a delayed effect of 1 to 2 years, attributed to the 0-2 year age structure of the main chub mackerel stock.

**Climate Drivers and Mechanisms:**
- TSI in different areas was affected by Arctic Oscillation Index (AOI), Monsoon Index (MOI), and Southern Oscillation Index (SOI).
- Non-stationarity in the TWC area was linked to declined variance in the Siberian High, while non-stationarity in the Pacific area was linked to the Aleutian Low.
- The regime shifts in AOI, MOI, and SHI in the late 1980s caused weakening monsoon and decreasing cold air intrusion, increasing water temperatures.
- The Pacific stock's late 1970s step change was related to interannual-decadal variability in the Aleutian Low and ENSO.
- Spatio-temporal variation in spawning temperature suitability had an important impact on the recovery of the Pacific stock after the 2000s, including a northward movement trend of the spawning area.
- The study follows an "atmosphere-ocean-biology" or "double-integration" process mechanism, demonstrating that climate variability influences biological variability through intermediary environmental variability.

**Conclusions:**
The research provides a reasonable explanation for variations in the two chub mackerel stocks and their responses to TSI variability, offering improved understanding of climate-induced non-stationary relationships between chub mackerel abundance and physical drivers. The authors note that biotic factors (e.g., spawning-stock biomass) should also be considered in future research for comprehensive population dynamics understanding and resource management.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results showed that the TSIs in the shelf waters of China seas and the waters of the Tsushima Strait displayed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock, whereas the TSI in the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Synchronous spatio-temporal changes in potential habitats of Trachurus murphyi and Dosidicus gigas off Chile in relation to regime shift of Pacific decadal oscillation ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0924796322000598

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Journal of Marine Systems (Volume 233, September 2022, Article 103758), investigates synchronous spatio-temporal changes in potential habitats of Chilean jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi) and jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) off the coast of Chile in relation to Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) regime shifts from 1950 to 2017.

**Key Environmental Factors Identified:**
- For D. gigas: sea surface salinity (SSS), sea surface height anomaly (SSHA), and water temperature at 400m (Temp_400m)
- For T. murphyi: sea surface temperature (SST), mixed layer depth (MLD), and Temp_400m
- All environmental factors were significantly related to the PDO

**Methodology:**
- Used habitat suitability index (HSI) models
- Fisheries data from the National Distant-water Fisheries Data Center of China (NDFDC), Shanghai Ocean University
- Fishing data for D. gigas covered March–May 2011–2017; T. murphyi covered March–May 2013–2017
- PDO regimes identified: two cold regimes (1950–1976 and 1999–2017) and one warm regime (1977–1998)

**Key Findings:**
- A significantly negative relationship was found between the HSI of D. gigas and the PDO index, while a significantly positive correlation was observed for T. murphyi
- In the warm PDO regime: MLD was shallower, SST increased, and SSHA decreased from northeast to southwest off Chile; D. gigas suitable habitats contracted and shifted southwestward; T. murphyi habitat quality enhanced with little distribution change
- In the cold PDO regime: SST and SSHA decreased, MLD deepened; D. gigas suitable habitats enlarged and moved northeastward; T. murphyi suitable habitats slightly reduced
- The study concluded that Chilean T. murphyi dominated in the warm PDO regime while D. gigas dominated in the cold PDO regime

**Context:**
- Both species are key economic species in the Humboldt Current System (HCS) off Chile
- Chilean T. murphyi catches account for the highest proportion among world oceans; D. gigas is distributed from northern California (37°N) to southern Chile (47°S)
- Both are regulated by the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO)
- China began fishing D. gigas in 2001 and T. murphyi in 2000 in Chilean waters
- T. murphyi fishing grounds are primarily in southern Chilean waters; D. gigas mostly in northern waters, with some geographic overlap

**Funding:** Supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China, Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai, Shanghai talent development funding, National Key R&D Program of China, and open fund of State Key Laboratory of Satellite Ocean Environment Dynamics.

**Citation metrics:** The article has been cited 5 times and has 17 Mendeley readers. The paper has 50 references.

--- SOURCE 9: Pacific decadal oscillation - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_decadal_oscillation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin, detected as warm or cool surface waters in the Pacific north of 20°N. It varies irregularly at interannual-to-interdecadal timescales. The PDO was named by Steven R. Hare in 1997, who noticed it while studying salmon production patterns. The PDO index is the leading empirical orthogonal function (EOF) of monthly sea surface temperature anomalies over the North Pacific, with signals reconstructed back to 1661 (and as far back as 993) through tree-ring chronologies.

**Mechanisms:** The PDO is not a single physical mode of ocean variability but rather the superposition of several processes with different dynamic origins:
- **ENSO teleconnections/atmospheric bridge**: El Niño events generate Rossby waves that propagate poleward, modifying surface fluxes over the North Pacific within 2–6 weeks.
- **SST reemergence**: Winter SST anomalies are sequestered beneath the shallow summer mixed layer and reemerge the following winter when the mixed layer deepens again.
- **Stochastic atmospheric forcing**: Random storm forcings integrated into the ocean mixed layer can contribute up to 1/3 of PDO variability at decadal timescales.
- **Ocean dynamics**: Including advective resonance, Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension variability, and North Pacific gyre circulation adjustments driven by westward-propagating Rossby waves.

**Impacts:** During a positive phase, the Aleutian Low deepens, warming the Pacific Northwest to Alaska while cooling Mexico and the Southeast US. Winter precipitation increases in Alaska's coastal range, Mexico, and the Southwest US but decreases in Canada, Eastern Siberia, and Australia. The PDO also affects the Indian summer monsoon (stronger during negative phase) and, along with the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, strongly influences multidecadal drought patterns in the US.

**Regime shifts:** Documented reversals around 1924/25, 1945/46, and 1976/77, with additional shifts in 1988/89 and 1997/98. A 2014 flip to a warm phase coincided with record-breaking global surface temperatures. The last two major reversals corresponded with dramatic shifts in salmon production regimes in the North Pacific. Reconstructions show a 50–70 year periodicity, with a persistent negative phase during medieval times (993–1300).

**Predictability:** NOAA produces PDO forecasts using linear inverse modeling (LIM), with predictability largely arising from ENSO and limited to approximately 4 seasons (~14 months). ENSO tends to lead PDO cycling. The PDO is related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO), a similar but more global phenomenon covering 50°S to 50°N.
</summary>
