A Monte Carlo filtering approach is used to identify viable r-K pairs. Parameter pairs (ri, Ki) are randomly sampled from their respective prior distributions. An initial biomass (BFYR) is randomly drawn from its defined B/K range. Biomass trajectories are projected forward using Equations (13) and (14). A likelihood function based on a Bernoulli distribution (Equation (15)) is used to evaluate the agreement between simulated and observed catches, filtering for the most plausible r-K combinationswhere θ = (r,K) is the parameter vector, Cobs is the observed catch series, Csim is the simulated catch series, I(·) is an indicator function, and δ is an acceptable error threshold. To characterize the distribution of r, K, and derived MSY accurately, the geometric mean of the viable parameter combinations is used as the final point estimate. MSY is calculated using the Schaefer model equation: MSY = r × K/4. Uncertainty is quantified using the standard deviation (SD) of the log-normal distribution, deriving approximate 95% confidence intervals. Stock status is evaluated based on the criteria: A stock is considered healthy if B/Bmsy > 1 and F/Fmsy < 1; experiencing fishing overfishing if B/Bmsy > 1 and F/Fmsy > 1; experiencing recruitment overfishing if B/Bmsy < 1 and F/Fmsy < 1; and severely overfished if B/Bmsy < 1 and F/Fmsy > 1.

#### 2.3.2. Parameterization

To assess the current status of the S. japonicus stock in the North Pacific, catch data from 1995 to 2024 were used. Based on information from the FishBase database and studies by Palomares et al. (2018) [[25](#B25-fishes-11-00276)] and Wang et al. (2020) [[30](#B30-fishes-11-00276)], the population resilience of S. japonicus is considered moderate. Consequently, the prior distribution for the intrinsic growth rate (r) was set between 0.2 and 0.8. Following the approach of Froese et al. [[15](#B15-fishes-11-00276)], the initial prior for the carrying capacity (K) was set to 50 × CMAX.

### 2.4. Resource Management

In the field of fishery resource assessment and management, core objectives include quantifying stock status, predicting the effects of management measures, and mitigating the risk of overfishing. The Kobe Plot and the Kobe II Strategy Matrix (K2SM) are widely recognized tools used by international fisheries management organizations, such as Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMOs). Both tools use maximum sustainable yield (MSY) as the central reference point, integrating stock biomass, fishing mortality, and sustainable yield reference points to provide an intuitive, probabilistic analytical framework for scientific evaluation and management decisions.

To scientifically evaluate the sustainable utilization potential of the S. japonicus resource in the Northwest Pacific, this study first established a management baseline. The average annual catch from 2019 to 2024 in this region (352,100 t) was set as the constant future baseline total allowable catch (TAC). The K2SM was then employed to project resource dynamics over future time horizons of 5, 10, 15, and 20 years.

Based on all viable r-K parameter combinations identified from the model fitting process and using the estimated biomass in 2019 (B2019) as the initial stock status, projections were simulated under the constant baseline TAC specified above. For each projection year, the probabilities of two key performance indicators were calculated: (1) the probability that current biomass exceeds the biomass at MSY (Bcur > BMSY), and (2) the probability that the current fishing mortality rate is below the fishing mortality rate at MSY (Fcur < FMSY). BMSY (biomass at MSY), Fn (fishing mortality in projection year n), and FMSY (fishing mortality at MSY) were calculated using the standard Schaefer model equations

All model construction, parameterization, and projection simulations in this study were conducted using R software version 4.0.3 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria, 2020) [[26](#B26-fishes-11-00276)].

The assessment based on the most recent six years of data indicates that the S. japonicus stock is currently overfished. The ratio of length at first capture to optimal length at first capture (Lc/Lc-opt) ranged from 0.60 to 0.84. With the exception of a lower value in 2021 (0.60), this ratio remained between 0.75 and 0.84 in other years. The ratio has shown a year-on-year increase since 2021, reaching its peak (0.84) in 2024. This suggests that under the prevailing fishing pressure, the mean length of captured fish has been relatively well-aligned with the theoretical optimum in most years, and the proportion of large individuals in the population has been increasing.

Resource parameters (fork length, biomass, fishing pressure, etc.) and stock status exhibited significant interannual fluctuations from 2019 to 2024. The asymptotic length (Linf) varied between 39.4 cm and 46.0 cm, peaking in 2020 (46.0 cm), reaching its lowest point in 2022 (39.4 cm), and increased to 41.2 cm in 2024. This overall pattern shows no clear long-term trend, indicating no fundamental shift in the population’s growth potential. The trends for relative biomass (B/B0) and biomass relative to the level at maximum sustainable yield (B/BMSY) were highly congruent. The ratios F/M (fishing to natural mortality) and F/K showed a significant negative correlation with biomass estimates. The stock was assessed as healthy in 2019, 2021, and 2022, indicating sufficient biomass and controlled fishing pressure. It was classified as overfished in 2020 due to elevated, though not critically high, fishing pressure. In 2024, despite some signs of recovery (relative biomass B/B0 increased from 0.09 in 2023 to 0.22 in 2024, [Table 3](#table_body_display_fishes-11-00276-t003)), the stock was assessed as overfished owing to high fishing mortality.

The annual LBB assessments for 2019–2024 revealed pronounced interannual variability in stock status indicators. Specifically, years 2020, 2023, and 2024 showed low B/B0 and high F/M, indicating states ranging from overfished to severely overfished. In contrast, adjacent years (2019, 2021, and 2022) were assessed as healthy. Such sharp reversals in status over short periods are unlikely to be attributed solely to true population dynamics. They are more plausibly influenced by sampling error inherent in single-year length-frequency data, interannual environmental perturbations, and other stochastic noise.

To enhance the robustness of the assessment, this study further conducted LBB analyses by pooling length-frequency data across consecutive two-year periods. This approach mitigates the impact of short-term fluctuations by increasing the effective sample size. The results from the pooled data present a more coherent temporal trend: the stock remained healthy (B/BMSY > 1) during the periods 2019–2020 and 2021–2022. However, a significant deterioration occurred in the 2023–2024 period, with B/BMSY dropping to 0.51, classifying the stock as overfished.

### 3.2. Catch-MSY

The assessment results for chub mackerel under the baseline scenario using the Catch-MSY model are presented in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004). The model estimates the MSY to be 278,000 t (95% confidence interval: 162,000 t to 475,000 t) ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)a). This suggests that a stable annual catch of approximately 300,000 t is sustainable without jeopardizing the population, and this estimate is considered reliable. [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)b illustrates the viable combinations of the intrinsic growth rate (r) and carrying capacity (K) identified by the model filtering process. The feasible parameter pairs are concentrated in a region of relatively low r and high K, showing a clear negative correlation between the two parameters. The posterior distribution for K is relatively narrow compared to the broader posterior distribution for r, which covers much of its prior range. The negative correlation between r and K is further evidenced in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)c, where ln(K) decreases with increasing ln(r). This indicates that changes in r and K jointly influence the estimated MSY. The posterior probability density distributions for r, K, and MSY under the specified prior for K are shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)d–f, which include the 95% confidence intervals. [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)d shows that the posterior density for r peaks at 0.2 (95% CI: 0.06–0.7), confirming that the intrinsic growth rate for S. japonicus in the study area is generally moderate, with most probable values lying within this central range. The frequency distribution for K ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)e) shows a peak at 5,406,100 t (95% CI: 2,355,000 t to 12,410,500 t). The increasing posterior frequency of K toward the upper bound suggests that the prior upper limit (100 × CMAX) was not restrictive, and the model could not precisely estimate an upper carrying capacity. This reflects the data-limited nature of the assessment; however, the MSY estimate remained within a relatively narrow 95% CI, indicating that MSY is more reliably estimated than K alone ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_fishes-11-00276-f004)f). The increasing frequency with higher K values suggests that the population’s maximum theoretical carrying capacity under natural conditions is approximately 5.4 million tonnes, and environmental capacity tends to be relatively high in most scenarios.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1. LBB Model

As a small pelagic fish with a short life cycle and rapid population turnover [[32](#B32-fishes-11-00276)], the biomass of S. japonicus is susceptible to the combined effects of environmental factors and fishing pressure. In recent years, rising sea surface temperatures have forced a northward shift in adult distribution, while larval survival rates are constrained by changes in ocean circulation and thermohaline conditions [[33](#B33-fishes-11-00276),[34](#B34-fishes-11-00276)]. Methodologically, research on the growth patterns of S. japonicus remains limited due to difficulties in data acquisition [[35](#B35-fishes-11-00276)]. Traditional age-structured assessment models are often hampered by insufficient data. In contrast, growth parameters, which are among the most accessible foundational data [[36](#B36-fishes-11-00276)], allow the corresponding length structure to effectively reflect the true age composition of the population [[15](#B15-fishes-11-00276)]. The von Bertalanffy growth equation, characterized by its parsimonious parameters and clear biological interpretation, not only fits fish growth processes with few parameters but has also been widely applied in various fishery stock assessment models, demonstrating its utility under data-limited conditions.

The Length-based Bayesian Biomass (LBB) estimator is a fisheries stock assessment method based on a Bayesian statistical framework. By analyzing length-frequency data from catches and incorporating prior life-history information such as asymptotic length and growth coefficient, it infers key population parameters including total mortality, optimal length at first capture, and biomass status. A key advantage of this method is its adaptability to data-poor assessment scenarios. It relies solely on short time-series of length-composition data, eliminating the need for complex information like age determination or fishing effort, thereby significantly lowering the technical threshold for resource assessment [[24](#B24-fishes-11-00276)]. Consequently, the LBB model is particularly suitable for fish populations like S. japonicus, which exhibit smaller body sizes and younger age structures, enabling it to capture the dynamics of their population structure with reasonable accuracy. Given that the length-frequency data for S. japonicus in recent years showed an asymmetric distribution pattern, this study selected the LBB model—an assessment tool designed for data-limited fisheries—to provide a reasonable evaluation of the resource status of North Pacific S. japonicus and offer management advice. The FAO has incorporated LBB into its Guidelines for the Assessment of Data-Limited Fisheries Resources, endorsing it as a key tool for fisheries management in developing countries [[19](#B19-fishes-11-00276)]. The NPFC has utilized the LBB model in managing North Pacific armorhead (Pseudopentaceros richardsoni) to inform dynamic mesh-size regulations [[5](#B5-fishes-11-00276)].

The Linf for S. japonicus estimated in this study was 45.7 cm. To enhance the precision of the LBB model, this value was used as a fixed prior input parameter in the model computations. The assessment based on the LBB model indicated that the Lc/Lc-opt ratio for North Pacific S. japonicus exceeded 0.75 in most years, both in the annual assessments for the recent six years and in the analyses of pooled biennial length-frequency data. Conversely, the relative biomass indicators (B/BMSY and B/B0) derived from the pooled biennial data did not show significant improvement. Specifically, B/B0 values were generally poor, mostly below 0.5. Only in 2021 and 2022 did the values reach 0.8 and 0.67, respectively, while in other years they did not exceed this threshold. Overall, the model results indicate a deteriorating trend in the resource status of North Pacific S. japonicus in recent years.

However, over the last three years, the stock status has transitioned from good to overfished, presenting an overall concerning trend. Fishing mortality, with the exception of 2021 and 2022, has been relatively high in most years, indicating that current fishing intensity exerts a significant overall impact on the resource structure. These results also underscore the effective assessment capability of the LBB model even in scenarios with limited catch and biological data.

This study provides a supplementary assessment of the North Pacific S. japonicus resource status based on recently acquired length-frequency data. The LBB model analysis indicates that during 2021–2022, several parameters, including B/B0, F/FMSY, and Lc/Lc-opt showed temporary positive trends, suggesting a potential phase of stock recovery during that period. This scientific article, published in the journal *Fishes* (Volume 11, Issue 5, 2026, Article 276), assesses the stock status and management implications for chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the North Pacific Ocean. The study was conducted by researchers from the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Shanghai Ocean University, Anhui Normal University, and the Wenchang Innovation Research Center.

**Authors:** Sisi Huang, Famou Zhang, Heng Zhang (corresponding author), Ming Gao, and Kangbo Li.

**Study Methods:** The research integrates two data-limited stock assessment models: (1) the Length-based Bayesian Biomass (LBB) estimator, using length-frequency data from 6,061 chub mackerel specimens sampled from light purse seine fisheries on the high seas of the North Pacific (38°00′N–46°00′N, 147°00′E–162°00′E) during April–December 2019–2024; and (2) the Catch-MSY model, using historical catch data from 1995 to 2024. Management implications were analyzed using the Kobe plot and Kobe II Strategy Matrix (K2SM).

**Key Results:**
1. The LBB model revealed significant interannual variability in stock status. The stock was within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, but suffered overfishing in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Pooled two-year data analysis showed that B/BMSY dropped to 0.51 during 2023–2024, reflecting marked stock deterioration.
2. The Catch-MSY model estimated MSY at 278,000 t (95% CI: 162,000–475,000 t). The estimated intrinsic growth rate (r) peaked at 0.2 (95% CI: 0.06–0.7), and carrying capacity (K) peaked at 5,406,100 t (95% CI: 2,355,000–12,410,500 t).
3. The Kobe plot showed only 23.2% probability of a healthy stock state in the final assessment year. Probabilities of recruitment-overfished, fishing-overfished, and severely overfished were 37.6%, 14.9%, and 24.3%, respectively. With B/BMSY < 1 and F/FMSY < 1, the final-year stock status was diagnosed as recruitment overfishing.
4. Management recommendations: TAC should be set at 60–80% of the baseline TAC (352,100 t) during the medium-term (5–10 years), corresponding to 211,300–281,700 t. Long-term TAC could be gradually increased to MSY levels if the stock recovers.

**Context:** Chub mackerel is a priority species managed by the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC). The study notes that fishing mortality exceeded natural mortality in recent years (F/M > 1.5), making fishing pressure the primary driver of overfishing. Notably, new regulations effective 2025 have reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). The findings contrast with earlier research (Zhao, based on 2016–2021 data) that suggested the stock was in good condition, indicating a recent transition to overfished status.

Although the stock was within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, it suffered from overfishing or was heavily overfished in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Notably, integrated data analysis indicated that during 2023–2024, the B/BMSY ratio dropped to 0.51, reflecting a marked deterioration in the stock condition."

Краткое описание

The effects of temperature and prey density on the recent growth rate (RGR) of chub mackerel, Scomber japonicus, were examined. Scomber spp. larvae and juveniles were collected along the Boso–Kashimanada Pacific coast in Japan between March and July in 2015 and 2016. Larvae and juveniles identified as S. japonicus using DNA were subjected to stomach-content and otolith-increment analyses. The effects of temperature and prey density on RGR were analyzed using a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM), which showed that temperature positively affected the RGR of larvae in the body length (BL) classes < 5 mm, 5–7 mm, 7–9 mm and 9–11 mm. Prey density also affected growth in the < 5 mm, 5–7 mm, 7–9 mm and > 11 mm classes and effects of prey density on RGR for larger (> 11 mm) larvae and juveniles were stronger than those for smaller (< 9 mm) larvae. S. japonicus larvae transform into juveniles at around 12 mm BL, and the increased feed demands of juveniles likely lead to prey-density-dependent growth. The otolith increment widths of larvae and juveniles were significantly narrower than those during the same stages in 1-year-old S. japonicus collected from purse seine fisheries operated in the Joban or Kashimanada areas, suggesting growth-dependent mortality.

args.summary:
This is a journal article page from Colab (colab.ws) documenting the publication "Effects of water temperature and prey density on recent growth of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus larvae and juveniles along the Pacific coast of Boso–Kashimanada" published in Fisheries Science (Springer Nature), Volume 85, Issue 6, pages 931-942, on September 7, 2019. The authors are Makoto Taga, Yasuhiro Kamimura, and Yoh Yamashita. DOI: 10.1007/s12562-019-01354-8.

The study examined the effects of temperature and prey density on the recent growth rate (RGR) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) larvae and juveniles. Specimens were collected along the Boso–Kashimanada Pacific coast of Japan between March and July in 2015 and 2016. Larvae and juveniles were identified as S. japonicus using DNA analysis, then subjected to stomach-content and otolith-increment analyses. A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) was used to analyze the effects of temperature and prey density on RGR.

Key findings: Temperature positively affected RGR of larvae in body length (BL) classes <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and 9-11mm. Prey density affected growth in the <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and >11mm classes, with effects of prey density on RGR being stronger for larger (>11mm) larvae and juveniles than for smaller (<9mm) larvae. S. japonicus larvae transform into juveniles at around 12mm BL, and the increased feed demands of juveniles likely lead to prey-density-dependent growth. Otolith increment widths of collected larvae and juveniles were significantly narrower than those of 1-year-old S. japonicus from purse seine fisheries in the Joban or Kashimanada areas, suggesting growth-dependent mortality.

The article has 29 total citations, with 7 citations from 2025 (24.14%). The most-citing journal is Frontiers in Marine Science (4 citations, 13.79%) and the most-citing publisher is Springer Nature (9 publications, 31.03%). Abstract This study contrasts diet composition patterns of larval fish categorized as strong and weak foragers, identified from quadratic relationships between larval length and the number of prey eaten, for 11 fish species. Two sets of alternative hypotheses test whether strong foragers (1) exhibit precocious behaviour by eating later developmental stages of copepods, and (2) take advantage of random encounters with zooplankton, based on the contrast between the two categories in each 1 mm length-class. Results indicate that strong foragers shift their feeding toward earlier copepod developmental stages, which was most apparent in four flatfish species, and demonstrate stronger overall prey selectivity than weak foragers. ##### [Climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index of chub mackerel in the spawning season and its effect on the abundance](/en/works/lDXVPNLl/)

Journal Article Scopus WoS   [Crossref: 14](/en/?backlinks_to=10.3389/fmars.2022.996626)

Liangming Wang, Shuyang Ma, Yang Liu, Jianchao Li, Dianrong Sun, Yongjun Tian

Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) is widely distributed in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and is utilized by China, Korea, and Japan in different seasons and areas. Generally, chub mackerel is divided into Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) and Pacific stocks based on its different distribution, migration, and life-history traits. The two stocks showed obvious interannual to decadal variability in abundance with evident different variation patterns. Chub mackerel has extensive spawning areas in the northwestern Pacific Ocean, with the main spawning period from March to June, and the suitable spawning SST (sea surface temperature) ranging from 15°C to 22°C. To explore the temperature effects on different variations of the two stocks, we estimated the average temperature suitability index (TSI) for chub mackerel in main spawning areas during the spawning period from March to June based on the relationship between the probability of spawning and the specific SST. Results showed that the TSIs in the shelf waters of China seas and the waters of the Tsushima Strait displayed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock, whereas the TSI in the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock. The spatio-temporal variation in spawning temperature suitability may have had an important impact on the recovery of the Pacific stock after the 2000s. We also found that there is a non-stationary relationship between chub mackerel abundance and TSI, which is driven by climate variabilities such as the Siberian High and the Aleutian Low. Moreover, TWC stock showed non-stationary relationship with TSI, and the threshold years was identified in the 1990s, and the non-stationary relationship between TSI and Pacific stock, with thresholds occurring in the late 1970s. Our research provides a reasonable explanation for the variations in the two stocks and their responses to TSI variability and offers an improved understanding of the climate-induced non-stationary relationships between chub mackerel abundance and physical drivers.

## Abstract

The density dependence of growth and body condition have important impacts on fish population dynamics and fisheries management. Although population density is known to affect the temperature of the habitat selected, how this affects the density dependence of growth and body condition remains unclear. Here, we investigated annual changes in body condition, habitat temperature, and cohort-specific growth of chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_) in the western North Pacific and examined quarterly changes in the density dependence of body condition. We hypothesized that chub mackerel body condition is affected both directly (e.g., through competition for food) and indirectly (through changes in habitat temperature) by the abundance of both conspecifics (i.e., chub mackerel) and heterospecifics (the Japanese sardine _Sardinops melanostictus_). Indeed, chub mackerel body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific abundance. Mean annual growth rates in chub mackerel were positively corelated with body condition. The best model showed that conspecific and/or heterospecific abundance had strong negative effects on chub mackerel body condition in all seasons, and influenced habitat temperature in some seasons. By contrast, temperature effects on body condition were weak. Therefore, direct effects likely have more impact than indirect effects on density-dependent body condition and growth.

## Introduction

Density-dependent processes are fundamental to fish population dynamics ([Rose _et al._, 2001](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-52); [Andersen _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-3)). Growth, survival, movement, and reproduction are all affected by population density, and can contribute to a decrease or increase in population growth rate at high or low densities ([Rose _et al._, 2001](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-52)). In general, density-dependent mortality is a dominant factor in fish population dynamics in the early juvenile stage, and density-dependent growth becomes dominant in the late juvenile and adult stages ([Lorenzen and Enberg, 2002](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-40); [Lorenzen, 2008](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-41); [Van Gemert and Andersen, 2018](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-66); [Zimmermann _et al._, 2018](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-81)). Although the density dependence of recruitment is a stronger regulator of fish population size, the density dependence of growth affects productivity and catch composition and may be particularly important for fisheries management ([Zimmermann _et al._, 2018](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-81)). In addition, rapid changes in fish population density and the subsequent drastic changes in growth and maturation often complicate stock assessment and fisheries forecasting ([Eero _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-14)). There is an urgent need to understand the density dependence of growth to inform effective management decisions.

As with growth, body condition is often used as a proxy of individual fitness, as it reflects the size of individual energy reserves. Many studies have sought to identify determinants of body condition, such as conspecific and heterospecific density, temperature, prey availability, and fishing impacts, as a way to understand fish population dynamics ([Rueda _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-53); [Brosset _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-8)). It is widely accepted that fish body condition can affect growth, reproductive potential, and survival ([Blackwell _et al._, 2000](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-6); [Lloret _et al._, 2002](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-38)) and is an important data point for stock assessment and fisheries management ([Blackwell _et al._, 2000](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-6); [Dahl _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-13)).

Temperature is one of the most important abiotic factors for fish growth and body condition ([Houde, 1989](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-20); [Rueda _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-53)). Many studies have considered temperature to be a density-independent factor when examining its effects on growth and body condition ([Brunel and Dickey-Collas, 2010](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-9); [Casini _et al._, 2011](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-10), [2016](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-11); [Brosset _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-7); [Cormon _et al._, 2016](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-12)). However, because the temperature of habitats selected by fish can vary with population density ([Swain and Kramer, 1995](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-60)), population density can indirectly affect growth and body condition through changes in habitat temperature. In addition, this indirect effect can vary with season. Comprehensive analyses of the effect of density-dependent changes in habitat temperature on growth and body condition, and how these effects change over the seasons, are required to properly understand the process of density dependence.

Chub mackerel (_Scomber japonicus_) is widely distributed across the North Pacific and is one of the most productive and economically important fisheries resources in the world, with annual catches reaching ca. 1.5 million metric tons ([FAO, 2020](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-15)). However, the abundance of the Pacific stock of chub mackerel declined in the 1990s and early 2000s ([Yukami _et al._, 2020a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-79)). Since 2013, when a strong year class occurred, its abundance has dramatically increased ([Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#T1)). Although previous studies reported changes in factors such as growth and maturity during the period of population decline ([Watanabe and Yatsu, 2004](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-68), [2006](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-69)), limited information is available for the period of population increase, especially for recent years. In addition, although much attention has been paid to the impact of environmental and endogenous factors (e.g., temperature, food availability, and age/size) on chub mackerel growth in the larval and early juvenile stages ([Hunter and Kimbrell, 1980](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-21); [Sassa and Tsukamoto, 2010](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-54); [Kamimura _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-25); [Higuchi _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-19); [Kaneko _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-27); [Taga _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-62); [Nakamura _et al._, 2020](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-44)), comparatively little research has been conducted on later growth stages ([Parrish and Mallicoate, 1995](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-49); [Watanabe and Yatsu, 2004](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-68); [Yatsu _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-77)).

Chub mackerel mainly spawns in the waters around the Izu islands and the Boso peninsula, Japan ([Figure 1a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F1)) from March to June ([Watanabe and Yatsu, 2006](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-69); [Kanamori _et al._, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-26)). Larvae and early juveniles are transported offshore from April to September by the Kuroshio and Kuroshio extension to a large region in the western North Pacific stretching from the Kuroshio–Oyashio transition region to the Oyashio region, after which juveniles begin to migrate to the coastal waters of northern Japan ([Watanabe and Nishida, 2002](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-67); [Takahashi _et al._, 2014](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-63); [Kamimura _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-25)). Age-1+ mackerel typically migrate northward along the Japanese coast from July to September and southward from October to December ([Watanabe, 1970](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-71); [Usami, 1973](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-65)).

Japanese sardine (_Sardinops melanostictus_) is also an important fishery resource in Japan, and the size of the Pacific stock has been increasing over the past ten years ([Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#T1)). Seasonal changes in its distribution are similar to those of chub mackerel ([Watanabe and Nishida, 2002](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-67); [Yatsu _et al._, 2005](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-75); [Yatsu, 2019](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-78)). The major prey items of juveniles and adults, such as Copepoda, Eupausiidae, Decapoda, and Amphipoda ([Yamashita, 1955](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-73); [Nakai, 1962](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-43); [Kawasaki, 1984](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-29); [Yamamoto and Katayama, 2012](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-72)), overlap with those of late-juvenile and adult chub mackerel ([Sato _et al._, 1975](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-56); [Nakatsuka _et al._, 2010](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-45); [Taga and Yamashita, 2018](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-61)). Therefore, Japanese sardine is a potential competitor of chub mackerel ([Kishida and Matsuda, 1993](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-31); [Yatsu _et al._, 2005](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-75)), and a previous study has indicated that Japanese sardine density has a negative effect on chub mackerel recruitment ([Kishida and Matsuda, 1993](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-31)). However, the mechanisms of inter-specific density dependence of chub mackerel growth and body condition remain unknown.

The principal aim of this study was to clarify the density dependence of growth and body condition of late-juvenile and adult chub mackerel in the Pacific by considering the direct (e.g., through competition for food) and indirect (i.e., through changes in habitat temperature) effects of conspecific and heterospecific density. In addition, we also aimed to identify seasonal changes in density dependence and the drivers of fluctuations in body condition. First, individual size-at-age, relative condition factor, and habitat temperature were estimated to analyze the relationship between mean annual growth rate and mean body condition on a quarterly basis. Second, we used structural equation models (SEMs) to examine the effects of chub mackerel and Japanese sardine abundance, environmental conditions (i.e., the location of the Oyashio Current and the locations of sample capture), and an endogenous factor (age) on body condition and habitat temperature by quarter.

## Materials and methods

### Fish sampling and laboratory procedures

A total of 18,302 chub mackerel landed in fishing ports on the Pacific coast of northern Japan between 2006 and 2019 were used for the study ([Figure 1b](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F1)). Fishing gear included purse seines, dipnets, setnets, and vertical long lines. Most of the samples (12,379 individuals, or 68%) were captured by purse seine fisheries. Fork length (FL) was measured to the nearest 1 mm by using digital calipers. Total weight (TW), gonad weight (GW), and stomach content weight (SCW) were measured to the nearest 0.1 g by using digital scales. Sex was determined by direct gonad observation.

Ages were determined by counting annual rings on scales ([Kondo and Kuroda, 1966](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-34)) or sectioned sagittal otoliths ([Kawashima _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-30)) under electronic microscopes. Previous studies have used gonad observation of mature fish and otolith microstructure analysis of juveniles to reveal that spawning mainly occurs in April ([Watanabe, 2010](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-70); [Kamimura _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-25)). Therefore, we assumed that the hatch date was in April and calculated ages as _t = A + m_/12, where _A_ is age (in years) estimated from scale and otolith observations, and _m_ is the number of months between the catch month and the preceding April.

### Growth analysis

A total of 15,415 fish in the 2006 to 2016 year classes were used for growth analysis. ([Table 2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#T2)). The von Bertalanffy (VB) equation was fitted separately to the FL-at-age data for each year class to estimate cohort-specific growth parameters: ![Image 5: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2021/03/26/2021.03.25.436928/embed/graphic-5.gif) where _L_ _t_, _L_ inf, _K_, and _t_ 0 are FL at age _t_, asymptotic FL, growth coefficient, and hypothetical age at zero FL, respectively. Non-linear least-squares regression was used to estimate these parameters. Initial values were estimated by using the Ford–Walford plot. Sex-specific models were calculated for each year class, and VB growth formulae were compared between males and females within each year class by using the _F_ test.

### Body condition

Relative condition factor (_K n_; [Le cren, 1951](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-36); [Froese, 2006](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-16)) was computed to examine individual fish condition by using 8429 age-1+ chub mackerel from the 2006–2016 year classes (caught from 2007 to 2018 in 510 hauls) whose catch locations were recorded. ![Image 9: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2021/03/26/2021.03.25.436928/embed/graphic-7.gif) where _W_ is body weight (excluding GW and SCW) and _W_ pred is the predicted _W_ from a weight–length relationship of the form: ![Image 11: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2021/03/26/2021.03.25.436928/embed/graphic-8.gif) where _L_ is FL, _a_ is the allometric coefficient between weight and length, and _b_ is the exponent of that relationship. We estimated these parameters by using non-linear least-squares regression.

### Abundance indices of the Pacific stock of chub mackerel and Japanese sardine

Abundances of the Pacific stock of chub mackerel and Japanese sardine were estimated by virtual population analysis from the 1970s to 2018 ([Furuichi _et al._, 2020](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-17); [Yukami _et al._, 2020a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-79)). We used these estimates as abundance indices for this study. As mentioned above, the distributions of age-0 chub mackerel and Japanese sardine are different from those of older individuals; hence, the age-1+ abundances were used as the abundance indices. Age-1+ chub mackerel abundances (_N_ _m_) ranged from 8.5 × 10 9 (2007) to 141.2 × 10 9 individuals (2017), and Japanese sardine abundances (_N_ _s_) ranged from 5.2 × 10 9 (2008) to 313.6 × 10 9 individuals (2018; [Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#T1)). _N_ _m_ increased dramatically in 2014 and reached about 140 × 10 9 individuals. _N_ _s_ gradually increased after 2011 and stabilized at about 300 × 10 9 individuals after 2016.

### Confirmation of overlapping distributions of chub mackerel and Japanese sardine by comparing catch locations

To confirm the distributional overlap of chub mackerel and Japanese sardine in recent years, we compared mackerel (chub and spotted mackerel, _S. australasicus,_ were combined) and Japanese sardine catch locations by season by using catch reports of purse seine fisheries made by the Japan Fisheries Agency from 2010 to 2017.

### Habitat temperature

Seasonal changes in the vertical distribution of chub mackerel were reported in previous studies ([Usami, 1973](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-65); [Sato, 1974](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-55)). Hence, we examined mean monthly habitat depths based on 266 school-depth records from fishing vessel logbooks recorded by the North Pacific district purse seine fishery for 2008–2019. Mean monthly school depths showed that mackerel habitat was deeper in winter (November to February) than in summer (May to August; [Figure 2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F2)).

We used the temperatures at which chub mackerel had been caught (TC) as a proxy for habitat temperature in this study. Temperature data were obtained from reanalysis data of the Regional Ocean Modelling System (ROMS) developed by the Japan Fisheries and Education Agency (FRA) for fisheries science (FRA-ROMS; [Kuroda _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-35)). Temperatures were estimated by using fishing locations and dates recorded in the logbooks. FRA-ROMS provides averaged daily temperatures at 1/10-degree scale at depths of 0, 10, 30, 50, 75, 100, and 200 m in the Kuroshio–Oyashio region. Therefore, we extracted temperatures for the depths provided by FRA-ROMS that were closest to the mean monthly school depths estimated above (i.e., 75 m in January and February; 50 m in March, November, and December; 30 m in April, September, and October; and 10 m in May, June, July, and August) ([Figure 2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F2)).

### The First Oyashio Intrusion

The Oyashio Current is a western boundary current of western subpolar gyre in the North Pacific ([Qiu, 2001](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-50)) that transports cold, low-salinity subarctic water together with chemical and organic matter along the Kuril, Hokkaido, and Honshu (the main island in the Japanese archipelago) islands ([Figure 1a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F1)). The southward current on the continental slope along the east coast of Honshu is referred to as the First Oyashio Intrusion (FOI), and plays an important role in the supply of nutrients and copepods to the region ([Shimizu _et al._, 2009](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-57); [Kuroda _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-35)). Therefore, the FOI could potentially impact the growth and body condition of fisheries species. In this study, the southernmost position of the FOI (the SFOI) was determined from FRA-ROMS reanalysis data by using a procedure described in previous studies ([Murakami, 1994](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-42); [Kuroda _et al._, 2017](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-35)). We defined the SFOI as the point at which the southward convex locations of the 5-°C isotherm at a depth of 100 m (as calculated from approximately 10-d means) was the closest to the coast of Honshu. SFOIs were averaged for each month during 2006–2018.

### Statistical analysis

The piecewise SEM ([Lefcheck, 2016](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-37)) was used to investigate the effects of biotic and abiotic factors on the body condition of age-1+ chub mackerel. Classical SEMs assume that all observations are independent and that all variables are normally distributed. By contrast, in the piecewise SEM, the path diagram is translated to a set of linear equations and parameters are calculated by solving each equation separately; hence, the piecewise SEM can include random effects and distributions of various shapes ([Lefcheck, 2016](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-37)). We developed an _a priori_ SEM (Figure S1) by using previous studies to parameterize the relationships between fish condition factor (_K_ _n_), chub mackerel abundance (_N_ _m_), Japanese sardine abundance (_N_ _s_), age (_A_), the southernmost position of the FOI (SFOI), habitat temperature (TC), catch latitude (Lat), and catch longitude (Lon) ([Parrish and Mallicoate, 1995](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-49); [Watanabe and Yatsu, 2004](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-68)). We hypothesized that these causal variables affect body condition indirectly through TC, as well as directly. Because monthly mackerel condition factor and temperature are most closely correlated at short lag times (i.e., a lag of 0 or 1 month) ([Parrish and Mallicoate, 1995](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-49)), TC was used as a causal variable for _K_ _n_ in this study. Piecewise SEMs were constructed for each quarter starting in April, with the quarters defined as follows: Q1, April to June; Q2, July to September; Q3, October to December; and Q4, January to March. We assumed Q1 as the spawning season, Q2 as the season for the northward feeding migration, Q3 as the season for the southward migration, and Q4 as the pre-spawning season, based on previous studies of seasonal distribution ([Watanabe, 1970](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-71); [Usami, 1973](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-65)) and reproductive surveys of chub mackerel ([Watanabe and Yatsu, 2006](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-69)). The goodness-of-fit of each model was evaluated using Shipley’s d-separation test ([Shipley, 2000](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-58), [2009](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-59)), which tests the assumption that all variables are conditionally independent, and we considered the final SEM consistent with the data if Fisher’s _C_ statistic was _p_> 0.05. The model with the lowest Bayesian information criterion (BIC) was considered the final model; BIC is appropriate for confirmatory analyses and for finding the correct model ([Aho _et al._, 2014](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-1)). Standardized path coefficient estimates were calculated for each path model.

To construct the piecewise SEM, the _K_ _n_ model and TC model were separately fitted with individual regressions by using linear mixed models (LMMs). For the _K_ _n_ model, _K_ _n_ was used as a response variable; _N_ _m_, _N_ _s_, TC, _A_, SFOI, Lat, and Lon were used as explanatory variables; and sex (male, female, and unidentified) and haul ID (a categorical variable) were included as random variables. For the TC models, TC was used as a response variable; _N_ _m_, _N_ _s_, _A_ _t_, SFOI, Lat, and Lon were used as explanatory variables; and sex was included as a random variable. The multicollinearity of models was checked by calculating a variance inflation factor for each explanatory variable. Collinearity was assessed with a cut-off value of 5 ([James _et al._, 2013](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-23)); as a result, _N_ _s_ and Lon were eliminated from the models in Q1 and Lon was eliminated in Q4.

To examine whether chub mackerel body condition was related to _G_ _L_, relationships between mean _K_ _n_ in each quarter and _G_ _L_-at-age were analyzed by using LMMs. We used _G_ _L_ for ages 1–5 as a response variable and mean _K_ _n_ by age as explanatory variables with age as a random intercept. A likelihood-ratio test was conducted to examine the significance of _K_ _n_ in this analysis.

All statistical tests were performed in R v. 3.6.3 ([R Core Team, 2020](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-51)). VB parameters were estimated by using the package _FSA_ ([Ogle _et al._, 2020](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-47)). Piecewise SEMs were constructed with the package _piecewiseSEM_ ([Lefcheck, 2016](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-37)), and LMMs were analyzed with the package _lme4_ ([Bates _et al._, 2015](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-4)).

## Results

Chub mackerel was caught mainly from January to June in the waters offshore of the central Japanese archipelago between 34°N and 39°N ([Figure 1b](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F1)). During summer (July to September), catch locations were mainly in northern waters between 37°N and 43°N, and after October, they moved southward. The catch locations of mackerels (i.e., chub and spotted mackerel) and Japanese sardine in purse seine fisheries followed similar seasonal patterns and overlapped from 2010 to 2017 (Figure S2). We used catch data on chub mackerel ([Yukami _et al._, 2020a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-79)) and spotted mackerel ([Yukami _et al._, 2020b](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#ref-80)) to calculate the percentage of chub mackerel in the total mackerel catch in the Pacific stock. The percentages for each study year were 2010, 40.4%; 2011, 36.1%; 2012, 47.8%; 2013, 67.0%; 2014, 71.6%; 2015, 84.5%; 2016, 90.7%; and 2017, 93.6%. We estimated that most of the catches from 2010 to 2017 were in fact chub mackerel.

The mean monthly SFOI changed seasonally, with high latitudes in October–January followed by a rapid transition to low latitudes ([Figure 3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F3)). The highest (farthest north) SFOI was observed in December 2015 (42°4’N), and the lowest (farthest south) in March 2017 (37°4’N).

Monthly changes in the southernmost position of the First Oyashio Intrusion from January 2006 to December 2018.

The FLs of individuals used in the VB growth formulae ranged from 121 to 470 mm, and ages ranged from 0.2 to 11.1 years. VB growth formulae were fitted to each year class by sex. We found significant differences between male and female formulae in the 2008, 2009, and 2013 year classes (Figure S3 and Table S1). However, differences by sex in these year classes were small after age 1; therefore, we combined data from males, females, and individuals of unidentified sex to establish VB growth formulae for each year class.

Estimates of _L_ _inf_, _K_, and _t_ 0 ranged from 339.9 (for the 2016 year class) to 440.5 (the 2006 year class), from 0.25 (for the 2015 year class) to 0.55 (the 2012 year class), and from −2.88 (for the 2011 year class) to −1.26 (the 2007 year class), respectively ([Table 2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#T2)). _G_ _L_ ranges were 29.6–51.2 at age 1, 20.8–33.3 at age 2, 13.4–25.6 at age 3, 7.7–19.6 at age 4, and 4.4–15.1 at age 5 (Table S2). The estimated FLs were especially high for the 2007–2011 year classes and low for the 2013–2016 year classes, with the 2012 year class showing intermediate growth ([Figure 4](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F4) and Table S2). The _G_ _L_ s of 2012 year class were lower after age 2 than the other year classes (Table S2).

The weight–length relationship was estimated as _W_ = 1.09 × 10−6 _L_ 3.41. Values of _K_ _n_ followed a generally downward trend in recent years and were lower in Q1 among older individuals and higher in Q3 and Q4 ([Figure 5a](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.03.25.436928.full#F5) and Tables S3 and S4). This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2021.03.25.436928) titled "Intra- and inter-specific density dependence of body condition, growth, and habitat temperature in chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus)" by Yasuhiro Kamimura, Makoto Taga, Ryuji Yukami, Chikako Watanabe, and Sho Furuichi (Japan Fisheries Research and Education Agency). It has since been published in ICES Journal of Marine Science (doi: 10.1093/icesjms/fsab191).

**Research Question & Hypothesis:** The study investigated how conspecific (chub mackerel) and heterospecific (Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanostictus) abundance affects body condition, growth, and habitat temperature in chub mackerel in the western North Pacific. The authors hypothesized that body condition is affected both directly (competition for food) and indirectly (through changes in habitat temperature) by population density.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific abundance.
- Mean annual growth rates were positively correlated with body condition in all four quarters (Q1: χ²=34.6, p<0.001; Q2: χ²=7.23, p=0.007; Q3: χ²=6.50, p=0.011; Q4: χ²=4.83, p=0.028).
- The best structural equation model (SEM) showed that conspecific and/or heterospecific abundance had strong negative effects on body condition in all seasons, and influenced habitat temperature in some seasons, but temperature effects on body condition were weak.
- Direct effects (food competition) likely have more impact than indirect effects (habitat temperature changes) on density-dependent body condition and growth.

**Methodology:**
- 18,302 chub mackerel landed in fishing ports on the Pacific coast of northern Japan (2006–2019) were sampled; 68% from purse seine fisheries.
- 15,415 fish from 2006–2016 year classes used for growth analysis with von Bertalanffy growth equations.
- 8,429 age-1+ fish used for relative condition factor (Kn) analysis.
- Habitat temperature estimated using FRA-ROMS ocean model reanalysis data.
- Piecewise structural equation models (SEMs) with linear mixed models used for statistical analysis, applied quarterly (Q1 spawning, Q2 northward feeding migration, Q3 southward migration, Q4 pre-spawning).
- Age-1+ chub mackerel abundance ranged from 8.5×10⁹ (2007) to 141.2×10⁹ individuals (2017); Japanese sardine abundance ranged from 5.2×10⁹ (2008) to 313.6×10⁹ individuals (2018).
- Weight-length relationship: W = 1.09 × 10⁻⁶ L³.⁴¹.
- VB parameter estimates: Linf ranged 339.9–440.5, K ranged 0.25–0.55, t0 ranged −2.88 to −1.26.

**Context:**
Chub mackerel is a globally important fishery resource with annual catches around 1.5 million metric tons. The Pacific stock declined in the 1990s–early 2000s but dramatically increased after a strong 2013 year class. Japanese sardine, a potential competitor with overlapping prey (Copepoda, Eupausiidae, Decapoda, Amphipoda) and distributions, has also increased over the past decade. This study addresses gaps in understanding density-dependent processes during periods of population increase.

## ORIGINAL RESEARCH article

Front. Mar. Sci., 27 April 2022

Sec. Marine Fisheries, Aquaculture and Living Resources

Volume 9 - 2022 | <https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2022.856483>

# Impacts of Morphological Characteristics on Target Strength of Chub Mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the Northwest Pacific Ocean

Jianfeng Tong 1,2,3,4\*

Minghua Xue 1

Zhenhong Zhu 1

Weiqi Wang 1

Siquan Tian 1,2,3,4

1. College of Marine Sciences, Shanghai Ocean University, Shanghai, China

2. National Engineering Research Center for Oceanic Fisheries, Shanghai Ocean University, Shanghai, China

3. Key Laboratory of Sustainable Exploitation of Oceanic Fisheries Resources, Ministry of Education, Shanghai, China

4. Key Laboratory of Oceanic Fisheries Exploration, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Shanghai, China

Article metrics

## Abstract

Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is an important commercial fish in the Northwest Pacific Ocean. Accurate target strength (*TS*) underpins acoustic stock assessment but the *TS* of *S. japonicus* is still poorly understood. In this study, the Kirchhoff-ray mode (KRM) model was used to estimate the *TS* of *S. japonicus* and its relationship with sound wave frequency and fish morphology. The results revealed that *TS* values varied with pitch angle shifts, with the impact on fish scattering strength being greater at higher frequency. This is less important because 38 kHz has been used for the biomass assessment of these fish resources. At frequencies of 38 kHz, 70 kHz, 120 kHz and 200 kHz, *TS* was greatest at a pitch angle range of -10° to 0°, which was related to the angle of the swim bladder tilt. There were almost no differences between *TS* estimated using the measured pitch angle distributions and using the universal distribution. When the measured pitch angle was *N*[-3°,4°], the average *TS* of *S. japonicus* with body length of 12.04–22.17 cm at four frequencies was -48.88 dB, -49.14 dB, -49.75 dB and -48.55 dB, respectively. The regression intercept (*b20*) in *TS*–body length equation was -73.27 dB, -73.56 dB, -74.18 dB and -73.46 dB, respectively. Variation in *TS* range at 0–300 m depth was about 10 dB. The simulated broadband target strength spectrum shows the scattering characteristics of individuals with different swim bladder length between 0–250 kHz. These results could be used for identification of *S. japonicus* in echograms and provide reference for acoustic stock assessment of *S. japonicus* in the Northwest Pacific Ocean.

## Introduction

The Northwest Pacific Ocean has abundant fishery resources (Chiba et al., 2009; Miyamoto et al., 2020). As the most productive marine fishery area in the world, total catches in this area reached 20.06 million tons in 2018, accounting for 23.76% of total marine catches (FAO, 2020). Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is a warm-water pelagic fish. As one of the most economically important fish species in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, it plays an important role in the marine fisheries of China, Japan, and South Korea. Total global catch of *S. japonicus* was 1.56 million tons in 2018, accounting for 2% of total marine catches (FAO, 2020). However, *S. japonicus* biomass has declined sharply since 1997 and has remained low over the past few decades (Takahashi et al., 2014). To develop appropriate fishery management measures and sustainably use *S. japonicus* resources, it is necessary to assess its biomass accurately.

Underwater acoustic surveys can provide high-resolution information in large-scale bodies of water and are widely used in monitoring behavior of marine organisms (Muñoz et al., 2020), habitat distribution research (Zhang et al., 2020), and stock assessment (Stierhoff et al., 2019; Escobar-Flores et al., 2020). Target strength (*TS*) is a key parameter used to identify species in the echogram and convert the echo signal into biomass. *TS* varies between species and is affected by many factors including swim bladder characteristics (Foote, 1980), body size (Lu et al., 2011), swimming pitch angle (Horne, 2003), water depth (Mukai and Iida, 1996), and incident sound wave frequency (Foote, 1982). Therefore, it is very important to correctly identify target species, estimate their *TS*, and understand the factors that affect *TS* variation to accurately assess stocks of marine fish.

Estimation methods of *TS* mainly include *in situ*, *ex situ*, and theoretical models (Sobradillo et al., 2021). The *in situ* method records the *TS* of fish in their natural environment. This method requires the target fish to be discretely distributed and single-species (Simmonds and MacLennan, 2005). However, these conditions are difficult to satisfy, especially in mixed species aggregations. The *ex situ* method measures the *TS* of target fish in an artificial acoustic experimental arena; however, the experimental arena is challenging to set up and has poor flexibility. Theoretical models approximate the main source of acoustic scattering to a regular geometric model based on scattering theories and biological characteristics of the fish. Then, computer simulations are used to estimate *TS*. Because the model method is simple, flexible and low-cost, it could enable the study of the factors affecting *TS* (Hazen and Horne, 2003). Additionally, theoretical models could improve the ability to identify and classify targets in echograms (Jech and Horne, 2002) and reduce the uncertainty of stock assessment (Khodabandeloo et al., 2021).

The Kirchhoff-ray mode (KRM) model could simulate the process of sound waves from seawater into the body and swim bladder of fish. It uses low-mode solutions and Kirchhoff-ray approximations to estimate resonant and geometric backscatter from the body and swim bladder of fish (Gauthier and Horne, 2004). The results of the KRM model are consistent with those of *in situ* and *ex situ* methods (Horne, 2003; Kang et al., 2004; Kusdinar et al., 2014). Some researchers have used the KRM model to study the effects of different factors on *TS*. For example, Hazen and Horne (2003) used KRM to determine that pitch angle and frequency had greater effects on walleye pollock (*Theragra chalcogramma*) *TS* compared to length, while depth had the least effect. Gauthier and Horne (2004) established the *TS*–length equation for five pelagic fish species in the Bering Sea and the Gulf of Alaska.

The purpose of this study was to estimate the impacts of morphological characteristics on the *TS* of *S. japonicus* in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, so as to improve the acoustic stock assessment accuracy. First, the morphological characteristics of the swim bladder and its changes with fish growth were described based on X-ray images. Then, the KRM model was used to calculate the*TS* of *S. japonicus* and to analyze variation in *TS* with fish body and swim bladder shape at different frequencies. Four common frequencies used in acoustic fishery surveys, including 38 kHz, 70 kHz, 120 kHz and 200 kHz, were selected. Finally, a broadband *TS* spectrum was produced by simulating the variation of *TS* with frequency in the range of 0–250 kHz. Our work could provide a scientific basis for signal identification of *S. japonicus* in echograms and provide reference for acoustic stock assessment of *S. japonicus* in the Northwest Pacific Ocean.

## Materials and Methods

### Field Sampling

Samples were obtained from 147°E–165°E, 33°N–44°N in the Northwest Pacific Ocean by the Shanghai Ocean University research vessel (RV) Songhang. The survey was conducted from June 18 to August 7, 2021 using a four-panel midwater trawl with a mean speed of 4.6 knots. Samples were frozen in seawater immediately after being captured and stored in plastic bottles at -20°C onboard the research vessel.

### Morphological Measurements

One month after capture, frozen samples were transferred to the laboratory. There, the bottles were slowly thawed in cold water over a period of 20 h to minimize any changes in swim bladder shape (Yasuma et al., 2010). After the length and weight measurements of samples were recorded, a specialized MIKASA HF100HA X-ray imaging system, with input voltage of AC220 V maximum tube voltage of 100 kV, and maximum tube current of 40 mA, was used to map the outlines of each fish. Both lateral and dorsal aspects from 18 individuals were X-rayed. Morphological parameters of each sample were measured as shown in [**Figure 1**](#f1), including body length (*BL*), body height (*BH*), body width (*BW*), swim bladder length (*SL*), swim bladder height (*SH*) and swim bladder width (*SW*). The swim bladder tilt angle was also measured relative to the main axis of the lateral image aspect.

### TS Estimation

Since the lack of *in situ* data, the KRM model (Clay and Horne, 1994) was used to estimate *TS*. Acoustic parameters, such as the density contrast (*g*) and sound speed contrast (*h*), were needed in this model. Previous researchers found that fish flesh had *g* values ranging from ~1.02 to 1.06 and *h* values from ~1.02 to 1.08 (Love, 1978; Medwin and Clay, 1998; Gastauer et al., 2016). Typical acoustic parameters of fish with a swim bladder, measured using Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*), from literature (Clay and Horne, 1994) were chosen in our model ([**Table 1**](#T1)), which were also used in the jack mackerel (*Trachurus japonicus*) *TS* research performed by Hwang et al. (2015). *TS* of fish is closely related to the sound wave frequency and the swimming pitch angle. Broadband scattering characteristics with a frequency in the range of 0–250 kHz were simulated to plot the entire broadband *TS* spectrum. According to Yasuma et al. (2003), when the incidence sound wave is perpendicular to the dorsal aspect of the fish body, the pitch angle is defined as 0°. Shifts in *TS*, when the swimming pitch angle ranged from −50° (head-down) to 50° (head-up), were estimated at frequencies of 38 kHz, 70 kHz, 120 kHz, and 200 kHz. Average *TS* value was calculated from estimated *TS* across the pitch angle distribution. This value was used as the *TS* of individual fish (Yasuma et al., 2010). ## Results

### Morphology of *S. japonicus*

The range of body length of the 18 *S. japonicus* was 12.98–22.17 cm, with a mean of 16.08±3.15 cm (mean ± SD). The range of swim bladder length was 1.45–6.63 cm, with a mean of 3.64 ± 1.49 cm. Tilt angle was from 1.7° to 14.0° and mean tilt angle was 8.26° ± 3.62°.

### *TS* Variation With Body Pitch Angle Shifts

[**Figure 2**](#f2) shows *TS* variation of each sample in relation to pitch angle shifts. We used ∆*TS* (*TSmax*-*TSmin*) to represent this variation. When pitch angle shifted from −50° to 50°, the ∆*TS* range of the 18 *S. japonicus* at four frequencies was 12.33–52.68 dB, 28.81–45.34 dB, 26.38–52.30 dB, and 28.57–50.15 dB, respectively.

### The Broadband Scattering Characteristics

The broadband *TS* spectrum of the 18 *S. japonicus*, estimated using the pitch angle distribution *N*[−3°,4°], in the frequency range of 0–250 kHz, is shown in [**Figure 6**](#f6). *TS* values decreased along with swim bladder length but the resonance frequency dominated by Rayleigh scattering increased. As frequency increased and entered into the Mie scattering range, *TS* began to fluctuate over a range of 5 dB. However, individuals with different swim bladder lengths showed two trends after 150 kHz. *TS* of fish whose *SL*>*3 cm* increased, while the *TS* of fish with *SL>3 cm* maintained stability.

## Discussion

The KRM model requires precise measurements of the body and swim bladder to obtain detailed morphological parameters. Therefore, we used a specialized X-ray imaging system to map the outlines of the fish, which reliably reflects the size of the swim bladder and its relative position in the body. Sample preservation quality greatly influenced image quality as the swim bladder may not be obvious in the poorly preserved samples. In this study, *S. japonicus* samples were collected *in situ* and frozen in seawater, ensuring the relative stability of the internal structure of the fish and improved measurement accuracy. However, morphology will inevitably change during freezing and thawing, and temperature cannot be kept constant during long periods of time needed for transportation. Sobradillo et al. (2019) proposed using liquid nitrogen to freeze samples and thaw them in a temperature-controlled environment (0°C), which can minimize damage to biological structures. It is better to take X-rays *in situ* when conditions permit, to avoid freezing and transportation. The total catch of *S. japonicus* during the survey period was 1,299 and their body length distribution follows *N*[16.15,4.14]. Among these catches, 946 individuals with gonadal maturity of stage 1 and stage 2 indicate that they were mainly juveniles. In this paper, the body length distribution of the 18 samples was *N*[15.86,3.15], which is consistent with the overall catches. Although there were few samples used in *TS* estimation, it would not have a large impact on conclusions.

The *TS* of fish is influenced by many factors. There are even differences in the same species due to variation in individual morphology. The size of this difference depends on the frequency of the sound waves (Gauthier and Horne, 2004). At 38 kHz, *TS* was relatively stable with body pitch angle shifts and there were fewer side lobes. While at higher frequencies, wavelength interaction in the body produced more interference which caused greater fluctuation in *TS* and more side lobes. *TS* of *S. japonicus* was sensitive to body pitch angle shifts at high frequencies. However, this is less important because 38 kHz has been used for the biomass assessment of these fish resources. *S. japonicus* have a swim bladder, which is filled with gas and has a stronger scattering ability than the rest of the fish body. Researchers have shown that the swim bladder accounts for more than 90% of the total scattering of fish with swim bladders (Foote, 1980) and that is why the maximum *TS* of the sample with a body length of 14.81 cm in [**Figure 3**](#f3) appeared at a pitch angle of about −10°. Because the tilt angle of this sample was 8.4°, the swim bladder reached its normal aspect and intercepted the sound wave the most when the pitch angle was −10°.

Fish have different pitch angles due to differences in body size, swimming speed, and living conditions. In this paper, three pitch angle distributions were used to calculate *TS* of *S. japonicus*. Results show that there were almost no differences between *TS* calculated using the measured *S. japonicus* angle distributions and that estimated by using the universal distribution and this is consistent with the results of Furusawa (1988). Therefore, we conclude that the difference between the measured and universal angle distributions had little effect on the KRM results for *S. japonicus*. However, due to low samples sizes used to obtain these two measured distributions, *N*[−3°,4°] was observed using four samples and *N*[−0.5°,0.09°] was observed using only one; these conclusions are not generalizable. In addition, these two distributions were quite different, indicating differences in individual swimming patterns. To improve the accuracy of acoustic stock assessment, it is better to estimate *TS* of *S. japonicus* using the measured distribution. It is necessary to carry out comprehensive studies on the swimming posture of *S. japonicus* and to use more samples to measure the angle distribution.

There are few studies on TS of *S. japonicus*: Miyanohana et al. (1990) used four frequencies to measure *TS* of *S. japonicus* but they did not show the explicit values. Mukai et al. (1993) measured the *b20* of individuals with a total length of 23.0–26.8 cm using the *ex situ* method, which was −64.1 dB at 25 kHz and −65.5 dB at 100 kHz. Gutiérrez and Maclennan (1998) reported the *b20* of *S. japonicus* with a total length of 26–30 cm using the *in situ* method, which was −70.95 dB at 38 kHz and −70.8 dB at 120 kHz. The *TS* calculated using their *b20* and our total length data were 2–8 dB higher than our KRM model results. Lee and Shin (2005) used the *ex situ* method to obtain the *b20* for individuals with a total length of 26.2–38.3 cm which was −66.9 dB at 120 kHz and −71.1 dB at 200 kHz. *TS* calculated using their *b20* were 6–12 dB higher than ours at 120 kHz and 1–7 dB higher at 200 kHz. Svellingen and Charouki (2008, cited in Palermino et al., 2021) used the *in situ* method to measure the *b20* of *S. japonicus* with an average length of 21.8 cm which was −77.6 dB at 38 kHz and −79.8 dB at 120 kHz. Our *TS* were 0–6 dB higher than results calculated using their *b20*. Kurnia et al. (2011) reported that the *TS* of a *S. japonicus* with *BL*=21.4 cm was −40.02 dB at 50 kHz when the incidence wave was perpendicular to the dorsal aspect. While the sample with *BL=*21.33 cm in this paper had a simulated *TS* of −36.28 dB under the same frequency and pitch angle. These difference of these results indicate that there may be errors in the KRM estimation. However, the length of *S. japonicus* in most studies was larger than ours, which may be another reason that caused these differences in *TS*.

Density contrast value (*g*) and sound speed contrast value (*h*) of a fish’s body and swim bladder are not only important parameters in the KRM model but also in most *TS* models. Changes in *g* and *h* will affect the *TS* estimation (Chu and Wiebe, 2005; Kang et al., 2006; Matsukura et al., 2009). The results of Yasuma et al. (2009) showed that using *g* and *h* values in the primary research may lead to an error of about 10 dB when using the deformed cylinder model to calculate *TS* of fish without a swim bladder. For zooplankton *TS* estimation, small changes in *g* and *h* in the distorted wave born approximation model can result in errors of up to 20 dB (Chu et al., 2000). Therefore, the use of measured *g* and *h* is better for the accurate estimation of the *TS* of *S. japonicus*. In addition, the results of KRM model are affected by the sound speed and density of seawater. Eulachon (*Thaleichthys pacificus*) has a *TS* of 3–4 dB higher in freshwater than in seawater (Gauthier and Horne, 2004). For fish with a swim bladder, their volume has a greater effect on *TS* than *g* and *h* values (Mukai and Iida, 1996; Gorska and Ona, 2003). Studies showed that some mackerel species have a diel vertical migration behavior (Bertrand et al., 2004; Li et al., 2014; Tsuda et al., 2014; Paramo et al., 2015). They usually aggregate in deeper water during the daytime and move to the surface at night. These differences have strong implications for the estimation of biomass. Therefore, *TS* in different depths should be attended. According to Boyle’s law, there is a negative correlation between swim bladder volume and water depth. With increasing depth, pressure increases on the swim bladder causing a decrease in volume and the effective backscattering cross-section, which leads to a decrease in *TS*. Morphological characteristics in this study were obtained by taking X-ray images of fish out of the water. However, *TS* in different depths still needs further study and experimental data on *TS* at different depths are needed to validate the theoretical model.

In recent years, using broadband techniques to identify and classify species in echograms has become a hot topic in fishery acoustics (Stanton et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2020; Hasegawa et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2021). At the same time, a growing number of research vessels are equipped with broadband fish finders. The broadband scattering spectrum of *S. japonicus* produced by us can provide a reference for identifying *S. japonicus* in a mixed population echogram. The two observed trends in *TS* variation of individuals with different swim bladder lengths above 150 kHz may be related to the ratio of swim bladder lengths to acoustic wavelengths. It is necessary to select the appropriate frequency for the body length of the fish to improve accuracy when using the dB-difference method for stock assessment.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (Vol. 9, 27 April 2022) by Jianfeng Tong, Minghua Xue, Zhenhong Zhu, Weiqi Wang, and Siquan Tian from Shanghai Ocean University, China. The study investigates the impacts of morphological characteristics on the target strength (TS) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Northwest Pacific Ocean using the Kirchhoff-ray mode (KRM) model.

Key methodology: 18 S. japonicus samples (body length 12.98–22.17 cm, mean 16.08±3.15 cm) were collected from 147°E–165°E, 33°N–44°N in the Northwest Pacific Ocean by the RV Songhang (June 18 to August 7, 2021). Morphological measurements (body length, height, width, swim bladder length, height, width, and tilt angle) were obtained using a MIKASA HF100HA X-ray imaging system. The KRM model was used to estimate TS at frequencies of 38, 70, 120, and 200 kHz across pitch angles from -50° to 50°, and a broadband TS spectrum was simulated from 0–250 kHz.

Key results: TS varied with pitch angle shifts, with greater impact on scattering strength at higher frequencies. TS peaked at pitch angles of -10° to 0°, related to swim bladder tilt angle (mean tilt 8.26°±3.62°). There was almost no difference between TS estimated using measured pitch angle distributions (N[-3°,4°] and N[-0.5°,0.09°]) versus the universal distribution (N[-5°,10°]). Average TS for fish with body lengths of 12.04–22.17 cm was -48.88 dB, -49.14 dB, -49.75 dB, and -48.55 dB at 38, 70, 120, and 200 kHz respectively. The b20 regression intercepts were -73.27, -73.56, -74.18, and -73.46 dB at these four frequencies. TS variation from 0–300 m depth was about 10 dB due to swim bladder compression per Boyle's law. The regression slopes exceeded 20 in all cases, indicating backscattering cross-section increases faster than the square of body length. Broadband TS spectra showed resonance frequency increasing as swim bladder length decreased, with two distinct trends above 150 kHz for individuals with swim bladder length >3 cm versus <3 cm.

Significance: These results provide reference for acoustic stock assessment and echogram-based species identification of S. japonicus in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, where this species is an economically important commercial fish for China, Japan, and South Korea, with a global catch of 1.56 million tons in 2018 but declining biomass since 1997. Comparison with prior studies showed TS differences of 2–12 dB due to fish size differences and potential model errors. The study was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China.
args.key_excerpts: "The results revealed that TS values varied with pitch angle shifts, with the impact on fish scattering strength being greater at higher frequency. This is less important because 38 kHz has been used for the biomass assessment of these fish resources."
