PO Box 3797, Wellington 6140, New Zealand P: +64 4 499 9893 – E: secretariat@sprfmo.int – www.sprfmo.int 12th MEETING OF THE SCIENTIFIC COMMITTEE 30 September to 05 October 2024, Lima, Peru SC 12 - HM 05 Habitat for jack and chub mackerel Peru 2022-2024 Peru 12th MEETING OF THE SCIENTIFIC COMMITTEE Lima, 30 September – 05 October 2024 HABITAT CONDITIONS OF JACK MACKEREL (Trachurus murphyi), Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) AND OTHER SPECIES IN THE PERUVIAN SEA BETWEEN 2021 AND 2024 by MARIANO GUTIÉRREZ1, ALMENDRA TARAZONA1, CARLOS VALDEZ2, LUCERO MORENO3, CLAUDIA JUAREZ3, SALVADOR PERALTILLA4, GLORIAS MENESES4 (1) Instituto Humboldt de Investigación Marina y Acuícola - IHMA (2) Instituto del Mar del Perú – IMARPE (3) Tecnológica de Alimentos S.A: - TASA (4) Sociedad Nacional de Pesquería - SNP 2024 This report contains information on the Jack mackerel fish stock and fishery in Peruvian jurisdictional waters that, we reiterate, the delegation of Peru, in use of its discretionary powers, voluntarily provides for the purpose of information and support to the scientific research work within the Scientific Committee of the SPRFMO. In doing so, while referring to Article 5 of the Convention on the Conservation and Management of High Seas Fishery Resources in the South Pacific Ocean and reiterating that Peru has not given the express consent contemplated in Article 20 (4) (a) (iii) of the Convention, Peru reaffirms that the decisions and conservation and management measures adopted by the SPRFMO Commission are not applicable within Peruvian jurisdictional waters. 1 South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization 12th Meeting of the Scientific Committee September 30th – October 5th 2024 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 Lima, August 2024 2 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 Mariano Gutiérrez1, Almendra Tarazona1, Carlos Valdez2, Lucero Moreno3, Claudia Juarez3, Salvador Peraltilla4, Glorias Meneses4 (1) Instituto Humboldt de Investigación Marina y Acuícola - IHMA (2) Instituto del Mar del Perú – IMARPE (3) Tecnológica de Alimentos S.A: - TASA (4) Sociedad Nacional de Pesquería - SNP Summary An update of the analysis on changes in the habitat of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel has been carried out, emphasizing what was observed between 2021 and 2024, in addition to aspects of the abundance of other species of top predators. The summer of 2024 has been dominated by positive temperature anomalies until the beginning of March, when the sea began to cool from north to south. In March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that began a year earlier. In this context, and regarding the habitat, it was observed that during the summer of 2024 the presence of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel has again occurred in a typical way, that is, along the fronts between oceanic and coastal waters, unlike the year 2020 when they were observed in oceanic waters, which was considered unusual at least for that season. From the analysis of the various variables regarding the habitat of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel, it is concluded that there have been different conditions in recent years, where the only parameter analyzed that remained within a narrow range is salinity. Another striking fact is that both species have been available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll concentration and relatively high altimetry values and high sea surface anomaly. In the case of Jack mackerel, its distribution on the central coast during January is noteworthy compared to its southern distribution in previous seasons. In the case of Chub mackerel, a higher availability was observed in the southern zone during the summer of 2024. However, it should be noted that there were no trips during February and March, due in most cases to the maintenance needs of the fishing vessels. At the moment of drafting this document, the fleet was fishing for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel in the southern area. A significant presence of marine fauna has been recorded in the areas of operation of three fishing vessels. A total of 2,671 individuals were observed between seabirds, whales, dolphins and sea lions, with the most numerous taxonomic group being seabirds with 1,772 individuals, dolphins were the second group with 810 individuals, then sea lions with 77 individuals and whales with 12 individuals. In the habitat reports submitted in the previous years (2019 to 2023) to the SPRFMO Habitat Monitoring Working Group, as well as in the present case, it should be specified that what has generally been mapped and modeled the ideal environmental conditions (habitat) for adult fish of Jack and Chub mackerel only. A similar type of study is pending for the early stages of both species. 3 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 TABLE OF CONTENTS 1. Introduction 4 2. Description of jack mackerel and chub mackerel habitat using satellite and fisheries data 4 2.1. Sea surface temperature (SST, °C) between 2020 and 2022 4 2.2. Sea surface temperature anomaly (ATSM, °C) between 2020-22 5 2.3. Sea surface salinity (SSM, ups) between 2020 and 2022 6 2.4. Sea surface chlorophyll (ug/Lt) between 2020 and 2022 7 2.5. Sea level anomaly (SLA, cm) between 2020 and 2022 8 2.6. Jack mackerel fishing sets in national waters during September 2023 9 2.7. Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets on the high seas during June and July 2023 9 2.8. Analysis of variability for Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel according to fishing sets carried out between 2019 and 2023 in relation to satellite oceanography variables 12 2.8.1 Variability in the case of Jack mackerel 12 2.8.2. Variability in the case of Chub mackerel 13 2.9. Potential Habitat Model for Mackerel (MHPJ) 14 3. Top Predators Sighting 2024 15 4. Conclusions 17 5. References 18 Lima, August 2024 4 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 1. Introduction The Scientific Research Committee (CIC) of the National Fisheries Society (SNP), in cooperation with the Humboldt Institute for Marine and Aquaculture Research (IHMA) organized the Eleventh SNP Workshop on the habitat conditions of jack mackerel and other species of the Peruvian Current in the Humboldt System, which was held virtually from 24 to 28th June 2024. It has counted, as usual, with the valuable participation and contribution of researchers from the Institute of Sea Research of Peru (IMARPE). This activity is a contribution to the national and international effort to research and diagnose the changing conditions of jack mackerel and chub mackerel populations, as well as other species of the South Pacific, with particular emphasis on aspects related to their habitats since the first workshop conducted in 2011. 2. Description of jack mackerel and chub mackerel habitats using oceanographic satellite and fisheries data Various oceanographic parameters are presented for the summers (January, February, March) of the years 2022, 2023 and 2024 with an indication of the fishing sets of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel (represented by symbols), since -in general- they are the months in which the fishing seasons took place. Figures 2.1.1 to 2.1.5. shows the oceanographic parameters of January 15, February 15, and March 15 of each year, from left to right, in order to appreciate the changes that have occurred in the last three years and their relationship with the relative distribution of Jack and Chub mackerel. 2.1. Sea surface temperature (SST, °C) between 2022 and 2024 In the period described, the presence of Lack mackerel and Chub mackerel has been observed along the thermal fronts; Jack mackerel fishing sets were carried out outside the continental shelf. It is considered that, in general, the moderate thermal conditions of the last five years (since 2019, with the exception of the warm year 2023) have led to a higher concentration of Jack mackerel, especially in the southern area. Chub mackerel, on the other hand, has tended to be distributed – as usual – more northwards to the extent that in that area the presence of Surface Equatorial Waters has predominated in the summers that favor it. However, unlike previous years, in 2024 adult Chub mackerel predominated in the southern area. (Figure 2.1.1). 5 Figure 2.1.1. Sea surface temperature (SST, °C) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel. 2.2. Sea surface temperature anomaly (ATSM, °C) between 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and January 2023, there were negative anomalies, as in previous years. Under these conditions, the main jack mackerel fishing areas were distributed in the area located south of the Paracas Peninsula, where negative thermal anomalies were higher during 2022. Chub mackerel, on the other hand, had some distribution areas in the center and south, but also in areas where it coincided with Jack mackerel in the north. The conditions in which Jack mackerel was detected and caught during January 2024 is similar to that of January 2022; and it is since February 2023 that warm conditions begin to develop until March 2024 (Figure 2.2.1). 6 Figure 2.2.1. Sea surface temperature anomaly (ATSM, °C) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In the months of March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches were observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel. 2.3. Sea surface salinity (SSM, ups) between 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and 2024, Chub mackerel fishing areas were distributed both in the center and in the south along the front between cold coastal waters (CCW) and surface subtropical waters (SSA); in the case of Jack mackerel, in 2023 its fishing areas have been located approximately the same as in previous years. that is, south of the Paracas Peninsula along the front between ACF and ASS (Figure 2.3.1). 7 Figure 2.3.1 Sea surface salinity (SSM, ups) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In the month of March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both species. 2.4. Sea surface chlorophyll (ug/Lt) between years 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and 2024, Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel were found on the outer edges of the highest concentration of chlorophyll in the central and southern areas. For 2023, lower primary productivity was evident, as occurs during El Niño events, unlike 2024 where there was higher primary productivity than in previous years (Figure 2.4.1). 8 Figure 2.4.1. Sea surface chlorophyll (ug/Lt) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both species. 2.5. Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA, cm) between 2022 and 2024 The summer months of 2022 to 2024 presented a higher oceanic dynamic than in previous years, which is associated with a denser presence of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel, but mainly in the southern area. More specifically, the presence of both species has been related to intermediate to high SLA values (Figure 2.5.1) 9 Figure 2.5.1. Sea level anomaly (SLA, cm) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both horse mackerel and mackerel. 2.6. Jack mackerel fishing sets in national waters during September 2023 In September 2023, Jack mackerel fishing sets were carried out in the southern zone in which the following conditions were present: cold temperatures, salinity of 34.9-35.4 UPS, low chlorophyll values, intermediate and high SLA levels, neutral and positive thermal anomalies (Figure 2.6.1). 10 Figure 2.6.1. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (SST), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll, Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during September 2023. The fishing sets are indicated by black circles. 2.7. Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets on the high seas during June and July 2023 During June and July 2023, the fishing areas for jack mackerel and chub mackerel were located outside 200 nautical miles, where cold temperatures, low chlorophyll levels, neutral thermal anomalies, intermediate and high SLA levels were present (Figures 2.7.1 and 2.7.2). 11 Figure 2.7.1. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll (ug/Lt), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during June 2023 on the high seas. Fishing sets for jack mackerel are indicated by black circles, and chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. Figure 2.7.2. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll (ug/Lt), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during July 2023 on the high seas. Fishing sets for jack mackerel are indicated by black circles, and chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. 12 2.8. Analysis of variability for Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel according to fishing sets carried out between 2019 and 2023 in relation to satellite oceanography variables. Figures 2.8.1 and 2.8.2 present the comparative results of the analysis of variability of parameters relevant to the distribution of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel between 2019 and 2024. The parameters analyzed are: Sea Surface Temperature (TSM, °C), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (ATSM, °C), Sea Surface Salinity (SALINIDAD, ups), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA ug/Lt), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA, cm), Sea Surface Altimetry (ALT, cm), latitude (LAT), distance from the coast (DC) and month of the year (MESES). 2.8.1 Variability in the case of Jack mackerel In the case of Jack mackerel, Figure 2.8.1 is presented, which shows notable differences between several parameters during years 2019 to 2024. For the TSM, a wide range of thermal values (between 18 and 25°C) is appreciated, with a preference for relatively high temperatures during years 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2024; in years 2021 and 2022 the thermal values have been below average. As for the ATSM (in a range between -4 to +3°C), there has been a larger presence of Jack mackerel in slightly positive values with the exception of 2021 in which all catches were made in the midst of negative values. On the other hand, salinity remained in a discrete range of values (35 to 35.4 ups) and low chlorophyll concentration values (< 4 ug/Lt) with the exception of 2021 when the highest values were observed. As for SLA and ALT, the presence of Jack mackerel is almost entirely limited to positive values, but not beyond values of 10 cm. Latitudinally, the distribution of Jack mackerel presented a range restricted to the central-southern zone. As for its distribution according to its distance from the coast, Jack mackerel was at relatively close distances, around 50 nm from the coast on average between 2019 and 2024, with the exception of 2020 and 2023 when it was located at more than 100 nm on average. Finally, the timing of the distribution of fishing sets on Jack mackerel is usually limited to the summer months, when the fishing quota has been completed (Figure 2.8.1.1.) with the exception of 2023. At the time of the 2024 workshop Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets were beginning in the southern zone. Figure 2.8.1.1. Box plots on the variability of parameters in the case of Jack mackerel between 2019 to 2024: Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinidad), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA), Altimetry (ALT), latitude 13 (LAT), distance to the coast (DC) and months (MESES). The red line on each box indicates the average value of all measurements. 2.8.2. Variability in the case of Chub mackerel For TSM, different ranges of thermal values are seen (between 18 and 24°C), having been distributed in warmer conditions during 2019, 2020, part of 2023 and 2024, and in colder conditions during 2021, 2022 and part of 2023. Likewise, the distribution of Chub mackerel is related to a rather wide range of ATSM (between -4 to +2°C), but discrete in the case of SSM (34.9 to 35.4 ups), and with low chlorophyll concentration values (< 4 ug/Lt) with the exception of 2021 when the highest values are observed. As for SLA and ALT, the presence of Chub mackerel is almost entirely limited to positive values, but not beyond values of 10 cm. Latitudinally, the distribution of Chub mackerel was wide during 2019 and 2023, with a southward trend in 2020 and 2024, and with a denser presence in the center during 2021 and 2022. In terms of its distribution according to its distance from the coast, Chub mackerel was relatively close to the coast during 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, and further away from it in 2020 and 2023. Finally, the timing of the distribution of Chub mackerel, as it is the same fleet that fishes for Jack mackerel, indicates that during 2023 it was also fished during June. At the time of the 2024 workshop Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets were beginning in the southern zone. Figure 2.8.1.2. Box plots on the variability of parameters in the case of Chub mackerel between 2019 to 2024: Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinidad), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA), Altimetry (ALT), latitude (LAT), distance to the coast (DC) and months (MESES). The red line on each box indicates the average value of all measurements. 14 2.9. Potential Habitat Model for Mackerel (MHPJ) Valdez et al. (2015) developed a deterministic and probabilistic 2D model of potential Jack mackerel habitat (MHPJ) using satellite oceanography data and positional variables. Originally, six variables were considered for the model, but due to the high prevalence of cloud cover in the coastal zone, it was decided to exclude chlorophyll, whose remote measurement is affected by the atmospheric conditions. Jack mackerel catches showed a more robust correlation with the model when the probability exceeded the threshold of 0.45 on a scale of 0 to 1. The used satellite oceanographic parameters, including salinity and temperature, were obtained from the HYCOM platform. Thermal anomalies from an annual pattern were also incorporated. The MHPJ model was run biweekly only during periods with confirmed jack mackerel catches, using biweekly averages of oceanographic variables. This analysis covered from May 2023 (May, June, September and December) to January 2024 (first and second half of January), coinciding with the industrial Jack mackerel fishing season and the data available at the time of the study. The results of the model are presented in Figure 2.9.1. Regarding the areas represented by the model, during fortnight 1 (May 16 to 30, 2023), a wide extension with a high density (> 0.6) is observed south of 15th south degree; no coincidences were found in the northern area, specifically north of Pimentel. For fortnights 2 and 3 (July 16 to 30 and September 16 to 30, 2023), the area begins to retreat from the coast, increasing its probability at the edge of the shelf. On the other hand, the coincidences with the fishing sets were observed mainly in the southern zone with probabilities close to ~0.5. In the fourth half of December (December 1 to 15, 2023), an expansion of the area and an increase in probability are observed along the entire coast. In fortnight 5, a similar pattern is presented to the fourth fortnight, highlighting the coincidence of the fishing sets with the main distribution area in the southern zone. In fortnight 6, a reduction in the area of the model is observed, as well as a decrease in the higher probability values, with coincidences observed in the fishing sets. In addition, the average probability value of fishing sets was calculated, finding a high assertiveness (~0.55). 15 Figura 2.9.1. Resultados de seis quincenas del MHPJ entre mayo del 2023 y enero del 2024. Los puntos azules marcados en los mapas indican las capturas efectuadas por los barcos industriales. La escala de color indica probabilidad de encontrar jurel (valores de 0 a 1). 3. It occurred in a range of 5 to 240 nautical miles from the coast, with a latitudinal distribution that ranges from 12 to 21th south degrees. args.summary:
This document is a scientific report submitted to the 12th Meeting of the Scientific Committee (SC12) of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO), held in Lima, Peru from September 30 to October 5, 2024. The report, prepared by researchers from the Instituto Humboldt de Investigación Marina y Acuícola (IHMA), IMARPE, TASA, and the Sociedad Nacional de Pesquería (SNP), analyzes habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus), and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024.

KEY FINDINGS:
- The summer of 2024 was dominated by positive temperature anomalies until early March, when the sea began cooling from north to south. In March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that had begun a year earlier.
- During summer 2024, both jack mackerel and chub mackerel were again found in typical coastal-oceanic front zones, unlike 2020 when they were found in unusual oceanic waters.
- Moderate thermal conditions over the last five years (since 2019, except warm 2023) led to higher concentration of jack mackerel, especially in the southern area. In 2024, adult chub mackerel unusually predominated in the southern area.
- Salinity was the only parameter that remained within a narrow range (35-35.4 ups for jack mackerel; 34.9-35.4 ups for chub mackerel) across the study period.
- Both species were available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll concentration (<4 ug/Lt) and intermediate-to-high sea level anomaly and altimetry values (positive but not exceeding 10 cm).
- Jack mackerel distribution on the central coast during January was noteworthy compared to southern distribution in previous seasons. Jack mackerel typically fished within ~50 nm of the coast on average (2019-2024), except in 2020 and 2023 when located over 100 nm offshore.
- No fishing occurred during March 2022, February and March 2024, despite quotas being provided, due to vessel maintenance needs.
- During June-July 2023 on the high seas (outside 200 nm), fishing areas had cold temperatures, low chlorophyll, neutral thermal anomalies, and intermediate-high SLA levels.
- The Potential Jack Mackerel Habitat (MHPJ) model (developed by Valdez et al., 2015) using satellite oceanography variables showed high assertiveness (~0.55 average probability) in matching fishing set locations during May 2023 to January 2024. The model excluded chlorophyll due to cloud cover issues in coastal zones.

TOP PREDATOR SIGHTINGS (2024):
From three TASA company vessels operating between June-September 2023 (5-240 nm from coast, 12-21°S), 2,671 individuals were observed: seabirds (1,772 individuals), dolphins (810), sea lions (77), and whales (12). Notable species included black-browed albatross (400 individuals, 81-200 nm range), Peruvian gull (249 within 80 nm), blue whale (6 within 80 nm), bottlenose dolphin (400 within 80 nm), common dolphin (385), and fur seals (67 within 80 nm). ~87 of 791 records included top predator sightings.

CONCLUSIONS:
- Thermal conditions of recent years favored jack mackerel availability, especially in southern areas.
- South latitudes 13 and 14 degrees concentrate the largest catches in the last two years, located along the front between coastal cold and subtropical waters.
- At the time of the 2024 workshop, fishing for both species had just begun in the southern zone (June-July 2024).
- The report notes that habitat modeling has so far covered adult fish only; similar studies for early life stages are pending.
- Peru reiterates that SPRFMO decisions and conservation measures do not apply within Peruvian jurisdictional waters.

# Analysis of the inter-annual variation of chub mackerel abundance in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea during 1999-2011

* [WANG Congjun](javascript:void(0);),
* [ZOU Lijin](javascript:void(0);),
* [LI Gang](javascript:void(0);),
* [CHEN Xinjun](javascript:void(0);)

![]()

[Abstract](javascript:void(0);)

* ### Abstract

  Relative abundance index is often used to measure the level of fisheries resources biomass.Based on chub mackerel(*Scomber japonicus*)catch data of the large lighting-purse seine fishery from 1999 to 2011,the impacts of temporal(Year,Month),spatial(Longitude,Latitude),environmental factors(Sea surface temperature,Sea surface height and Sea surface chlorophyll-a concentration)and fishing performance(Vessel name)on catch per unit effort(CPUE)were analyzed using generalized linear model(GLM)and generalized additive model(GAM).The Year effect of CPUE,extracted from GAM,was used as the annual abundance index(AI)to reflect the inter-annual variation of chub mackerel abundance in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea.The relationship between AI and SST in the chub mackerel spawning ground and fishing effort was also investigated.The GAM with the eight variables explains 11.69% of the total variance in nominal CPUE,and the impact of Year on CPUE is the foremost factor,contributing to 53.9% of the total reduction in deviance.The extracted Year effect indicates that chub mackerel abundance shows a declining trend over the past 13 years,especially after 2008,and the AI fell from 1.22 in 2008 to 0.82 in 2011.The AI shows a significantly positive relationship with the SST of the spawning ground,and it is expressed as AI=-3.5+023SST(*P*<0.05).This result indicates that SST of the spawning ground has a positive impact on the abundance of chub mackerel.The decrease of chub mackerel abundance in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea resulted from the rapidly increasing number of purse seine vessels in the recent years.

This webpage presents the abstract and article details for a scientific paper titled "Analysis of the inter-annual variation of chub mackerel abundance in the East China Sea and Yellow Sea during 1999-2011" published in the Journal of Fisheries of China (2014, 38(1): 56-64, DOI: 10.3724/SP.J.1231.2014.48737). The paper was authored by WANG Congjun, ZOU Lijin, LI Gang, and CHEN Xinjun.

The study analyzed chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) catch data from the large lighting-purse seine fishery (1999-2011) using generalized linear models (GLM) and generalized additive models (GAM). Eight variables were examined: temporal factors (Year, Month), spatial factors (Longitude, Latitude), environmental factors (Sea surface temperature, Sea surface height, Sea surface chlorophyll-a concentration), and fishing performance (Vessel name) on catch per unit effort (CPUE).

Key findings include:
- The GAM with eight variables explains 11.69% of total variance in nominal CPUE, with "Year" being the foremost factor, contributing 53.9% of total reduction in deviance.
- Chub mackerel abundance showed a declining trend over the 13-year period, especially after 2008, with the abundance index (AI) falling from 1.22 in 2008 to 0.82 in 2011.
- The AI showed a significantly positive relationship with sea surface temperature (SST) of the spawning ground, expressed as AI = -3.5 + 0.23SST (P < 0.05).
- The decline in chub mackerel abundance is attributed to the rapidly increasing number of purse seine vessels in recent years, suggesting overfishing pressure as a primary driver of population decline.

## Abstract

Population dynamics of small pelagic fishes (SPF) and their management in Japan were reviewed for Japanese sardine _Sardinops melanostictus_, Japanese anchovy _Engraulis japonicus_, chub mackerel _Scomber japonicus_, and Pacific saury _Cololabis saira_. The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly “regime shifts,” of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations, and the proposed hypothetical mechanisms of recruitment variability are summarized herein. Although overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented the recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, they have been recovering since the mid-2000s owing to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing was derived from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity since the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF began to shift from sardine to anchovy. Recommendations for fisheries management of SPF around the Japanese Archipelago are proposed, considering climate change and naturally and drastically changing SPF populations.

## Introduction

Population dynamics and Japan’s fishery management of the principal small pelagic fishes (SPF) around the Japanese Archipelago were reviewed on the basis of available information, including long-term trajectories of commercial catch, biomass, spawning stock biomass (SSB), recruitment, recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS, No./kg), fishing mortality coefficient (_F_), and exploitation rate (ER, catch weight/biomass). Potential mechanisms of population fluctuations of target SPF including the effects of “regime shifts” (Kawasaki [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR33 "Kawasaki T (2013) Regime shift—fish and climate change. Tohoku University Press, Sendai")) and climate change were also summarized. Finally, recommendations for fisheries management of SPF around the Japanese Archipelago were proposed. The target stocks reviewed are the Pacific and Tsushima Current stocks of Japanese sardine _Sardinops melanostictus_ and chub mackerel _Scomber japonicus_; the Pacific, Seto Inland Sea, and Tsushima Current stocks of Japanese anchovy _Engraulis japonicus_; and Pacific saury _Cololabis saira_, which is considered the only stock over the North Pacific Ocean and its marginal seas (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1), Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig1)). Table[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab2) describes the abbreviations, mathematical constants, and biological reference points for fisheries management used herein.

Decadal-scale variability in catch trajectories of SPF (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig2)), accompanied by shifts in dominant species, is often linked to global- or basin-scale variability in environmental factors; a famous example is the sardine/anchovy cycle associated with the Pacific Decadal Oscillation index (Chavez et al. [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR8 "Chavez FP, Ryan J, Lluch-Cota SE, Niquen CM (2003) From anchovies to sardines and back: multidecadal change in the Pacific Ocean. Science 299:217–221")). Decadal-scale alternation in the dominant species is known as “species replacements” (Matsuda et al. [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR49 "Matsuda H, Wada T, Takeuchi Y, Matsumiya Y (1992) Model analysis of the effect of environmental fluctuation on the species replacement pattern of pelagic fishes under interspecific competition. Res Pop Ecol 34:309–319"); Barange et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR4 "Barange M, Bernal M, Cercole MC, Cubillos L, Cunningham CL, Daskalov GM, De Oliveira JAA, Dickey-Collas M, Hill K, Jacobson L, Køster FW, Masse J, Nishida H, Niquen M, Oozeki Y, Palomera I, Saccardo SA, Santojanni A, Serra R, Somarakis S, Stratoudakis Y, van der Lingen CD, Uriarte A, Yatsu A (2009) Current trends in the assessment and management of small pelagic fish stocks. In: Checkley D et al (eds) Climate change and small pelagic fish. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, pp 191–255")). Species replacements can also be detected by analyzing the stomach contents of minke whales _Balaenoptera acutorostrata_ (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig3)), which is an opportunistic feeder, and predatory fishes (Tamura et al. [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR73 "Tamura T, Fujise Y, Shimazaki K (1998) Diet of minke whales Balaenoptera auctorostrata in the northwestern part of the North Pacific in summer, 1994 and 1995. Fish Sci 64:71–76"); Yatsu et al. [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR94 "Yatsu A, Nagasawa K, Wada T (2003) Decadal changes in abundance of dominant pelagic fishes and squids in the Northwestern Pacific Ocean since the 1970s and implications to fisheries management. Trans Am Fish Soc Symp 38:675–684")).

**Fig.2**

PICES, Sidney"); gray). N.B.: Development of efficient fishing technologies occurred with stick-held dip nets for Pacific saury and purse seine for mackerels during the 1950s and 1960s, respectively

**Fig.3**

![Image 9: Fig. 3](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs12562-019-01305-3/MediaObjects/12562_2019_1305_Fig3_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3/figures/3)

As catch trajectories of jack mackerel _Trachurus japonicus_ and common squid _Todarodes pacificus_ showed decadal-scale variability similar to that of Japanese anchovy (Yatsu et al. [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR95 "Yatsu A, Watanabe T, Ishida M, Sugisaki H, Jacobson LD (2005) Environmental effects on recruitment and productivity of the Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanostictus, and chub mackerel, Scomber japonicus, with recommendations for management. Fish Oceanogr 14:263–278"); Gong and Suh [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR16 "Gong Y, Suh YS (2012) Climate change and fluctuations of pelagic fish populations in the Far East region. J Ecol Field Biol 35:15–25")), these species were excluded from this review. Although the trophic level of chub mackerel is higher than that of other SPF, as it preys on anchovy in addition to zooplankton (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1)), this species was included in this review for three seasons. First, its longevity, natural mortality rate, and migration routes are similar to those of sardine (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1)). Second, the principal prey of its larvae and juveniles (copepod nauplii) is similar to that of other SPF (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1)). Third, this species has been often regarded to replace SPF and is one of the major target species of purse seine fishery, which suggests its high potential biomass and commercial catch in spite of its higher trophic level (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig2); Matsuda et al. [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR49 "Matsuda H, Wada T, Takeuchi Y, Matsumiya Y (1992) Model analysis of the effect of environmental fluctuation on the species replacement pattern of pelagic fishes under interspecific competition. Res Pop Ecol 34:309–319"); Takasuka et al. [2008a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR71 "Takasuka A, Oozeki Y, Kubota H (2008a) Multi-species regime shifts reflected in spawning temperature optima of small pelagic fish in the western North Pacific. Mar Ecol Prog Ser 360:211–217"); Kawasaki [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR33 "Kawasaki T (2013) Regime shift—fish and climate change. Tohoku University Press, Sendai")).

### Overview of oceanographic and geographic characteristics

The Northwestern Pacific Ocean (FAO Statistical Area 61) is the most productive area worldwide, comprising oceanic waters where interactions of western boundary currents (the Tsushima, Kuroshio, Kuroshio Extension, and Oyashio Currents) create zones of enrichment and concentration of biological processes, as well as marginal seas (the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan Sea, Seto Inland Sea, and Sea of Okhotsk) with broad continental shelves (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig1); Yatsu and Ye [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR93 "Yatsu A, Ye Y (2011) Northwest Pacific (FAO statistical area 61). FAO Fish Aquac Tech Pap 569:141–150")). The net primary productivity is extremely high in the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, and Seto Inland Sea because of high nutrient supply from shallow sea floor and river discharge (Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab3)). Among oceanic areas, Kuroshio (a subtropical area, including the Kuroshio Extension and Kuroshio recirculation area) is the least productive, mainly due to a strong stratification of the water column (Chiba et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR10 "Chiba S, Aita M, Tadokoro K, Saino T, Sugisaki H, Nakata K (2008) From climate regime shifts to lower-trophic level phenology: synthesis of recent progress in retrospective studies of the western North Pacific. Prog Oceanogr 77:112–126")), whereas the productivity in other areas is similar. The net primary productivity of Oyashio and Okhotsk Seas (subarctic areas) is high during spring and summer, unlike other areas where the maximum productivity occurs in spring. Furthermore, the ratio of seasonal maximum/minimum productivity in the subarctic area is much higher than that in other areas around Japan (Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab3)), which is consistent with the findings of Brown et al. ([2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR7 "Brown CW, Uz SS, Corliss BH (2014) Seasonality of oceanic primary production and its interannual variability from 1998 to 2007. Deep Sea Res I 90:166–175")). The East China Sea and Yellow Sea have undergone drastic changes during recent decades as witnessed by species shifts, increasing blooms of harmful algae (red tide) and jellyfish, and eutrophication, suggesting that the ecosystem structure is rapidly shifting (Yoo et al. [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR99 "Yoo S, An YR, Bae S, Choi S, Ishizaka J, Kang YS, Kim ZG, Lee C, Lee JB, Li R, Park J, Wang Z, Wen Q, Yang EJ, Yeh SW, Yeon I, Yoon WD, Zhang CI, Zhang X, Zhu M (2010) Status and trends in the Yellow Sea and East China Sea region. Harmful algae and/or jellyfish blooms are also common in the Japan Sea, Seto Inland Sea, and semi-closed bays in Japan, where anthropogenic effects are prominent (Trainer and Yoshida [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR76 "Trainer VL, Yoshida T (eds) (2014) Proceedings of the workshop on economic impacts of harmful algal blooms on fisheries and aquaculture. PICES, Sidney")). Moreover, the annual average sea surface temperature (SST) around Japan has increased by +1.11°C over the last 100 years, which exceeds the corresponding figure for the global ocean and the North Pacific (+0.54°C and +0.51°C, respectively) according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) (JMAWeb: [https://www.data.jma.go.jp/gmd/kaiyou/english/long_term_sst_japan/sea_surface_temperature_around_japan.html](https://www.data.jma.go.jp/gmd/kaiyou/english/long_term_sst_japan/sea_surface_temperature_around_japan.html) Accessed 15 Oct 2018). This warming affects marine ecosystems and SPF around Japan and its adjacent countries (Yoo et al. [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR99 "Yoo S, An YR, Bae S, Choi S, Ishizaka J, Kang YS, Kim ZG, Lee C, Lee JB, Li R, Park J, Wang Z, Wen Q, Yang EJ, Yeh SW, Yeon I, Yoon WD, Zhang CI, Zhang X, Zhu M (2010) Status and trends in the Yellow Sea and East China Sea region. In: McKinnell SM, Dagg ML (eds) Marine ecosystems of the North Pacific Ocean, 2003-2008. PICES, Sydney, pp 360–393"); Yatsu et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR97 "Yatsu A, Chiba S, Yamanaka Y, Ito S, Shimizu Y, Kaeriyama M, Watanabe Y (2013) Climate forcing and the Kuroshio/Oyashio ecosystem. ICES J Mar Sci 70:922–933")).

### Biology, migration, and fisheries of the target stocks

SPF are short-lived and fast-growing, and are characterized by high and often variable levels of natural mortality, resulting in the dependence of their stock size on recruitment (Barange et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR4 "Barange M, Bernal M, Cercole MC, Cubillos L, Cunningham CL, Daskalov GM, De Oliveira JAA, Dickey-Collas M, Hill K, Jacobson L, Køster FW, Masse J, Nishida H, Niquen M, Oozeki Y, Palomera I, Saccardo SA, Santojanni A, Serra R, Somarakis S, Stratoudakis Y, van der Lingen CD, Uriarte A, Yatsu A (2009) Current trends in the assessment and management of small pelagic fish stocks. In: Checkley D et al (eds) Climate change and small pelagic fish. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, pp 191–255")). Recruitment is generally highly variable in response to complex trophodynamics, maternal effects, and environmental factors such as changes in temperature and prey availability (Houde [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR21 "Houde ED (2008) Emerging from Hjort’s shadow. J Northwest Atl Fish Sci 41:53–70"); Aoki et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR1 "Aoki I, Yamakawa T, Takasuka A (eds) (2018) Fish population dynamics, monitoring, and management—sustainable fisheries in the eternal ocean. Springer Nature, Tokyo")).

Spawning of the target SPF around Japan generally takes place in subtropical waters such as the Tsushima and Kuroshio Currents and the Kuroshio Extension, where small zooplankton, including copepod nauplii, are numerically abundant, thus playing an important role as a prey for the larvae and juveniles of the target SPF (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1), Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig4); Chiba et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR10 "Chiba S, Aita M, Tadokoro K, Saino T, Sugisaki H, Nakata K (2008) From climate regime shifts to lower-trophic level phenology: synthesis of recent progress in retrospective studies of the western North Pacific. Prog Oceanogr 77:112–126")). The spawning season generally extends from winter to spring, except for anchovy, whose spawning period extends from spring to autumn. Meanwhile, subarctic waters such as the Oyashio Current and Yellow Sea, and the northern areas of the Japan Sea and East China Sea are important feeding grounds for SPF during summer and autumn. Here, the SST becomes suitable for SPF, and large-sized zooplankton such as _Euphausia pacifica_, _Neocalanus_ spp., and _Calanus sinicus_ become available during these seasons (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig4); Sugisaki and Kurita [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR63 "Sugisaki H, Kurita Y (2004) Daily rhythm and seasonal variation of feeding habit of Pacific saury (Cololabis saira) in relation to their migration and oceanographic conditions off Japan. Fish Oceanogr 13(Suppl 1):63–73"); Yoo et al. [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR99 "Yoo S, An YR, Bae S, Choi S, Ishizaka J, Kang YS, Kim ZG, Lee C, Lee JB, Li R, Park J, Wang Z, Wen Q, Yang EJ, Yeh SW, Yeon I, Yoon WD, Zhang CI, Zhang X, Zhu M (2010) Status and trends in the Yellow Sea and East China Sea region. In: McKinnell SM, Dagg ML (eds) Marine ecosystems of the North Pacific Ocean, 2003-2008. PICES, Sydney, pp 360–393")). The transitional regions between subtropical and subarctic waters including the Kuroshio–Oyashio Transition Zone (KOTZ) are also important feeding grounds for both the adults and juveniles of SPF. Particularly during spring, abundant small neritic copepods such as _Paracalanus parvus_ are available in the KOTZ, owing to the spring bloom and entrainment of coastal waters by the Kuroshio and Kuroshio Extension Currents (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1); Takagi et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR65 "Takagi K, Yatsu A, Itoh H, Moku M, Nishida H (2009) Comparison of feeding habits of myctophid fishes and juvenile small epipelagic fishes in the western North Pacific. Mar Biol 156:641–659")). Therefore, the life history and migration of SPF are associated with seasonal changes in temperature and prey availability around the Japanese Archipelago.

SPF are important for worldwide fisheries and marine ecosystems, owing to their abundance and intensive consumption by various marine predators (Barange et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR4 "Barange M, Bernal M, Cercole MC, Cubillos L, Cunningham CL, Daskalov GM, De Oliveira JAA, Dickey-Collas M, Hill K, Jacobson L, Køster FW, Masse J, Nishida H, Niquen M, Oozeki Y, Palomera I, Saccardo SA, Santojanni A, Serra R, Somarakis S, Stratoudakis Y, van der Lingen CD, Uriarte A, Yatsu A (2009) Current trends in the assessment and management of small pelagic fish stocks. In: Checkley D et al (eds) Climate change and small pelagic fish. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, pp 191–255"); Checkley et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR9 "Checkley DM Jr, Asch RG, Rykaczewski RR (2017) Climate, anchovy, and sardine. Annu Rev Mar Sci 9:469–493")). SPF are indispensable for food security in developing countries, while in developed countries, SPF are largely processed into fish meal and fish oil. In Japan, the principal SPF fishery uses purse seining (Makino [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR47 "Makino M (2018) Rebuilding and full utilization of alternating pelagic species around Japan: a social-ecological approach. FAO Fish Aquac Tech Pap 630(2):61–73")), and various other methods are also used. Fishing grounds are located almost entirely in coastal and offshore areas around Japan. The target species of the Japanese purse seine fishery are generally Japanese sardine, Japanese anchovy, chub mackerel, spotted mackerel _Scomber australasicus_, jack mackerel, common squid, and skipjack tuna _Katsuwonus pelamis_. This fishery changes the target species by season and area, depending on availability and commercial demands of potential target species, under designated management restrictions. In Japan, chub and spotted mackerels fetch a high market price and are used mainly for human consumption, while sardine and anchovy are inexpensive and mainly used for human consumption and animal feed (Makino [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR47 "Makino M (2018) Rebuilding and full utilization of alternating pelagic species around Japan: a social-ecological approach. FAO Fish Aquac Tech Pap 630(2):61–73")). The Japanese catch of Pacific saury is almost exclusively derived from the stick-held dip net fishery, mainly in waters from the eastern area of Hokkaido Island to the Kanto area of Honshu Island during its southwestward spawning migration from August to December (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig1)). Large saury draws a high market price and is used for human consumption, whereas small-sized saury and mackerels are inexpensive and used in a manner similar to that of sardine and anchovy. It must be noted that the market price of juveniles (“shirasu” or whitebait) of sardine and anchovy is high, as this is a traditional and popular Japanese food.

In the Pacific Ocean, Pacific saury fishing grounds belonging to Japan and Russia are generally located within their exclusive economic zone (EEZ), whereas China, South Korea, and Taiwan harvest this species in international waters (Suyama et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR64 "Suyama S, Nakagami M, Naya M, Kato Y, Shibata Y, Sakai M, Takeuchi Y (2016) Stock assessment and evaluation for the Pacific saury (fiscal year 2015/2016). In: Marine fisheries stock assessment and evaluation for Japanese waters (fiscal year 2015/2016). Fisheries Agency and Fisheries Research Agency of Japan, Tokyo, pp 283–336 (in Japanese)")), i.e., the Convention area of the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC). This was formally established in 2015, and is responsible for stock assessment and management of commercially important species and the surrounding ecosystems (with the exception of tunas and salmons, for which other international organizations are responsible; Yatsu and Ye [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR93 "Yatsu A, Ye Y (2011) Northwest Pacific (FAO statistical area 61). FAO Fish Aquac Tech Pap 569:141–150")). The pacific stocks of Japanese sardine and chub mackerel were also harvested by Russia for a long period when their stock was abundant, and China recently began to catch them just outside the Japan’s EEZ near Hokkaido Island. In the Japan Sea, East China Sea, and Yellow Sea, the distribution, population structure, and migration of SPF, including the Tsushima Current stocks of Japanese sardine, anchovy, and chub mackerel, are not well known, particularly in the waters of China (for details, see descriptions of these stocks in later sections).

### Climatic and oceanic environmental drivers

Six climatic and oceanic environmental indices have been reported to affect the dynamics of target stocks included in this review (Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig5)), namely, the North Pacific index in winter (NPI; Trenberth and Hurrell [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR77 "Trenberth KE, Hurrell JW (1994) Decadal atmosphere-ocean variations in the Pacific. Clim Dyn 9:303–319")), Pacific Decadal Oscillation index in winter (PDO; Mantua et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR48 "Mantua NJ, Hare SR, Zhang Y, Wallace JM, Francis RC (1997) A Pacific decadal-scale climate oscillation with impacts on salmon production. Bull Am Meteor Soc 78:1069–1079")), SST of the Kuroshio Extension South Area in February (KESA; Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig1); Noto and Yasuda [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR53 "Noto M, Yasuda I (1999) Population decline of the Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanostictus, in relation to sea surface temperature in the Kuroshio extension. Can J Fish Aquat Sci 56:973–983")), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation index in winter (NPGO; Di Lorenzo et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR12 "Di Lorenzo E, Schneider N, Cobb KM, Franks PJS, Chhak K, Miller AJ, McWilliams JC, Bograd SJ, Arango H, Curchitser E, Powell TM, Riviére P (2008) North Pacific gyre oscillation links ocean climate and ecosystem change. Geophys Res Lett 35:L08607")), Arctic Oscillation index in winter (AO; Thompson and Wallace [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR74 "Thompson DWJ, Wallace JM (1998) The Arctic oscillation signature in the wintertime geopotential height and temperature fields. Geophys Res Lett 25:1297–1300")), and Monsoon index in winter (MOI; Hanawa et al. [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR17 "Hanawa K, Watanabe T, Iwasaka N, Suga T, Toba Y (1988) Surface thermal conditions in the Western North Pacific during the ENSO events. J Meteor Soc Jpn 66:445–456")).

Trajectories of winter (January–March) anomalies and their 5-year running means (shaded areas) of the North Pacific index (_NPI_), Pacific Decadal Oscillation index (_PDO_), sea surface temperatures in the Kuroshio Extension South Area (_KESA SST_) in February, winter North Pacific Gyre Oscillation index (_NPGO_), winter Arctic Oscillation index (_AO_), and monsoon index (_MOI_) during December–February. The vertical lines indicate years of regime shifts

The NPI in winter is linked to winter activity of the Aleutian Low, which affects subarctic circulation, Kuroshio Current transport, and oceanic states in the Central North Pacific, as well as the anomalies of basin-scale (PDO and NPGO) and regional SST, mixed layer depth (MLD), upwelling, and productivity of lower trophic ecosystems. It may also affect the probability of encountering predators of SPF (Yatsu et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR96 "Yatsu A, Aydin KY, King JR, McFarlane G, Chiba S, Tadokoro T, Kaeriyama M, Watanabe Y (2008) Elucidating dynamic responses of North Pacific fish populations to climate forcing: influence of life-history strategy. Prog Oceanogr 77:252–268"); Di Lorenzo et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR13 "Di Lorenzo E, Combes V, Keister JE, Strub PT, Thomas AC, Franks PJS, Ohman MD, Furtado JC, Bracco A, Bograd SJ, Peterson WT, Schwing EB, Chiba S, Taguchi B, Hormazabal S, Parada C (2013) Synthesis of Pacific Ocean climate and ecosystem dynamics. Oceanography 26:68–81")). The PDO and NPGO are the first and second modes of empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis of detrended SST in the North Pacific Ocean (north of 20°N), respectively. The variability of NPGO has been greater than that of PDO since the 1990s (Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig5); Di Lorenzo et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR12 "Di Lorenzo E, Schneider N, Cobb KM, Franks PJS, Chhak K, Miller AJ, McWilliams JC, Bograd SJ, Arango H, Curchitser E, Powell TM, Riviére P (2008) North Pacific gyre oscillation links ocean climate and ecosystem change. Geophys Res Lett 35:L08607")). The AO is the first mode of EOF analysis of monthly anomalies in sea-level pressure in the Northern Hemisphere, north of 20°N. The MOI is the December–February average difference in sea-level air pressure between Irkutsk (Russia) and Nemuro (eastern area of Hokkaido Island).

In the positive phase of PDO, the SST in the Northwestern and Central North Pacific Ocean, approximately between 30°N and 50°N, becomes cooler, while the SST in coastal and offshore areas of North America becomes warmer (Mantua et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR48 "Mantua NJ, Hare SR, Zhang Y, Wallace JM, Francis RC (1997) A Pacific decadal-scale climate oscillation with impacts on salmon production. Bull Am Meteor Soc 78:1069–1079")). In the positive phase of NPGO, the SST of the Northwestern and Central North Pacific Ocean becomes warmer south of approximately 40°N, while the SST becomes cooler in waters north of approximately 40°N and the entire area of the Northeastern North Pacific Ocean (Di Lorenzo et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR12 "Di Lorenzo E, Schneider N, Cobb KM, Franks PJS, Chhak K, Miller AJ, McWilliams JC, Bograd SJ, Arango H, Curchitser E, Powell TM, Riviére P (2008) North Pacific gyre oscillation links ocean climate and ecosystem change. Geophys Res Lett 35:L08607")). The PDO- and NPGO-derived Rossby waves drive changes in the meridional position and strength of the Kuroshio Oyashio Extension Currents (KOE), respectively, with a lag of 2–3 years; in the positive phases of PDO and NPGO, the KOE shifts south and intensifies (Di Lorenzo et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR13 "Di Lorenzo E, Combes V, Keister JE, Strub PT, Thomas AC, Franks PJS, Ohman MD, Furtado JC, Bracco A, Bograd SJ, Peterson WT, Schwing EB, Chiba S, Taguchi B, Hormazabal S, Parada C (2013) Synthesis of Pacific Ocean climate and ecosystem dynamics. Oceanography 26:68–81")). During the negative phase of AO, the cold Arctic air slides south into the Northern Hemisphere, causing cold winter temperatures around Japan. In the positive phase of MOI, strong NW winds prevail in winter, enhancing vertical mixing of the water column and reducing the SST. The winter KESA SST can be regarded as a proxy of winter MLD and SST near the axes of the Kuroshio and Kuroshio Extension Currents (Nishikawa et al. [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR52 "Nishikawa H, Yasuda I, Itoh S (2011) Impact of winter–spring SST and MLD along the Kuroshio jet on the recruitment of Japanese sardine (Sardinops melanostictus). Fish Oceanogr 20:570–582")), where the eggs and larvae of the Pacific stocks of Japanese sardine, Japanese anchovy, chub mackerel, and Pacific saury are distributed (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Tab1)). Anomalies in the SST at the spawning and nursery grounds are important as they primarily influence the survival rate of eggs, growth rates, and physiological conditions of larvae after hatching (Takasuka et al. [2008b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR72 "Takasuka A, Oozeki Y, Kubota H, Lluch-Cota SE (2008b) Contrasting spawning temperature optima: why are anchovy and sardine regime shifts synchronous across the North Pacific? Prog Oceanogr 77:225–232")). Variability of MLD is also important for nutrient supply from deeper layers during winter, and it affects the primary productivity (Chiba et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR10 "Chiba S, Aita M, Tadokoro K, Saino T, Sugisaki H, Nakata K (2008) From climate regime shifts to lower-trophic level phenology: synthesis of recent progress in retrospective studies of the western North Pacific. Prog Oceanogr 77:112–126")).

### Population fluctuations of the target stocks

During the 20th century, the Pacific populations of sardines flourished during periods of warmer-than-average global air temperatures and positive phases of the PDO index, whereas anchovies flourished during the negative PDO phases (Figs.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig2) and [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig5); Kawasaki and Omori [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR34 "Kawasaki T, Omori M (1988) Fluctuations in the three major sardine stocks in the Pacific and the global trend in mean temperature. In: Wyatt T, Larrañeta MG (eds) International symposium: long-term changes in marine fish populations. Imprento REAL, Bayona, pp 37–53"); Chavez et al. [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR8 "Chavez FP, Ryan J, Lluch-Cota SE, Niquen CM (2003) From anchovies to sardines and back: multidecadal change in the Pacific Ocean. Science 299:217–221")). Thus, synchronized sardine/anchovy cycles coupled with global or basin-scale climatic/oceanographic jumps or shifts lead to the concept of “regime shift” (Kawasaki [1983](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR32 "Kawasaki T (1983) Why do some pelagic fishes have wide fluctuations in their numbers? FAO Fish Rep 201:1055–1080"), [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR33 "Kawasaki T (2013) Regime shift—fish and climate change. Tohoku University Press, Sendai"); Lluch-Belda et al. [1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR43 "Lluch-Belda D, Crawford RJM, Kawasaki T, McCall AD, Parrish RH (1989) World-wide fluctuations of sardine and anchovy stocks: the regime problem. S Afr J Mar Sci 8:195–205")).

Kuwae et al. ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR41 "Kuwae M, Yamamoto M, Sagawa T, Ikehara K, Irino T, Takemura K, Takeoka H, Sugimoto T (2017) Multidecadal, centennial, and millennial variability in sardine and anchovy abundances in the western North Pacific and climate–fish linkages during the late Holocene. Prog Oceanogr. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2017.09.011
                  
                
                        ")) demonstrated that the Japanese sardine scale deposition rate (SDR) over the last 2850 years, obtained from Beppu Bay, Southern Japan (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#Fig1)) indicated periodicities at approximately 50, 100, and 300 years, whereas the SDR variations in Japanese anchovy showed periodicities at approximately 30 and 260 years. This finding indicates that the decadal-scale alternations in the sardine and anchovy populations observed in the 20th century did not necessarily occur during earlier periods. This is consistent with the results described by Baumgartner et al. ([1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR5 "Baumgartner TR, Soutar A, Ferreira-Bartrina V (1992) Reconstruction of the history of Pacific sardine and northern anchovy populations over the past two millennia from sediments of the Santa Barbara Basin, California. CalCOFI Rep 33:24–40")), who estimated variability in the abundance of sardine and anchovy based on SDR from 270 A.D. obtained from the Santa Barbara Basin off California. In the same study, spectral analysis of the SDR indicated that sardine and anchovy both tended to vary over a period of approximately 60 years, and anchovy also fluctuated at a period of approximately 100 years. Kuwae et al. ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3#ref-CR41 "Kuwae M, Yamamoto M, Sagawa T, Ikehara K, Irino T, Takemura K, Takeoka H, Sugimoto T (2017) Multidecadal, centennial, and millennial variability in sardine and anchovy abundances in the western North Pacific and climate–fish linkages during the late Holocene. Prog Oceanogr. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2017.09.011
                  
                
                        ")) also reported that since the late 15th century, the SDR variability nearly coincided with good/poor cycles in Japanese archives of catch records obtained from the Kanto area of Honshu Island to the northeast of Kyushu Island. Kuwae et al. This is an open-access peer-reviewed review article published in Fisheries Science (Springer/journal 12562) on April 3, 2019, by Akihiko Yatsu (Volume 85, pages 611-639). The article reviews the population dynamics and management of small pelagic fishes (SPF) around the Japanese Archipelago, focusing on four target species: Japanese sardine (Sardinops melanostictus), Japanese anchovy (Engraulis japonicus), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus), and Pacific saury (Cololabis saira). The article has 20k accesses and 113 citations.

Key findings:
- SPF catch and biomass show decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s, driven largely by climatic/oceanic variability and "regime shifts." The 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s.
- Variability in early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations.
- Overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, but both have been recovering since the mid-2000s due to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates.
- The fundamental cause of overfishing stemmed from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity following the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF shifted from sardine to anchovy.

Population dynamics context:
- Paleoecological evidence (scale deposition rates from Beppu Bay, Japan) covering 2,850 years shows sardine periodicities of approximately 50, 100, and 300 years, while anchovy shows periodicities of approximately 30 and 260 years—indicating decadal-scale alternations in the 20th century did not necessarily occur in earlier periods.
- During the 20th century, Pacific sardines flourished during warmer global air temperatures and positive PDO phases, while anchovies flourished during negative PDO phases.

Oceanographic setting:
- The Northwestern Pacific (FAO Statistical Area 61) is the most productive area worldwide, involving interactions of the Tsushima, Kuroshio, Kuroshio Extension, and Oyashio Currents, plus marginal seas (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan Sea, Seto Inland Sea, Sea of Okhotsk).
- Annual average sea surface temperature around Japan has increased +1.11°C over the last 100 years, exceeding the global ocean (+0.54°C) and North Pacific (+0.51°C) averages.

Management considerations:
- Six climatic/oceanic indices affect target stock dynamics: North Pacific Index (NPI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Kuroshio Extension South Area SST (KESA), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), and Monsoon Index (MOI).
- Management challenges arise because recruitment and surplus production are strongly affected by environmental variability, including regime shifts.
- Pacific saury is managed internationally under the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC), established 2015.
- The article provides recommendations for SPF fisheries management around Japan considering climate change and naturally fluctuating SPF populations.

# Impacts of El Niño on Fish Distribution

# Impacts of El Niño on Fish Distribution

*from NOAA Fisheries*

El Niño events are associated with physical and biological changes in our oceans that affect fish distribution. Among the variations in oceanographic features that are observed following an El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) event are changes in sea-surface temperatures, changes in the vertical, thermal structure of the ocean (particularly in coastal regions), and altered coastal and upwelling currents. These changes can directly affect the species composition and abundance of fishes. In the northern hemisphere, El Niño events typically result in observations of tropical, warm water species moving north (thereby extending their range). Cold water species move north or into deeper water (thereby restricting their range). Surface-oriented, schooling fish often disperse and move into deeper waters. Fishes that remain in an affected region experience reduced growth, reproduction, and survival.

Observations during the ongoing 1997 El Niño event are generally consistent with what has been recorded during previous events along the coastal regions of California, Oregon, and Washington, and in the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea. Recent reports include the capture near San Francisco of the equatorial game fish mahi mahi, and swordfish, striped marlin, and blue marlin have been observed off California and along the Washington coast. Movement of yellowtail, Pacific bonito, and albacore into northerly waters has also been observed. Their onshore movement has been particularly surprising as these fish are typically found 100 miles offshore. Other members of the tuna family, such as the Pacific and jack mackerel, have also moved north. Whitebait smelt, thresher shark, finescale triggerfish, spotted cuskeel, Pacific saury, common dolphinfish, white seabass, fantail ragfish, halfmoon, ocean sunfish, barracuda, California tonguefish, and California lizardfish all have been reported in areas where they are not typically observed.

A major consequence of an El Niño is the loss of commercially important species where they traditionally occur. A notable example is the movement of the market squid to cooler waters to the north, away from established fisheries in California. This phenomenon is also true for many rockfish species that move from nearshore areas to deeper or more northerly and cooler waters. Pacific whiting likewise shift northward from their spawning and feeding areas off California, Oregon, and Washington to the more temperate latitudes centered off Vancouver Island.

Pacific salmon are also affected by El Niño induced changes to their marine habitat. Increased mortalities and reduced growth have been noted in Pacific salmon populations off Oregon and Washington after previous El Niño events. With respect to the current El Niño, the loss of millions of adult sockeye salmon in the Bering Sea is being attributed to a nearly 10°C increase in summer water temperatures which occurred while the sockeye salmon were migrating back to their natal streams. Changes in the migration patterns of adult sockeye salmon have also been recorded for Fraser River (Canada) stocks. During an El Niño event, sockeye salmon use a more northerly approach, entering the Fraser River from the eastern side of Vancouver Island rather than using the more traditional entry through the more southerly Strait of Juan de Fuca.

The ocean is not a uniform and constant environment. El Niño events provide an excellent opportunity to observe and evaluate how changes in microhabitats influence fish distribution. Identifying changes in fish distribution will increase our understanding of the habitat requirements of important marine resources and will help us better manage our fisheries in the future.

This webpage from NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory (PMEL), sourced from NOAA Fisheries, explains how El Niño events affect fish distribution in the oceans. El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events cause physical and biological ocean changes—including shifts in sea-surface temperatures, changes in vertical thermal structure of coastal waters, and altered coastal and upwelling currents—that directly impact fish species composition and abundance.

Key effects documented include: (1) tropical warm-water species extending their range northward in the Northern Hemisphere; (2) cold-water species moving north or into deeper water; (3) surface-oriented schooling fish dispersing into deeper waters; and (4) reduced growth, reproduction, and survival for fish remaining in affected regions.

Observations during the 1997 El Niño along California, Oregon, Washington, the Gulf of Alaska, and the Bering Sea showed: mahi mahi captured near San Francisco; swordfish, striped marlin, and blue marlin off California and Washington coast; yellowtail, Pacific bonito, and albacore moving into northern waters (surprisingly onshore since these fish typically remain 100 miles offshore); and many other species (including whitebait smelt, thresher shark, ocean sunfish, barracuda, and California lizardfish) appearing in atypical areas.

Commercial impacts included: market squid moving to cooler northern waters away from established California fisheries; rockfish moving from nearshore to deeper/northerly waters; and Pacific whiting shifting northward from California, Oregon, and Washington to temperate latitudes off Vancouver Island.

Pacific salmon are particularly affected: increased mortality and reduced growth were noted off Oregon and Washington after previous El Niño events, and millions of adult sockeye salmon in the Bering Sea were lost due to a nearly 10°C increase in summer water temperatures during their migration. Fraser River sockeye salmon also changed migration patterns, entering from the eastern side of Vancouver Island instead of the traditional Strait of Juan de Fuca route.

The page concludes that El Niño events provide an excellent opportunity to study how microhabitat changes influence fish distribution, improving understanding of habitat requirements for marine resources and future fisheries management.

We’re not even one month into [“super” El Niño](https://grist.org/food-and-agriculture/the-super-el-nino-is-here-what-happens-next-could-upend-farming-worldwide/), the natural Pacific weather pattern characterized by warmer than average sea surface temperatures, and fisheries around the world are already getting scrambled.

In Peru, government officials have effectively canceled the fishing season for anchovies, one of the country’s most important exports and a leading source of fish oil and animal feed globally. The Indian government is preparing for a season of smaller, [less plentiful Indian mackerel](https://www.indiatoday.in/science/story/el-nino-to-hit-fisheries-sardine-mackerel-fish-species-to-shrink-in-indian-ocean-2933099-2026-06-24). Meanwhile, in Southern California, recreational and commercial fishers have reported some of the most successful months of tuna fishing they’ve ever seen.

The divergent situations show how El Niño can create [winners and losers](https://en.ird.fr/assessing-el-ninos-impact-fisheries-and-aquaculture-around-world) across the fishing industry, decimating some species while making others easier to catch. For fishers, the result is instability, with many forced to consider seasonal diversification. And consumers can expect fluctuations in the price of key fish products.

“People are worried,” said Juan Carlos Sueiro, an economist and fisheries director for the nonprofit Oceana Peru. As climate change is expected to drive [more frequent, stronger](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/grantham/publications/climate-change-faqs/what-is-el-nino/) El Niños, “our vulnerability is increasing.”

El Niño is a [weather phenomenon](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/dyk/el-nino) that happens every two to seven years in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It was named by Peruvian fishers who, hundreds of years ago, noticed periodic fluctuations in their catches, with huge declines occurring every few years around Christmas. They called it El Niño, after the baby Jesus.

The reason it has such disparate impacts on different fisheries has to do with the way it moves around ocean water.

Under normal conditions, trade winds blowing west along the equator move warm water from South America toward Asia. This causes cold, nutrient-dense water to rise up from the depths, a process known as “upwelling” that encourages the growth of tiny algae near the ocean’s surface. During an El Niño, however, weakening trade winds slow or even stop this upwelling. Less algae at the surface means species that depend on it, like anchovies, are forced to search for grub in deeper waters. Not only does this make the fish harder to catch, it can also [stress and shrink their populations](https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/how-climate-works/el-nino-fish-tale).

At the same time, those ocean dynamics can boost other fisheries. El Niño often sees warm-water species like the [skipjack tuna](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html) straying toward coastal waters of the Americas, where temperatures would normally be too frigid for them. Nearer to the shore, these species become easier to catch.
