[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Humboldt_current.jpg/500px-Humboldt_current.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humboldt_current.jpg)

Humboldt Current

The **Humboldt Current**, also called the **Peru Current**, is a cold, low-[salinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinity "Salinity") [ocean current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_current "Ocean current") that flows north along the western coast of [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) It is an [eastern boundary current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_boundary_current "Eastern boundary current") flowing in the direction of the [equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator"), and extends 500–1,000 km (310–620 mi) offshore. The Humboldt Current is named after the German naturalist [Alexander von Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Humboldt "Alexander von Humboldt") even though it was discovered by [José de Acosta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_de_Acosta "José de Acosta") 250 years before Humboldt.[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 1846, von Humboldt reported measurements of the cold-water current in his book *[Cosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosmos_(Humboldt) "Kosmos (Humboldt)")*.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

The current extends from southern [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") (~[45th parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_parallel_south "45th parallel south")) to northern [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") (~[4th parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_parallel_south "4th parallel south")) where cold, upwelled, waters intersect warm tropical waters to form the [Equatorial Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_Front?action=edit&redlink=1 "Equatorial Front (page does not exist)").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) [Sea surface temperatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature") off the coast of Peru, around [5th parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_parallel_south "5th parallel south"), reach temperatures as low as 16 °C (61 °F).[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) This is highly uncharacteristic of tropical waters, as most other regions have temperatures measuring above 25 °C (77 °F). Upwelling brings nutrients to the surface, which support phytoplankton and ultimately increase biological productivity.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

The Humboldt Current is a highly productive [ecosystem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem "Ecosystem"). It is the most productive eastern boundary current system.[[4]](#cite_note-4) It accounts for roughly 18-20% of the total worldwide marine fish catch. The species are mostly [pelagic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagic_fish "Pelagic fish"): [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"), [anchovies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchovy "Anchovy") and [jack mackerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_mackerel "Jack mackerel"). The system's high productivity supports other important fishery resources as well as marine mammals ([eared seals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eared_seal "Eared seal") and [cetaceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacea "Cetacea")) and [seabirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabird "Seabird"). Periodically, the upwelling that drives the system's productivity is disrupted by the [El Niño-Southern Oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Niño-Southern_Oscillation "El Niño-Southern Oscillation") (ENSO) event, often with large social and economic impacts.

The Humboldt has a considerable cooling influence on the [climate of Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Chile "Climate of Chile"), [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Peru "Climate of Peru") and [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Ecuador "Climate of Ecuador"). It is also largely responsible for the aridity of the [Atacama Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert "Atacama Desert") in [northern Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norte_Grande,_Chile "Norte Grande, Chile") and coastal areas of Peru and also of the aridity of southern Ecuador. Marine air is cooled by the current and thus is not conducive to generating precipitation (although clouds and fog are produced).

## Physical oceanography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Humboldt_Current&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physical oceanography")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Tropical_cyclones_1945_2006.png/500px-Tropical_cyclones_1945_2006.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tropical_cyclones_1945_2006.png)

The presence of the Humboldt Current and its associated wind shear makes for conditions that inhibit the formation of [tropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone").[[5]](#cite_note-5)  
(Worldwide tropical cyclone tracks, 1945–2006.)

The [trade winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds "Trade winds") are the primary drivers of the Humboldt Current circulation.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Variability in this system is driven by latitudinal shifts between the Intertropical Convergent Zone and the trade winds in the north. Shifts within the South Pacific High at mid-latitudes, as well as cyclonic storms and movement of the Southern [Westerlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerlies "Westerlies") southward also contribute to system changes. Atmospheric variability off central Chile is enhanced by the aggravation of coastal low pressure systems trapped between the marine boundary layer and the coastal mountains. This is prominent poleward from [27th parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/27th_parallel_south "27th parallel south") to [42nd parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_parallel_south "42nd parallel south").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

The Humboldt current, occupying the upper ocean, flows equatorward carrying fresh, cold Sub-Antarctic surface water northward, along the outskirts of the [subtropical gyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_gyre "Subtropical gyre").[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The main flow of the current veers offshore in southern Peru, as a weaker limb continues to flow equatorward. Around [18th parallel south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_parallel_south "18th parallel south") the fresh, cold waters begin to mix with the warm, high salinity Subtropical Surface waters. This collision causes partial [subductions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction "Subduction"). Within this region, the [equatorial undercurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_Undercurrent "Equatorial Undercurrent") (EUC) flows eastward along the equator, feeding the [Peru-Chile undercurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru-Chile_undercurrent?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peru-Chile undercurrent (page does not exist)") (PCU) that moves poleward.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

Off the coast of central Chile, there is a coastal transition zone (CTZ), which is characterized by high eddy kinetic energy.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) This energy forms [mesoscale eddies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_eddies "Mesoscale eddies") which extend 600–800 km (370–500 mi) offshore. The CTZ has three distinct regions within its boundaries:

1. high chlorophyll-a concentrations in wide regions off the coast of Peru (10–15°S),
2. high chlorophyll-a concentrations in wide regions off the coast of Chile (30°S), and
3. high chlorophyll-a concentrations in narrow regions off the coast of northern Chile (Montecino and Lange 2008). High chlorophyll-a concentrations are generally found within 50 km of the coast.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

The limb of the Humboldt Current System that veers off the coast of Peru creates a decrease in ventilation within the system.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) This lack of ventilation is the primary driver of an intense [oxygen minimum zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_minimum_zone "Oxygen minimum zone") (OMZ) which is formed in the sub-surface to intermediate depths. In the north, the EUC ventilates the OMZ, and in the south the PCU [advects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advection "Advection") low oxygen waters southward towards northern Chile.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) This OMZ is the fourth largest permanent hypoxic zone in the world's oceans. It occupies an area about 2.18 ± 0.66 million km3. The core of this zone is centered off Peru, creating a shallow upper boundary that reaches from about 100 m (330 ft) down to 600 m (2,000 ft).[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Another factor contributing to the OMZ is sinking and decay of primary productive resources.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

Consequently, the OMZ forces many organisms to stay near the surface where nutrients and oxygen are obtainable.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) The presence of a shallow OMZ restricts the migration of [zooplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zooplankton "Zooplankton") within the water column. Between 0 and 600 m (0–1,969 ft), many species of zooplankton occupy this space within the OMZ. This allows for a substantial exchange of carbon between the euphotic layer and the OMZ. 75% of the total zooplankton biomass move in and out of the OMZ. The OMZ also serves as a refuge for organisms that can live in [hypoxic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoxia_(environmental) "Hypoxia (environmental)") conditions.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

Coastal upwelling is the main factor contributing to the high biological productivity of the Humboldt current.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Upwelling within the current is not uniform across the entire system. Three notable upwelling subsystems are produced by this current:

1. seasonal upwelling in Chile only during the spring and summer, because of the displacement of the subtropical center of high pressure during the period January–March,
2. upwelling "shadow" that is less productive, but still large in northern Chile and Southern Peru, and
3. highly productive year-round upwelling in Peru.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The upwelling shadow identified between 35°S and 15°S is caused by the oligotrophic subtropical gyre impinging on the coast. This creates a narrow, but highly productive, upwelling zone.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

## Biological productivity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Humboldt_Current&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Biological productivity")]

Due to the upwelling zones within the Humboldt current, biological diversity is extremely high. The Humboldt Current is considered a Class I, highly productive (>300 gC/m2/yr) ecosystem. The current hosts a wide range of organisms including multiple species of [plankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plankton "Plankton"), [mollusks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusca "Mollusca"), [sea urchins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_urchin "Sea urchin"), [crustaceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crustacean "Crustacean"), fish, and marine mammals.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The food web starts with the [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton"). The conditions of the Humboldt current are prime for these organisms to thrive. This causes a cascade effect in which larger and larger organisms are drawn to the area.

## Fisheries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Humboldt_Current&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Fisheries")]

The Humboldt current produces some of the most successful commercial [fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisheries "Fisheries") in the world.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The major catches include: [sardines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardine "Sardine"), [anchovies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchovy "Anchovy"), [mackerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackerel "Mackerel"), [hake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hake "Hake"), and [squid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squid "Squid"). Three major stocks of [anchoveta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchoveta "Anchoveta") are distributed between 4°S and 42°S within the Humboldt Current System. North-central Peru's fishery is primarily composed of one stock of anchoveta. Sardines, [chub mackerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chub_mackerel "Chub mackerel"), and [bonito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonito "Bonito") are also common catches, but not as prominent, in Peru.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Southern Peru and Northern Chile host a major sardine fishery. Other common stocks include: a second anchoveta stock, [jack mackerel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_mackerel "Jack mackerel"), [tuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuna "Tuna"), and [swordfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swordfish "Swordfish"). Anchoveta, jack mackerel, and sardines are the primary commercial stocks in central Chile.

Anchoveta are found in more recently upwelled waters, close to the coast. Sardines, on the other hand, are typically found farther offshore.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Seasonal upwelling plays a major role in the spawning behaviors of both sardines and anchoveta. By spawning at the end of winter, egg and larval survival is greatly enhanced. This is due to the moderate upwelling, which causes lower turbulence, as well as a weakened Ekman drift offshore. These two species experience population shifts related to climate changes and environmental events such as [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Niño "El Niño"). This is due to changes in the availability of each species habitat. Anchoveta are an important component in the diets of marine mammals, seabirds, and larger fish. Shifts in these populations ultimately cause a shift in the energy processing within the Humboldt Current System.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

Jack mackerel (jurel) is the second largest fishery in the Humboldt Current System.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) As with the anchoveta in Peru, this species is believed to be composed of a single stock. Jurel are a straddling species. This means the species is found both within and outside of the 200-mile economic exclusive zone. Jurel became an important fishery in the 1970s to alleviate the pressure put on the anchoveta stock. During the 1980s, however, the jurel decreased in population size due to poor recruitment and [overfishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfishing "Overfishing"). Restrictions of jurel fishing were imposed in 1998 which led to regrowth of the population. Since 2002, the jurel population is now under full exploitation.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

Between 1993 and 2008, the hake fishery in Peru declined significantly.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) This was due to overfishing, environmental stress, and decreased reproductive capacity. The Chilean hake population in central-south Chile catch exceeded 100,000 tons, and dropped to 40,000 tons in 2007.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

## Influence of El Niño

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Humboldt_Current&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Influence of El Niño")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Sitting_at_the_Top_of_a_Cloud.jpg/330px-Sitting_at_the_Top_of_a_Cloud.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sitting_at_the_Top_of_a_Cloud.jpg)

[La Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Silla_Observatory "La Silla Observatory") observatory is in the Southern outskirts of the [Atacama Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert "Atacama Desert"), one of the driest places on Earth, it may come as a surprise to see cloud formations result of the Humboldt Current.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The productivity of the Humboldt Current System is strongly affected by [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Niño "El Niño") and [La Niña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Niña "La Niña") events.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) During an El Niño event, the [thermocline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermocline "Thermocline") and upper region of the [OMZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_minimum_zone "Oxygen minimum zone") deepen to greater than 600 m. This causes a loss of nitrogen and decrease in export of carbon. El Niño also causes poleward currents to increase in velocity. During non-El Niño years, productivity is very high due to the high nutrient contents, nitrogen recycling through processes such as denitrification, increased carbon export, and remineralization.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

During El Niño events, fish abundance and distribution are significantly affected, often leading to stock crashes and cascading social and economic impacts. These events have led to sequential changes, where sardines and anchovies have replaced each other periodically as the dominant species in the ecosystem. These species changes can have negative consequences for the fishing industry and the economies of the countries that fish the system. The anchoveta fishery in Peru was booming during the 1960s.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) In 1970, catches were reported to exceed 12 million tons per year. This accounted for 20% of the world's catches. An El Niño event occurred during 1972 and caused the anchoveta population to collapse. However, sardine populations saw a dramatic increase in the next 15–20 years. Consequently, sardine fisheries grew in this "[regime shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regime_shift "Regime shift")".[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

## Humboldt Current (Peru Current)

The **Humboldt Current**, also called the **Peru Current**, is a cold, low-salinity ocean current flowing north along the western coast of South America. It is an eastern boundary current extending 500–1,000 km (310–620 mi) offshore, named after German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt (though discovered earlier by José de Acosta). The current extends from southern Chile (~45th parallel south) to northern Peru (~4th parallel south), where cold upwelled waters meet warm tropical waters at the Equatorial Front. Sea surface temperatures off Peru reach as low as 16°C (61°F), unusually cold for tropical waters (other regions typically exceed 25°C/77°F).

### Key Characteristics
- The most productive eastern boundary current system in the world, accounting for roughly 18-20% of the total worldwide marine fish catch.
- Species are mostly pelagic: sardines, anchovies, and jack mackerel, supporting marine mammals (eared seals, cetaceans) and seabirds.
- The current has a considerable cooling influence on the climate of Chile, Peru, and Ecuador, and is largely responsible for the aridity of the Atacama Desert and coastal regions.

### Physical Oceanography
- Trade winds are the primary drivers of circulation, with variability influenced by the Intertropical Convergent Zone, South Pacific High, cyclonic storms, and Southern Westerlies.
- The current flows equatorward carrying fresh, cold Sub-Antarctic surface water, with the main flow veering offshore in southern Peru.
- A major oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) — the fourth largest permanent hypoxic zone in the world — occupies ~2.18 ± 0.66 million km³, with a core centered off Peru extending from ~100m to 600m depth. The OMZ forces organisms near the surface, with 75% of total zooplankton biomass moving in and out of the zone.
- Three notable upwelling subsystems: seasonal upwelling in Chile (spring/summer), a less-productive upwelling "shadow" in northern Chile and southern Peru, and highly productive year-round upwelling in Peru.
- The current and associated wind shear inhibit tropical cyclone formation.
- The coastal transition zone (CTZ) features mesoscale eddies extending 600–800 km offshore with three distinct regions of high chlorophyll-a concentrations.

### Biological Productivity
- Classified as a Class I, highly productive (>300 gC/m²/yr) ecosystem hosting plankton, mollusks, sea urchins, crustaceans, fish, and marine mammals. Upwelling-driven phytoplankton support a cascading food web.

### Fisheries
- Major commercial catches include sardines, anchovies, mackerel, hake, and squid. Three major anchoveta stocks distributed between 4°S and 42°S.
- Anchoveta are found in recently upwelled waters near the coast; sardines typically farther offshore. Both spawn at end of winter to enhance egg/larval survival.
- Jack mackerel (jurel) is the second largest fishery; restrictions imposed in 1998 led to population regrowth, though since 2002 the population is under full exploitation.
- Peruvian hake fishery declined significantly between 1993 and 2008 due to overfishing, environmental stress, and decreased reproductive capacity. Chilean hake catches dropped from over 100,000 tons to 40,000 tons in 2007.

### El Niño Influence
- Productivity is strongly affected by El Niño and La Niña events. During El Niño, the thermocline and upper OMZ deepen beyond 600m, causing nitrogen loss and decreased carbon export.
- The 1972 El Niño caused the Peruvian anchoveta population to collapse (catches had exceeded 12 million tons/year in 1970, accounting for 20% of world catches), while sardine populations increased dramatically over the next 15-20 years in a "regime shift" with sardines and anchovies replacing each other periodically as dominant species.

### Sources
Primary references include Montecino & Lange (2009), Chavez et al. (2008), Penven et al. (2005), and Ruminski (1991). The article relies heavily on a single source (NOAA) and includes public domain material.

# Connecting the Current: Ecosystem-based management of the Humboldt Current large marine ecosystem

[Feature Story](/newsroom/feature-stories)

![Connecting the Current template.png](/sites/default/files/styles/main_image_content_width/public/Connecting%20the%20Current%20template.png?h=e85f6c07&itok=yaoEt6Rk "Between 2011 and 2016, UNDP provided support to the Governments of Chile and Peru to implement ecosystem-based management as a strategy for restoring and sustaining the health, productivity, resilience and biological diversity of the Humboldt Current Large Marine Ecosystem, and the quality of life of the people who depend on its bounty.")

Connecting the Current template.png

Cold, slow, and bursting with life – this is the Humboldt Current, a stream of sub-Antarctic water that flows in a northerly direction along the coasts of Chile and Peru, before veering westward across the Pacific to bathe the Galapágos Islands. These nutrient-rich waters support some of the densest populations of fish found anywhere in the world – millions of anchovies, sardines and jack mackerel provide food for an extraordinary abundance of other marine fauna both at sea and on the shore.

The high productivity of this ecosystem is caused by upwelling – a process in which wind-displaced surface waters are replaced by cool, nutrient-rich water that ‘wells up’ from beneath. The Humboldt Current is the largest upwelling system in the world, supporting one of the most productive of the large marine ecosystems. It provides six percent of the global fish catch (down from 20 percent in 2010), generates goods and services valued at about US$20 billion annually, and hosts globally significant biodiversity.

This unique ecosystem is being placed at risk by over-fishing and rapid coastal development which results in habitat destruction and pollution. It is also particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. During El Niňo events, shifting wind patterns and increased sea temperatures result in the layer of warm surface water extending to greater depths and this prevents upwelling. Lower productivity causes fish stocks to collapse, which, in turn, triggers a cascade of negative environmental, social and economic impacts.

Between 2011 and 2016, UNDP provided support to the Governments of Chile and Peru to implement ecosystem-based management as a strategy for restoring and sustaining the health, productivity, resilience and biological diversity of the Humboldt Current Large Marine Ecosystem, and the quality of life of the people who depend on its bounty. This project, which was funded as part of the GEF International Waters programme, set out to establish and strengthen priority marine protected areas and fisheries management tools as part of a bi-national strategic action programme to implement ecosystem-based management. It also put in place measures to address policy and capacity gaps that presented barriers to the design and implementation of the strategic action programme.

Ecosystem-based management is a proactive and holistic approach to managing ecosystems in a way that balances conservation with sustainable use of marine resources and ecosystem services. It addresses multiple issues to manage ecosystems within the limits of their ecological functioning, whilst considering the economic and social context of management actions. Importantly, it recognizes that people are an integral part of natural ecosystems and that effective management solutions must involve all relevant sectors of society. The role of marine protected areas within ecosystem-based management approaches varies depending on the spatial scale and the extent and nature of the stressors in the system.

Peru has implemented a system of land-based ‘Natural Protected Areas,’ with a marine protection component comprising an area of two nautical miles around a cape or island. These protected areas are closely associated with centres of human settlement and activity, and play an important role in reducing the cumulative impacts of overfishing and other stressors, in addition to maintaining connectivity between protected areas along the entire length of the Peruvian coastline. An important intervention of the Humboldt Current project was to facilitate the participatory processes necessary to secure the zoning of the 22 islands and 11 capes making up the Guano Islands and Capes National Park, and to negotiate inclusive co-management schemes with local communities to manage local fisheries and protect biodiversity.

In Chile, the majority of coastal and marine protected areas are not situated close to fishing villages. While some protected areas are close to the mainland, the majority encompass extensive areas of ocean some distance offshore. In the Juan Fernández Multiple Use Marine Protected Area, which centres on Robinson Crusoe and Alejandro Selkirk Islands, the main income for the 285 households living in the islands comes from the endemic rock lobster fishery and tourism. A priority of the project was participatory development of tourism and lobster management plans within the protected area. The lobster fishery became the first artisanal fishery to be certified by the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) in the south-east Pacific. The success with which ecosystem-based management has been applied by the local authorities and island communities is demonstrated by the fact that it was the islanders who initiated the requests for certification of the fishery, and the establishment of the Juan Fernández Multiple Use Marine Protected Area (and its five associated Marine Parks).

# Using scientific models to understand ecosystem changes in the Humboldt Current
## Humboldt Tipping
125 subscribers


### Description
875 views
Posted: 24 Aug 2020
The Humboldt Current with its upwelling system at the coast of Peru is, in terms of fishing catches, the most productive system in the world. 
Aside from Anchovy and other fishery resources, it is home to many differing species forming an abundant food web. Food webs change over time. For example, marine animals can appear or disappear from ecosystems, depending on living conditions shaped by temperature, oxygen or other factors.  
To understand these changes, scientists monitor ocean conditions and analyse a lot of different data. Scientists want to understand the changes in marine ecosystems which the future will bring. They are testing these future scenarios not in the actual ocean, but with computer models. 
These models can be used to simulate the mentioned changes and can help in developing suitable adaptation measures. This way, scientists can work hand in hand with local fishers, communities and other professionals to help protect and sustainably use the ecosystem in the future.


The project is funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (Germany) and is part of the Bio-Tip call of the FONA- Research for sustainable Development program.

args.summary:
This video, posted on 24 August 2020 by the Humboldt Tipping project, explains how scientists use computer models to understand and predict ecosystem changes in the Humboldt Current off the coast of Peru. The Humboldt Current is described as the most productive fishing system in the world, home to anchovies and many other species forming an abundant food web. The video explains that marine animals can appear or disappear from ecosystems depending on living conditions shaped by temperature, oxygen, and other factors.

A key scenario explored is the potential expansion of the oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) due to rising water temperatures and reduced coastal winds. Since anchovies require oxygen and feed on small crustaceans while hiding from predators, they cannot survive in low-oxygen zones. If the OMZ expands closer to the surface, anchovies would need to migrate further south, which would impact marine mammals, seabirds, and larger fish that depend on them as a food source, as well as artisanal fishers who fish near shore (only large fishing boats could reach the migrated fish). Alternative species like bonito, tuna, and mahi-mahi—warm-water fish favored by warmer climate conditions—could potentially be caught instead.

Scientists use computer models to simulate these future scenarios rather than testing in the actual ocean, enabling them to develop suitable adaptation measures. The project works hand-in-hand with local fishers, communities, and professionals to protect and sustainably use the ecosystem. The project is funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (Germany) and is part of the Bio-Tip call of the FONA-Research for Sustainable Development program. The storyboard was created by Dr. Frederike Tirre and production by wekao | Jan Heinecke.
args.key_excerpts: "The Humboldt Current with its upwelling system at the coast of Peru is, in terms of fishing catches, the most productive system in the world."

# The Humboldt Current: A sea full of life to feed the planet

This South Pacific current has global significance for fisheries and biodiversity.

June 08, 2025

View page in: [English](https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/where-we-work/latin-america/stories-in-latin-america/humboldt-current-fishing-biodiversity/) | [Español](https://www.nature.org/es-us/sobre-tnc/donde-trabajamos/tnc-en-latinoamerica/historias-en-latinoamerica/corriente-humboldt-mar-de-vida-pesca-planeta/)

***Covering just 0.1% of the ocean’s surface, the Humboldt Current is the most productive fishing area in the world. Preserving it means securing a future food supply for millions of people.***

Along the coasts of Chile, Peru and Ecuador, air currents push warm surface waters westward, allowing cold waters rich in life and nutrients to rise from the depths of the ocean. This ecosystem is known as the Humboldt Current, home to schools of horse mackerel, anchovies, tuna and sardines, as well as giant squid, sharks (more than 70 species), whales and sea lions, among other iconic species.

Despite covering only 0.1% of the global marine surface, the Humboldt Current, also known as the Peruvian Current, is capable of providing up to 15% of the world’s fish catch and is responsible for 50% of the world’s fishmeal production, used as animal feed in aquaculture, poultry farming and livestock.

## Humboldt Current in Numbers

* ### 0.1%

  global ocean surface area
* ### 15%

  of the world's fishing comes from this current
* ### 50%

  of the world's fishmeal is produced here

This makes it the world’s richest marine ecosystem and most productive fishing area. In addition to the sea life, the region is home to more than four million birds that also take advantage of the rich food chain, including the iconic [Humboldt penguins](https://blog.nature.org/2025/03/15/humboldt-penguins-on-the-edge/), which are endemic to this part of the world and can live in the equatorial zone due to the low water temperatures. The albatross, Chilean pelican, Peruvian booby and gray gull are other species that forage the seas from the air.

However, the excessive extraction of resources from this current presents several challenges, including decreased biological productivity, disruption of marine and terrestrial ecosystems and threats to food security, mainly for countries such as Chile and Peru. In addition, global warming may alter species distribution, cause forced migration and reduce the availability of fishery resources for coastal communities. Extreme events such as El Niño, which are intensified by climate change, disrupt the ecosystem’s natural cycles, generating significant economic and social impacts. Given this situation, there is an urgent need to strengthen the resilience of the Humboldt Current by conserving its biodiversity, reducing emissions and empowering local communities to adapt to a changing environment.

For Natalio Godoy, marine biologist and leader of TNC Chile’s Oceans Strategy: “*The big challenge lies in coastal fisheries. Many people and many resources are working in the areas with the greatest biodiversity. And coastal areas account for more than 80% of the biodiversity we want to conserve. So there is also an opportunity there.*”

Since 2015, TNC has been working closely with several communities along the coast of Ecuador, Chile and Peru to ensure that the Humboldt Current remains a source of life, culture and livelihood for current and future generations.

### **How can we feed the planet without perishing in the attempt?**

According to the FAO, food production will have to [increase by 60%](https://www.un.org/en/chronicle/article/feeding-world-sustainably) to supply a world population that, by 2050, will be close to 9.3 billion people. It also states that the per capita consumption of aquatic animals has increased from 9.1 kg in 1961 to 20.6 kg in 2021, more than doubling. Add to this the overexploitation of fisheries, 70% of which are estimated to be completely depleted.

**Juvenal Antillanca, president of the Huiro Indigenous Fishermen’s Association**, in Chile’s Los Ríos region, has seen it first-hand: *“For many years we have been facing a decline in production due to a decrease in the populations of some species."*

The collapse of the fisheries and the resulting loss of biodiversity call for a change in approach. *“Conceptually, that is where TNC comes in: asking ourselves how to make more sustainable fisheries that allow these productive natural systems to maintain all their components,”* adds Natalio.

## Fishing is essential to global food security

The Humboldt Current plays an important role.

### **Science and technology for sustainable fishing**

In the late 1990s, fishermen in the community of Ancón, just north of Lima, Peru, began to notice a significant decline in species that they used to catch in large quantities, such as snails, octopuses and crabs.

Fisherman **Héctor Samillán** recalls that his community then introduced protective measures such as closed seasons, prohibiting the harvesting of certain species at certain times of year. *“We made those agreements empirically. But we had doubts about whether we were doing the job correctly. That’s when we contacted TNC,”* says Héctor.

It has now been more than a decade of work between scientists and fishing communities in Peru and Chile. The accumulated knowledge has been centralized in [FishPath](https://fishpath.org), a tool that seeks to improve decision-making and expand markets for artisanal fishing, an activity that approximately 93,000 people depend on in Chile, along with more than 55,000 in Peru and around 28,000 in Ecuador.

![Fishermen and their products in Ancón, Perú.](https://natureconservancy-h.assetsadobe.com/is/image/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/latin-america/159-MAG19005_181201_20568.jpg?crop=114%2C0%2C1820%2C1365&wid=800&hei=600&scl=2.275) ![Fishing boat at sea with the coast in the background.](https://natureconservancy-h.assetsadobe.com/is/image/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/latin-america/64-MAG19005_181120_7699.jpg?crop=228%2C0%2C1820%2C1365&wid=800&hei=600&scl=2.275)

**Seafood in Ancón** The fishermen in this area of Peru decided to establish management plans to conserve their resources. © Jason Houston

 

![Fishermen and their products in Ancón, Perú.](https://natureconservancy-h.assetsadobe.com/is/image/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/latin-america/159-MAG19005_181201_20568.jpg?crop=114%2C0%2C1820%2C1365&wid=800&hei=600&scl=2.275)

**Fishing along the Peruvian coast** In the Ancón area, north of Lima. © Jason Houston

 

![Fishing boat at sea with the coast in the background.](https://natureconservancy-h.assetsadobe.com/is/image/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/latin-america/64-MAG19005_181120_7699.jpg?crop=228%2C0%2C1820%2C1365&wid=800&hei=600&scl=2.275)

It is important to strengthen scientific knowledge to better manage small-scale and artisanal fisheries, which often do not have enough information or, when they do have it, do not have the methods to understand the state of their fisheries.

Matías Caillaux, Coordinator of TNC Peru’s Oceans Program

Meanwhile, in Ecuador, the aim is to support more responsible production of industrial purse seine tuna fishing. *“Electronic monitoring involves the installation of cameras in strategic locations so that inappropriate fishing practices can be identified in real time, such as the capture of vulnerable species like sharks, sea turtles and dolphins,"* explains Marco Robles, director of conservation at TNC Ecuador.

TNC Ecuador is also working to ensure that shrimp production implements more sustainable practices, including the conservation and restoration of mangroves, an ecosystem that is interconnected with the Humboldt Current. It is worth mentioning that Ecuador is the world’s leading shrimp exporter.

**Mangroves of Ecuador (3:17)** Learn about the work of TNC Ecuador in support of mangrove conservation.

Through science and the leadership of communities such as these, it is possible to envision a future in which the largest fish stock in Latin America maintains its equilibrium. Conserving the Humboldt Current is essential not only for its extraordinary biodiversity and its role in global food security, but also for the well-being of the coastal communities that directly depend on it. These communities, with their ancestral fishing traditions combined with sustainable fishing practices, are resilient guardians before the environmental challenges facing this sea full of life.

args.summary:
The article, published by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) on June 8, 2025, examines the Humboldt Current (also known as the Peruvian Current) — a marine ecosystem along the coasts of Chile, Peru, and Ecuador where cold, nutrient-rich waters rise from ocean depths. Despite covering only 0.1% of the global ocean surface, this current provides up to 15% of the world's fish catch and is responsible for 50% of global fishmeal production used in aquaculture, poultry, and livestock. It is home to horse mackerel, anchovies, tuna, sardines, giant squid, more than 70 species of sharks, whales, sea lions, Humboldt penguins (endemic to the region), and over four million birds, making it the world's most productive fishing area.

The article highlights growing threats to the ecosystem: excessive resource extraction leading to decreased biological productivity, disruption of marine and terrestrial ecosystems, threats to food security in Chile and Peru, climate change altering species distribution, and intensified El Niño events disrupting natural cycles.

Key expert quotes include Natalio Godoy, TNC Chile's marine biologist and Oceans Strategy leader, who notes that coastal areas account for more than 80% of the biodiversity they aim to conserve. Juvenal Antillanca, president of Chile's Huiro Indigenous Fishermen's Association, describes long-term declines in species populations. Héctor Samillán, former president of Peru's Ancón shellfish harvesters association, explains how his community established protective measures (closed seasons) empirically before partnering with TNC.

TNC's work since 2015 includes: using the FishPath tool (centralizing knowledge from over a decade of scientific-community collaboration) to improve decision-making for artisanal fishing — an activity supporting approximately 93,000 people in Chile, 55,000+ in Peru, and around 28,000 in Ecuador; implementing electronic camera monitoring for Ecuador's industrial tuna fisheries to detect bycatch of sharks, sea turtles, and dolphins; and supporting sustainable shrimp production with mangrove conservation in Ecuador (the world's leading shrimp exporter).

The article cites FAO data indicating food production must increase 60% to feed a world population of ~9.3 billion by 2050, while per capita aquatic animal consumption has more than doubled (9.1 kg in 1961 to 20.6 kg in 2021), and an estimated 70% of fisheries are fully depleted. The core message is that conserving the Humboldt Current is essential for global food security, biodiversity, and the well-being of coastal communities that depend on it, requiring sustainable fishing practices, emission reductions, and community empowerment.

The summer of 2024 has been dominated by positive temperature anomalies until the beginning of March, when the sea began to cool from north to south. In March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that began a year earlier. In this context, and regarding the habitat, it was observed that during the summer of 2024 the presence of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel has again occurred in a typical way, that is, along the fronts between oceanic and coastal waters, unlike the year 2020 when they were observed in oceanic waters, which was considered unusual at least for that season. From the analysis of the various variables regarding the habitat of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel, it is concluded that there have been different conditions in recent years, where the only parameter analyzed that remained within a narrow range is salinity. Another striking fact is that both species have been available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll concentration and relatively high altimetry values and high sea surface anomaly. In the case of Jack mackerel, its distribution on the central coast during January is noteworthy compared to its southern distribution in previous seasons. In the case of Chub mackerel, a higher availability was observed in the southern zone during the summer of 2024. However, it should be noted that there were no trips during February and March, due in most cases to the maintenance needs of the fishing vessels. At the moment of drafting this document, the fleet was fishing for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel in the southern area. A significant presence of marine fauna has been recorded in the areas of operation of three fishing vessels. A total of 2,671 individuals were observed between seabirds, whales, dolphins and sea lions, with the most numerous taxonomic group being seabirds with 1,772 individuals, dolphins were the second group with 810 individuals, then sea lions with 77 individuals and whales with 12 individuals. In the habitat reports submitted in the previous years (2019 to 2023) to the SPRFMO Habitat Monitoring Working Group, as well as in the present case, it should be specified that what has generally been mapped and modeled the ideal environmental conditions (habitat) for adult fish of Jack and Chub mackerel only. A similar type of study is pending for the early stages of both species. 3 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 TABLE OF CONTENTS 1. References 18 Lima, August 2024 4 Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024 1. Introduction The Scientific Research Committee (CIC) of the National Fisheries Society (SNP), in cooperation with the Humboldt Institute for Marine and Aquaculture Research (IHMA) organized the Eleventh SNP Workshop on the habitat conditions of jack mackerel and other species of the Peruvian Current in the Humboldt System, which was held virtually from 24 to 28th June 2024. It has counted, as usual, with the valuable participation and contribution of researchers from the Institute of Sea Research of Peru (IMARPE). This activity is a contribution to the national and international effort to research and diagnose the changing conditions of jack mackerel and chub mackerel populations, as well as other species of the South Pacific, with particular emphasis on aspects related to their habitats since the first workshop conducted in 2011. 2. Description of jack mackerel and chub mackerel habitats using oceanographic satellite and fisheries data Various oceanographic parameters are presented for the summers (January, February, March) of the years 2022, 2023 and 2024 with an indication of the fishing sets of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel (represented by symbols), since -in general- they are the months in which the fishing seasons took place. Figures 2.1.1 to 2.1.5. shows the oceanographic parameters of January 15, February 15, and March 15 of each year, from left to right, in order to appreciate the changes that have occurred in the last three years and their relationship with the relative distribution of Jack and Chub mackerel. 2.1. Sea surface temperature (SST, °C) between 2022 and 2024 In the period described, the presence of Lack mackerel and Chub mackerel has been observed along the thermal fronts; Jack mackerel fishing sets were carried out outside the continental shelf. It is considered that, in general, the moderate thermal conditions of the last five years (since 2019, with the exception of the warm year 2023) have led to a higher concentration of Jack mackerel, especially in the southern area. Chub mackerel, on the other hand, has tended to be distributed – as usual – more northwards to the extent that in that area the presence of Surface Equatorial Waters has predominated in the summers that favor it. However, unlike previous years, in 2024 adult Chub mackerel predominated in the southern area. (Figure 2.1.1). 5 Figure 2.1.1. Sea surface temperature (SST, °C) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel. 2.2. Sea surface temperature anomaly (ATSM, °C) between 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and January 2023, there were negative anomalies, as in previous years. Under these conditions, the main jack mackerel fishing areas were distributed in the area located south of the Paracas Peninsula, where negative thermal anomalies were higher during 2022. Chub mackerel, on the other hand, had some distribution areas in the center and south, but also in areas where it coincided with Jack mackerel in the north. The conditions in which Jack mackerel was detected and caught during January 2024 is similar to that of January 2022; and it is since February 2023 that warm conditions begin to develop until March 2024 (Figure 2.2.1). 6 Figure 2.2.1. Sea surface temperature anomaly (ATSM, °C) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In the months of March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches were observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel. 2.3. Sea surface salinity (SSM, ups) between 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and 2024, Chub mackerel fishing areas were distributed both in the center and in the south along the front between cold coastal waters (CCW) and surface subtropical waters (SSA); in the case of Jack mackerel, in 2023 its fishing areas have been located approximately the same as in previous years. that is, south of the Paracas Peninsula along the front between ACF and ASS (Figure 2.3.1). 7 Figure 2.3.1 Sea surface salinity (SSM, ups) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In the month of March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both species. 2.4. Sea surface chlorophyll (ug/Lt) between years 2022 and 2024 Between 2022 and 2024, Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel were found on the outer edges of the highest concentration of chlorophyll in the central and southern areas. For 2023, lower primary productivity was evident, as occurs during El Niño events, unlike 2024 where there was higher primary productivity than in previous years (Figure 2.4.1). 8 Figure 2.4.1. Sea surface chlorophyll (ug/Lt) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both species. 2.5. Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA, cm) between 2022 and 2024 The summer months of 2022 to 2024 presented a higher oceanic dynamic than in previous years, which is associated with a denser presence of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel, but mainly in the southern area. More specifically, the presence of both species has been related to intermediate to high SLA values (Figure 2.5.1) 9 Figure 2.5.1. Sea level anomaly (SLA, cm) during years 2022, 2023 and 2024, for the summer season. Jack mackerel fishing sets are indicated by black circles, and Chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. In March 2022, February and March 2024, no catches are observed due to no fishing effort despite having provided a fishing quota for both horse mackerel and mackerel. 2.6. Jack mackerel fishing sets in national waters during September 2023 In September 2023, Jack mackerel fishing sets were carried out in the southern zone in which the following conditions were present: cold temperatures, salinity of 34.9-35.4 UPS, low chlorophyll values, intermediate and high SLA levels, neutral and positive thermal anomalies (Figure 2.6.1). 10 Figure 2.6.1. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (SST), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll, Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during September 2023. The fishing sets are indicated by black circles. 2.7. Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets on the high seas during June and July 2023 During June and July 2023, the fishing areas for jack mackerel and chub mackerel were located outside 200 nautical miles, where cold temperatures, low chlorophyll levels, neutral thermal anomalies, intermediate and high SLA levels were present (Figures 2.7.1 and 2.7.2). 11 Figure 2.7.1. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll (ug/Lt), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during June 2023 on the high seas. Fishing sets for jack mackerel are indicated by black circles, and chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. Figure 2.7.2. Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinity), Chlorophyll (ug/Lt), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), and Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA) during July 2023 on the high seas. Fishing sets for jack mackerel are indicated by black circles, and chub mackerel fishing sets are indicated by purple crosses. 12 2.8. Analysis of variability for Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel according to fishing sets carried out between 2019 and 2023 in relation to satellite oceanography variables. Figures 2.8.1 and 2.8.2 present the comparative results of the analysis of variability of parameters relevant to the distribution of Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel between 2019 and 2024. The parameters analyzed are: Sea Surface Temperature (TSM, °C), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (ATSM, °C), Sea Surface Salinity (SALINIDAD, ups), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA ug/Lt), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA, cm), Sea Surface Altimetry (ALT, cm), latitude (LAT), distance from the coast (DC) and month of the year (MESES). 2.8.1 Variability in the case of Jack mackerel In the case of Jack mackerel, Figure 2.8.1 is presented, which shows notable differences between several parameters during years 2019 to 2024. For the TSM, a wide range of thermal values (between 18 and 25°C) is appreciated, with a preference for relatively high temperatures during years 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2024; in years 2021 and 2022 the thermal values have been below average. As for the ATSM (in a range between -4 to +3°C), there has been a larger presence of Jack mackerel in slightly positive values with the exception of 2021 in which all catches were made in the midst of negative values. On the other hand, salinity remained in a discrete range of values (35 to 35.4 ups) and low chlorophyll concentration values (< 4 ug/Lt) with the exception of 2021 when the highest values were observed. As for SLA and ALT, the presence of Jack mackerel is almost entirely limited to positive values, but not beyond values of 10 cm. Latitudinally, the distribution of Jack mackerel presented a range restricted to the central-southern zone. As for its distribution according to its distance from the coast, Jack mackerel was at relatively close distances, around 50 nm from the coast on average between 2019 and 2024, with the exception of 2020 and 2023 when it was located at more than 100 nm on average. Finally, the timing of the distribution of fishing sets on Jack mackerel is usually limited to the summer months, when the fishing quota has been completed (Figure 2.8.1.1.) with the exception of 2023. At the time of the 2024 workshop Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets were beginning in the southern zone. Figure 2.8.1.1. Box plots on the variability of parameters in the case of Jack mackerel between 2019 to 2024: Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinidad), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA), Altimetry (ALT), latitude 13 (LAT), distance to the coast (DC) and months (MESES). The red line on each box indicates the average value of all measurements. 2.8.2. Variability in the case of Chub mackerel For TSM, different ranges of thermal values are seen (between 18 and 24°C), having been distributed in warmer conditions during 2019, 2020, part of 2023 and 2024, and in colder conditions during 2021, 2022 and part of 2023. As for SLA and ALT, the presence of Chub mackerel is almost entirely limited to positive values, but not beyond values of 10 cm. Latitudinally, the distribution of Chub mackerel was wide during 2019 and 2023, with a southward trend in 2020 and 2024, and with a denser presence in the center during 2021 and 2022. In terms of its distribution according to its distance from the coast, Chub mackerel was relatively close to the coast during 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, and further away from it in 2020 and 2023. Finally, the timing of the distribution of Chub mackerel, as it is the same fleet that fishes for Jack mackerel, indicates that during 2023 it was also fished during June. At the time of the 2024 workshop Jack mackerel and Chub mackerel fishing sets were beginning in the southern zone. Figure 2.8.1.2. Box plots on the variability of parameters in the case of Chub mackerel between 2019 to 2024: Sea Surface Temperature in °C (TSM), Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly in °C (ATSM), Sea Surface Salinity in ups (salinidad), Chlorophyll (CLOROFILA), Sea Surface Anomaly (SLA), Altimetry (ALT), latitude (LAT), distance to the coast (DC) and months (MESES). The red line on each box indicates the average value of all measurements. 14 2.9. Potential Habitat Model for Mackerel (MHPJ) Valdez et al. (2015) developed a deterministic and probabilistic 2D model of potential Jack mackerel habitat (MHPJ) using satellite oceanography data and positional variables. Originally, six variables were considered for the model, but due to the high prevalence of cloud cover in the coastal zone, it was decided to exclude chlorophyll, whose remote measurement is affected by the atmospheric conditions. Jack mackerel catches showed a more robust correlation with the model when the probability exceeded the threshold of 0.45 on a scale of 0 to 1. The used satellite oceanographic parameters, including salinity and temperature, were obtained from the HYCOM platform. Thermal anomalies from an annual pattern were also incorporated. The MHPJ model was run biweekly only during periods with confirmed jack mackerel catches, using biweekly averages of oceanographic variables. This analysis covered from May 2023 (May, June, September and December) to January 2024 (first and second half of January), coinciding with the industrial Jack mackerel fishing season and the data available at the time of the study. The results of the model are presented in Figure 2.9.1. Regarding the areas represented by the model, during fortnight 1 (May 16 to 30, 2023), a wide extension with a high density (> 0.6) is observed south of 15th south degree; no coincidences were found in the northern area, specifically north of Pimentel. For fortnights 2 and 3 (July 16 to 30 and September 16 to 30, 2023), the area begins to retreat from the coast, increasing its probability at the edge of the shelf. On the other hand, the coincidences with the fishing sets were observed mainly in the southern zone with probabilities close to ~0.5. In the fourth half of December (December 1 to 15, 2023), an expansion of the area and an increase in probability are observed along the entire coast. In fortnight 5, a similar pattern is presented to the fourth fortnight, highlighting the coincidence of the fishing sets with the main distribution area in the southern zone. In fortnight 6, a reduction in the area of the model is observed, as well as a decrease in the higher probability values, with coincidences observed in the fishing sets. In addition, the average probability value of fishing sets was calculated, finding a high assertiveness (~0.55). 15 Figura 2.9.1. Resultados de seis quincenas del MHPJ entre mayo del 2023 y enero del 2024. Los puntos azules marcados en los mapas indican las capturas efectuadas por los barcos industriales. La escala de color indica probabilidad de encontrar jurel (valores de 0 a 1). 3. args.summary:
This document is a report presented to the 12th Meeting of the Scientific Committee (SC12) of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO), held September 30–October 5, 2024 in Lima, Peru. The report, titled "Habitat conditions of jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and other species in the Peruvian sea between 2021 and 2024," was authored by Mariano Gutiérrez, Almendra Tarazona, Carlos Valdez, Lucero Moreno, Claudia Juarez, Salvador Peraltilla, and Glorias Meneses, representing the Instituto Humboldt de Investigación Marina y Acuícola (IHMA), Instituto del Mar del Perú (IMARPE), Tecnológica de Alimentos S.A. (TASA), and Sociedad Nacional de Pesquería (SNP). Peru emphasizes it provides this information voluntarily and reiterates that SPRFMO decisions do not apply within Peruvian jurisdictional waters.

The report updates analyses of jack mackerel and chub mackerel habitat changes between 2021 and 2024. Key findings include: the summer of 2024 was dominated by positive temperature anomalies until March, when the Coastal El Niño (announced as ended by ENFEN in March 2024) subsided. Jack mackerel and chub mackerel returned to typical habitat patterns along fronts between oceanic and coastal waters during summer 2024, unlike 2020 when they occurred in oceanic waters. Salinity was the only parameter that remained in a narrow range across recent years; both species were available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll concentrations, relatively high altimetry values, and high sea surface anomalies.

Oceanographic analysis of summers 2022–2024 examined sea surface temperature, temperature anomaly, salinity, chlorophyll, and sea level anomaly. Jack mackerel fishing sets occurred outside the continental shelf along thermal fronts, with higher concentrations in the southern area during the moderate thermal conditions of the last five years. Chub mackerel tended to distribute northward but in 2024 adults predominated in the southern area. Notably, in several months (March 2022, February and March 2024) no fishing occurred despite provided quotas, due to vessel maintenance needs.

Variability analysis of fishing sets from 2019–2024 shows: for both species, sea surface temperatures ranged 18–25°C (jack mackerel) and 18–24°C (chub mackerel), preferring warmer conditions in 2019, 2020, 2023, and 2024; salinity remained between 34.9–35.4 UPS; chlorophyll was below 4 ug/Lt except in 2021; sea level anomaly and altimetry were mostly positive but not exceeding 10 cm; and distances from coast averaged ~50 nautical miles except in 2020 and 2023 when jack mackerel was found beyond 100 nm. Fishing was generally limited to summer months except in 2023.

A Potential Habitat Model for Jack Mackerel (MHPJ), originally developed by Valdez et al. (2015), was run biweekly from May 2023 to January 2024 using HYCOM platform oceanographic variables and excluding chlorophyll due to cloud cover issues. The model showed high-density areas (>0.6 probability) south of 15°S in May 2023, coastal retreat during mid-2023, expansion along the entire coast in December 2023, and an average probability value of ~0.55 for fishing sets, indicating high model assertiveness.

Top predator sightings from three TASA company vessels between June and September 2023 (5–240 nautical miles from coast, latitudes 12–21°S) recorded 2,671 individuals: seabirds were most numerous (1,772 individuals), followed by dolphins (810), sea lions (77), and whales (12). Within 80 miles, Peruvian gulls (249), Peruvian boobies (128), and Guanay cormorants (120) dominated; between 81–200 miles, black-browed albatross (400) and gray-headed albatross (20) were most sighted; beyond 200 miles, Parkinson's Petrel (150) dominated. Cetaceans sighted included blue whales (6), humpback whales (4 total), and sperm whales (2, one within 80 miles and one beyond 200 miles). Dolphins sighted within 80 miles included Bottlenose Dolphin (400) and Common Dolphin (385). Fur seals were the only sea lion species observed (67 within 80 miles, 10 between 81–200 miles). Species identification confidence by trained fishermen ranged from 25% to 100%.

The report notes that habitat mapping thus far covers only adult jack and chub mackerel, with a study on early life stages pending. Conclusions highlight that the last five years' thermal conditions increased jack mackerel availability in the south despite the warm 2023, chub mackerel distributed northward but shared southern areas with jack mackerel, and latitudes 13–14°S concentrated the largest catches in the last two years along the front between coastal cold and subtropical waters.
args.key_excerpts: "The summer of 2024 has been dominated by positive temperature anomalies until the beginning of March, when the sea began to cool from north to south. In March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that began a year earlier."

## Effects of western boundary currents and sea surface temperature anomalies on interannual variability of chub mackerel abundance in the Northwest Pacific

 Show affiliations Loading affiliations affiliations loading

*   [Li, Jiasheng](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/search/q=author:%22Li%2C+Jiasheng%22&sort=date%20desc,%20bibcode%20desc) ;

#### Abstract

The abundance of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Northwest Pacific has undergone significant changes in recent decades. To investigate the long-term and short-term impacts of environmental factors on the abundance of chub mackerel, Kuroshio volume transport in summer and winter, the Oyashio area, the Oyashio southern limit, and the Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (SSTA), were selected to construct the ARDL-ECM model based on the Autoregression Distributed Lag (ARDL) method for 3 age groups with resource abundance as the response variable. The results showed that in short term effects there is a positive correlation between Kuroshio intensity and the chub mackerel abundance in winter, but a negative correlation in summer. Oyashio area can impact the fish abundance under 2 years old significantly (p < 0.001) and the change of Oyashio sourth limit only has a significant impact on the abundance of 0-age fish (p < 0.001). In the long-term relationship, Kuroshio significantly influences the abundance of fish aged 3 years and older (p < 0.001). SSTA had a significant impact on the abundance of all 3 age groups (p < 0.05), while Oyashio area may influence the fish abundance under 2 years old (p < 0.05). Furthermore, Oyashio south limit was found to affect the abundance of fish aged over 1 year (p < 0.01). SSTA can increase the abundance in both short term (p < 0.001) and long term (p < 0.001).The findings of this research may enhance our understanding of the variations in chub mackerel abundance in the Northwest Pacific.

This is an Astrophysics Data System (ADS) abstract page for a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Sea Research (Volume 203, id.102561, February 2025, DOI: 10.1016/j.seares.2024.102561, Bibcode: 2025JSR...20302561L).

The study, titled "Effects of western boundary currents and sea surface temperature anomalies on interannual variability of chub mackerel abundance in the Northwest Pacific," investigates how environmental factors influence the abundance of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Northwest Pacific. The authors are Li, Jiasheng; Zhou, Weifeng; Dai, Yang; Tang, Fenghua; Wu, Yumei; Zhang, Heng; Fan, Xiumei; and Cui, Xuesen.

Methodology: The researchers constructed an ARDL-ECM model (Autoregression Distributed Lag - Error Correction Model) using four environmental predictors: Kuroshio volume transport (summer and winter), Oyashio area, Oyashio southern limit, and Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (SSTA). The model was applied to 3 age groups of chub mackerel, with resource abundance as the response variable.

Key findings:
- Short-term effects: Positive correlation between Kuroshio intensity and chub mackerel abundance in winter, but negative correlation in summer.
- Oyashio area significantly impacts fish under 2 years old (p < 0.001).
- Changes in Oyashio southern limit only significantly impact 0-age fish (p < 0.001).
- Long-term: Kuroshio significantly influences fish aged 3 years and older (p < 0.001).
- SSTA had a significant impact on all 3 age groups (p < 0.05) in both short-term (p < 0.001) and long-term (p < 0.001), increasing abundance.
- Oyashio area influences fish abundance under 2 years old in long-term relationships (p < 0.05).
- Oyashio southern limit affects fish aged over 1 year (p < 0.01) in long-term.

Keywords: Chub mackerel, Abundance, Kuroshio, Oyashio, Sea surface temperature anomaly, Northwest Pacific. The article is available as open access via Elsevier.

Abstract:

Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is an important pelagic fish in the Northwest Pacific Ocean. It is necessary for us to find the relationship between the abundance and influence factors, which are beneficial to exploit and utilize this resource. In this study, based on the recruitment data and the spawning stock biomass (SSB) data of the Pacific-cohort of *S.japonicus* during 1980—2016 obtained from Japan fisheries institution, the normality test of natural logarithm of recruitment was finished and the time period that passed the normality test was during 1980—1999, with the environmental data of spawning ground, we analyzed the relationship between the sea surface height (SSH), sea surface salinity (SSS), sea surface temperature (SST) and the natural logarithm of SSB [ln(SSB)] and the recruitment during 1980—1999 with generalized linear model (GLM) and generalized additive model (GAM). The GLM results revealed the order of importance of variables ranked by decreasing magnitude was ln(SSB)×Year, ln(SSB), SSS×Year and SSS, which were significant (*P*<0.05) and considered the combined effects of factors. Considering the single factor in GLM models affecting the recruitment, order of the importance of variables ranked by decreasing magnitude was SST, SSS, Year, ln(SSB) and SSS. The GAM results indicated that the model which contained Year, SST and SSH was the optimal model based on Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC), the importance ranked by decreasing magnitude was Year, SST and SSH. However, considering the single factor in GAM models affecting the recruitment, the importance of variables ranked by decreasing magnitude was Year, SSS, ln(SSB), SST and SSH. The suitable range of SSH was 62—65 cm, the suitable range of SSS was 34.72—34.74 and 34.78—34.83 and the suitable range of SST was 20.2—20.6 ℃. When ln(SSB)>6.0，the recruitment was at a high level, based on GAM analysis.

## Highlights

*   •Water temperature significantly affected the growth of _Scomber japonicus_ larvae in the northern Satsunan area. 
*   •Growth of _S. japonicus_ larvae was not linked to prey abundance or density. 
*   •_Scomber japonicus_ larvae had no significant impact on the mesozooplankton production. 
*   •The northern Satsunan area provides a good food environment for larvae. 

## Abstract

In the northern Satsunan area, southern Japan, upwellings generated by the intrusion of the Kuroshio branch current into Kagoshima Bay are observed at the bay's mouth once every two weeks in winter and spring, and the resulting nutrient supply promotes phytoplankton blooms. Currently, this is a key spawning and nursery habitat for chub mackerel _Scomber japonicus_ in Japan. This study examined how water temperature and prey density influenced the growth, mortality, and predatory effects of _S_. _japonicus_ larvae in the northern Satsunan area. Recent growth (measured as the average width of the last three otolith increments) of _S. japonicus_ larvae was positively correlated with water temperature but not with prey density, indicating that prey abundance was adequate for larvae and that water temperature controlled their growth rate in the study area. The instantaneous daily mortality rate of _S_. _japonicus_ larvae was 0.322 in 2021 and 0.252 in 2022 (equivalent to 27.5% mortality d−1 in 2021 and 22.3% in 2022). The food requirements of _S_. _japonicus_ larvae and mesozooplankton production were 0.00427±0.00334 and 6.37±3.04 mg DW m−3 d−1, respectively. _S_. _japonicus_ larvae had no significant predatory impact on mesozooplankton (0.0869±0.0796%). The present study suggests that none of the plankton feeders have a significant top-down regulating effect on mesozooplankton biomass in the northern Satsunan area, which provides a good food environment for S. _japonicus_ larvae.

2026, Progress in Oceanography  Show abstract The Kuroshio Current and its neighboring waters are nursery grounds for the early life stages of migratory fish, despite poor food availability under oligotrophic conditions. Although recent findings suggest that standing stocks of mesozooplankton are not low and provide good prey availability for fish larvae, no information is available at their prey quality. Here, we investigated the spatial and temporal variations in the fatty acid content of mesozooplankton communities from transect lines across the Kuroshio to evaluate the nutritional quality of mesozooplankton as prey for fish larvae. We identified 5 saturated fatty acids (SFAs), 4 mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), and 13 poly-unsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) in the mesozooplankton community. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that fatty acid contents in mesozooplankton dry mass were more variable between the seasons than at the sites, with increasing SFA in summer. Long-chain PUFA (LC-PUFA) content, represented by arachidonic, eicosapentaenoic, and docosahexaenoic acids, was comparable between the Kuroshio and its neighboring waters. These LC-PUFA contents exhibited significant positive correlations with the relative abundance of Eucalanidae copepods and molluscans determined with metabarcoding analysis. These contents were also positively correlated with the fatty acid content of the haptophyte biomarker. Beaked sandfish larvae had higher LC-PUFA contents than those of Anguilliformes leptocephali. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that the fatty acid composition of omnivorous crustaceans, such as decapods and Eucalanidae copepods, was synchronized with that of beaked sandfish larvae. These findings suggest that the LC-PUFA contents of mesozooplankton communities accumulate in omnivorous crustaceans feeding on nano- to micro-sized phytoplankton and are transferred to planktivorous fish larvae.

This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the journal Continental Shelf Research (Volume 285, February 2025, Article 105399) titled "Growth, mortality, and predatory impact on mesozooplankton of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus larvae in an upwelling system, southern Japan." The article is open access under a Creative Commons license.

**Study Context and Methods:** The research was conducted in the northern Satsunan area of southern Japan, where upwellings are generated by the intrusion of the Kuroshio branch current into Kagoshima Bay, occurring once every two weeks in winter and spring. These upwellings promote phytoplankton blooms through nutrient supply. The area is a key spawning and nursery habitat for chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in Japan. The study examined how water temperature and prey density influenced larval growth, mortality, and predatory effects. Growth was measured using the average width of the last three otolith increments.

**Key Findings:**
- Water temperature was the primary factor controlling larval growth in the study area; recent growth was positively correlated with water temperature but NOT with prey density, indicating prey abundance was adequate for larvae.
- Instantaneous daily mortality rates were 0.322 in 2021 (27.5% mortality d⁻¹) and 0.252 in 2022 (22.3% mortality d⁻¹).
- Food requirements of S. japonicus larvae and mesozooplankton production were 0.00427 ± 0.00334 and 6.37 ± 3.04 mg DW m⁻³ d⁻¹, respectively.
- S. japonicus larvae had no significant predatory impact on mesozooplankton (0.0869 ± 0.0796%).
- The study suggests that none of the plankton feeders exert significant top-down regulation on mesozooplankton biomass in the northern Satsunan area, which provides a good food environment for S. japonicus larvae.

**Authors:** Gen Kume, Hiroki Oba, Masafumi Kodama, Taichi Shigemura, Kazuhiro Shiozaki, Mutsuo Ichinomiya, Tomohiro Komorita, Takafumi Azuma, and Toru Kobari.

**Keywords:** Food requirement, Mortality, Otolith, Recent growth rate, Scomber japonicus.

**Data availability:** Data will be made available on request. The article has 7 figures, 3 tables, and is cited by 2 subsequent articles (one on fatty acid contents of mesozooplankton in the Kuroshio Current published in Progress in Oceanography 2026, and one on gut content and isotopic composition of Anguilliformes leptocephali in ICES Journal of Marine Science 2025).
args.key_excerpts: "Water temperature significantly affected the growth of Scomber japonicus larvae in the northern Satsunan area. Growth of S. japonicus larvae was not linked to prey abundance or density. Scomber japonicus larvae had no significant impact on the mesozooplankton production. The northern Satsunan area provides a good food environment for larvae."
