# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act), [16 U.S.C. 1801](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/16/1801)
*et seq.,*
NMFS manages the Pacific mackerel fishery in the U.S. EEZ off the West Coast in accordance with the CPS FMP. The CPS FMP and its implementing regulations ([50 CFR 660.508](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-50/section-660.508)) require NMFS to set annual harvest specifications for the Pacific mackerel fishery based on the annual specification framework and control rules in the FMP. The Pacific mackerel fishing season runs from July 1 to June 30. The purpose of this action is to implement harvest specifications for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 fishing seasons: OFL, ABC, ACL, HG, and ACT. Any Pacific mackerel harvested between July 1, 2025, and the effective date of the final rule will count toward the aforementioned reference points for 2025-2026.

During public meetings held every other year, the NMFS Southwest Fisheries Science Center (SWFSC) presents biomass estimates for Pacific mackerel to the Pacific Fishery Management Council's (Council) CPS Management Team (CPSMT), the Council's CPS Advisory Subpanel (CPSAS) and the Council's Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC), and the biomass estimates and the status of the fisheries are reviewed and discussed. The CPSMT, CPSAS, and SSC then provide recommendations and comments to the Council regarding the OFL, ABC, ACL, HG, and ACT. Following Council review and after hearing public comment, the Council adopts biomass estimates and makes its harvest specification recommendations to NMFS. Pursuant to regulations at [50 CFR 660.508(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-50/section-660.508#p-660.508(e)), NMFS publishes biennial harvest specifications in the
**Federal Register**
that establish the OFLs, ABCs, ACLs, HCs and ACTs for the upcoming two Pacific mackerel fishing seasons.

The control rules in the CPS FMP include the formula-based control rule for the HG, which is used, in conjunction with the OFL and ABC control rules, to manage Pacific mackerel. The HG is based, in large part, on the estimate of stock biomass for the fishing year. The biomass estimate is an explicit part of the various harvest control rules for Pacific mackerel, and as the estimated biomass decreases or increases from one year to the next, the resulting allowable catch levels similarly trend. The following is the formula-based harvest control rule for the HG:

HG = [(Biomass−Cutoff) × Fraction × Distribution]

The parameters in the formula are described as follows:

1.
*Biomass.*
The estimated stock biomass of Pacific mackerel is 61,737 mt for the 2025-2026 management season, and 67,954 mt the 2026-2027 management season.

2.
*Cutoff.*
This is the biomass level below which the directed commercial fishery is not allowed to fish. The FMP establishes this level at 18,200 mt.

3.
*Fraction.*
The harvest fraction is the percentage of the biomass above 18,200 mt that may be harvested. This is set in the FMP at 30 percent.

4.
*Distribution.*
Pacific mackerel range from Mexico to Alaska and regularly migrate between Mexico and the U.S. West Coast. Because some of the Pacific mackerel stock exists outside of U.S. waters, the Distribution parameter is used to estimate the proportion of the total biomass in U.S. waters and to calculate U.S. catch limits. The average portion of the total Pacific mackerel biomass estimated in the U.S. West Coast EEZ is set in the FMP at 70 percent. The 70 percent distribution estimate is based on the average historical larval distribution data obtained from scientific cruises and the distribution of the resource according to the logbooks of aerial fish-spotters.

The proposed Pacific mackerel harvest specifications for both the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 fishing seasons, as recommended by the Council, are presented in Table 1.

Table 1—Pacific Mackerel Harvest Specifications for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 Fishing Seasons

| Harvest specifications | 2025-2026 (mt) | 2026-2027 (mt) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OFL | 12,965 | 14,270 |
| ACL = ABC | 10,084 | 11,099 |
| HG | 9,143 | 10,448 |
| ACT | 8,143 | 9,448 |

Table 1—Pacific Mackerel Harvest Specifications for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 Fishing Seasons

These catch specifications are based on the OFL and ABC control rules established in the CPS FMP, recommendations from the Council's SSC and other advisory bodies, and biomass estimates of 61,737 mt (2025-2026) and 67,954 mt (2026-2027). The biomass estimates are the result of a catch-only stock assessment the NMFS SWFSC completed in March 2025. At the April 2025 Council meeting, the Council's SSC reviewed and approved, and the Council adopted, the 2025 catch-only stock assessment and resulting biomass estimates as the best scientific information available for setting harvest specifications for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 Pacific mackerel fishing seasons. Additionally, the uncertainty surrounding these biomass estimates for Pacific mackerel for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 fishing seasons were explicitly taken into consideration in the development of these harvest specifications.

Under this proposed action, in the unlikely event that catch reaches the ACT in either fishing season, directed fishing would close, while the difference between the HG and ACT (1,000 mt) would be reserved as a set-aside for incidental landings in other fisheries and other sources of mortality.[[1](#footnote-1-p41377)] 
For the remainder of the fishing season, incidental landings in CPS fisheries would be constrained to a 45 percent incidental catch allowance (in other words, no more than 45 percent by weight of the CPS landed per trip may
( printed page 41378)
be Pacific mackerel); and in non-CPS fisheries, up to 3 mt of Pacific mackerel incidental catch may be landed per fishing trip. The incidental catch set-aside is intended to allow continued operation of fisheries for other stocks, particularly other CPS stocks that may school with Pacific mackerel. The NMFS West Coast Regional Administrator will publish a notice in the
**Federal Register**
announcing the date of any closure of directed fishing if and when harvest levels reach or exceed the ACT. Additionally, to ensure the regulated community is informed of any closure, NMFS will also make announcements through other means available, including by email to fishermen, processors, and state fishery management agencies.

Comments on this proposed rule and on NMFS' determination that this proposed rule, if adopted, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities (as discussed below in the Classification section), may be submitted via
*<https://www.regulations.gov>*
(see
**DATES**
and
**ADDRESSES**
).

## Classification

Pursuant to section 304(b)(1)(A) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, the NMFS Assistant Administrator has determined that this proposed rule is consistent with the CPS FMP, other provisions of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and other applicable law, subject to further consideration after public comment.

This proposed rule has been determined to be not significant for purposes of [Executive Order 12866](/executive-order/12866). This proposed rule is not an [Executive Order 14192](/executive-order/14192) regulatory action because this action is not significant under [Executive Order 12866](/executive-order/12866).

The purpose of this rulemaking is to set harvest specifications (
*i.e.,*
OFL, ABC, ACL, HG, and ACT) and management measures for the Pacific mackerel fishery, consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act and the CPS FMP. The OFL, ABC, and ACT are based on the harvest control rules in the CPS FMP. These specific harvest control rules are applied to year specific stock biomass estimates to derive these catch specifications, which are used to manage the commercial take of Pacific mackerel. A component of these control rules is that, as the estimated biomass decreases or increases from one year to the next, so do the applicable quotas. The harvest control rules in the CPS FMP remain unchanged by this proposed action.

The Chief Counsel for Regulation of the Department of Commerce certified to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration that this proposed rule, if adopted, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, for the reasons described below.

For Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) purposes only, NMFS has established a small business size standard for businesses, including their affiliates, whose primary industry is commercial fishing (see [50 CFR 200.2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-50/section-200.2)). A business primarily engaged in commercial fishing (NAICS code 11411) is classified as a small business if it is independently owned and operated, is not dominant in its field of operation (including its affiliates), and has combined annual receipts not in excess of $11 million for all its affiliated operations worldwide. The small entities that would be affected by this proposed action are those vessels that harvest Pacific mackerel as part of the West Coast CPS purse seine fleet and are all considered small businesses under the above size standards.

The CPS FMP and its implementing regulations require NMFS to set an OFL, ABC, ACL, HG, and ACT for the Pacific mackerel fishery based on the harvest control rules in the FMP. These specific harvest control rules are applied to the current stock biomass estimate to derive these catch specifications, which are used to manage the commercial take of Pacific mackerel. A component of these control rules is that, as the estimated biomass decreases or increases from one year to the next, so do the applicable quotas.

Pacific mackerel harvest is one component of CPS fisheries off the U.S. West Coast. Pacific mackerel are principally caught off southern California within the limited entry portion (south of 39 degrees N lat.; Point Arena, California) of the fishery. Currently there are 59 vessels permitted in the Federal CPS limited entry fishery off California. The average annual per vessel revenue in the 2023-2024 fishing season for the 33 vessels that landed mackerel in the Federal CPS limited entry fishery off California was well below the threshold level of $11 million; therefore, all 59 of these vessels are considered small businesses under the RFA. Because each affected vessel is a small business, this proposed rule is considered to equally affect all of these small entities in the same manner. Additionally, the harvest specifications proposed in this rule would not constrain catch disproportionately for small entities in different size categories, as they remain well above the annual coastwide landings. Therefore, this rulemaking would not create disproportionate costs between small and large entities or between different size categories of small entities.

NMFS used the ex-vessel revenue information for a profitability analysis, as the cost data for the harvesting operations of CPS finfish vessels was limited or unavailable. For the 2023-2024 fishing year, the HG was 7,871 mt with an ACT of 6,871 mt and an incidental set-aside of 1,000 mt. Approximately 778 mt of Pacific mackerel were harvested in the 2023-2024 fishing year with an estimated ex-vessel value of approximately $406,702. For the 2025-2026 fishing season the proposed HG is 9,143 mt and the ACT is 8,143 mt. For the 2026-2027 fishing season the proposed HG is 10,448 mt and the ACT is 9,448 mt. Each fishing season will have an incidental set-aside of 1,000 mt. The proposed ACTs for these fishing seasons are slightly greater than those of the prior two fishing season (6,871 mt for 2023-2024, 7,943 mt for 2024-2025), and are well above recent catches, which have not exceeded 1,000 mt since the 2019-2020 fishing season. Therefore, the ACTs proposed in this rule are not expected to affect the profitability of the fleet compared to last season. Accordingly, under this rulemaking, vessel income from fishing is not expected to be altered from the vessel income from fishing under the previous season's specifications as a result of this rulemaking.

For the reasons described above, we find that the proposed action, if adopted, will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. As a result, an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis is not required, and none has been prepared.

This action does not contain a collection-of-information requirement for purposes of the Paperwork Reduction Act. There are no relevant Federal rules that may duplicate, overlap, or conflict with the proposed action.

This is a Federal Register proposed rule published August 25, 2025 (FR Doc. 2025-16233) by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), proposing annual harvest specifications and management measures for Pacific mackerel in the U.S. exclusive economic zone (EEZ) off the West Coast for the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 fishing years (July 1 through June 30 each year).

**Key Harvest Specifications (Table 1):**
- **2025-2026 season:** OFL = 12,965 mt; ACL = ABC = 10,084 mt; HG = 9,143 mt; ACT = 8,143 mt
- **2026-2027 season:** OFL = 14,270 mt; ACL = ABC = 11,099 mt; HG = 10,448 mt; ACT = 9,448 mt

**Harvest Control Rule Formula:** HG = [(Biomass − Cutoff) × Fraction × Distribution], where Cutoff = 18,200 mt, Fraction = 30%, and Distribution = 70% (proportion of biomass in U.S. waters).

**Management Measures:** If the fishery reaches the ACT in either season, directed fishing closes, with the 1,000-mt difference between HG and ACT reserved as a set-aside for incidental landings in other coastal pelagic species (CPS) fisheries. **Regulatory Impact:** The rule is certified as not having significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. All 59 vessels permitted in the Federal CPS limited entry fishery off California are considered small businesses (annual receipts under $11 million). Recent catches have not exceeded 1,000 mt since the 2019-2020 fishing season, and the proposed ACTs are well above recent harvest levels. Prior fishing season (2023-2024) had HG of 7,871 mt and ACT of 6,871 mt with roughly 778 mt harvested (ex-vessel value ~$406,702). The rule proposes amendments to 50 CFR 660.511 paragraphs (i)(1) and (2). The Pacific mackerel fishing season runs July 1 to June 30. The rule was determined not significant under Executive Order 12866.

![School of blue-green, silvery Pacific chub mackerel fish swimming together in dark waters.](/s3//styles/full_width/s3/dam-migration/900x600-pacific-chub-mackerel-shutterstock.jpg?itok=n4Bugvkp) Pacific mackerel. Credit: Shutterstock

U.S. wild-caught Pacific mackerel is a smart seafood choice because it is sustainably managed and responsibly harvested under U.S. regulations.

![Population Status Icon](/themes/custom/noaa_components/images/species--fish-population.png)

### Population

The stock is not overfished.

![Fishing Status Icon](/themes/custom/noaa_components/images/species--fish-status.png)

### Fishing Rate

Not subject to overfishing.

![Habitat Impacts Icon](/themes/custom/noaa_components/images/species--habitat.png)

### Habitat Impact

The gear used to catch Pacific mackerel is used at the surface and has little impact on bottom habitat.

![Bycatch Icon](/themes/custom/noaa_components/images/species--bycatch.png)

### Bycatch

Bycatch is low because gear used is selective.

### Population Status

* Pacific mackerel is not overfished (2023 stock assessment), and not subject to overfishing based on 2023 catch data. Summary stock assessment information can be found on [Stock SMART](https://www.st.nmfs.noaa.gov/stocksmart?stockname=Pacific%20chub%20mackerel%20-%20Pacific%20Coast&stockid=10163).
* Pacific mackerel naturally experience “boom and bust” cycles of abundance, which is typical of other small pelagic species that have relatively short life spans and high reproduction rates.
* The Pacific mackerel stock is well above its target population level. However, in historical terms, the population remains at a relatively low abundance level, due primarily to oceanographic conditions.

### Appearance

* The body of the Pacific mackerel tapers at both ends.
* They have a pointy head and a large mouth.
* The head is dark blue, the back is dark blue with about 30 dark wavy lines, and the undersides are silver green.
* Pacific mackerel can be distinguished from other mackerel by counting the finlets on their back; Pacific mackerel typically have four to six finlets.

### Biology

* Pacific mackerel grow fast, up to 25 inches and more than 6 pounds.
* They can live up to 18 years but are able to reproduce by age 4, and sometimes as early as age 1.
* They spawn at different times of the year, depending on where they live. Pacific mackerel spawn from late April to September off California, year-round off central Baja California peaking from June through October, and from late fall to early spring off Cabo San Lucas.
* They spawn several times a year, releasing batches of almost 70,000 eggs each time. The eggs usually hatch within 4 to 5 days.
* Pacific mackerel feed on plankton (tiny floating plants and animals) and the younger stages of all the pelagic species such as anchovies and sardines, as well as their own young.
* Various larger fish (such as sharks and tunas), marine mammals, and seabirds eat Pacific mackerel.
* Pacific mackerel school as a defense against predators. Often they will school with other pelagic species such as jack mackerel and sardines.
* As adults, they migrate north to Washington in the summer and south to Baja California in the winter. The northerly movement in summer is accentuated during El Niño events.
* They also travel inshore and offshore off California—they’re more abundant inshore from July to November and more abundant offshore from March to May.

### Where They Live

#### Range * Pacific mackerel are found from southeastern Alaska to Mexico but are most common south of Point Conception, California. Habitat * Pacific mackerel live within 20 miles of shore in water ranging from 50˚ to 72˚ F. * When the population is small, they tend to occupy only the warmer part of their habitat. * Juveniles live off sandy beaches, around kelp beds, and in open bays. * Adults are found near shallow banks from the surface to waters almost 1,000 feet deep. Fishery Management * [NOAA Fisheries](http://www.westcoast.fisheries.noaa.gov/) and the [Pacific Fishery Management Council](https://www.pcouncil.org/) manage the Pacific mackerel fishery. * Managed under the [Coastal Pelagic Species Fishery Management Plan](http://www.pcouncil.org/coastal-pelagic-species/fishery-management-plan-and-amendments/): + Catch limits are in place to end and prevent overfishing. + Permits are needed to harvest Pacific mackerel. + Gear restrictions are in place to reduce bycatch. Harvest * Commercial fishery: + In 2024, commercial landings of Pacific mackerel totaled 3.3 million pounds and were valued at $800,000, according to the NOAA Fisheries [commercial fishing landings database](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/foss/f?p=215:200:3577333744020::NO:::). + There is no directed fishery for mackerel in Oregon or Washington, but small amounts are taken incidentally by whiting trawlers and salmon trollers. * Gear types, habitat impacts, and bycatch: + Round haul nets are used to catch Pacific mackerel. + Habitat and bycatch impacts are minimal because the gear is used at the surface. * Recreational fishery: + Recreational fishermen catch Pacific mackerel in California but seldom target them. + The statewide recreational harvest makes up a small fraction (less than 5 percent in weight) of the total landings. + California’s recreational catch of Pacific mackerel is included within the fishery harvest guideline, but there are no other restrictions on this fishery. Last updated by NOAA Fisheries on 06/26/2026

Interannual variations in body weight and length measurements of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus). Research how body weight and standard length or fork length of chub mackerel fluctuate year over year across Pacific populations (e.g., the Tsushima Warm Current stock and Pacific stock in Japan, the East China Sea stock, the California Current stock, the Peruvian/Humboldt stock). --- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Moving beyond controversy: is the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) stock recovering? ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1814806/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (May 14, 2026, Volume 13) that assesses the stock status of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in Korean waters of the Northwest Pacific. The study was conducted by Dong-Jin Kwak, Do-Hoon Kim, and Kyounghoon Lee from Pukyong National University, Busan, Republic of Korea.

**Purpose and Context:** The chub mackerel has been managed under Korea's Total Allowable Catch (TAC) system since 1999, but prior stock assessments have yielded conflicting results regarding whether the stock has recovered or remains overfished, complicating management decisions. This study aims to resolve discrepancies using two complementary models.

**Methods:** The study employed CMSY++ (which uses an Artificial Neural Network/ANN to objectively estimate prior biomass ranges) and a Bayesian State-Space (BSS) model. Crucially, the BSS model incorporated a 2% annual technical creep correction to CPUE data—a factor frequently overlooked in previous research. The analysis used 55 years of catch data (1970–2024) from Korea, China, and Japan (Tsushima Current stock), plus 27 years of CPUE data (1997–2023) from Korea. Gross tonnage was selected as the primary effort variable (correlation coefficient 0.976, R²=0.950).

**Key Findings:**
- In 2024, the relative biomass (B/BMSY) was estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), classifying the stock as "Overfished" (still below the Biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield).
- CMSY++ estimated: r=0.255, k=2,273,005 tons, MSY=145,462 tons, B2024=779,191 tons.
- BSS estimated: r=0.310, k=1,802,382 tons, MSY=139,902 tons, B2024=549,884 tons.
- Kobe plot analysis revealed sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s has impeded recovery, with 87.6% (CMSY++) and 95.3% (BSS) posterior probability of the stock remaining in the "overfished and overfishing" red quadrant.
- Korean catch peaked at 415,003 tons in 1996, reached a historical low of 77,603 tons in 2020, and was 124,928 tons in 2024. The large purse seine fishery accounts for 82.2% of domestic catch (average 91,349 tons, 2020–2024).
- Fishing effort has effectively increased despite fleet reduction: vessels decreased from 342 (1992) to 106 (2024), but GT/vessel rose from 131 to 188 and EHP/vessel from 827 to 1,471.
- Sensitivity analysis showed B2024 estimates varied by up to 34% depending on technical creep correction (0%: 824,168 tons vs. 2%: 549,884 tons).

**Conclusions:** The study demonstrates CMSY++ as an effective tool for reconciling discrepancies in data-limited stock assessments and underscores the necessity of correcting for technical creep. Landing data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market shows an increasing proportion of small-sized (≤250g, ~29.7cm TL, below the L50 of 31.4cm) immature individuals in the catch (from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024), providing biological evidence of stock depletion. The authors recommend more stringent TAC reductions, extended closed seasons, vessel buyback programs, and upward revision of minimum legal size limits for the stock's recovery.
</summary>

URL: https://www.pcouncil.org/documents/2025/03/g-4-attachment-1-catch-only-stock-assessment-of-pacific-mackerel-for-u-s-management-in-2025-26-and-2026-27-fishing-years.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a NOAA Technical Memorandum (NOAA-TM-NMFS-SWFSC-718, March 2025) presenting a catch-only stock assessment of Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) for U.S. management in the 2025-26 and 2026-27 fishing years. Authors include Alexander J. Jensen, Caitlin Allen Akselrud, Juan P. Zwolinski, Peter T. Kuriyama, and Kevin T. Hill from NOAA Southwest Fisheries Science Center and UC Santa Cruz.

**Purpose and Framework:** The Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) follows a management schedule with full benchmark assessments every four years (last conducted 2023) and catch-only projection assessments every four years (last in 2021). This 2025 catch-only assessment provides biomass estimates and harvest guidelines for the period July 2025 through June 2027. It uses the same model as the 2023 benchmark assessment, updating only catch data—including new landings for model years 2022-2023 and forecasted landings for 2024-2026.

**Stock Description:** Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California. Three spawning aggregations are hypothesized: Gulf of California, Cabo San Lucas area, and the Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos (Baja California). The PFMC manages this transboundary stock with an assumed long-term average distribution of approximately 70% in U.S. waters.

**Catch Data:** Landings data (2008-2024) came from commercial purse-seine fisheries in the U.S. and Mexico (Ensenada and Magdalena Bay), recreational fisheries in California, and bycatch from the Pacific whiting at-sea fishery. Data sources included CONAPESCA, PacFIN, and CDFW reports. 'Unidentified' mackerel landings from CA and WA were excluded for consistency. Total landings ranged from roughly 3,331 mt (2009) to 32,027 mt (2020). Assumed/forecasted landings for 2025 and 2026 were set at 16,661 mt each based on 2021-2023 averages.

**Stock Assessment Results:** The model (Stock Synthesis v3.30.22.1) converged successfully. Recruitment was relatively high for model years 2011, 2016, and 2018. Stock biomass (age 1+) generally declined between 2008 and 2022, then was estimated at:
- 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26
- 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for fishing year 2026-27

Estimates for 2023 onward are highly uncertain and informed primarily by the stock-recruit relationship due to missing acoustic-trawl (AT) survey data for 2020 and 2022.

**Sensitivity Analyses:** All sensitivity scenarios produced lower forecasted biomass than the base model. Fixing forecasted recruitment to 2019-2021 average recruitment produced the largest decrease (56,390 mt by 2026-27). A scenario fixing age-0 fecundity to zero during forecast years highlighted an issue in Stock Synthesis where age-0 fish erroneously contribute to spawning stock biomass in single-season models; this represents best available information but departs from the benchmark calculation method.

**Harvest Control Rules:** The stock remains above the 18,200 mt management cutoff threshold. With an EMSY of 0.30, U.S. distribution factor of 0.70, and P-star of 0.45:
- 2025-26: OFL = 12,965 mt; HG = 9,143 mt
- 2026-27: OFL = 14,270 mt; HG = 10,448 mt

**Exploitation and Management Performance:** Instantaneous fishing mortality (F) fluctuated from roughly 0.05 to 0.35 yr⁻¹ between 2008-2023. Annual exploitation rates ranged from ~1% to 27%. U.S. fisheries harvested only 7-39% of harvest guidelines across model years 2008-2023. The annual catch limit for 2024-25 was 10,073 mt.

**Ecosystem Considerations:** Pacific mackerel are part of the coastal pelagic species assemblage in the California Current, serving as both predators of plankton and smaller CPS (anchovy, sardine, squid) and prey for larger fish, marine mammals, and seabirds. Their abundance can spike during favorable oceanographic conditions.

**Uncertainties and Research Needs:** Major uncertainties include missing AT survey data for 2020 and 2022, variable stock distribution in U.S. waters, and survey catchability issues. Research needs include exploring natural mortality (M) estimates for similar CPS, characterizing spatial stock structure, and continuing survey data collection in Mexican waters (the 2024 survey achieved expanded Mexican coverage). The 2024 summer AT survey estimated Pacific mackerel biomass at 11,129 mt (preliminary).
</summary>

URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2615/15/8/1135

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the journal Animals (MDPI) on April 15, 2025, by Guoqing Zhao (East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University), Heng Zhang, and Fenghua Tang. The study examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO) using commercial fishing data from Chinese light purse seine vessels during 2016–2021, comprising 38,123 fishing operations and 4,440 biological samples. The study area covers 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E.

Key findings: (1) High catches were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan's and Russia's exclusive economic zone lines; the gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward, driven largely by climate warming and marine heatwaves since 2014. (2) CPUE decreased year by year (strong negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01). (3) Using the length-based Bayesian (LBB) method for stock assessment, the population of chub mackerel was found to be healthy during 2016–2021, with no overfishing: F/M values were all less than 0.5, E (exploitation ratio) ranged from 0.17 to 0.32 (below 0.5), B/B0 exceeded 0.5, and B/Bmsy exceeded 1. Body length structure was reasonable with no miniaturization and large individuals still present (L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt close to 1; Lc/Lopt greater than 1). Total mortality (Z) ranged from 1.01 (2016) to 1.64 (2021), natural mortality (M) from 0.59–0.85, and fishing mortality (F) from 0.23–0.79, with natural mortality being the dominant contributor to total mortality. The asymptotic length (Linf) varied from 36–42.35 cm, with growth coefficient K from 0.31–0.65. Sex ratios (female:male) ranged from 1.09–2.55, and fork lengths ranged from 102–400 mm.

However, the E value showed an increasing year-by-year trend, reaching 0.48 in 2021, suggesting the population may soon reach a critical exploitation threshold. The authors emphasize that managers should focus on the impact of climate warming on marine ecosystem population composition. The decline in catches/CPUE is attributed to multiple factors including fishing effort dynamics, interspecific competition with Japanese sardine (Sardinops melanostictus), and potential changes in spawning grounds affected by the Kuroshio Current. The LBB method was selected because chub mackerel is a data-poor fishery in the high seas of the NPO, requiring only length-frequency data for stock assessment. Funding was provided by the National Key Research and Development Programme (2019YFD0901405) and Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Polar Science Base Open Subject Fund (SOO2024-15). DOI: 10.3390/ani15081135.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Animals (an open-access MDPI journal) in April 2025, examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO). - Study area: High seas of the NPO between 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E
- Data: 38,123 fishing operations from Chinese commercial light purse seine vessel logs (2016–2021), plus 4,440 biological samples
- Methods: Length-weight relationships, Von Bertalanffy growth equations (ELEFAN I in FISAT II), mortality estimation (Pauly's equations), and Length-based Bayesian (LBB) stock assessment using the TropFishR package in R

**Key Findings:**
1. **Spatio-temporal distribution**: High catches were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan and Russia's EEZ lines. The gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward from 2016-2021, with a northeast-southwest-northeast pattern. CPUE decreased year by year, with large values dominating 2016-2018 and small values dominating 2019-2021. Strong negative correlation existed between CPUE and year (r = -0.489, p < 0.01).

2. **Biological characteristics**: Sex ratios (female:male) ranged from 1.09 to 2.55 across years (all >1). Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020). 3. **Stock assessment (LBB results)**: No overfishing occurred during 2016-2021. F/M ratios were all <0.5, E (exploitation rate) values ranged 0.17-0.32 (all below 0.5), B/B0 were all >0.5, B/Bmsy were all >1, L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt were close to 1, and Lc/Lopt were >1. 4. **Concerns**: Although not currently overexploited, the exploitation ratio (E) showed an increasing trend, reaching 0.48 by 2021 (from conventional methods), suggesting it may soon reach critical thresholds. **Conclusions**: (1) Fishing ground gravity center moved northward with year-by-year CPUE decline; (2) Chub mackerel grew well with no miniaturization and reasonable length structure; (3) Fishing mortality was low, no overfishing occurred; (4) E value increase warrants attention from international management organizations. Managers should consider climate warming impacts on marine ecosystem population composition.

Funding: National Key Research and Development Programme (2019YFD0901405) and Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Polar Science Base Open Subject Fund (SOO2024-15).

Model fitting and statistical analyses were performed in R (Version 4.0.3) using packages including lme4, Matrix, nlme, Metrics, rjstat, and FSA.

**Taxonomy & Distribution:** Scomber japonicus belongs to Scombriformes order and Scombridae family (Mackerels, tunas, bonitos), subfamily Scombrinae. It is distributed in the Indo-Pacific, is anti-tropical, and is absent from the Indian Ocean except for South Africa (KZN to Western Cape). Reports from the Atlantic including the Mediterranean are actually Scomber colias, and reports from the Red Sea and northern Indian Ocean are Scomber australasicus.

**Habitat & Environment:** This is a marine, pelagic-neritic, oceanodromous species with a depth range of 0-300 m (usually 50-200 m). It prefers subtropical waters with temperatures of 10°C-27°C, spanning latitudes 60°N to 48°S and longitudes 116°E to 70°W.

The interpelvic process is small and single, no well-developed corselet, swim bladder present. The back has narrow zigzag undulating stripes; the belly is unmarked (Pacific population) or has wavy lines (Atlantic population). Caudal peduncle has 5 finlets on upper and lower edges. Body shape is fusiform with an oval cross-section.

**Size & Age:** Lm at first maturity is 26.1 cm; max length 64.0 cm TL; common length 30.0 cm FL; max published weight 2.9 kg; max reported age 18 years.

**Biology:** This coastal pelagic species schools by size starting at approximately 3 cm, and may form schools with Sarda chiliensis, Trachurus symmetricus, and Sardinops sagax. Adults stay near the bottom during the day and rise to open water at night to feed on copepods, other crustaceans, fishes, and squids. They spawn in batches at water temperatures of 15°-20°C, with 250-300 eggs per gram of fish, totaling 100,000-400,000 eggs per female. Eggs and larvae are pelagic. In Asian waters, they move to deeper water and remain inactive during winter.

**Human Uses & Conservation:** The species is highly commercial in fisheries, commercially cultured in Japan, and used as gamefish and bait. Marketed fresh, frozen, smoked, salted, and occasionally canned; eaten fried, broiled, and baked; and used in Chinese medicine. IUCN Red List status: Least Concern (LC), assessed 01 June 2022. The assessment provides management advice for Pacific mackerel for the 2015-16 and 2016-17 fishing years (July-June seasons).

### Stock Status
- Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California, with majority distributed from Monterey Bay, California to Cabo San Lucas, Baja California Sur. Three spawning aggregations are hypothesized (Gulf of California, Cabo San Lucas, and Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos extending to southern California/Pacific Northwest).
- The assessment uses a Stock Synthesis (SS) age-structured model, specifically "Model H3," which closely resembles the previously accepted model XA from 2011.
- Model H3 uses data from 1983-2014 including: catch time series, age compositions from the commercial California fishery, and CPFV (commercial passenger fishing vessel) index of abundance with length compositions.

### Population Trends
- SSB has continually declined since the mid-1980s, remaining consistently low over the last decade, with some recent increase.
- High recruitment periods last occurred mid-1980s and mid-1990s (1-2.7 billion fish); very low recruitment from mid-1990s to 2012, with somewhat higher levels recently (highly uncertain).
- Since the late 1990s, abundance has remained at historically low levels (<150,000 mt).

### Harvest Control Rules
The FMP harvest rule is: **Harvest = (Biomass - Cutoff) × EMSY × Distribution**, where:
- Cutoff = 18,200 mt (lowest biomass above which harvest allowed)
- EMSY = 30% (fraction of biomass above cutoff harvestable)
- Distribution = 70% (assumed proportion of stock in USA waters)

**2016-17 Management Year:** Biomass = 118,968 mt; OFL = 24,983 mt; HG = 21,161 mt

ABC calculations provided using P-star buffers (0.45 to 0.05) for both Tier 1 and Tier 2.

### Management History
- 1970: State of California imposed moratorium after stock decline in mid-1960s.
- 1977: Fishery reopened under quota system.
- 1985: Regulations imposed moratorium when biomass <18,200 mt; fishing year set July 1-June 30.
- 2000: Federal FMP for coastal pelagic species implemented.
- HGs: ~15,000 mt average (2001-06); 40,000 mt (2007-08); reduced to 10,000 mt (2009-2010-11); ~31,000 mt (2011-13); ~39,000 mt (2013-14); ~29,000 mt (2014-15).
- Fishery has not fully utilized HGs recently, with average landings ~5,000 mt over the last decade.

Field surveys were conducted during the main spawning season (February-May) onboard the T/S Nansei-maru, sampling at 11-15 fixed stations across the mouth of Kagoshima Bay (KB1-KB6) and the Osumi Strait (OS1-OS9) using an ORI net (160 cm diameter, 335 μm mesh).

**Key Methodology:** Larval specimens were identified using polymerase chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) analysis of mitochondrial cytochrome b genes. Feeding habits were assessed via morphological gut content analysis (n=139 larvae from 2018), DNA metabarcoding of gut contents (n=68 larvae from 2019), and stable isotope analysis. Larval growth was estimated from sagittal otolith increment analysis (n=227 larvae from 2018-2019).

**Key Findings:**

1. **Species identification:** Of 305 Scomber spp. specimens (2017-2019), S. japonicus larvae were dominant (273 vs. 32 S. australasicus). S. japonicus comprised 96.8% of larvae in Kagoshima Bay and 87.7% in the Osumi Strait, contradicting previous assumptions that the northern Satsunan area was primarily a spawning ground for S. australasicus.

2. **Distribution:** Larval densities increased dramatically from 2016 (10.8 individuals per 1,000 m³) to 2018 (724.0 in Kagoshima Bay, 343.2 in Osumi Strait), corresponding with the increasing Pacific stock population of S. japonicus, which grew from 153,000 tons in 2001 to 6,808,000 tons in 2019. A significant negative relationship was found between larval density and chlorophyll a concentration.

3. **Feeding habits:** Both morphological and DNA metabarcoding analyses showed copepods (particularly Calanidae, Paracalanidae, Oithonidae, Oncaeidae) and appendicularians (Oikopleuridae) were the primary prey. Appendicularians were more prominent in metabarcoding analysis (%N: 24.9-32.5%, %F: 42.3-54.8%) than morphological analysis (%N: 1.7%), likely due to the difficulty of detecting fragmented appendicularian houses microscopically. Larger larvae (≥6.0 mm) fed on appendicularians more actively (45.4% for %N). Stable isotope analysis confirmed Scomber spp. larvae have lower δ13C values than copepod-feeding species (E. japonicus, T. japonicus), indicating substantial appendicularian consumption and suggesting the microbial loop supports S. japonicus feeding.

4. **Growth:** The exponential model fitted larval growth well. Instantaneous growth rate (G) was 0.072 in 2018 and 0.078 in 2019 (not significantly different, ANCOVA P=0.256). Daily specific growth rate (K) was 7.5% BL d⁻¹ in 2018 and 8.1% BL d⁻¹ in 2019. These rates were comparable to those in the southern East China Sea (the species' main spawning ground).

5. **Environmental conditions:** Water temperature and salinity were significantly higher in the Osumi Strait (due to Kuroshio Current influence), while chlorophyll a concentrations were consistently higher in Kagoshima Bay (due to winter-spring upwellings), which may create favorable feeding conditions for S. japonicus larvae.

**Conclusions:** The study strongly supports the northern Satsunan area as a major spawning and nursery ground for the Pacific stock of S. japonicus during high-stock periods. The area provides favorable conditions for sustaining high larval population densities, and findings provide important insights for fisheries management of S. japonicus in the Japanese Pacific coastal area.
</summary>

Management quotas have remained at approximately 21,000-27,000 mt since 2015, with landings notably below recommended catches since the late 1990s.

**Stock Structure:** The full range extends from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California. Three spawning aggregations are hypothesized: one in the Gulf of California, one near Cabo San Lucas, and one along the Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos extending to southern California and beyond. The latter sub-stock is harvested by U.S. and Mexican fishermen and is the population assessed.

**Major Uncertainties:** 1) The portion of the stock distributed in U.S. waters each year is never known definitively due to extensive range driven by environmental factors; 2) Improvements needed in production ageing programs for quality age data; 3) Highly variable recent recruitment (age-0 fish) estimation, as age 0-2 fish typically comprise roughly 80% of total population biomass.

--- SOURCE 1: Assessment and Management Implications for Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the North Pacific: Integrating Length-Based Bayesian and Catch-MSY Models ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/11/5/276

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in the journal *Fishes* (Volume 11, Issue 5, 2026, Article 276), assesses the stock status and management implications for chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the North Pacific Ocean. The study was conducted by researchers from the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Shanghai Ocean University, Anhui Normal University, and the Wenchang Innovation Research Center.

**Authors:** Sisi Huang, Famou Zhang, Heng Zhang (corresponding author), Ming Gao, and Kangbo Li.

**Study Methods:** The research integrates two data-limited stock assessment models: (1) the Length-based Bayesian Biomass (LBB) estimator, using length-frequency data from 6,061 chub mackerel specimens sampled from light purse seine fisheries on the high seas of the North Pacific (38°00′N–46°00′N, 147°00′E–162°00′E) during April–December 2019–2024; and (2) the Catch-MSY model, using historical catch data from 1995 to 2024. Management implications were analyzed using the Kobe plot and Kobe II Strategy Matrix (K2SM).

**Key Results:**
1. The LBB model revealed significant interannual variability in stock status. The stock was within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, but suffered overfishing in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Pooled two-year data analysis showed that B/BMSY dropped to 0.51 during 2023–2024, reflecting marked stock deterioration.
2. The Catch-MSY model estimated MSY at 278,000 t (95% CI: 162,000–475,000 t). The estimated intrinsic growth rate (r) peaked at 0.2 (95% CI: 0.06–0.7), and carrying capacity (K) peaked at 5,406,100 t (95% CI: 2,355,000–12,410,500 t).
3. The Kobe plot showed only 23.2% probability of a healthy stock state in the final assessment year. Probabilities of recruitment-overfished, fishing-overfished, and severely overfished were 37.6%, 14.9%, and 24.3%, respectively. With B/BMSY < 1 and F/FMSY < 1, the final-year stock status was diagnosed as recruitment overfishing.
4. Management recommendations: TAC should be set at 60–80% of the baseline TAC (352,100 t) during the medium-term (5–10 years), corresponding to 211,300–281,700 t. Long-term TAC could be gradually increased to MSY levels if the stock recovers.

**Context:** Chub mackerel is a priority species managed by the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC). The study notes that fishing mortality exceeded natural mortality in recent years (F/M > 1.5), making fishing pressure the primary driver of overfishing. Notably, new regulations effective 2025 have reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). The findings contrast with earlier research (Zhao, based on 2016–2021 data) that suggested the stock was in good condition, indicating a recent transition to overfished status.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The LBB model revealed significant interannual variability in stock status of S. japonicus. Although the stock was within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, it suffered from overfishing or was heavily overfished in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Notably, integrated data analysis indicated that during 2023–2024, the B/BMSY ratio dropped to 0.51, reflecting a marked deterioration in the stock condition."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: is the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) stock recovering? ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1814806/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (May 14, 2026, Volume 13) that assesses the stock status of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in Korean waters of the Northwest Pacific. The study was conducted by Dong-Jin Kwak, Do-Hoon Kim, and Kyounghoon Lee from Pukyong National University, Busan, Republic of Korea.

**Purpose and Context:** The chub mackerel has been managed under Korea's Total Allowable Catch (TAC) system since 1999, but prior stock assessments have yielded conflicting results regarding whether the stock has recovered or remains overfished, complicating management decisions. This study aims to resolve discrepancies using two complementary models.

**Methods:** The study employed CMSY++ (which uses an Artificial Neural Network/ANN to objectively estimate prior biomass ranges) and a Bayesian State-Space (BSS) model. Crucially, the BSS model incorporated a 2% annual technical creep correction to CPUE data—a factor frequently overlooked in previous research. The analysis used 55 years of catch data (1970–2024) from Korea, China, and Japan (Tsushima Current stock), plus 27 years of CPUE data (1997–2023) from Korea. Gross tonnage was selected as the primary effort variable (correlation coefficient 0.976, R²=0.950).

**Key Findings:**
- In 2024, the relative biomass (B/BMSY) was estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), classifying the stock as "Overfished" (still below the Biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield).
- CMSY++ estimated: r=0.255, k=2,273,005 tons, MSY=145,462 tons, B2024=779,191 tons.
- BSS estimated: r=0.310, k=1,802,382 tons, MSY=139,902 tons, B2024=549,884 tons.
- Kobe plot analysis revealed sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s has impeded recovery, with 87.6% (CMSY++) and 95.3% (BSS) posterior probability of the stock remaining in the "overfished and overfishing" red quadrant.
- Korean catch peaked at 415,003 tons in 1996, reached a historical low of 77,603 tons in 2020, and was 124,928 tons in 2024. The large purse seine fishery accounts for 82.2% of domestic catch (average 91,349 tons, 2020–2024).
- Fishing effort has effectively increased despite fleet reduction: vessels decreased from 342 (1992) to 106 (2024), but GT/vessel rose from 131 to 188 and EHP/vessel from 827 to 1,471.
- Sensitivity analysis showed B2024 estimates varied by up to 34% depending on technical creep correction (0%: 824,168 tons vs. 2%: 549,884 tons).

**Conclusions:** The study demonstrates CMSY++ as an effective tool for reconciling discrepancies in data-limited stock assessments and underscores the necessity of correcting for technical creep. Landing data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market shows an increasing proportion of small-sized (≤250g, ~29.7cm TL, below the L50 of 31.4cm) immature individuals in the catch (from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024), providing biological evidence of stock depletion. The authors recommend more stringent TAC reductions, extended closed seasons, vessel buyback programs, and upward revision of minimum legal size limits for the stock's recovery.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2024, the relative biomass (B/BMSY) was estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), indicating that the stock remains overfished and below the Biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (BMSY)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Spatio-Temporal Distribution and Population Dynamics of Chub ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12024016

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Animals (an open-access MDPI journal) in April 2025, examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO). Authors: Guoqing Zhao, Heng Zhang, and Fenghua Tang (corresponding author: f-h-tang@163.com).

**Study Methodology:**
- Study area: High seas of the NPO between 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E
- Data: 38,123 fishing operations from Chinese commercial light purse seine vessel logs (2016–2021), plus 4,440 biological samples
- Methods: Length-weight relationships, Von Bertalanffy growth equations (ELEFAN I in FISAT II), mortality estimation (Pauly's equations), and Length-based Bayesian (LBB) stock assessment using the TropFishR package in R

**Key Findings:**
1. **Spatio-temporal distribution**: High catches were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan and Russia's EEZ lines. The gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward from 2016-2021, with a northeast-southwest-northeast pattern. CPUE decreased year by year, with large values dominating 2016-2018 and small values dominating 2019-2021. Strong negative correlation existed between CPUE and year (r = -0.489, p < 0.01).

2. **Biological characteristics**: Sex ratios (female:male) ranged from 1.09 to 2.55 across years (all >1). Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020). Mean lengths varied from 212.07 mm (2016) to 268.28 mm (2018). Growth parameters: asymptotic length (L inf) ranged 36-42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged 0.31-0.65.

3. **Stock assessment (LBB results)**: No overfishing occurred during 2016-2021. F/M ratios were all <0.5, E (exploitation rate) values ranged 0.17-0.32 (all below 0.5), B/B0 were all >0.5, B/Bmsy were all >1, L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt were close to 1, and Lc/Lopt were >1. All years were classified as "healthy" stock status with reasonable body length structure and presence of large individuals.

4. **Concerns**: Although not currently overexploited, the exploitation ratio (E) showed an increasing trend, reaching 0.48 by 2021 (from conventional methods), suggesting it may soon reach critical thresholds. The study emphasizes that climate warming, marine heatwaves (frequent in NPO since 2014), and increased competition with Japanese sardine are important factors affecting chub mackerel population dynamics.

**Explanations for CPUE decline despite healthy stock**: (1) Reasonable resource fluctuation not reaching critical population thresholds; (2) spawning grounds in south-central Pacific coast of Japan may have changed, reducing recruitment via Kuroshio Current transport; (3) increasing food competition with Japanese sardine, which also serves as a food source for adult chub mackerel; (4) interactions among proliferating fishing vessels' fish-attracting light systems.

**Conclusions**: (1) Fishing ground gravity center moved northward with year-by-year CPUE decline; (2) Chub mackerel grew well with no miniaturization and reasonable length structure; (3) Fishing mortality was low, no overfishing occurred; (4) E value increase warrants attention from international management organizations. Managers should consider climate warming impacts on marine ecosystem population composition.

Funding: National Key Research and Development Programme (2019YFD0901405) and Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Polar Science Base Open Subject Fund (SOO2024-15).
</summary>

"From 2016 to 2021, high catches of chub mackerel were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan or Russia's exclusive economic zone line, and the gravity center of the fishing grounds moved to the northwest gradually, with a decrease in the average value of catch per unit effort (CPUE) year by year."

--- SOURCE 5: Stock assessment of Chub Mackerel Tsushima stock (2019) ---
URL: https://www.fra.go.jp/shigen/fisheries_resources/meeting/peer_review_meeting/files/2020/assess_masaba_t.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Chub Mackerel Tsushima Stock Assessment (2019)

### Stock Status Overview
The stock assessment of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Tsushima stock was conducted by the National Research Institute of Fisheries Science and Saikai National Fisheries Research Institute. The stock biomass was around 1 million tons during 1973-1996, decreased to ~500,000 tons after 2000, then recovered to 650,000 tons in 2018 supported by strong recruitments. SSB in 2018 was estimated at ~238,000-240,000 tons.

### Key Reference Points
- **SBmsy**: 310,000 tons
- **Fmsy**: (0.33, 1.07, 0.69, 0.69) for ages 0, 1, 2, 3+ respectively
- **%SPR(Fmsy)**: 20%
- **MSY**: 323,000 tons
- **SB2018/SBmsy**: 0.77 (below SBmsy)
- **F2018/Fmsy**: 1.24 (above Fmsy)
- Stock-recruitment relationship: Hockey Stick (HS) model, no autocorrelation (parameters: a=0.00755, b=237,192 tons)

### Stock Status Summary (2018)
- SSB: Below SBmsy (warning level)
- Fishing pressure (F): Above Fmsy
- SSB trend (2014-2018): Increasing

### Biology and Ecology
- **Distribution**: Southern East China Sea to northern Japan Sea, Yellow Sea, and Bo Hai
- **Growth**: 25-28cm FL at age 1, 29-32cm at age 2, 33-35cm at age 3, 36cm at age 4, 37cm at age 5; longevity ~6 years
- **Spawning**: Main grounds in East China Sea off Chinese coast, Korean Peninsula coastal waters, and Kyusyu/Sanin coastal waters of Japan; season Jan-Apr in south, May-Jun in north
- **Maturity**: 60% at age 1, 85% at age 2, 100% at age 3+
- **Natural mortality (M)**: 0.4 per year

### Fisheries and Catches
- Mainly caught by purse seine fisheries in East China Sea, Korean coastal waters, northwest Kyusyu, and western Japan Sea
- Japanese catch 2018: 150,000 tons (0- and 1-year old fish dominate); Korean catch 2018: 140,000 tons (age composition unknown); Chinese catch up to 500,000 tons since 2010 (species composition unknown, NOT included in analysis)
- Total catch 2018 (Japan + Korea): 292,000 tons
- Fishing effort (purse seine nets) at lowest level (4,710 nets) in 2018 due to shift to Pacific fishing grounds

### Assessment Methodology
- Cohort analysis (VPA) using catch-at-age data from Japan and Korea, tuned with abundance indices from purse seine fisheries
- Abundance indices from purse seine logbooks, Sakai port landing data, neuston-net larval surveys, acoustic surveys, and bottom trawl surveys
- Chinese catch excluded due to unreliable species composition data
- Results used as qualitative information due to insufficient accuracy of survey estimates

### Historical Trends
- **Biomass**: 1,000,000 tons (1973-1989), peaked 1,370,000 tons (1996), fell to 370,000 tons (2013, lowest), recovered to 654,000 tons (2018)
- **SSB**: Peaked 470,000 tons (1993-1996), dropped to 120,000 tons (2003), fluctuated 110,000-190,000 until 2014, increased to 240,000 tons (2018)
- **Recruitment**: Peak 3,300 million (1995), dropped to 800 million (2013), strong year classes 1,500 million (2014) and 2,000 million (2017), 1,329 million (2018)
- **Fishing ratio (U)**: Rapidly increased 1996, stayed high at 40-50%, was 45% in 2018
- **%SPR**: Lowest in 1996 (8.31%), was 16.7% in 2018 and 15.6% for F2016-2018 (below Fmsy level of 20%)

### Management Context
- Management via effort control (licensed vessels for purse seine) and TAC for "mackerels" (including blue mackerel) since 1997
- Stock rebuilding plan for western Japan Sea/western Kyusyu (2009-2011) focused on protecting juveniles
- Major uncertainty from lack of Chinese catch data; satellite night vision monitoring of Chinese fishing vessels started 2014
- Future projections complicated by inaccurate Chinese/Korean predictions and TAC combining chub and blue mackerel
- Recommended international cooperation for fisheries monitoring and further study of recruitment fluctuation and migration patterns
</summary>

"For this stock, we propose the Hockey Stick (HS) model of reproduction curve, and SBmsy was estimated as 310,000 tons. Following the reference, SSB in 2018 is below MSY. Recently fishing pressure on the stock stay at similar level and is above Fmsy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Effects of water temperature and prey density on recent growth of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus larvae and juveniles along the Pacific coast of Boso–Kashimanada | CoLab ---
URL: https://colab.ws/articles/10.1007%2Fs12562-019-01354-8

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a journal article page from Colab (colab.ws) documenting the publication "Effects of water temperature and prey density on recent growth of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus larvae and juveniles along the Pacific coast of Boso–Kashimanada" published in Fisheries Science (Springer Nature), Volume 85, Issue 6, pages 931-942, on September 7, 2019. The authors are Makoto Taga, Yasuhiro Kamimura, and Yoh Yamashita. DOI: 10.1007/s12562-019-01354-8.

The study examined the effects of temperature and prey density on the recent growth rate (RGR) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) larvae and juveniles. Specimens were collected along the Boso–Kashimanada Pacific coast of Japan between March and July in 2015 and 2016. Larvae and juveniles were identified as S. japonicus using DNA analysis, then subjected to stomach-content and otolith-increment analyses. A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) was used to analyze the effects of temperature and prey density on RGR.

Key findings: Temperature positively affected RGR of larvae in body length (BL) classes <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and 9-11mm. Prey density affected growth in the <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and >11mm classes, with effects of prey density on RGR being stronger for larger (>11mm) larvae and juveniles than for smaller (<9mm) larvae. S. japonicus larvae transform into juveniles at around 12mm BL, and the increased feed demands of juveniles likely lead to prey-density-dependent growth. This article from the Global Seafood Alliance's Responsible Seafood Advocate, authored by Sukgeun Jung, Ph.D. (Jeju National University, Republic of Korea), summarizes a study published in Fishes (2025, 10(1), 20) by Go, S. et al. that projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Western North Pacific Ocean.

**Key background:** Chub mackerel are forage fish crucial to marine food webs, feeding on zooplankton/phytoplankton and serving as prey for larger marine predators. The Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock is an economically valuable fishery exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the East China Sea (ECS) and Korea Strait (KS) from February to June before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the Japan/East Sea (JES) and Yellow Sea (YS).

**Study methodology:** Researchers developed spawning ground indices and used the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to estimate and project water temperature and salinity at 10 meters depth in the western North Pacific. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010 to 2059 under an IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (IPCC AR5) climate change scenario, comparing the 2010s (2010–2019) and 2050s (2050–2059) periods.

**Key findings:**
- Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to the 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s and become less influenced by the Kuroshio Current.
- This northward shift is expected to cause a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds (from the Pacific side of Japan and JES toward waters off Jeju Island), consistent with earlier work by Li et al.
- Ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production are expected to increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the JES.
- Model outputs were generally compatible with previous observations, though the model did not perfectly align with observational data in the same space and time; data assimilation methods were suggested for future improvements.
- Spawning grounds were assumed to be limited to continental shelf areas (50–300 meters depth), though other research suggests chub mackerel may also spawn in shallower coastal areas (<50 meters), including Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait.
- The study only considered environmental conditions at 10 meters depth and used only temperature and salinity variables; other factors (turbulence, currents, dissolved oxygen) and photoperiod influences on spawning periods require further research.

**Conclusions:** The study enhances the reliability of stock assessment for fisheries management of chub mackerel and contributes to the development of individual-based bio-physical coupled models for predicting recruitment and spatiotemporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel. The results are expected to inform fisheries policies accounting for climate change in the region.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to 2050s, and these suggested that chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s compared to the 2010s, which means that spawning will become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: A Study on the Impact of Environmental Factors on Chub Mackerel Scomber japonicus Fishing Grounds Based on a Linear Mixed Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/9/8/323

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the journal Fishes (2024, Volume 9, Issue 8, Article 323; DOI: 10.3390/fishes9080323), examines how marine environmental factors affect Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific using a linear mixed model (LMM). Authors include Jiasheng Li, Fenghua Tang, Yumei Wu, Shengmao Zhang, Weifeng Zhou, and Xuesen Cui (corresponding author), affiliated with the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute (Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences) and Shanghai Ocean University. The study was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (grant 2023YFD2401303) and received on 14 June 2024, published 14 August 2024.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used fishery data from China's high-sea light-purse seine operations (2014–2020) covering fishing grounds between 140–165°E and 30–50°N, combined with monthly averaged sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL) data from Oregon State University's Ocean Productivity database. Data were aggregated at 0.5° × 0.5° spatial resolution. CPUE was calculated as catch per net-haul (t/net). Square-root transformation of CPUE and natural logarithm of CHL were applied to achieve normal distributions; VIF values of 1.990 confirmed no multicollinearity between SST and logCHL. The LMM included SST and logCHL as fixed effects, with Year, Month, and fishing Zone as random effects, using the lme4 package in R. Among 256 candidate models, the optimal model (scenario 5) was selected based on lowest AIC, BIC, and logLik values.

KEY RESULTS: (1) SST had a significant fixed effect on CPUE with a negative slope (p < 0.001), meaning CPUE increases as SST decreases. (2) logCHL had no fixed effect on CPUE but showed significant random effects by month. (3) logCHL was positively correlated with CPUE during spawning and wintering periods (April–May, November–December) and negatively correlated during the summer feeding period (June–October), consistent with patterns observed in neon flying squid. (4) Annual average CPUE decreased from 2014 to 2020, peaking at 15.501 t/net (2015) and 11.363 t/net (2018), with a low of 8.355 t/net in 2020; monthly CPUE peaked in November (14.426 t/net). (5) Low CPUE areas (<5 t/net) were south of 34°N, while high CPUE areas (>15 t/net) were between 148–159°E. (6) The random intercept for Year showed highest value (0.353) in 2015 and lowest (−0.480) in 2019; a high-random-intercept zone at 150–152°E, 39–41°N corresponded to high catch rates. Residuals approximated a normal distribution (skewness 0.031, kurtosis 3.532).

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS: The negative SST-CPUE relationship aligns with prior studies in the East China Sea and Japan coastal waters. Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019). The optimal SST range for fishing grounds is 14–18°C (~16°C ideal), and optimal chlorophyll-a range is 0.3–0.8 mg/m³. LIMITATIONS: Interpretation complexity with crossed random effects, high parameterization risks (overfitting), and incomplete spatial/temporal data coverage (no data from Japan/Russia EEZs, no January–March data).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SST had a significant fixed effect on the CPUE. In contrast, the natural logarithm of chlorophyll (logCHL) had no fixed effect on the CPUE. Based on the monthly analysis, random fluctuations were observed in the impact of logCHL on the CPUE. LogCHL and CPUE show a positive correlation during spawning and wintering periods and a negative correlation during the feeding period."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/10/1/20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Fishes* (2025, Volume 10, Issue 1, Article 20) by authors Seonggil Go (Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology), Joon-ho Lee (Underwater Survey Technology 21), and Sukgeun Jung (Jeju National University, corresponding author). The study projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the western North Pacific Ocean.

**Methodology:** The researchers developed a spawning ground index (SGI) based on a Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′ E, 20°00′–52°00′ N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers), driven by the IPCC AR5 RCP85 scenario. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010–2059. SGI was calculated using four parameters: water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m). The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001).

**Key Findings:**
- In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June.
- By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes).
- Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea.
- The study suggests biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea.

**Limitations noted:** The model results did not perfectly align with observations in the same space and time (though trends were similar); the assumed spawning period may shift due to photoperiod changes; only 10 m depth environmental conditions were considered; and chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m depth).

**Funding:** Supported by the Korea Institute of Marine Science and Technology (KIMST), Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries (RS-2023-00256330 and RS-2022-KS221566), and Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST grant PEA0306).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite some uncertainty, our model based on climate change scenarios projected that, by the 2050s, spawning grounds will shift northward due to warming of the ocean surface, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Effects of oceanographic conditions on fishery distribution: A case study of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in northeastern Taiwan ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0141113624004641

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Marine Environmental Research (Volume 202, November 2024, Article 106803) as part of a special issue on "Climate Change and the Oceans," edited by Fangli QIAO of the First Institute of Oceanography. The study examines the effects of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) distribution in northeastern Taiwan.

**Authors:** Sandipan Mondal, Frank Muller-Karger, Aratrika Ray, Shin-Ichi Ito, Ming-An Lee, and Hsueh-Jung Lu.

**Methodology:** The researchers constructed a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery data, climatic oscillation data, and oceanography data. Fishery and oceanographic data were rescaled using MATLAB (2022a) to a consistent spatial and temporal grid, then standardized using a generalized linear model (GLM). Five single-algorithm models were used: GLM, generalized additive model (GAM), gradient boosting method (GBM), random forest (RF), and classification models, combined into an ensemble approach.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO), which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792).
- NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level.
- Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect.
- Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m.
- Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E.

**Background Context:** Global climate change is significantly affecting marine ecosystems, with ocean warming causing coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, and sea-level rise. Under RCP 8.5 scenario, a predicted 40% decline in tropical fish catch by the 2050s in some economic zones (Lam et al., 2020) highlights the urgency of this research. Chub mackerel is economically crucial to Taiwan, with Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries accounting for 98.66% of captures. The study addresses a research gap by using multiple algorithms to confirm oceanographic significance, unlike previous studies that relied on single models.

**Funding:** National Science & Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC) grant 112-2811-M-019-004 and Fisheries Agency, Council of Agriculture, Taiwan grant 112-FM-2.31-A-03.

**Applications:** Findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in northeastern Taiwan waters and may aid decision-makers in protecting other ocean fisheries and dependent communities under changing climate conditions. The article has been cited by 5 subsequent publications (as of the page retrieval date).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304380014001604

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Ecological Modelling (Volume 283, 10 July 2014, Pages 70-84) titled "Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea" by Yuesong Li, Xinjun Chen, Changsheng Chen, Jianzhong Ge, Rubao Ji, Rucheng Tian, Pengfei Xue, and Liuxiong Xu. DOI: 10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2014.03.016.

The study developed an early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The researchers examined how regional physical processes affect larval dispersal and survival under climatological spring-summer conditions, both with and without short-time fluctuations from a typhoon.

Key findings include:
- Seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages.
- Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location.
- Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing. Comparison of cases with and without Typhoon Alice showed that cancellation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents limits typhoon influence on low-frequency flow and larval dispersion, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds.
- Temperature and food play significant roles in early larval development; water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March-July.
- Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June).
- Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion.

The article provides background on the ECS physical oceanography, including the Kuroshio Current (which acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf), the Taiwan Warm Current, and the Changjiang Coastal Current (which tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East Strait). Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. The study is the first IBM developed to examine chub mackerel recruitment in the ECS.

The paper has 41 references and has been cited 27 times. It was supported by multiple Chinese national research projects including the National 863 project, Shanghai Education Committee, and Shanghai Ocean University programs.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Cambridge University Press journal article (published online October 30, 2013, in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom) titled "Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data." The study addresses the chub mackerel, an important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea that rose to prominence after the decline of traditional demersal economic species. The research methodology involved separating sample catches from 2009-2010 into three age groups based on an age–fork length key, estimating maximum sustainable yield (MSY), and building a spawner–recruitment relationship using fishery statistics from purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels, and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Ocean University of China (Volume 20, pages 1483–1494, 2021) titled "Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea." Published on November 21, 2021, the study was conducted by authors Wei Yu, Jian Wen, Xinjun Chen, Gang Li, Yuesong Li, and Zhong Zhang, affiliated with Shanghai Ocean University and the Qingdao National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology.

The study investigated how the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) impacts the habitat range and distribution of the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the East China Sea (ECS).
