x 1 Introduction 1.1 Stock Structure and Management Units The full range of Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus, also referred to as chub or blue mackerel) in the northeastern Pacific Ocean is from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay (Puerto Vallarta), Mexico, including the Gulf of California (Hart 1971). Although stock structure of this species off the Pacific coast of North America is not known definitively, it is generally hypothesized that three spawning aggregations exist currently: one in the Gulf of California; one in the vicinity of Cabo San Lucas (Baja California, Mexico); and one along the Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos (Baja California) that extends north to areas off southern California, and even further during favorable oceanographic periods to waters off the U.S. Pacific Northwest. The latter sub-stock is harvested by fishermen in the U.S. and Mexico, and is the population considered in this assessment.
The Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) manages the northeastern Pacific Ocean stock along the Pacific coast of North America as a single unit, with no area- or sector-specific allocations. However, the formal Fishery Management Plan (FMP) harvest control rule does include a stock distribution adjustment, based on a long-term assumption that on average, roughly 70% of this transboundary population resides in U.S. waters in any given year (PFMC 1998).
1.2 Distribution and Movement Although the northeastern Pacific Ocean stock ranges from southeastern Alaska to southern Baja California, the species is more common from Monterey Bay, CA to Cabo San Lucas, Mexico (Figure 1). Over the last few decades, the stock has been observed to more fully occupy the northernmost portions of its range in response to warmer oceanographic conditions that have persisted in the northeastern Pacific Ocean, being found at times as far north as British Columbia, Canada (Ware and Hargreaves 1993, Hargreaves and Hungar 1995). To date, there exists only a general understanding of the seasonal movement patterns exhibited by this species along the coast of North America (Fry Jr and Roedel 1949, Roedel 1949, Parrish and MacCall 1978, Hill et al. 1999), with northward movement from waters off Baja and southern California beginning in the late spring/summer to feed in productive areas of upwelling off Oregon and Washington (potentially, more extensive geographical range during El Ni˜ no events, MBC (1987)); and southerly movement in the late fall/winter back to spawning grounds off southern and Baja California. Pacific mackerel sampled from Pacific Northwest incidental fisheries (e.g., Pacific hake and salmon spp.) during the mid-1990s indicated the fish were generally older and larger than those captured in the southern California fishery (Hill et al. 1999). In recent years, the stock has been observed to be relatively abundant in waters off the Pacific Northwest as documented in cruise reports for the acoustic-trawl (AT) survey, conducted annually since the mid-2000s by the Southwest Fisheries Science 1 Center (SWFSC), e.g., Stierhoff et al. (2019a) and Zwolinski et al. (2019). Thus, the stock is assumed to be most abundant in U.S. waters during the summer and fall months of each year; however, determination of the exact portion of the population that occupies U.S. waters each summer/fall is necessarily problematic and subject to some level of uncertainty.
It is further hypothesized that the stock exhibits east-west (inshore-offshore) movement along the U.S. Pacific coast, with increased inshore abundance during July to November and increased offshore abundance during March to May (Cannon 1967, Sciences 1987). Pacific mackerel usually occur within 30 km of shore, but have been captured as far as 400 km offshore (Fitch 1969, Frey 1971, Sciences 1987, Allen et al. 1990). Pacific mackerel adults are found in water ranging from 10 to 22.2°C (Sciences 1987) and larvae are found in water around 14°C (Allen et al. 1990). Adult fish are commonly found near shallow banks. Juveniles are found off sandy beaches, around kelp beds, and in open bays. Adults are found from the surface to 300 m depth (Allen et al. 1990). Pacific mackerel often school with other small pelagic species, particularly jack mackerel and Pacific sardine, likely based on size/age attributes as well (Parrish and MacCall 1978).
1.3 Life History Pacific mackerel found off the Pacific coast of North America are the same species found elsewhere in the Pacific and Indian Oceans (Collette and Nauen 1983). Synopses regarding the biology of Pacific mackerel are presented in Kramer (1969) and Schaefer (1980). Spawning occurs from Point Conception, California to Cabo San Lucas from 3 to over 300 km offshore (Moser et al. 1993). Off California, spawning occurs from March to October (primarily, late April through August) at depths to 100 meters (Knaggs and Parrish 1973). Off central Baja California, spawning can occur year round at some level. Around Cabo San Lucas, spawning occurs primarily from late fall to early spring. Pacific mackerel are believed to seldomly spawn north of Point Conception (Fritzsche 1978, Sciences 1987).
As exhibited by similar CPS, Pacific mackerel have indeterminate fecundity and appear to spawn whenever sufficient food is available and favorable oceanographic conditions prevail.
Individual fish may spawn eight times or more each year and can release batches of at least 68,000 eggs per spawning. Actively spawning fish appear capable of spawning daily or every other day(Dickerson et al. 1992). New research on Mediterranean Sea S. japonicus reproduction showed a wide range of relative fecundity by length and weight [420 to 2,553 eggs per cm for total length, and 76 to 379 eggs per gram for total weight; Farrag et al.
(2022)]. The length at 50% maturity for this population was 19.7 cm for females and 19.5 cm for males. Farrag et al. (2022) also include a literature summary of length at first maturity for global S. japonicus populations, which ranges from about 18-30 cm. Research from the western North Pacific Ocean shows an effect of maternal age on egg and larval success (Yoneda et al. 2022). Yoneda et al. (2022) found significantly larger and more nutrient-rich eggs, higher starvation tolerance, larger body size, and faster growth rates of larvae from 3 year-old females compared to 1 year-old females. Currently, Stock Synthesis does not 2 provide an option for directly increasing egg or larval survival based on female age, therefore any model explorations would have to indirectly address this relationship by increasing the number of eggs by length or weight.
Pacific mackerel larvae eat copepods and other zooplankton, including fish larvae (Collette and Nauen 1983, Sciences 1987). Juvenile and adult mackerel feed on small fish (e.g., northern anchovy), fish larvae, squid, and pelagic crustaceans, such as euphausids (Clemmens and Wilby 1961, Turner and Sexsmith 1967, Fitch 1969, Fitch and Lavenberg 1971, Frey 1971, Hart 1971, Collette and Nauen 1983). Pacific mackerel larvae are subject to predation from a number of invertebrate and vertebrate planktivores. Juveniles and adults are eaten by larger fishes, marine mammals, and seabirds. Principal predators include porpoises, California sea lions, pelicans, and large piscivorous fish, such as sharks and tunas. Pacific mackerel likely school as a defense against predation, often with other CPS, such as jack mackerel and Pacific sardine.
Population dynamics of the Pacific mackerel stock off U.S. Pacific coast, particularly California, have been extensively studied in the past and of particular importance was pioneering research conducted during the 1970s and 1980s, e.g., Parrish (1974), Parrish and MacCall (1978), Mallicoate and Parrish (1981), MacCall et al. (1985), and Prager and MacCall (1988). Since the mid-1990s, various age-structured population dynamics models have been used to assess the Pacific mackerel stock for providing management advice (e.g., Jacobson et al. 1994, Hill and Crone 2005, Crone et al. 2009, Crone and Hill 2015), see History of modeling approaches below.
Pacific mackerel experience cyclical periods of notable abundance, a phenomenon exhibited by CPS in general, which are characterized by relatively short life spans and highly variable productivity/abundance driven primarily by large-scale environmental factors (e.g., Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), and related oceano-graphic drivers, such as sea-surface temperature, sea-surface height, upwelling, cholorophyll, etc.). Analysis of mackerel scale-deposition data (Soutar and Isaacs 1974) indicates that periods of high biomass, such as during the 1930s and 1980s, are relatively rare events that might be expected to occur, on average, about once every 60 years (MacCall et al. 1985).
Results from the ongoing assessment of this stock generally support past research, with periods of high recruitment success observed no more frequently than every few decades.
As presented above, recruitment is generally variable both spatially and temporally in the northeastern Pacific Ocean, and unlikely to be related strongly to spawning stock size (Parrish 1974, Parrish and MacCall 1978).
One of the largest recorded Pacific mackerel was 63.0 cm in length (FL) and weighed 2.9 kg (Roedel 1938, Hart 1971), but the largest Pacific mackerels taken by commercial fishing (CA) were a 47.8 cm FL fish and a 1.72 kg fish. The oldest recorded age for a Pacific mackerel was 14 years, but most commercially caught Pacific mackerel recorded by CDFW are less than 4 years old, with few living beyond age 8 and larger than 45 cm. Historical data of generally older and larger Pacific mackerel sampled from Pacific Northwest incidental fisheries in the 1990s exists, and have been reported on previously (Hill et al. 1999). The oldest Pacific 3 mackerel from Washington state was 16 years old and measured 69 cm.
As addressed in earlier assessments/reviews, size-at-age relationships by sex and sex ratio data indicated no notable sexual dimorphism in growth or mortality rate is exhibited by this species. Combined sex models have been used in all Pacific mackerel assessments used to advise management.
1.4 Fishery Descriptions Pacific mackerel are currently harvested by three fisheries (Table 1 and Figure 2): the USA commercial fishery that primarily operates out of southern California, as well as Oregon and Washington; a sport fishery based largely in southern California; and the Mexico commercial fishery that is based in Ensenada, Baja California and Magdalena Bay, Baja California Sur. In the commercial fisheries, Pacific mackerel are landed by the same boats that catch Pacific sardine, northern anchovy, jack mackerel, and market squid (commonly referred to as the west coast ‘wetfish’ fleet). In recent years, Oregon and Washington have landed limited amounts of Pacific mackerel, with a combined annual average catch of roughly 500 mt over the last decade. Pacific mackerel are also (incidentally) harvested in small volumes by whiting trawlers and salmon trollers. Available information concerning bycatch and discard mortality of Pacific mackerel, as well as other members of the small pelagic fish assemblage of the California Current, is presented in PFMC (2021). Limited information from observer programs implemented in the past indicated little bycatch of other species and/or discard of Pacific mackerel in the commercial purse seine fishery off the U.S. Pacific coast.
The history of California’s Pacific mackerel fishery has been reviewed by Croker (1933), Croker (1938), Roedel (1952), and Klingbeil (1983). Historically, Pacific mackerel have been landed in moderate amounts, supporting a viable fishery off California during the 1930s and 1940s and more recently, during the 1980s and early 1990s. During the early years of the fishery, Pacific mackerel were taken by lampara and pole-and-line boats, which were replaced in the 1930s by the same purse seine fleet that fished for Pacific sardine. Before 1929, Pacific mackerel were taken incidentally, in relatively small volumes with sardine and sold as a fresh product (Frey 1971). Canning of Pacific mackerel began in the late 1920s and increased as greater processing capacities and more marketable ‘packs’ were developed.
Landings decreased in the early 1930s due to the economic depression and subsequent decline in demand, but increased significantly by the mid-1930s (66,400 mt in 1935-36). During this period, Pacific mackerel were second only to Pacific sardine in total (annual) landings.
Subsequently, harvests underwent a long-term decline and for many years, a continued demand for canned mackerel exceeded supply. Supply reached record low levels in the early 1970s, at which time the State of California implemented a ‘moratorium’ on the directed fishery, allowing only limited amounts of incidental landings.
The moratorium was lifted following a period of ‘recovery’ that spanned from the mid to late 1970s. During the 1980s through mid-1990s, catches of Pacific mackerel by California 4 fishermen supported an economically viable fishery. The market for canned mackerel during the 1980s through early 1990s fluctuated substantially due largely to economic factors.
Domestic demand for canned Pacific mackerel eventually waned and the last mackerel cannery in California closed in 1992. Presently, the limited landings of Pacific mackerel caught by U.S. fishermen are used for human consumption (e.g., canned, frozen, fresh) or pet food.
Pacific mackerel are caught by recreational anglers in southern California using commercial passenger fishing vessels (CPFV), private boats, piers, beaches, etc., but are not typically considered a target species (Young 1969), with comparatively minimal catches to landings from commercial operations (Table 1). Pacific mackerel are also harvested in California’s recreational fishery as bait for directed fishing on larger pelagic species, such as tunas, sharks, and billfishes. Additionally, Pacific mackerel are caught by anglers in central California, Oregon, and Washington, but typically, in only limited amounts. The sport harvest of Pacific mackerel in California comprises a very small fraction of the total landings of Pacific mackerel, e.g., over the last decade, recreational catch is less than 5% of the total weight landed (Table 1). Although some mackerel are likely discarded in some recreational fishing sectors for this non-targeted species, accurate determination of discard magnitude from available creel survey data is not straightforward, potentially subject to problematic sampling biases in the field.
In summary, Pacific mackerel landings in the U.S. have remained low over the last two decades, with total annual landings averaging rougly 7,000 mt since the late 1990s (Table 1).
Relatedly, mackerel catches from fisheries have not realized allowable yields via stipulated harvest guidelines imposed since the late 1990s (see Table 2 and “Management performance” below).
The Mexico fishery for Pacific mackerel is primarily based in Ensenada and to a lesser extent, Magdalena Bay, Baja California Sur. The Mexico purse seine fleet has slightly larger vessels, but is similar to southern California’s fleet with respect to gear (mesh size) and fishing practices. The fleet operates in the vicinity of the nearby ports and also targets other CPS. Demand for Pacific mackerel in Baja California increased after World War II. Mexico landings remained stable for several years, increased to over 10,000 mt in the mid-1950s, declined to under 500 mt during the mid-1970s, and remained relatively low through the late 1980s. Landings of Pacific mackerel in Ensenada peaked during the 1990s, but have remained relatively low over the last two decades. For the most part, the Ensenada fishery has been generally comparable in volume to the southern California fishery since 1990 (averaging about 10,000 mt/yr), with some differences for particular years (Table 1). In Mexico, harvested Pacific mackerel have been canned for human consumption or reduced to fish meal.
1.5 Ecosystem Considerations Pacific mackerel are part of the CPS assemblage of the northeastern Pacific Ocean, which represents an important forage base in the California Current Ecosystem (CCE). Pacific mackerel do not typically represent a dominant species of this assemblage in any given year, 5 with abundances likely less than more productive CPS, such as northern anchovy and Pacific sardine. However, mackerel population biomass can increase to relatively high levels during periods of favorable oceanographic conditions, which likely occur less regularly than observed for anchovy and sardine stocks. Relatedly, periods of low recruitment success driven by prevailing oceanic phenomena can lead to low population abundance over extended periods of time. Readers should consult Field et al. (2001), PFMC (1998, 2021), and NMFS (2022) for comprehensive information regarding environmental processes generally hypothesized to influence small pelagic species that inhabit the CCE.
1.6 Management History The state of California first implemented formal management associated with the Pacific mackerel stock in 1970, after the stock was thought to have declined substantially during the mid-1960s. A moratorium was placed on the fishery at this time, with a small allowance for incidental catch in mixed-fish landings. In 1972, legislation was enacted that imposed a quota based on the estimate of age-1+ biomass (>1-yr old fish) generated from formal stock assessments. Some very strong year classes in the late 1970s led to a brief period of moderately high stock abundance, which was followed by the fishery being reopened under a quota system in 1977. From 1977 to 1985, various adjustments were made to quotas for the directed harvest of Pacific mackerel and related incidental catch limits. It is important to note that even during the moratorium, substantial allowances were made for incidental catches associated with this species (Parrish and MacCall 1978).
State regulations enacted in 1985 imposed a moratorium on directed fishing when the total biomass was less than 18,200 mt, and limited incidental landings of Pacific mackerel to 18% (about 3,000 mt) during such periods. At this time, the ‘fishing year’ was set to extend from July 1st to June 30th of the following year. In summary, seasonal quotas, equal to 30% of the total biomass in excess of 18,200 mt, were allowed when the biomass was between 18,200 and 136,000 mt, with no quota limitations in effect when the total biomass was estimated to be 136,000 mt or higher.
A federal fishery management plan (FMP) for CPS, including Pacific mackerel, was imple-mented by the PFMC in January 2000 (PFMC 1998). The FMP’s harvest policy for Pacific mackerel, originally implemented by the State of California, was based on simulation analysis conducted during the mid-1980s (MacCall et al. 1985), with the addition of a proration to account nominally for the portion of the assessed stock assumed to inhabit U.S. waters (PFMC 1998). The following maximum sustainable yield (MSY) control rule for Pacific mackerel has been generally used for management from the early 2000s to the present: 𝐻𝑎𝑟𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡= (𝐵𝑖𝑜𝑚𝑎𝑠𝑠−𝐶𝑢𝑡𝑜𝑓𝑓)𝐸𝑀𝑆𝑌* 𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑏𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 where Harvest is the harvest guideline (HG), Cutoff (18,200 mt) is the lowest level of estimated biomass above which harvest is allowed, 𝐸𝑀𝑆𝑌(30%, also referred to as exploitation fraction 6 in earlier PFMC documents) is the proportion of biomass above the Cutoff that can be harvested by fisheries, and Distribution (70%) is the average proportion of total Biomass (ages 1+) assumed to reside in U.S. waters. The HGs under the federal FMP are applied to a July to June fishing year. Detailed description of the current management actions applicable to Pacific mackerel, including quotas and related fishing quantities (e.g., allowable biological catch-ABC, annual catch limit-ACL, overfishing limit-OFL, etc.), can be found in the most recent CPS SAFE document (PFMC 2021). Also, see Harvest Control Rules for U.S. Management (2019-20 and 2020-21).
Total annual harvest of Pacific mackerel by the Mexico fishery is not regulated by quotas, but there has been minimum legal size limits (e.g., 25.5 cm) imposed in the past. International management agreements between the U.S. and Mexico regarding transboundary stocks, such as Pacific mackerel, have not been developed to date (see Research and data needs below).
1.7 Management Performance From 1985 to 1991, the catch biomass exceeded 136,000 mt and no state quota restrictions were in effect. State quotas for 1992-00 fishing years averaged roughly 24,000 mt. The HGs averaged roughly 15,000 mt from 2001-06. In 2007, the HG was increased substantially to 40,000 mt and remained at this level until 2009, when the calculated HG (55,408 mt) was reduced by management to 10,000 mt based on limited landings in recent years, with the quota applicable through the 2010-11 fishing year that included an additional 1,000 mt incidental landing allowance (11,000 mt). Following the full stock assessment conducted in 2011, a harvest guideline of roughly 31,000 mt was implemented for two consecutive fishing years. Catch-based projection assessments were used to set quotas for 2013-14 (˜39,000 mt) and 2014-15 (˜29,000 mt). Quotas have remained at roughly 20,000-25,000 mt since 2015.
Note that from a management context, the CPS fishery has not fully utilized HGs since the late 1990s, with total landings far below recommended catches (see Table 2 for harvest regulations from 2008-18).
2 Data The available data between 2008 and 2021 are shown in Figure 3. Data for model year 2022 were available but not finalized nor included in this base model.
2.1 Fishery-dependent data Fishery data for assessing Pacific mackerel included landings from California, Oregon, and Washington commercial fisheries, the California recreational fishery, and the Mexico commer-7 cial fishery from Ensenada, BC and Magdalena Bay, BCS. Additionally, port sample data (ages, lengths, and weights) from from California’s commercial fishery were included.
Since 1929, CDFW has collected biological data for Pacific mackerel landed in the southern California fishery (primarily, San Pedro). Limited samples have also been collected from the Monterey fishery when available. Sample data collected from 2008 through 2022 were incorporated in this assessment (Table 4). There was one fishery sample from San Pedro from August 2022 (model year 2022) which was not included. Biological samples from the commercial fishery generally include whole body weight, fork length, sex, maturity (visual), and otoliths for age determination. Currently, CDFW strives to collect 12 ‘random’ (port) samples per month (typically, 25 fish per sample) to determine length/age compositions, as well as catch-at-age, weight-at-age, etc. for the directed fishery.
Additionally, port sampling data for the commercial fishery in Mexico have been collected by the National Fisheries Institute (INAPESCA) since 1989; however, this information has not been made formally available to date and thus, commercial fishery data from the California purse seine fleet were assumed to be representative of the combined fisheries. Lack of data from the Pacific Northwest and Baja California may not be a serious problem for some years when catches were low. However, in some recent years, Baja California catches have equaled or exceed California catches by volume (Table 1), which necessarily increases the likelihood that potential biases associated with the omission of (and subsequent assumptions concerning) sample data from the Mexico and Pacific Northwest fisheries.
Pacific mackerel are aged by CDFW biologists based on identification of annuli in whole sagittae. Historically, a birth date of May 1st was used to assign year class (Fitch 1951). In 1976, ageing protocols changed to a July 1st birth date, which coincided with an increasing population, resumed fishery sampling, and a change in the management season from a May 1st opening to a July 1st start date. Fishery inputs for this assessment were compiled by ‘biological year,’ based on the birth dates used to assign age. The biological year used in this assessment is synonymous with the ‘fishing year’ defined previously, as well as with ‘fishing season’ as reported in the historical literature (from 1976 onwards). All landings and biological compositions included in this assessment were developed on a fishing year (July – June) basis. Sample sizes associated with biological data used in this assessment are presented in (Table 4).
2.1.1 Landings The assessment includes commercial and recreational landings from calendar years 2008 to 2022. Catch estimates are based on model years and presented by region in Table 1 and Figure 2. Commercial catch statistics compiled in the CPS assessment data base are from the state fishery agencies CDFW (T. Nguyen, pers. comm.), Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW, C. Schmitt, pers. comm.), and Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW, L. Wargo, pers. comm.). California recreational catch (mt) time series 8 from 2008 to the present are based on all sport fishery modes (man-made, beach/bank, party/charter, and private/rental) and obtained from CDFW (K. Lynn, pers. comm.).
As in the last assessment (Crone et al. 2019), commercial and recreational catch have been combined into one fishery, given similar selectivity properties between the two fisheries and the limited sport-related catches. To date, the sport fishery has contributed only limited catches to the overall landings of this species. Discards were assumed to be negligible, as in previous assessments, in both the commercial and recreational fisheries associated with this species. The total values summed across region are shown in Table 5 and Figure 4 Mexico landings reflect catches in Baja California from commercial purse seine fleets operating off Ensenada and in Magdalena Bay. Commercial landings from 2008 to 2022 were taken from the National Commission of Aquaculture and Fishing (CONAPESCA) website that archives Mexico’s fishery yearbook statistics e.g. CONAPESCA (2020).
Landings values were updated at the STAR panel to reflect removals from the Pacific whiting at-sea fishery for 2008-2022. Additionally, Washington state landings in 2012 were corrected to exclude 126 mt of ‘unspecified’ mackerel previously ascribed to Pacific mackerel in the PacFIN database. The differences between the catch time series are shown in Table 3, and the base model and associated sensitivities used this updated catch time series.
2.1.2 Age compositions Presently, age data are only available from the California commercial fishery, which typically contributes the majority of fish landed at U.S. Pacific coast ports (Table 1). Biological sampling directed towards Pacific mackerel has recently begun in the states of Oregon and Washington, but only limited information is available at this time. Sample sizes (number of fishing trips) and number of measured individuals (specimens) associated with biological compositions included or considered in this assessment are presented in Table 4.
The nominal age compositions were weighted by the total monthly landings (𝐿𝑚). Port samplers biologically sample 25 individual fish per landed haul. args.summary:
This document is a stock assessment of Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) for U.S. management in the 2023-24 and 2024-25 fishing years, prepared by the Southwest Fisheries Science Center (SWFSC) scientists (Peter T. Kuriyama, Juan P. Zwolinski, Caitlin Allen Akselrud, Kevin T. Hill) in June 2023. The assessment was reviewed at a STAR Panel in April 2023.

**Stock and Management:** The assessment focuses on the Pacific mackerel sub-stock found along the Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos (Baja California) extending north to southern California and potentially the U.S. Pacific Northwest. The Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) manages this as a single stock unit with no area-specific allocations, though the harvest control rule includes a 70% U.S. distribution adjustment.

**Catches:** Landings from 2008-2022 were included from Mexico (Ensenada and Magdalena Bay) and the U.S. (California commercial and recreational, Oregon, Washington, plus bycatch from the Pacific whiting at-sea fishery). Total landings ranged from a low of 3,656 mt in 2009 to a high of 32,060 mt in 2020. Mexico landings reached 31,368 mt in 2020, while U.S. total landings peaked at 11,909 mt in 2013.

**Model:** The integrated assessment used Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3 version 3.30.20) with data from 2008-2021 (the 2022 acoustic-trawl survey value was unavailable). The model spans July-June biological years, combines sexes, ages 0-8+, has one fishery (MexCal) with annual selectivity, uses a Beverton-Holt stock-recruitment relationship with steepness 0.75, estimates age-specific natural mortality (Lorenzen), and includes an AT survey with time-varying catchability.

**Key Results:**
- Spawning stock biomass (SSB) projected: 43,864 mt in 2022, 46,167 mt in 2023, 50,372 mt in 2024
- Stock biomass (age-1+) for PFMC management: 49,977 mt in 2021, projected 46,682 mt in 2022
- Initial SSB estimated at 136,664 mt; virgin recruitment estimated at 917,938 thousand fish
- U.S. exploitation rate peaked at 27% in 2020, remaining below 30% throughout the model period

**Harvest Control Rule:** The MSY control rule is: Harvest = (Biomass − Cutoff) × E_MSY × Distribution, where Cutoff = 18,200 mt, E_MSY = 30%, and Distribution = 70%. Harvest guidelines have remained roughly 20,000-25,000 mt since 2015. The U.S. fishery has not fully utilized HGs since the late 1990s, with landings typically 7-39% of the HG (e.g., 990 mt USA landings in 2022 vs. 4,822 mt HG). Mexico's fishery is not regulated by quotas but has had minimum size limits (e.g., 25.5 cm); no international management agreements exist between the U.S. and Mexico for this transboundary stock.

**Ecosystem and History:** Pacific mackerel are part of the CPS (coastal pelagic species) assemblage in the California Current Ecosystem, though typically less abundant than anchovy or sardine. The stock experiences cyclical abundance periods (high biomass events roughly every 60 years). California first implemented management in 1970 with a moratorium. The federal FMP was implemented in January 2000 by the PFMC.

**Research Needs:** Top priorities include extending the AT survey into Mexican waters, continued coordination on age-composition data, and re-examining the harvest control rule (developed in the mid-1980s) using updated data and simulation methods.

--- SOURCE 1: A Study on the Impact of Environmental Factors on Chub Mackerel Scomber japonicus Fishing Grounds Based on a Linear Mixed Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/9/8/323

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the journal Fishes (2024, Volume 9, Issue 8, Article 323; DOI: 10.3390/fishes9080323), examines how marine environmental factors affect Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific using a linear mixed model (LMM). Authors include Jiasheng Li, Fenghua Tang, Yumei Wu, Shengmao Zhang, Weifeng Zhou, and Xuesen Cui (corresponding author), affiliated with the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute (Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences) and Shanghai Ocean University. The study was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (grant 2023YFD2401303) and received on 14 June 2024, published 14 August 2024.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used fishery data from China's high-sea light-purse seine operations (2014–2020) covering fishing grounds between 140–165°E and 30–50°N, combined with monthly averaged sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL) data from Oregon State University's Ocean Productivity database. Data were aggregated at 0.5° × 0.5° spatial resolution. CPUE was calculated as catch per net-haul (t/net). Square-root transformation of CPUE and natural logarithm of CHL were applied to achieve normal distributions; VIF values of 1.990 confirmed no multicollinearity between SST and logCHL. The LMM included SST and logCHL as fixed effects, with Year, Month, and fishing Zone as random effects, using the lme4 package in R. Among 256 candidate models, the optimal model (scenario 5) was selected based on lowest AIC, BIC, and logLik values.

KEY RESULTS: (1) SST had a significant fixed effect on CPUE with a negative slope (p < 0.001), meaning CPUE increases as SST decreases. (2) logCHL had no fixed effect on CPUE but showed significant random effects by month. (3) logCHL was positively correlated with CPUE during spawning and wintering periods (April–May, November–December) and negatively correlated during the summer feeding period (June–October), consistent with patterns observed in neon flying squid. (4) Annual average CPUE decreased from 2014 to 2020, peaking at 15.501 t/net (2015) and 11.363 t/net (2018), with a low of 8.355 t/net in 2020; monthly CPUE peaked in November (14.426 t/net). (5) Low CPUE areas (<5 t/net) were south of 34°N, while high CPUE areas (>15 t/net) were between 148–159°E. (6) The random intercept for Year showed highest value (0.353) in 2015 and lowest (−0.480) in 2019; a high-random-intercept zone at 150–152°E, 39–41°N corresponded to high catch rates. Residuals approximated a normal distribution (skewness 0.031, kurtosis 3.532).

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS: The negative SST-CPUE relationship aligns with prior studies in the East China Sea and Japan coastal waters. Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019). The optimal SST range for fishing grounds is 14–18°C (~16°C ideal), and optimal chlorophyll-a range is 0.3–0.8 mg/m³. LIMITATIONS: Interpretation complexity with crossed random effects, high parameterization risks (overfitting), and incomplete spatial/temporal data coverage (no data from Japan/Russia EEZs, no January–March data).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SST had a significant fixed effect on the CPUE. In contrast, the natural logarithm of chlorophyll (logCHL) had no fixed effect on the CPUE. Based on the monthly analysis, random fluctuations were observed in the impact of logCHL on the CPUE. LogCHL and CPUE show a positive correlation during spawning and wintering periods and a negative correlation during the feeding period."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/10/1/20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Fishes* (2025, Volume 10, Issue 1, Article 20) by authors Seonggil Go (Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology), Joon-ho Lee (Underwater Survey Technology 21), and Sukgeun Jung (Jeju National University, corresponding author). The study projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the western North Pacific Ocean.

**Methodology:** The researchers developed a spawning ground index (SGI) based on a Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′ E, 20°00′–52°00′ N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers), driven by the IPCC AR5 RCP85 scenario. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010–2059. SGI was calculated using four parameters: water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m). The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001).

**Key Findings:**
- In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June.
- By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes).
- Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea.
- The study suggests biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea.

**Limitations noted:** The model results did not perfectly align with observations in the same space and time (though trends were similar); the assumed spawning period may shift due to photoperiod changes; only 10 m depth environmental conditions were considered; and chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m depth).

**Funding:** Supported by the Korea Institute of Marine Science and Technology (KIMST), Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries (RS-2023-00256330 and RS-2022-KS221566), and Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST grant PEA0306).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite some uncertainty, our model based on climate change scenarios projected that, by the 2050s, spawning grounds will shift northward due to warming of the ocean surface, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Effects of oceanographic conditions on fishery distribution: A case study of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in northeastern Taiwan ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0141113624004641

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Marine Environmental Research (Volume 202, November 2024, Article 106803) as part of a special issue on "Climate Change and the Oceans," edited by Fangli QIAO of the First Institute of Oceanography. The study examines the effects of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) distribution in northeastern Taiwan.

**Authors:** Sandipan Mondal, Frank Muller-Karger, Aratrika Ray, Shin-Ichi Ito, Ming-An Lee, and Hsueh-Jung Lu.

**Methodology:** The researchers constructed a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery data, climatic oscillation data, and oceanography data. Fishery and oceanographic data were rescaled using MATLAB (2022a) to a consistent spatial and temporal grid, then standardized using a generalized linear model (GLM). Five single-algorithm models were used: GLM, generalized additive model (GAM), gradient boosting method (GBM), random forest (RF), and classification models, combined into an ensemble approach.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO), which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792).
- NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level.
- Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect.
- Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m.
- Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E.

**Background Context:** Global climate change is significantly affecting marine ecosystems, with ocean warming causing coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, and sea-level rise. Under RCP 8.5 scenario, a predicted 40% decline in tropical fish catch by the 2050s in some economic zones (Lam et al., 2020) highlights the urgency of this research. Chub mackerel is economically crucial to Taiwan, with Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries accounting for 98.66% of captures. The study addresses a research gap by using multiple algorithms to confirm oceanographic significance, unlike previous studies that relied on single models.

**Funding:** National Science & Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC) grant 112-2811-M-019-004 and Fisheries Agency, Council of Agriculture, Taiwan grant 112-FM-2.31-A-03.

**Applications:** Findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in northeastern Taiwan waters and may aid decision-makers in protecting other ocean fisheries and dependent communities under changing climate conditions. The article has been cited by 5 subsequent publications (as of the page retrieval date).
</summary>

"Our results indicated that the chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation. Moreover, sea-surface height and mixed-layer depth exerted the most and least significant effects on chub mackerel distribution, respectively."

--- SOURCE 4: Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304380014001604

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Ecological Modelling (Volume 283, 10 July 2014, Pages 70-84) titled "Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea" by Yuesong Li, Xinjun Chen, Changsheng Chen, Jianzhong Ge, Rubao Ji, Rucheng Tian, Pengfei Xue, and Liuxiong Xu. DOI: 10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2014.03.016.

The study developed an early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The researchers examined how regional physical processes affect larval dispersal and survival under climatological spring-summer conditions, both with and without short-time fluctuations from a typhoon.

Key findings include:
- Seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages.
- Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location.
- Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing. Comparison of cases with and without Typhoon Alice showed that cancellation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents limits typhoon influence on low-frequency flow and larval dispersion, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds.
- Temperature and food play significant roles in early larval development; water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March-July.
- Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June).
- Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion.

The article provides background on the ECS physical oceanography, including the Kuroshio Current (which acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf), the Taiwan Warm Current, and the Changjiang Coastal Current (which tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East Strait). Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. The study is the first IBM developed to examine chub mackerel recruitment in the ECS.

The paper has 41 references and has been cited 27 times. It was supported by multiple Chinese national research projects including the National 863 project, Shanghai Education Committee, and Shanghai Ocean University programs.
</summary>

"The model results show that the seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during the early life stages."

URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/stock-assessment-of-chub-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-in-the-central-east-china-sea-based-on-length-data/9AC92B324DD34E8BA019F5462A821E73

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Cambridge University Press journal article (published online October 30, 2013, in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom) titled "Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data." The study addresses the chub mackerel, an important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea that rose to prominence after the decline of traditional demersal economic species. The research methodology involved separating sample catches from 2009-2010 into three age groups based on an age–fork length key, estimating maximum sustainable yield (MSY), and building a spawner–recruitment relationship using fishery statistics from purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels, and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. Key findings: (1) The MSY of chub mackerel is approximately 18.8 × 10⁴ tonnes; (2) The fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (with lighting and deep-water purse seine vessels standardized to purse seine vessels), equivalent to a fishing mortality rate (F) of 0.4; (3) If fishing mortality remains at the current level (F = 0.7), the biomass will remain at 45.3 × 10⁴ tonnes; (4) At current fishing intensity, more than 40% of catches will consist of individuals smaller than 200mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300mm. The study concludes there is little potential for further exploitation of chub mackerel resources in the central East China Sea, and recommends reducing fishing mortality (F) to less than 0.4 for sustainable utilization. The chub mackerel resources are suffering over-exploitation due to increased fishing effort, and this paper represents the first analysis of their response to fishing because of previous data shortages.

URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11802-021-4760-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Ocean University of China (Volume 20, pages 1483–1494, 2021) titled "Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea." Published on November 21, 2021, the study was conducted by authors Wei Yu, Jian Wen, Xinjun Chen, Gang Li, Yuesong Li, and Zhong Zhang, affiliated with Shanghai Ocean University and the Qingdao National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology.

The study investigated how the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) impacts the habitat range and distribution of the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the East China Sea (ECS). A weighting-based Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) model was established using vertical water temperature data at depths of 2.5 m, 25 m, and 50 m. The study concludes that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of S. japonicus in the East China Sea. The article received 279 accesses, 7 citations, and 1 Altmetric score. The research was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2018YFD0900906), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 41906073), the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (No. 19ZR1423000), and the Shanghai Universities First-Class Disciplines Project (Fisheries A).

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index of chub mackerel in the spawning season and its effect on the abundance ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (25 November 2022) examining climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index (TSI) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and its effect on stock abundance.

**Study Context and Species:**
- Chub mackerel is widely distributed in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and is fished by China, Korea, and Japan in different seasons and areas.
- The species is divided into two stocks: the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock (distributed in the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and Sea of Japan) and the Pacific stock (inhabiting the Pacific coast of Japan and high seas of the northwestern Pacific).
- Main spawning period is March to June, with suitable spawning SST ranging from 15°C to 22°C and optimal at 18°C.

**Methods:**
- The authors estimated average TSI for chub mackerel in main spawning areas using the relationship between spawning probability and SST, assuming a Gaussian distribution with mean 18°C and variance 2.0°C.
- Data sources included FAO catch data (1950-2017), Japanese Fisheries Agency stock assessments (TWC and Pacific stock data, 1970-2017), and SST data from Japan Meteorological Agency (1970-2011), AVHRR (2012-2015), and GOES (2016-2017).
- Analytical techniques included Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis, sequential t-test analysis of regime shifts (STARS), Gradient Forest (GF) analysis, Generalized Additive Models (GAM), and Threshold GAMs (TGAM) to detect stationary vs. non-stationary relationships.
- Three main spawning areas were defined: coastal waters of China seas (24°N-36°N/118°E-124°E), southern Sea of Japan/Tsushima Strait (31°N-36°N/126°E-132°E), and Pacific coast of Japan (30°N-38°N/129°E-147°E).

**Key Results:**
- TSI in the shelf waters of China seas and Tsushima Strait showed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock.
- TSI on the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock.
- Chinese catch showed an increasing trend since the 1970s with step changes in 1986/1987, 1993/1994, and 2003/2004; TWC catch by Korea/Japan decreased in the late 1990s (step-change in 1998/1999).
- Pacific catch dramatically decreased in the late 1970s and 1980s but began recovering after the 2000s, with step changes in 1979/1980, 1988/1989, and 2014/2015.
- EOF analysis showed TSI had opposite loading on either side of the Kuroshio axis; first four EOFs explained 43.10% of total variance in TSI.
- TWC stock showed non-stationary relationships with TSI with threshold years in 1993/1994 and the late 1990s; Pacific stock showed non-stationary relationships with thresholds in the late 1970s to early 1980s.
- All relationships between chub mackerel abundance and TSI were better fitted by non-stationary TGAMs than stationary GAMs.
- Effects of spawning temperature suitability on abundance had a delayed effect of 1 to 2 years, attributed to the 0-2 year age structure of the main chub mackerel stock.

**Climate Drivers and Mechanisms:**
- TSI in different areas was affected by Arctic Oscillation Index (AOI), Monsoon Index (MOI), and Southern Oscillation Index (SOI).
- Non-stationarity in the TWC area was linked to declined variance in the Siberian High, while non-stationarity in the Pacific area was linked to the Aleutian Low.
- The regime shifts in AOI, MOI, and SHI in the late 1980s caused weakening monsoon and decreasing cold air intrusion, increasing water temperatures.
- The Pacific stock's late 1970s step change was related to interannual-decadal variability in the Aleutian Low and ENSO.
- Spatio-temporal variation in spawning temperature suitability had an important impact on the recovery of the Pacific stock after the 2000s, including a northward movement trend of the spawning area.
- The study follows an "atmosphere-ocean-biology" or "double-integration" process mechanism, demonstrating that climate variability influences biological variability through intermediary environmental variability.

**Conclusions:**
The research provides a reasonable explanation for variations in the two chub mackerel stocks and their responses to TSI variability, offering improved understanding of climate-induced non-stationary relationships between chub mackerel abundance and physical drivers. The authors note that biotic factors (e.g., spawning-stock biomass) should also be considered in future research for comprehensive population dynamics understanding and resource management.
</summary>

"Results showed that the TSIs in the shelf waters of China seas and the waters of the Tsushima Strait displayed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock, whereas the TSI in the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Synchronous spatio-temporal changes in potential habitats of Trachurus murphyi and Dosidicus gigas off Chile in relation to regime shift of Pacific decadal oscillation ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0924796322000598

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Journal of Marine Systems (Volume 233, September 2022, Article 103758), investigates synchronous spatio-temporal changes in potential habitats of Chilean jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi) and jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) off the coast of Chile in relation to Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) regime shifts from 1950 to 2017.

**Key Environmental Factors Identified:**
- For D. gigas: sea surface salinity (SSS), sea surface height anomaly (SSHA), and water temperature at 400m (Temp_400m)
- For T. murphyi: sea surface temperature (SST), mixed layer depth (MLD), and Temp_400m
- All environmental factors were significantly related to the PDO

**Methodology:**
- Used habitat suitability index (HSI) models
- Fisheries data from the National Distant-water Fisheries Data Center of China (NDFDC), Shanghai Ocean University
- Fishing data for D. gigas covered March–May 2011–2017; T. murphyi covered March–May 2013–2017
- PDO regimes identified: two cold regimes (1950–1976 and 1999–2017) and one warm regime (1977–1998)

**Key Findings:**
- A significantly negative relationship was found between the HSI of D. gigas and the PDO index, while a significantly positive correlation was observed for T. murphyi
- In the warm PDO regime: MLD was shallower, SST increased, and SSHA decreased from northeast to southwest off Chile; D. gigas suitable habitats contracted and shifted southwestward; T. murphyi habitat quality enhanced with little distribution change
- In the cold PDO regime: SST and SSHA decreased, MLD deepened; D. gigas suitable habitats enlarged and moved northeastward; T. murphyi suitable habitats slightly reduced
- The study concluded that Chilean T. murphyi dominated in the warm PDO regime while D. gigas dominated in the cold PDO regime

**Context:**
- Both species are key economic species in the Humboldt Current System (HCS) off Chile
- Chilean T. murphyi catches account for the highest proportion among world oceans; D. gigas is distributed from northern California (37°N) to southern Chile (47°S)
- Both are regulated by the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO)

--- SOURCE 9: Pacific decadal oscillation - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_decadal_oscillation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin, detected as warm or cool surface waters in the Pacific north of 20°N. It varies irregularly at interannual-to-interdecadal timescales. The PDO was named by Steven R. Hare in 1997, who noticed it while studying salmon production patterns. The PDO index is the leading empirical orthogonal function (EOF) of monthly sea surface temperature anomalies over the North Pacific, with signals reconstructed back to 1661 (and as far back as 993) through tree-ring chronologies.

**Mechanisms:** The PDO is not a single physical mode of ocean variability but rather the superposition of several processes with different dynamic origins:
- **ENSO teleconnections/atmospheric bridge**: El Niño events generate Rossby waves that propagate poleward, modifying surface fluxes over the North Pacific within 2–6 weeks.
- **SST reemergence**: Winter SST anomalies are sequestered beneath the shallow summer mixed layer and reemerge the following winter when the mixed layer deepens again.
- **Stochastic atmospheric forcing**: Random storm forcings integrated into the ocean mixed layer can contribute up to 1/3 of PDO variability at decadal timescales.
- **Ocean dynamics**: Including advective resonance, Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension variability, and North Pacific gyre circulation adjustments driven by westward-propagating Rossby waves.

**Impacts:** During a positive phase, the Aleutian Low deepens, warming the Pacific Northwest to Alaska while cooling Mexico and the Southeast US. Winter precipitation increases in Alaska's coastal range, Mexico, and the Southwest US but decreases in Canada, Eastern Siberia, and Australia. The PDO also affects the Indian summer monsoon (stronger during negative phase) and, along with the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, strongly influences multidecadal drought patterns in the US.

**Regime shifts:** Documented reversals around 1924/25, 1945/46, and 1976/77, with additional shifts in 1988/89 and 1997/98. A 2014 flip to a warm phase coincided with record-breaking global surface temperatures. The last two major reversals corresponded with dramatic shifts in salmon production regimes in the North Pacific. Reconstructions show a 50–70 year periodicity, with a persistent negative phase during medieval times (993–1300).

**Predictability:** NOAA produces PDO forecasts using linear inverse modeling (LIM), with predictability largely arising from ENSO and limited to approximately 4 seasons (~14 months). ENSO tends to lead PDO cycling. The PDO is related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO), a similar but more global phenomenon covering 50°S to 50°N.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the journal *Geosciences* (2026, Volume 16, Issue 6, Article 212) by Zengan Deng (Tianjin University) and Ruiyao Li. The study investigates the transport and distribution of Scomber japonicus (chub mackerel) larvae in the Pacific Ocean south of Japan using a coupled ocean–biophysical model (CROCO v2.0 ocean model coupled with Ichthyop v3.3 biophysical model).

**Background:** S. japonicus is a key economically important fish in the Northwest Pacific, harvested mainly by China, Japan, Russia, and South Korea. The population declined significantly in the 1980s and has been classified as overfished since the 1990s despite conservation efforts.

**Methods:**
- The modeling domain spans 122–152°E and 25–45°N, with 1/12° horizontal resolution and 32 sigma levels.
- Three Kuroshio path modes were studied: offshore non-large-meander (ONLM, represented by 2009), nearshore non-large-meander (NNLM, represented by 2013), and typical large-meander (TLM, represented by 2018).
- Two transport scenarios were simulated: passive drift (PD) and active swimming (AS).
- Four spawning grounds were defined: near the Izu Ridge, south of the Kii Peninsula, south of Shikoku, and south of Kyushu.
- Three nursery areas were defined: east of 132.5°E (area 1), between 132.5°E–140°E (area 2), and east of 140°E near the Kuroshio Extension (area 3).
- 200 particles were released daily per spawning ground throughout April (peak spawning month), with a 20-day transport duration.
- AS scenario included active swimming toward higher plankton aggregation (32 cm/s swimming speed), diel vertical migration after day 3, and a customized buoyancy formula for spherical eggs.

**Key Results:**
- Model validation showed strong agreement with observed currents, tides (max amplitude difference <2.5 cm, max phase lag difference <4.4°), and temperatures.
- Active swimming significantly reduced transport distances and shifted larval distributions northward, allowing larvae to reach areas with higher zooplankton aggregation, particularly the Kuroshio–Oyashio transition zone.
- The largest latitudinal shift (473.2 km northward) between AS and PD scenarios occurred during the TLM period between 142°E–144°E.
- In PD scenarios, mid-distance transport (400–600 km) dominated (30–35%), while in AS scenarios, short-distance transport (0–400 km) increased to over 25% with long-distance transport dropping substantially.
- Larvae from southern Kyushu–Shikoku spawning grounds were primarily transported to nursery area 2 (132.5°E–140°E), while those from the Kii Peninsula and Izu Ridge areas were distributed mainly in nursery area 3 (east of 140°E).
- The TLM period produced the widest larval distribution due to pronounced meandering flow and eddy activity, while the NNLM produced a narrower distribution.

**Conclusions and Implications:** The authors recommend that nursery areas 2 and 3 may warrant further attention in future spatial management assessments. They caution that results should be interpreted as case-based comparisons (single year per path mode) rather than long-term mean responses, and future work should incorporate multi-year simulations, stage-dependent larval behavior, direct prey fields, and independent observational validation.

--- SOURCE 12: Kuroshio Current - Wikipedia ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Wikipedia article on the Kuroshio Current (黒潮, "Black Stream"), also known as the Black Current or Japan Current, describes it as a north-flowing, warm ocean current on the west side of the North Pacific Ocean basin. Named for its deep blue waters, it is analogous to the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic and serves as the western boundary current of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre. Off the east coast of Japan, it merges with the Oyashio Current to form the North Pacific Current.

HISTORY: The current was discovered in 1565 by Andrés de Urdaneta during his voyage from Cebu (Philippines) to California, which opened the "tornaviaje" route and gave Spain hegemony over the Pacific via the Manila galleon trade. Europeans knew of it as early as 1650 from a map by Bernhardus Varenius, and Captain J. King noted it during Captain James Cook's expedition. Historians have debated its role in structuring Japan's economic geography, including fisheries, whaling, and maritime routes.

PHYSICAL PROPERTIES: The Kuroshio has an annual average sea-surface temperature of about 24°C (75°F), is approximately 100 km wide, and produces frequent small to meso-scale eddies. It originates from the Pacific North Equatorial Current, splits at Luzon (Philippines), enters the East China Sea via the Yonaguni Depression east of Taiwan, is steered by the Okinawa Trough, re-enters the Pacific through the Tokara Strait, flows along southern Japan, and separates at the Bōsō Peninsula as the Kuroshio Extension. Its branch into the Sea of Japan is the Tsushima Current. Transport is ~25 Sv in the Sea of Japan and reaches 65 Sv southeast of Japan, with significant seasonal variability. The warm waters sustain the northernmost coral reefs in the world (at 33.48°N). The current creates warm surface temperatures and moisture that fuel typhoons—the Western North Pacific averages about 25 typhoons annually, mostly July–October. Regarding the geologic past, there is conflicting evidence about whether lower sea levels prevented the Kuroshio from entering the Sea of Japan during the last glacial period.

SEDIMENT TRANSPORT: The current causes deep-sea erosion, notably on the Kenting Plateau offshore Southern Taiwan, where accelerating bottom currents (from 3500m to 400-700m depth) erode sediment and reveal the Kuroshio Knoll. Sediment grain sizes increase with depth as fine particles are swept away. The current also transports Yangtze River sediment, with deposition controlled by the interaction of the Kuroshio intrusion, China Coastal Current, and Taiwan Warm Current. Distinct elemental tracers (illite, chlorite from Taiwan; smectite from Luzon; kaolinite and titanium from the Pearl River) allow tracking of sediment sources.

EDDIES & TYPHOONS: Eddies contribute to fish larvae survival. Warm-core rings show productivity comparable to surrounding shelf waters, with nutrient upwelling at perimeters and deep convective mixing via thermostads. A 1998 study found primary productivity within a warm-core ring was nearly equal to the cold jet outside it. Typhoon-induced mixing brings nutrients to surface layers; two typhoons in 2003 produced two algal bloom events in the NW Pacific that negatively affected Japan.

NUTRIENT TRANSPORT: The Kuroshio is a "nutrient stream" with primary production of 150-300 grams of carbon per square meter per year. Maximum chlorophyll occurs around 100m depth. Downstream receives nutrients at rates of 100-280 kmol N·s⁻¹. Upwelling over the Okinawa Trough and Tokara Strait (with Coriolis-driven cyclonic activity) brings deep nutrients to surface layers, essential for phytoplankton photosynthesis.

MARINE LIFE: The region is a biodiversity hotspot but many species are threatened by overfishing/overharvest. Phytoplankton: Prochlorococcus dominates picophytoplankton; with Synechococcus, they may fix half of CO2 in the photic zone. Dust deposition from Gobi desert storms stimulates growth. Trichodesmium (a diazotroph) correlates with nitrogen fixation. Ten genera of seaweed reside in the region. Zooplankton: Copepod species C. sinicus and E. concinna are transported northward from the East China Sea. Tunicates (salps and doliolids) transport carbon to bottom waters and feed at least 202 marine species. Coral: Heliopora coerulea is threatened by warming, acidification, and dynamite fishing; Acropora japonica, A. secale, and A. hyacinthus are key reef-builders using zooxanthellae symbioses. Crown-of-thorns starfish and Drupella fragum prey on corals. The current connects coral reefs via larval transport along the Ryukyu Arc. Squid: Japanese flying squid (Todarodes pacificus) has winter-spawning populations associated with the Kuroshio; expanding spawning areas in the East China Sea have contributed to increased annual catches in Japan since the late 1980s. Fish: Thousands of species including reef fish (rabbitfish, parrotfish), pelagic fish (sardines, anchovies, mackerel, sailfish), and sharks. The Kuroshio-Oyashio intersection region supports major fisheries whose success depends on oceanographic conditions varying through the year.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Global Seafood Alliance's Responsible Seafood Advocate, authored by Sukgeun Jung, Ph.D. (Jeju National University, Republic of Korea), summarizes a study published in Fishes (2025, 10(1), 20) by Go, S. et al. that projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Western North Pacific Ocean.

**Key background:** Chub mackerel are forage fish crucial to marine food webs, feeding on zooplankton/phytoplankton and serving as prey for larger marine predators. The Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock is an economically valuable fishery exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the East China Sea (ECS) and Korea Strait (KS) from February to June before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the Japan/East Sea (JES) and Yellow Sea (YS).

**Study methodology:** Researchers developed spawning ground indices and used the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to estimate and project water temperature and salinity at 10 meters depth in the western North Pacific. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010 to 2059 under an IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (IPCC AR5) climate change scenario, comparing the 2010s (2010–2019) and 2050s (2050–2059) periods.

**Key findings:**
- Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to the 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s and become less influenced by the Kuroshio Current.
- This northward shift is expected to cause a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds (from the Pacific side of Japan and JES toward waters off Jeju Island), consistent with earlier work by Li et al.
- Ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production are expected to increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the JES.
- Model outputs were generally compatible with previous observations, though the model did not perfectly align with observational data in the same space and time; data assimilation methods were suggested for future improvements.
- Spawning grounds were assumed to be limited to continental shelf areas (50–300 meters depth), though other research suggests chub mackerel may also spawn in shallower coastal areas (<50 meters), including Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait.
- The study only considered environmental conditions at 10 meters depth and used only temperature and salinity variables; other factors (turbulence, currents, dissolved oxygen) and photoperiod influences on spawning periods require further research.

**Conclusions:** The study enhances the reliability of stock assessment for fisheries management of chub mackerel and contributes to the development of individual-based bio-physical coupled models for predicting recruitment and spatiotemporal distribution of exploitable chub mackerel. The results are expected to inform fisheries policies accounting for climate change in the region.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to 2050s, and these suggested that chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s compared to the 2010s, which means that spawning will become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current."
</key_excerpts>

This bimodal feature is unique to the Kuroshio and not observed in other western boundary currents. LM and NLM paths can persist from a year to a decade, while transitions occur over several months. The LM path typically forms via transition from the nNLM path, triggered by a small meander that first appears southeast of Kyushu, grows eastward, and develops into an LM.

(2013)—positive SSH anomalies east of Taiwan, westward propagation of cyclonic eddies, and a stable KE state; (2) its exceptionally long duration is attributed to low Kuroshio transport since 2017 and wind-forced stability of the KE system east of the Izu Ridge after 2018; (3) it exhibited unstable flow patterns in its early stages (meander trough shifting eastward, S-shaped curvature) similar to the 1981–1984 LM; and (4) it featured significant cyclonic eddy detachment in 2020, followed by reabsorption and merging that led to rapid LM recovery—a phenomenon only previously observed during the 1975–1980 LM.

KUROSHIO CHARACTERISTICS: The Kuroshio transports large amounts of heat, salt, and biogeochemical materials northward. Its current velocity has a subsurface maximum (>1 m/s) extending to ~1000 m depth, with net volume transport of approximately 42 Sv. The Kuroshio exhibits large horizontal SSH and temperature gradients in surface and subsurface layers.

IMPACTS COVERED: The review covers LM impacts on (1) oceanic conditions (coastal sea level, coastal circulation, water temperature, and mass distributions), (2) atmospheric phenomena (via SST distribution changes that alter heat and moisture supply to the atmosphere; LM-associated SST anomalies have mesoscale horizontal scales of several hundred kilometers), (3) lower trophic marine ecosystems (Kuroshio carries a "nutrient stream"—nutrient-rich water below the euphotic zone—with studies on vertical turbulent nitrate flux and eddy-driven nutrient transport), and (4) fisheries resources (the Kuroshio region and adjacent areas are spawning and nursery grounds for various fish species, especially in the coastal Kanto-Tokai area where the Kuroshio approaches the coast during S-shaped curvature phases, causing coastal warming).

RESEARCH CONTEXT: The review notes significant contributions from the "Hotspots in the Climate System" (hotspot1; 2010–2014) and "Midlatitude ocean-atmosphere interaction hotspots under the changing climate" (hotspot2; 2019–2023) research projects. It positions itself as the first comprehensive review covering both oceanic dynamics and the broad impacts of the Kuroshio LM across ocean conditions, atmosphere, ecosystems, and fisheries, and emphasizes that 21st-century research has shown mid-latitude oceanic fronts and WBCs actively influence atmospheric variability (not merely passively responding).

--- SOURCE 2: The Spatio-Temporal Distribution and Population ... ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2615/15/8/1135

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Animals* (Volume 15, Issue 8, Article 1135, DOI: 10.3390/ani15081135) on April 15, 2025, authored by Guoqing Zhao, Heng Zhang, and Fenghua Tang from the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, Shanghai. The study examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO).

**Study Design**: Analyzing data from 38,123 commercial light purse seine fishing operations (2016–2021) and 4,440 biological samples. The fishing ground covered 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E. Methods included length-weight relationships, Von Bertalanffy growth equations (using ELEFAN I in FISAT II), mortality estimations via catch curves and Pauly's equations, and the Length-Based Bayesian (LBB) stock assessment model using the TropFishR package in R.

**Key Results**:
1. Fishing activities concentrated along the outer edge of Japan and Russia's exclusive economic zones; the fishing ground gravity center moved northwestward over time.
2. CPUE decreased year by year (negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01), with high values from 2016–2018 and low values from 2019–2021.
3. Sex ratios varied from 1.09–2.55 (female-to-male); fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020); mean lengths ranged from 212.07 to 268.28 mm.
4. Growth parameters: asymptotic length (Linf) varied from 36–42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged from 0.31–0.65; total mortality (Z) ranged from 1.01–1.64; natural mortality (M) from 0.59–0.85; fishing mortality (F) from 0.23–0.79.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: The study investigated how marine heatwaves (MHWs) affect the distribution and abundance of Japanese chub mackerel, a small pelagic economically important fish species in the northwest Pacific Ocean, from June to November 2014–2021.

METHODOLOGY:
- Fisheries data from the Distant-Water Fisheries Data Center of Shanghai Ocean University (daily records from Chinese enterprise fishing logbooks, including time, coordinates, fishing effort in days, and catch in tons)
- Sea surface temperature (SST) data from NOAA Optimal Interpolated Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) product (0.25°×0.25° spatial resolution)
- MHWs defined per Hobday et al.: SST exceeding the 90th percentile of a 30-year (1982–2011) climatology for at least five consecutive days; events separated by ≤2 days merged
- Three MHW parameters analyzed: frequency, mean intensity (°C), and duration (days)
- Catch per unit effort (CPUE) used as abundance indicator
- Methods included spatiotemporal statistical analysis, centroid trajectory comparisons, Generalized Additive Model (GAM), Mann–Kendall tests, Pearson correlation, t-tests, and two-way ANOVA
- Study area: 135–170° E, 30–50° N; two high-density fishing subregions analyzed in detail: Region a (150–155° E, 38–43° N) and Region b (144–149° E, 35–40° N)

KEY RESULTS:
1. Japanese chub mackerel CPUE concentrated within 145–160° E and 35–45° N, with significant interannual variability. CPUE declined overall from 2014 to 2021, peaking at 20 t/d in 2014–2015 and dropping below 10 t/d after 2018, with lowest values in 2019 and 2021. Monthly CPUE peaked in October. Two-way ANOVA confirmed significant year (p<0.001), month (p<0.001), and interaction effects (p<0.001).

2. MHWs showed significant interannual variability with increasing trends in frequency, intensity, and duration. MHW intensity peaked at 3.5–4.5 °C in 2016, while durations exceeded 90 days in the central region from 2020–2021 (up from 10–25 days in earlier years). MHW duration surpassed 50 days in 2016 and 2018, and reached 80 days locally in 2019. Mann–Kendall test confirmed significant upward trend in MHW frequency (p<0.001). Autumn MHWs exhibited stronger intensity and longer durations than summer ones.

3. MHWs negatively impacted mackerel: CPUE significantly lower during MHWs (p<0.001, Welch two-sample t-test). Pearson correlation between MHW frequency and CPUE was strongly negative (r = −0.72, p < 0.001).

4. Spatial analysis revealed the CPUE geographic centroid shifted eastward (mean longitude from ~151° E to ~153° E) and latitudinal distributions shifted northward in summer, deviating significantly from MHW centroid locations — consistent with the thermal displacement hypothesis (species moving poleward/cooler waters to avoid thermal stress).

5. CPUE decreased as MHW intensity increased, with frequencies dropping substantially at high intensities (6.5–7.0 °C). GAM analysis showed MHW intensity exerted a significant non-linear effect on CPUE (edf = 6.49, F = 15.74), explaining 33.9% of deviance (adjusted R² = 0.336). The partial effect of intensity dropped rapidly at low intensity levels (~1.5–2.3 °C), flattened at intermediate levels (~3–4.8 °C), and decreased sharply at higher intensities (>5 °C).

The species was noted as a thermally sensitive species, with rising SST adversely affecting reproductive ecology, larval survival, and food web dynamics. Key contribution: MHWs played an important role in regulating the distribution and abundance dynamics of Japanese chub mackerel.

LIMITATIONS: Narrow environmental focus (excluding salinity, currents), limited fishery data (7,800 MHW-CPUE matched records), and model complexity constraints. Future research should expand datasets, integrate additional environmental variables, and employ multi-model frameworks.
