<webpage_content>
93 Current stock status and management of chub mackerel, Scomber japonicas, along the Pacific coast of Japan an example of allowable biological catch determination AKIHIKOYATSU, TAKUMI MITANI1, CHIKAKO WATANABE, HIROSHI NISHIDA1, ATSUSHI KAWABATA2, AND HIROYUKI MATSUDA3 1National Research Institute of Fisheries Science, Yokohama 236-8648, Japan (yatsua@fra.affrc.go.jp),2Tohoku National Fisheries Research Institute, Hachinohe 031-0841, Japan and,3Ocean Research Institute, University of Tokyo, Tokyo 164-8639, Japan SUMMARY. Stock biomass of the Pacific stock of Scomber japonicus decreased from ca. 4-6 million tons during the early and mid 1970's to less than one million tons in the 1990's. This decline was probably caused from over-fishing and decreased reproductive success corresponding to regime shifts in the late 1970's and 1980's. We decided to keep the spawning stock biomass (SSB) above 0.45 million tons, because 1) no recruitment failures were observed above this level and 2) this SSB can be attained by preserving dominant year classes until their maturation (age-3). Problems of the allowable biological catch determination method in Japan were discussed and a practical solution was presented.
KEY WORDS: chub mackerel, stock assessment, stock management INTRODUCTION The Pacific stock of chub mackerel, Scomber japonicus, distributes from costal Japan to high seas as east as around the 1809 longitude.1 This stock has been harvested by Japanese and Russian fisheries. After the peak of the catch (1.5 million tons) in 1978, catch decreased to less than 25,000 tons in 1990. In 1992, 1996 and 2000, dominant year classes appeared, however, intensive fishing on immature fishes (age-0 and age-1) prevented recovery of the stock (Fig. 1).2,3 In order to rebuild this stock, we examined 1) current status of the Pacific stock of chub mackerel, 2) optimal harvest age and, 3) a stock rebuilding policy using dominant year classes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS Stock abundance was estimated by virtual population analysis (VPA)4,5 tuned with abundance indices from midwater trawls and driftnet surveys and wintering stock abundance index calculated from purse seine fishery data for age-0 stock numbers, and tuned with number of effective shots of the purse seine fishery, which account for approximately 80% of the total catch, for age-aggregated fishing mortality coefficient F. We also assumed an identical F for age-5 and a plus group (age-6 and older, abbreviated as 6+) for each year, because of no substantial differences in spatial distribution and body size between age-5 and the plus group. Catch-at-age data (Fig. 1) were calculated from monthly catch and length frequency data collected from the purse seine fishery and other fisheries, and an age-length-key. Natural mortality coefficient M was assumed 0.4 per year for all ages as a base-case, on the basis of empirical relationship between M and life span and reported values for chub mackerel.' Body weight and maturation rates for both sexes of chub mackerel were assumed as in Table 1 since growth and maturation were found density -dependent. In this paper, we used a fishing year system starting from July and ending in June of next year.
Equations (1)-(7) were used to determine selectivity of each age in the terminal year (in this case 2000)5: 94 where Nƒ¿,y is stock numbers of age a at year y, Ca ,y is catch, and p indicates a plus group.
F, except for terminal F, and F for terminal year and terminal age were determined with equations (5) and (6), and (7), respectively: Selectivity of age-0 fish in the terminal year was decreased to half of the original value, because the age-0 fish was unavailable in the first half fishing season owing to the prevailing Oyashio inshore branch in autumn of 2000.
Then, using the selectivity in the terminal year, we obtained age-aggregated F (arithmetic mean of age 0-6+) for terminal year by minimizing the sum of squares (SSQ): where, i is a tuning index (i=1, 2, 3) in year y, X is number of effective shots of purse seine fishery in yeary, qi is catchability coefficient for each index and Q is a inverse of catchability coefficient for purse seine fishery.
Table 1 Mean body weight and maturation rate at age used for VPA analysis during 1970-85 (high stock period) and after 1986 (low stock period) Fig. 1 Catch-at-age composition from 1970 to 2000 For projection of SSB using a forward VPA, we assumed 1) a constant future fishing mortality coefficient Fƒ¿ ,y, 2) a constant selectivity as in 2000, and, 3) occurrence of a dominant year class in 2004 and 2008 and average recruitment numbers in the 1990's except for 1992 and 1996 values, as a base case. In order to examine the effects of the assumption on recruitment numbers, we performed a bootstrap simulation based on 100 random resampling of the actual recruitment numbers during 1988-2000.
Optimal harvest age under a sustainable condition of a stock was determined following the method of Matsuda et al.7, where we ignored the discount rate and we adopted growth and M parameters for larvae and juveniles from Watanabes) and our unpublished data. Thus, we adopted a survival rate of 0.004% from prolarvae to the time of recruitment to fisheries at the age of 9 months. For older fish, growth and maturation parameters were derived from those observed in low stock period (Table 1) and M=0.4.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Stock status Stock biomass ranged from 4 to 6 million tons in the 1970's, decreased to about 2 million tons in the 1980's owing to the deteriorated recruitment success as defined by recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS) (Figs. 2 and 3) and further decreased to less than one million tons in the 1990's. Spawning stock biomass (SSB) ranged from 0.45 to 1.60 million tons during 1970-1985, and gradually decreased to around 0.1 million tons in the late 1990's (Fig. 3). Fishing mortality coefficient considerably varied (Fig. 4) with extremely low values in 1990 and 1991 when chub mackerel stock declined but sardine population was 95 still at the moderate level. Sensitivity analysis of M on SSB in 2000 indicated that estimated SSB were 90 % and 114 % of the base case in M=0.3 and 0.5, respectively and for biomass 87% and 118%, respectively.
Fig. 2 VPA-derived age-0 stock numbers and corresponding tuning indices Fig. 3 Age-0 stock numbers (R), spawning stock biomass (SSB) and R per SSB (RPS) Fig. 4 Age-aggregated fishing mortality coefficient and number of effective shots of purse seine fishery The stock recruitment relationship (Fig. 5) indicates that 1) two major shifts in RPS took place in the late 1970's and 1980's, probably corresponding to the large meandering periods of Kuroshio Path or regime shifts in the North Pacific Ocean and, 2) recruitment over fishing in the 1990's because dominant 1992 and 1996 year classes had not resulted in a recovery of SSB. Such quasi-decadal shifts in RPS are also reported for chub mackerel off southern California and for Japanese sardine.10,11 Fig. 5 Spawning stock biomass and recruitment (age-0) stock numbers from 1970 to 2000 Optimal harvest age The optimal harvest age for this stock was determined age-3 and older, and fishing is reasonable only for spawning season for age-3 (Fig. 6). This is compatible with the first age of 100% of maturation. The dominant ages in the catch of actual fisheries shifted from age-2 in the 1970's and 1980's to age-0 or age-1 in the 1990's (Fig. 1). Thus, the high exploitation rates on the immature fish during the 1990's, was considered growth and recruitment over-fishing.
Fig. 6 Current value, harvest value, reproductive value and optimal harvesting policy 96 Stock rebuilding Occurrences of dominant cohorts or extremely high RPS may indicate another regime shift favoring for chub mackerel recovery. In fact, Watanabe12,13 pointed out that drastic increases of stock abundance were resulted from consecutive occurrences of dominant year classes during 1955-58 and 1969-70. Also, Kawai et a1.3 concluded that if immature fish were conserved in the middle 1990's, especially for the 1992 and 1996 dominant year classes, SSB would have recovered to a level of 0.4 million tons in the late 1990's. The SSB-recruitment relationships indicates no recruitment failures for SSB above 0.45 million tons. Thus, we determined this SSB level as the target of stock rebuilding. We calculated annual allowable biological catch (ABC) and F corresponding to the target year of SSB recovery between 2004 and 2008. The most practical target year was judged 2006 taking the current fisheries conditions into consideration. The bootstrap results indicated that in 48% of scenarios the target SSB was attained in 2006 and that 68% attained in 2008.
CONCLUDSIONS Immature fishes must be preserved in order to rebuild SSB and to prevent growth over-fishing. Determination of annual ABC in Japan is, however, requested by the managers one or two years in advance depending on stocks. It is practically very difficult to predict recruitment numbers even for the next year, since we have neither revealed causes of RPS variability nor established an empirical relation of RPS and biological/non-biological environmental conditions. Thus, the current fishing that targets on immature fish renders more uncertainly for ABC determination. Recent studies on juvenile abundance in the Kuroshio-Oyashio Transition Zone in spring using a midwater trawl gear revealed that the survey-derived abundance had fairly good correlation to VPA-derived age-0 fish abundance for chub mackerel and Japanese sardine which recruited to fishing in autumn. Therefore, ABC for chub mackerel must be revised in a timely manner by using the spring trawl survey results and related information, in order to ensure preservation of immature fishes of dominant year classes.
ACKNOWLEDGMENTS We thank Dr. Kazuhiko Hiramatsu of the National Research Institute of Far Seas Fisheries, Fisheries Research Agency, for his comments on the stock assessment and ABC determination methods. args.summary:
This scientific paper documents the stock status, assessment, and management of the Pacific stock of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) along the Pacific coast of Japan, with a focus on allowable biological catch (ABC) determination.

**Stock Status & History:**
- Stock biomass ranged from approximately 4-6 million tons in the early-to-mid 1970s, declining to about 2 million tons in the 1980s and less than 1 million tons in the 1990s.
- Peak catch was 1.5 million tons in 1978; by 1990 the catch had fallen to less than 25,000 tons.
- Spawning stock biomass (SSB) ranged from 0.45 to 1.60 million tons during 1970-1985, declining to around 0.1 million tons in the late 1990s.
- Dominant year classes appeared in 1992, 1996, and 2000, but intensive fishing on immature fish (age-0 and age-1) prevented stock recovery.

**Methodology:**
- Stock abundance was estimated using virtual population analysis (VPA) tuned with abundance indices from midwater trawl and driftnet surveys, and purse seine fishery data.
- Natural mortality coefficient (M) was assumed at 0.4 per year for all ages.
- Sensitivity analysis showed estimated SSB in 2000 ranged from 90% to 114% of the base case depending on M values (0.3 to 0.5).

**Key Findings:**
- Two major regime shifts in recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS) occurred in the late 1970s and 1980s, likely corresponding to Kuroshio Path meandering or North Pacific regime shifts.
- The 1990s exhibited recruitment overfishing because dominant 1992 and 1996 year classes did not lead to SSB recovery.
- The optimal harvest age was determined to be age-3 and older, matching the first age of 100% maturation. Fishing on immature fish (age-0 to age-1) in the 1990s constituted growth and recruitment overfishing.

**Management Recommendations:**
- A target SSB of 0.45 million tons was established as the rebuilding threshold, since no recruitment failures were observed above this level.
- The most practical target year for SSB recovery was judged to be 2006, taking current fisheries conditions into account.
- Bootstrap simulation showed the target SSB would be attained by 2006 in 48% of scenarios and by 2008 in 68% of scenarios.
- ABC must be revised in a timely manner using spring trawl survey results for juvenile abundance in the Kuroshio-Oyashio Transition Zone, as these surveys correlate well with VPA-derived age-0 abundance.
- Immature fish must be preserved to rebuild SSB and prevent growth overfishing, though predicting recruitment remains difficult due to unexplained RPS variability.

This decline was probably caused from over-fishing and decreased reproductive success corresponding to regime shifts in the late 1970's and 1980's."

# Pacific Mackerel

### *Scomber japonicus*

D.R. Robertson, STRI [14]

* [## The Science](#tab-501)
* [## The Fishery](#tab-439)
* [## The Seafood](#tab-194)

#### THE SCIENCE

> Unlike its Atlantic counterpart, Pacific mackerel has an unmarked belly! [5]

### 

Image

![Pacific mackerel on ice.](/sites/default/files/styles/seafood_profile_1100/public/importedFiles/mackerel_Pacific_JHO22021.jpg?itok=uyqRKDxK)

Pacific mackerel on ice. Jason Houston/California Sea Grant

 

### Taxonomic description

* Has a tapered, large-mouthed fish with dark blue, pointy head. [1]
* Has a dark blue back with wavy dark lines, silvery green undersides. [1]
* Reaches lengths up to 63 cm (25 in) and weight up to 2.7 kg (6 lbs). [1]
* Swim bladder is attached to its esophagus via a pneumatic duct. [2,15]
* Has large eyes relative to other mackerel species. [2]

### Distribution

* Ranges from southeastern Alaska to Mexico. [1]
* Most common south of Point Conception, California. [1]
* Migrates north to Washington in summer, south to Baja California in winter. [1,2]

### Life history

* Can live up to 18 years.
* As a fast grower, it is able to reproduce by 4 years of age.
* Spawns from late April to September off of California, spawning events take place several times a year and yields about 70,000 eggs each time.
* Found in dense schools as a defense mechanism against predators, often with other pelagic species. [2]
* Feeds on plankton, other pelagic fish (e.g. sardine, anchovy) and its own young. [1,2]
* Is eaten by sharks, tunas, marine mammals, and seabirds. [1,2]

### Habitat

* Usually lives within 20 miles offshore in water between 50 and 72 degrees.
* Moves inshore and offshore seasonally off California, and is more abundant inshore from July to November, and offshore March to May. [1]
* Juveniles frequent sandy beaches, kelp beds, open bays, and congregate at piers. [1]

#### THE FISHERY

> Pacific mackerel reached its catching peak in 1978 with 3,412,602 tons!

Image

![fisherman in a boat holds up a pacific mackerel and a fishing pole as another fisherman looks on](/sites/default/files/styles/seafood_profile_1100/public/importedFiles/pacificmackerel_fishery.jpeg?itok=icvJYf1O)

Fisherman in a boat holds up a pacific mackerel. Alex Krohn/iNaturalist

 

### Seasonal availability

* Available year-round, though it is more abundant in summer. [1]

### Regulatory and managing authority

* The Pacific Mackerel fishery is managed federally by the NOAA fisheries and, as established by the Magnuson-Stevens Act, the Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) through the Coastal Pelagic Species Fishery Management Plan (CPSFMP). [1]
* As established by the Marine Life Management Act, the California Fish and Game Commission (CFGC) regulates the fishery in state waters, and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) collects data and helps enforce FMP management rules for this fishery through the Pelagic Fisheries and Ecosystems Program. [6,8]
* The California Wetfish Producers Association combines input from the industry and government entities to inform regulatory and management measures for this fishery. [7]

### Gear type

* Commercial fisheries use round haul gear consisting of purse-seines, lampara nets, drum seines, and dip nets. [2]

### Status of the fishery

* Currently harvested by two fisheries, commercial and sport fishing, both localized in Southern California. [1,3]
* The stock collapsed in 1960s, resulting in moratorium on the fishery in the 1970s. [2]
* The stock recovered in the late 1970s, but demand has not rebounded for canned mackerel so harvest remains low. [2]
* The last mackerel cannery in Southern California closed in 1992 with diminished demand for the product. [2]
* Recent landings fall well under sustainable harvest limits. [1,3]

### Potential ecosystem impacts

* Harvesting with round haul gear takes place in surface waters, minimally impacting the environment. [1]
* The schooling lifestyle of Pacific mackerel means bycatch is low, as individuals are densely grouped together. [1]
* Bycatch primarily consists of other coastal pelagic fish species. [1]

#### THE SEAFOOD

> In the kitchen and market, the fish is in the best condition if the meat is firm and the eyes are clear with the colors bright.

Image

![Grilled mackerel with rice, miso soup, and vegetable side dishes.](/sites/default/files/styles/seafood_profile_1100/public/importedFiles/Okhostk_atka_mackerel%2Chokke-yakizakana-teisyoku%2Csyari-town%2Cjapan.JPG?itok=e7U7cMzV)

Grilled mackerel with rice, miso soup, and vegetable side dishes. Katorisi/Wikipedia

 

![Pacific mackerel nutrition info](/sites/default/files/styles/400px/public/importedFiles/users/crystal.chan/PacificMackerel.png?itok=XKJsR-9o)

### Edible portions

* Pacific mackerel is sold fresh, frozen, or cured; whole or filleted.

### Description of meat

* It has firm, oily, dark meat with a strong flavor, rich in omega-3 fatty acids. [1]
* Mackerel has large bones which are easily removed from the cooked flesh. [4]
* The meat spoils quickly - this fish should be promptly frozen, refrigerated, or cured. [4]

### Culinary uses

* It is best prepared without adding additional oils or fats to the meat, i.e. roasted, baked, or grilled, as the naturally oily meat self-bastes during cooking. [4]
* Mackerel's robust flavor is well-complemented by acidic, spice-heavy, or fruity sauces. [4]
* For a Nigerian Mackerel and Tomato Sauce recipe, visit [Nigerian Lazy Chef](http://www.nigerianlazychef.com/2016/06/mackerel-and-tomato-sauce/). [9]
* For a Filipino recipe for Fish kinilaw, visit [SCMP Cooking](https://www.scmp.com/cooking/recipe/fish-kinilaw/article/3029585). [10]

### Nutritional information

* Nutritional information for 100g of Pacific Mackerel is shown on the table to the right. [1]

### Toxicity report

* No known contaminants. [1]

### Seasonal availability

* Year round. [1]

This webpage is a comprehensive seafood profile for Pacific Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) from the California Sea Grant. It covers three main sections: The Science, The Fishery, and The Seafood.

**The Science:** Pacific mackerel has an unmarked belly (unlike its Atlantic counterpart), a tapered large-mouthed fish with a dark blue, pointy head, dark blue back with wavy dark lines, and silvery green undersides. It reaches lengths up to 63 cm (25 in) and weights up to 2.7 kg (6 lbs), with a swim bladder attached to its esophagus via a pneumatic duct and large eyes relative to other mackerel species. Its range extends from southeastern Alaska to Mexico, most commonly south of Point Conception, California, migrating north to Washington in summer and south to Baja California in winter. It can live up to 18 years, reproduces by age 4, and spawns from late April to September off California (multiple times per year, yielding about 70,000 eggs per event). It lives in dense schools as a defense mechanism, feeds on plankton and other pelagic fish (including its own young), and is preyed upon by sharks, tunas, marine mammals, and seabirds. It typically lives within 20 miles offshore in water between 50-72°F, being more abundant inshore July-November and offshore March-May.

**The Fishery:** Pacific mackerel reached its catching peak in 1978 with 3,412,602 tons. The fishery is managed federally by NOAA fisheries and the Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) through the Coastal Pelagic Species Fishery Management Plan, and in state waters by the California Fish and Game Commission and California Department of Fish and Wildlife. Commercial fisheries use round haul gear (purse-seines, lampara nets, drum seines, and dip nets). The stock collapsed in the 1960s, resulting in a moratorium in the 1970s. It recovered in the late 1970s, but demand for canned mackerel never rebounded; the last mackerel cannery in Southern California closed in 1992. Current landings fall well under sustainable harvest limits, and harvesting is localized in Southern California. Environmental impacts are minimal due to surface-water harvesting and low bycatch (consisting primarily of other coastal pelagic fish species).

**The Seafood:** Pacific mackerel is sold fresh, frozen, or cured; whole or filleted. The meat is firm, oily, and dark with a strong flavor, rich in omega-3 fatty acids, with large bones easily removed after cooking. It spoils quickly and should be promptly frozen, refrigerated, or cured. It is best prepared by roasting, baking, or grilling without added oils (the naturally oily meat self-bastes), and pairs well with acidic, spice-heavy, or fruity sauces. No known contaminants exist, and it is available year-round. The page also links to recipes (Nigerian Mackerel and Tomato Sauce, Filipino Fish kinilaw) and provides nutritional information for 100g portions.

## Abstract

The stock abundance of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Pacific Ocean off Japan declined in the 1980s and remained at low levels through the 1990s. There were recruitment successes in 1992 and 1996. However, the cohorts born in these years were heavily fished before the age of maturity and chub mackerel has not begun to recover. To investigate the effects of conserving immature fish, we created four recovery policies: (i) policy 0, actual fishing mortality during the 1990s; (ii) policy 1, conserve strong year classes; (iii) policy 2, apply the average fishing mortality in the 1970s-1980s after 1992; and (iv) policy 3, a 55% reduction of the mortality adopted by policy 2. Policy 3 was considered to be the best in terms of final stock abundance and total catch from 1992 to 1999. We also calculate the future projection of stock and catch under these three policies as well as using average fishing mortality from 1993 to 1999. Using average fishing mortality from 1993 to 1999, the stock will not be recovered within the next 20 years. Even under the best policy, the risk that the final stock is not recovered to 3 million tons within the next 10 years is 40%.

This bulletin provides an in-depth analysis of the California Current Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) fishery. It includes descriptions of the fishery and the species population biology, a cohort analysis, density and environmental-dependent spawner-recruit models, and yield simulations. The cohort analysis (1928-1968), using an instantaneous natural mortality rate of M = 0.5, shows a fluctuating stock size with a maximum total biomass of 965 million pounds (438,000 MT) in 1933 and a minimum of 3.3 million pounds (1500 MT) in 1968. The number of recruits-per-spawner shows large fluctuations with considerable coherence between adjacent years. There was no marked downward trend in recruits-per-spawner over the 1928-1968 period. Density-dependent spawner-recruit models accounted for a maximum of 24 percent of the observed variation in recruitment. Multiple regression models, including both population and environmental variables, were fitted to the data available for two time periods; 1931-68 and 1946-68. The 1931-68 model accounted for 59 percent of the variation in recruitment; increased recruitment was associated with increased sea surface temperature, reduced sea level and reduced atmospheric pressure during the spawning season. The 1946-68 model accounted for 76 percent of the variation in recruitment; increased recruitment was associated with increased coastal upwelling and decreased offshore convergence during the spawning season. Maximum yield-per-recruit occurs with an age at recruitment of 1 or less, and with instantaneous fishing mortalities (F) in excess of 1.0. A dynamic pool model incorporating a Ricker spawner-recruit model predicts that extinction of the stock will occur with the above fishing strategy. Maximum sustained yield (MSY) with the steady state dynamic pool model is above 94 million pounds (41,000 MT). This MSY occurs with an ageat-recruitment of 4 and with an exploitation rate of 0.25. Simulations incorporating the density and environmental-dependent spawner-recruit functions predict that the above MSY cannot be attained when there is serial coherence in the annual recruitment fluctuations. Mean longterm annual yield with the above fishing strategy, under the environmental conditions occurring between 1931-1968, would have been only 56 million pounds (25,000 MT). With an age-at-recruitment of 1, maximum steady state yield (69 million pounds, 31,000 MT) occurs at an exploitation rate of 0.2. Maximum long-term yield with this fishing strategy, under the 1931-68 environmental conditions, would have been 45 million pounds (20,000 MT).

U.S. law requires that overfished fish populations be rebuilt within 10 years when biologically possible, and otherwise within the time it would take to rebuild in the absence of fishing plus one mean generation time (MGT). Most overfished populations can recover in less than 10 years; the exceptions are populations with very low productivity and some that are severely depleted. A range of harvest control policies, including constant fishing mortalities and variable harvest rate control rules, were compared in terms of their ability to rebuild overfished populations of five species within the required times. The North Atlantic swordfish Xiphias gladius and Gulf of Mexico red snapper Lutjanus campechanus populations were able to rebuild in 10 years, but the white marlin Tetrapturus albidus, sandbar shark Carcharhinus plumbeus, and darkblotched rockfish Sebastes crameri populations were not. The harvest policy that resulted in populations being rebuilt most rapidly was either a control rule that reduced fishing mortality with decreasing biomass or a constant harvest rate designed to meet the current rebuilding time requirement. The control rules we analyzed restricted catches at the beginning of the rebuilding period but allowed catches to increase rapidly as the population was rebuilt. Thus, there was a trade-off between relatively high catches early in the rebuilding period and high catches later in the rebuilding period when the population had been rebuilt and could sustain high catches. Whether the population was rebuilt more rapidly under a fixed rebuilding-time requirement or a control rule depended on the productivity of the population.

North American Journal of Fisheries Management, 2018

Maximum sustainable yield (MSY)-based reference points are often prescribed by national and international laws as the basis for catch limits (e.g., the Magnuson-Stevens Reauthorization Act in the United States). However, MSY is highly dependent on the assumed selectivity pattern and catch allocation of the fisheries. The addition of bycatch fleets or mortality from discarding further complicates MSY calculations, and no prescribed approach has been agreed upon for including complex fleet dynamics in dynamic pool models. Using the Gulf of Mexico Red Snapper Lutjanus campechanus fishery as an example, we demonstrate the various ways that MSY can be computed when multiple fleets and bycatch fisheries exist, and we illustrate the tradeoffs that occur between yield and spawning stock biomass (SSB). Presenting the full array of alternative MSY proxies, however, can lead to subjective decision making that may diminish the value of scientific advice by encouraging the maximization of yield at the expense of maintaining stocks within safe biological limits. We propose that the spawning potential ratio (SPR) associated with the global (theoretical maximum) MSY can be utilized as a reasonable proxy in most fishery applications. The yield streams required to achieve SPR MSY can then be calculated conditional on extant selectivity patterns and bycatch levels. Our approach utilizes the inherently sustainable SSB associated with the global MSY as a rebuilding target while limiting disruption to the fishery by accounting for current fleet dynamics and avoiding unsustainable proxies that may result when bycatch or discard rates are high.

There is considerable international concern and scientific debate about the current state and future of tuna stocks worldwide and the capacity of Regional Fisheries Management Organisations to manage the associated fisheries effectively. In some cases, this concern has extended to predictions of imminent collapse with minimal chances of recovery, even under a commercial catch moratorium. As a viable alternative to a full fishery closure, the Commission for the Conservation of Southern Bluefin Tuna (CCSBT) has adopted a scientifically tested, adaptive rebuilding strategy for the depleted southern bluefin tuna (Thunnus maccoyii) stock. The management procedure (MP) adopted involves a harvest control rule that fully specifies the total allowable catch as a function of key indicators of stock status, adjusting future harvest levels every three years so as to meet the rebuilding targets agreed by CCSBT. It was chosen from a subset of candidate MPs selected following extensive simulation testing. This involved first selecting a wide range of plausible scenarios for stock status and input data, ranging from pessimistic to optimistic, against which the alternative candidate MPs were tested to ensure that they were robust to important uncertainties. This is the first time that a comprehensively evaluated MP has been adopted for an internationally managed tuna stock. Both the process and the outcomes have broad applicability to other internationally managed stocks.

Recently, ecosystem management has become popular for forestry, agriculture and fisheries management. Carrying capacity and maximum sustainable yield for a particular species definitely depend on population sizes of other species in the same ecosystem. Natural stock fluctuations of sardine, anchovy and chub mackerel are well known examples of large, natural fluctuations. There is a negative correlation among their fluctuations. In accordance with the cyclic advantage hypothesis for replacement of pelagic fish species , we can predict the next dominant species, despite an uncertainty in the year of the next replacement. We recommend that commercial fisheries should switch their target to the next dominant species before the stock of the present dominant species collapses. Whilst total allowable catch (TAC) of the present dominant species can be as large as we can consume, TAC after the species collapses should be much smaller than the present catch level.

This webpage is an Academia.edu listing for a scientific paper titled "Recovery policy for chub mackerel stock using recruitment-per-spawning" by Akihiko Yatsu, published in Fisheries Science in 2002 (DOI: 10.1046/J.1444-2906.2002.00520.X). The paper is 9 pages and has been viewed 44 times.

**Paper Abstract/Findings:**
The stock abundance of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Pacific Ocean off Japan declined in the 1980s and remained at low levels through the 1990s. There were recruitment successes in 1992 and 1996, but cohorts born in these years were heavily fished before reaching maturity, preventing recovery. The study investigated four recovery policies: (i) Policy 0 - actual fishing mortality during the 1990s; (ii) Policy 1 - conserve strong year classes; (iii) Policy 2 - apply average fishing mortality from the 1970s-1980s after 1992; and (iv) Policy 3 - a 55% reduction of the mortality adopted by Policy 2. Policy 3 was considered the best in terms of final stock abundance and total catch from 1992 to 1999. The study also calculated future projections under these policies and using average fishing mortality from 1993-1999. Key finding: using average fishing mortality from 1993-1999, the stock will not recover within the next 20 years. Even under the best policy, the risk that the final stock is not recovered to 3 million tons within the next 10 years is 40%.

**Related Research Papers Listed:**
The page lists numerous related papers on fisheries management and stock recovery, including work on: optimal policies for rehabilitating overexploited fish stocks (Grossman, 1987), revised estimates of historical spawning biomass of Pacific mackerel (MacCall), East Atlantic Bluefin Tuna fisheries stock collapse or recovery (Bjørndal, 2006), yield-per-recruit models for sequential fisheries (Chen, 1998), optimal rebuilding of fish stocks in different nations (Sylvia, 2006), phased-in minimum size limits for Pacific Bluefin Tuna (Hoenig, 2018), global fisheries catches after rebuilding (Pedersen), and recent increased abundance of Pacific mackerel (MacCall, 1985).

**Author Information:**
The author, Akihiko Yatsu, has 26 papers and 6 followers on Academia.edu. Related papers by the same author address long-term changes in maturity at age of chub mackerel in relation to population declines in waters off northeastern Japan (2006) and changes in growth with fluctuation of chub mackerel abundance in Pacific waters off central Japan from 1970 to 1997 (2000).

**References:**
The paper cites 17 references, including works on cohort analysis of Pacific mackerel populations (Honma et al., 1987), stock assessment of chub mackerel (Yatsu et al., 2002), spawning stock biomass per recruit methodologies (Goodyear, 1993; Mace & Sissenwine, 1993), stock-recruitment relationships (Shepherd, 1982; Beverton & Holt, 1957), optimal harvesting policies (Matsuda et al., 1992), and ecological studies of Japanese mackerel (Usami, 1968; Wada, 1997).

args.summary:
This webpage presents a stock assessment presentation for the Pacific stock of Jack Mackerel (Trachurus japonicus) in Japan, covering biology, stock assessment methodology, stock-recruitment relationships, reference points, harvest control rules, and future projections. It includes reviewer comments and the assessment team's responses.

**Key Content:**

1. **Stock Structure and Distribution**: The Pacific stock distributes along Pacific coastal waters of the Japanese archipelago, with spawning grounds in the southern East China Sea and Pacific coastal areas of Japan. Reviewers questioned whether the Pacific and Tsushima stocks are truly separate stocks given overlapping spawning grounds in the East China Sea. The assessment team acknowledged uncertainty about juvenile/adult fish movement between Pacific and East China Sea areas due to the Kuroshio Current, and noted the magnitude of recruitment from the East China Sea to the Pacific is unclear.

2. **Catch Calculation**: Total catch is the sum of catch records from prefectures along the Pacific coast (between Aomori and Miyazaki). Catches by fleets in the East China Sea are removed and treated as the Tsushima/West Kyushu (TWC) stock. The stock is assumed not to extend into pelagic Pacific waters, and no non-Japanese fleet catches are included.

3. **Growth and Maturity**: Growth and maturity data presented by fork length, age, body mass, and percentage of maturation. Natural mortality M = 0.5, based on Tanaka 1960 (M = 2.5/Amax). Reviewers questioned whether Tanaka 1960 is the best available method given more recent meta-analyses like Hamel 2015, which would suggest a longer maximum age (~10-11 years) for M=0.5. The team committed to investigating M further using Hamel (2015) as a reference.

4. **Catch at Age (CAA)**: A fixed length-weight relationship (BW = 0.013 × FL³) and a fixed ALK (age-length key) developed by cohort slicing are used for all years. Reviewers raised concerns about: the fixed FL-BW relationship not varying by space/time, cohort slicing assigning a single length to a single age, ALKs not varying between years or fisheries, and the lack of aging data. The team acknowledged these limitations and reported recent progress: spatial and temporal differences in FL-BW and FL-Age relationships have been found, and methods are being improved (Watanabe et al. unpublished data showing differences across 6 areas).

5. **VPA Model**: Tuned VPA used with 6 tuning indices (Miyazaki CPUE, Uwajima CPUE, Sukumo Bay CPUE, Kushimoto catch, Ise Bay catch, Chiba catch) representing age-0 fish biomass, all treated equally and unstandardized. Indices cover about 32% of the total 2019 catch and are scattered across the central and western distribution area. Reviewers questioned the lack of standardization, equal weighting, and lack of indices for ages 1-3. Model diagnostics including residuals, jackknife analysis, and retrospective analysis were presented.

6. **Stock-Recruitment Relationships**: Two SR models compared - Ricker (AICc 27.18, SBmsy 44,000 tons, MSY 34,000 tons, 17% SPR) and Beverton-Holt (AICc 28.98, SBmsy 132,000 tons, MSY 53,000 tons, 34% SPR). Model averaging was used to reflect uncertainty. A cross-correlation lag analysis (Kurota et al. 2020) was conducted to investigate whether SSB influences recruitment. SSB and recruitment from VPA were assumed without error, though the team has started incorporating error into the model.

7. **Reference Points**: SBmsy = 60,000 tons; SBlimit = 15,000 tons; SBban = 1,700 tons. A Kobe plot was presented.

8. **Harvest Control Rule and Future Projections**: A harvest control rule based on SSB relative to reference points was presented. Future projections for catch in 2021 across beta values (0.1-1.0) showed: higher beta values give lower probability of exceeding SBmsy (39-99%), with catches ranging from 2,000 tons (beta=0.1) to 15,000 tons (beta=1.0). The probability of exceeding SBlimit remains 99-100% across all beta values.

9. **Terminal Year Uncertainty**: The review noted that terminal year N-at-age is calculated deterministically without error, and the team acknowledged this limitation.

# Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean

  title={Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean},
  author={Seonggil Go and Joon-ho Lee and Sukgeun Jung},

*   [Seonggil Go](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/Seonggil-Go/1500589561), [Joon-ho Lee](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/Joon-ho-Lee/2315948416), [Sukgeun Jung](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/Sukgeun-Jung/2281624161)
*   Published in [Fishes](https://www.semanticscholar.org/venue?name=Fishes)6 January 2025
*   Environmental Science

Spawning grounds may shift due to climate change and subsequent variations in the marine environment, but few studies have aimed to project shifts in the spawning grounds of chub mackerel driven by climate change. We projected the effects of climate change on the spawning grounds of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) by developing and applying a suitable spawning ground index based on a regional ocean circulation model for the western North Pacific. --- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | A new modeling strategy for the predictive model of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) central fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific Ocean based on machine learning and operational characteristics of the light fishing vessels ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2024.1451104/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (14 October 2024, Volume 11) that presents a new modeling strategy for predicting chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) central fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific Ocean. The study used 70,147 fishing logbook records from Chinese commercial light purse seine fishing vessels (2014-2022, March-December) in the high seas of the northwest Pacific (35°-45°N, 145°-165°E), obtained from the East China Sea and Pelagic Seas Data Service Center Database.

Key methodological elements:
- Six marine environmental variables were used: Sea Surface Temperature (SST), Sea Surface Salinity (SSS), Chlorophyll-a (Chla), Current Velocity (CV), Sea Level Anomaly (SLA), and Dissolved Oxygen (DO), sourced from Copernicus Marine Service at 0.25°×0.25° spatial resolution with daily temporal resolution.
- Data were divided into three datasets: Dataset A (no moonlight days: lunar days 1-10 and 20-30), Dataset B (bright moonlight days: lunar days 11-19), and Dataset C (all days).
- Two modeling approaches were compared: Approach One (based on light fishing vessel operational characteristics, modeling datasets A and B separately) and Approach Two (no distinction between moonlight conditions, modeling dataset C as a whole).
- Two machine learning models were compared: Random Forest (RF) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), with tuning via grid search and 5-fold cross-validation, using 80%:20% training:test split.
- Central fishing grounds were defined as those with daily catches at or above the daily median (label 1), others labeled 0.

Key results:
1) Stronger moonlight intensity (especially full moon) limits fishing efficiency. Most years showed a higher percentage of fishing days on bright moonlight days than catch percentages, with bright moonlight days accounting for 26.95%-34.24% of catches and 28.9%-32.87% of fishing days. No-moonlight days yielded higher catches with fewer fishing days.
2) Under Approach One, the LightGBM model achieved the best prediction results on all three datasets. The optimal prediction performance on the complete dataset C improved from 65.02% (RF model, Approach Two) to 66.52% (LightGBM model, Approach One).
3) Variable importance was highly similar between datasets A and C, suggesting that Approach Two (not accounting for operational characteristics) could misguide fisheries during bright moonlight days.
4) Under the optimal model (LightGBM, Approach One), the most important environmental variables were CV, SLA, and SSS for dataset A, and CV, DO, and SLA for dataset B. Chla was the least important variable, and SST had weaker influence. Year and lunar phase were most important temporal variables; longitude was more important than latitude spatially. Environmental variables were overall more important than spatiotemporal variables.

The study compared favorably with prior work by Han et al. (2023) that used 3DCNN models at coarser scales (monthly, 1°×1°), noting that fine spatial-temporal scales (0.25°, daily) used here are closer to fishery production needs but still affected by data bias from factors like fishermen decision-making and vessel production capacity differences. The authors recommend future research combining spatiotemporal models like 3DCNN, ConvLSTM, and vision Transformer with the current approaches, while expanding spatial-temporal scales to balance prediction performance and production needs. The study concludes that considering light fishing vessel operational characteristics (lunar phase effects) is critical for improving model selection and prediction accuracy, and contributes to more accurate guidance for fishermen on operating area and time for the Scomber japonicus fishery, supporting balanced ecological and economic fisheries development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) is one of the most influential small pelagic fish in the Northwest Pacific Ocean, and accurate modeling approaches and model selection are critical points in predicting the Scomber japonicus fishing grounds."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: CATCH-ONLY STOCK ASSESSMENT OF ... ---
URL: https://www.pcouncil.org/documents/2025/05/catch-only-stock-assessment-of-pacific-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-for-u-s-management-in-the-2025-26-and-2026-27-fishing-years.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a NOAA Technical Memorandum (NMFS-SWFSC-718) published in March 2025 presenting a catch-only stock assessment of Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) for U.S. management in the 2025-26 and 2026-27 fishing years. Authors include Alexander J. Jensen, Caitlin Allen Akselrud, Peter T. Kuriyama, and Kevin T. Hill (NOAA Southwest Fisheries Science Center) and Juan P. Zwolinski (UC Santa Cruz, affiliated with NOAA SWFSC).

The assessment follows the Pacific Fishery Management Council's (PFMC) schedule of benchmark assessments every 4 years (2015, 2019, 2023) and catch-only projection assessments every 4 years (2017, 2021, and now 2025). It uses the same model structure as the 2023 benchmark assessment (Stock Synthesis v3.30.22.1) with updated catch values for model years 2008-2022, new catch values for 2023 and 2024, and forecasted landings for 2025 and 2026 based on average landings from 2021-2023.

Key findings include: The estimated stock biomass (age 1+) is 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26 and 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for fishing year 2026-27. Stock biomass generally declined between 2008 and 2022, with relatively high recruitment in model years 2011, 2016, and 2018. Estimates for 2023-onwards are informed primarily by the stock-recruitment relationship and are highly uncertain.

Harvest guidelines are 9,143 mt for 2025-26 and 10,448 mt for 2026-27, with the stock projected to remain above the 18,200 mt management threshold. The OFL is 12,965 mt (2025-26) and 14,270 mt (2026-27). The SSC-selected tier 2 sigma (σ = 2.0) was adopted by the Council at their April 2025 meeting, using the tier 3 default because tier 2 values exceeded it.

Exploitation rates ranged from roughly 1-27% annually from model years 2008-2023, with U.S. fisheries harvesting between 7 and 39% of the harvest guideline. The 2024-25 annual catch limit was 10,073 mt, and U.S. landings have remained below annual catch limits.

Sensitivity analyses all resulted in lower forecasted biomass than the base model, with the scenario fixing recruitment to average 2019-2021 values producing the largest reduction (age-1+ biomass = 56,390 mt by 2026-27). A model issue was identified where age-0 fish incorrectly contributed to spawning stock biomass during forecast years; this was flagged as a Stock Synthesis issue and structural modifications (e.g., two-season model) may be considered in future assessments.

Uncertainties include the lack of AT survey data for 2020 and 2022 (no survey conducted in 2020; 2022 survey data not recommended for use), inherent uncertainty in stock distribution between U.S. and Mexican waters (with 70% assumed U.S. distribution), and oceanographic variability affecting recruitment success. Research needs include exploring natural mortality estimates for similar CPS and improving spatial variability characterization of stock structure and distribution, including prioritized survey data collection in Mexican waters.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The stock biomass was estimated to be 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26 and 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for fishing year 2026-27."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Spatio-Temporal Distribution and Population Dynamics of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the High Seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-2615/15/8/1135

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Animals* (Volume 15, Issue 8, Article 1135, DOI: 10.3390/ani15081135) on April 15, 2025, authored by Guoqing Zhao, Heng Zhang, and Fenghua Tang from the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, Shanghai. The study examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO).

**Study Design**: Analyzing data from 38,123 commercial light purse seine fishing operations (2016–2021) and 4,440 biological samples. The fishing ground covered 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E. Methods included length-weight relationships, Von Bertalanffy growth equations (using ELEFAN I in FISAT II), mortality estimations via catch curves and Pauly's equations, and the Length-Based Bayesian (LBB) stock assessment model using the TropFishR package in R.

**Key Results**:
1. Fishing activities concentrated along the outer edge of Japan and Russia's exclusive economic zones; the fishing ground gravity center moved northwestward over time.
2. CPUE decreased year by year (negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01), with high values from 2016–2018 and low values from 2019–2021.
3. Sex ratios varied from 1.09–2.55 (female-to-male); fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020); mean lengths ranged from 212.07 to 268.28 mm.
4. Growth parameters: asymptotic length (Linf) varied from 36–42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged from 0.31–0.65; total mortality (Z) ranged from 1.01–1.64; natural mortality (M) from 0.59–0.85; fishing mortality (F) from 0.23–0.79.
5. LBB assessment showed no overfishing during 2016–2021: F/M ratios were all below 0.5, exploitation rates (E) ranged from 0.17–0.32 (all below 0.5), B/B0 values exceeded 0.5, and B/Bmsy exceeded 1, indicating a healthy population at a high resource level.
6. Body length structure was reasonable with no miniaturization; large individuals remained present (L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt close to 1).

**Conclusions**: The chub mackerel population in the high seas of the NPO was healthy during 2016–2021, with fishing pressure not being the primary cause of catch declines. However, the increasing exploitation rate (reaching 0.48 in 2021) may soon approach critical thresholds. Climate warming is emphasized as a major factor driving the northward shift of fishing grounds and affecting population dynamics. The study also discusses competition with Japanese sardine (Sardinops melanostictus), changes in spawning grounds, and the value of the LBB method for data-poor fisheries. The research was funded by the National Key Research and Development Programme (2019YFD0901405) and the Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Polar Science Base Open Subject Fund (SOO2024-15).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"From 2016 to 2021, high catches of chub mackerel were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan or Russia's exclusive economic zone line, and the gravity center of the fishing grounds moved to the northwest gradually, with a decrease in the average value of catch per unit effort (CPUE) year by year."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Analysis of Relative Abundance Distribution and Environmental Differences for Blue Mackerel (Scomber australasicus) and Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) on the High Seas of the North Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12523857

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Animals (Basel) on September 27, 2025 (DOI: 10.3390/ani15192822), examining the relative abundance distribution and environmental differences between Blue Mackerel (Scomber australasicus) and Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean.

**Study Context and Problem:** These two economically important fish species look highly similar, leading to aggregated catch reporting in fishery logbooks that prevents accurate per-species stock assessments. Both species are priority stocks under the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC).

**Methods:**
- Integrated fishery logbook data from Chinese purse seine fleets (2014–2023) with field sampling data for species identification
- Introduced a Zero-One Inflated Beta Model (ZOIBM) built in a Bayesian framework (brms package in R) to quantify the proportional composition of the two co-occurring species in mixed catches—the first application of this model in marine fishery research
- Used a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to analyze environmental drivers of niche differentiation
- Seven candidate environmental variables were considered (SST, VO, UO, Chla, SSH, SSS, MLD); SSH was excluded due to high correlation with SSS (r=0.72), leaving six final variables
- ZOIBM used 4 MCMC chains × 4000 iterations, with adapt_delta=0.99 and max_treedepth=15, validated via 5-fold cross-validation
- Annual centroids were calculated to track distributional shifts

**Key Results:**
- ZOIBM performed excellently: R² = 0.63, RMSE = 0.305, MAE = 0.298; all Gelman-Rubin R-hat values (0.9996–1.0047) confirmed convergence; posterior predictive checks confirmed model adequacy
- Blue Mackerel high-abundance areas concentrated at 35–44°N, 145–160°E, with proportions decreasing at higher latitudes (below 10% north of 45°N)
- Chub Mackerel showed an opposite latitudinal pattern, with high-abundance areas spanning 35–47.5°N (a wider latitudinal range)
- Environmental driver analysis: SST was the most critical differentiating factor—Chub Mackerel showed a unimodal response peaking at 17–19°C (narrow optimal temperature, higher warm-water sensitivity), while Blue Mackerel increased monotonically with SST, tolerating temperatures up to ~23°C
- Chla and VO further amplified differences in resource utilization strategies
- Both species showed similar unimodal salinity responses (Chub peak ~33.9‰, Blue peak ~34.0‰); UO plays a weak role in niche differentiation; MLD positively correlated with both species
- From 2014–2023, both species shifted northward and eastward: Blue Mackerel centroid moved from 40.61°N to 43.46°N (0.3062°/year, R²=0.820) and from 150.82°E to 157.10°E (0.5736°/year); Chub Mackerel moved from 41.27°N to 43.72°N (0.2708°/year) and 151.45°E to 157.00°E (0.5125°/year)
- Spatial overlap between the two species has been continuously increasing as their distributions converge

**Hotels:** La Vista Tokyo Bay (from ¥20,000, closest to market) and Hotel JAL City Tokyo Toyosu (from ¥25,000) — recommended for tuna auction visitors.

**Toyosu vs. Tsukiji:** Tsukiji's outer market still exists and is worth visiting — it offers more food/shopping options. Walking between them takes ~30 minutes (3km over three bridges); by train ~15 minutes via Yurikamome to Toyosu then Yurakuchō Line to Shintomichō (750m walk). Taxi ~¥1,500.

**History:** The move cost over 600 billion yen (~$5.42 billion USD), including soil decontamination because the site was previously a gas production plant. Over 80% of Tsukiji fish traders originally opposed the move due to contamination concerns, though extensive cleanup appears to have addressed the issue. Tsukiji's old wholesale facilities (opened 1935) were outdated and raised food safety concerns.

**FAQs:** Recommended visit time is 2 hours; best time for auction is ~5 a.m. (by 6:30 a.m. at latest); market activity mostly finishes by 9 a.m.; most restaurants close by 1–2 p.m.; no boats land at Toyosu (99% of domestic catch arrives by truck from other Japanese ports).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: 豊洲市場の魚の価格はどう決まるのか？　マグロとサンマはまったく別…消費者が知らない裏側に迫る：時事ドットコム ---
URL: https://www.jiji.com/jc/v8?id=20220410toyosunews

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from Jiji Press (時事通信) published on April 15, 2022, explaining how fish prices are determined at the Toyosu Market in Tokyo, Japan's largest fish market. The article was written by Okayama Toshinori of Jiji Press's Fisheries Department.

**Three types of trading methods:**
1. **Auction (競り)** - The buyer offering the highest price wins. Used for tuna, sea urchin, and other premium items. Tuna auctions use finger signals ("teyari") as bids, taking only seconds per fish.
2. **Bidding (入札)** - Buyers submit written bids without knowing others' prices, a "one-shot gamble." Used for dried sardines and boiled-dried fish.
3. **Relative/negotiated trading (相対取引)** - Direct negotiations between sellers and buyers. Despite the market's auction image, nearly 90% of fish (by monetary value) at Toyosu are traded this way. Used for common fish like mackerel, sardines, saury, plus imported salmon and frozen shrimp/crab.

**Key price records:**
- January 2019: First New Year tuna auction at Toyosu after relocating from Tsukiji set a historic record - a bluefin tuna from Oma, Aomori Prefecture sold for ¥333.6 million (¥1.2 million/kg), the highest price ever.
- July 2020: First saury of the season sold for ¥125,000 per fish (¥100,000/kg), a record high during a period of poor catches. This unusually high price was partly motivated by a desire to liven up the market during COVID-19 restrictions.

**Price factors:**
- Supply (landing volume), origin, size, and quality determine prices.
- Poor catches have driven up prices for saury, squid (2-3x higher than a decade ago), and salmon roe (ikura). Meanwhile, abundant sardine harvests have prices below ¥50 per fish.
- Fishing methods matter: single-line fishing ("ippon-zuri") fetches premium prices (e.g., Oita's "Seki-aji" and Kanagawa's "Matsura saba" sell for 5x+ more than standard fish) due to better condition and freshness. Wild bluefin tuna caught by single-line or longline fishing is prized by sushi chefs, with large 100kg+ fish exceeding ¥10,000/kg (3x+ more than farmed tuna).
- Celebrity influence: Kei Nishikori's comment about wanting "nodoguro" (blackthroat sea perch) after his US Open performance boosted its popularity and price.
- Historical note: Fatty tuna (otoro), once discarded in the Edo period due to spoilage, became a luxury item with refrigeration and logistics advances.

**Market history:** During the Tsukiji era, almost all fish traded via auction. But "advance purchasing" (negotiating before auction times to secure supply) increased, causing auctions to become formalities for common fish. Law reforms led most fish to shift to relative trading. The article notes a decline in market-through distribution as direct producer-retailer trades increase, but Toyosu still serves as a national benchmark price-setting market.

**Consumer trends:** Ministry of Agriculture statistics show 40%+ of consumers cite "family prefers meat" and "fish is too expensive" as reasons for not buying fish more often - both ahead of "preparing fish is troublesome."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"取引手法は、最高値を提示した買い手が入手できる「競り」と「入札」、売り手と買い手が個別に交渉する「相対取引」の３種類。市場といえば競りのイメージが強いが、同市場では意外にも大半の魚が相対取引で、金額ベースで「全体の９割近く」（豊洲の卸会社）とされる。"
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://lib.suisan-shinkou.or.jp/column/ryutsu-korekara/vol06.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article is the 6th installment in a column series titled "The Future of Seafood Distribution" (水産物流通のこれから), written by Urawa Eisuke, Executive Director of the Tokyo Seafood Wholesalers Association, published in March 2025 in the Suisan Shinko (Fisheries Promotion) online magazine.

**Toyosu Market vs. Global Markets:**
- Toyosu Market's seafood handling volume (quantity and value) surpasses major global markets including Paris' Rungis Market, Spain's Mercamadrid, and London's Billingsgate Fish Market (using 2022 data).
- Rungis is three times the size of Toyosu by area (1.2 million m² vs. 400,000 m²) but is primarily an agricultural/livestock market with only one small seafood building.

**Toyosu Market within Japan:**
- Combining all categories (seafood and produce), Ota Market leads in quantity (~1 million tons) but Toyosu leads in value (~450 billion yen) nationwide.
- Only Toyosu, Ota, and Osaka Main Market are large; most other markets fall below 50 billion yen / 200,000 tons.
- Total central wholesale market seafood handling fell from ~4.3 million tons (1988) to ~1.3 million tons (2020+), mirroring Japan's national catch decline from ~12 million tons (1988 peak) to ~4 million tons.
- Toyosu (Tsukiji) seafood volume declined from ~800,000 tons (1988) to ~330,000 tons recently, but Toyosu's share of the national market increased from under 20% to 26%, showing increasing concentration.

**Category-wise Volume Trends (Toyosu, 2000 vs. 2023):**
- Total volume halved: 638,000 tons → 295,000 tons.
- Tuna (大物): halved from 70,000 to 33,000 tons.
- Specialty items (特種): nearly halved from 76,000 to 40,000 tons (shellfish decline notable due to coastal development).
- Fresh fish (鮮魚): -30% (136,000 → 95,000 tons), holding steady until ~2018 but recent declines driven by reduced catches of saury and squid.
- Salted/dried processed (塩干) and frozen products (冷凍): dropped to 34% and 39% of 2000 levels (-60%+), as supply chain vertical integration and cold chain limitations at Tsukiji drove these trades off-market. Toyosu's improved cold chain infrastructure offers potential for future recovery.

**Value Trends (Toyosu, 2000 vs. 2023):**
- Total value declined only 23% (535.2 billion → 411.3 billion yen) despite volume halving; prices recovered strongly from 2022 due to post-COVID economic reopening, inflation, and global seafood demand.
- Fresh fish and specialty items maintained ~100% and 98% of 2000 value levels; tuna value at 65% despite 50% volume reduction, reflecting higher unit prices.
- Overall pattern: declining volume with rising unit prices; seafood consumption decline is a concern.

**Household Expenditure Analysis (Statistics Bureau "Family Income and Expenditure Survey"):**
- Total household consumption expenditure (2+ person households): ~310,000 yen/month in 1990 and 2000, dropped below 300,000 in 2010, fell to 278,000 in 2020 (COVID), recovered to ~290,000 in 2022-2023.
- Increasing expenditure categories: Food, Housing, Fuel/Light/Water, Medical Care (aging population), Transportation/Communication (smartphone costs).
- Decreasing categories: Clothing/Footwear (fast fashion replacing high-end purchases), Education, and Culture/Recreation (declining birth rate).
- Engel's coefficient rose from 25.4% (1990) to 27.8% (2023), primarily due to declining real income; Japan's coefficient is comparable to China's (28.2%) and much higher than the US, Germany, or UK.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: Report Name:Korea Seafood Market Update 2025 ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) Voluntary Report (Report Number: KS2025-0046) providing a comprehensive overview of the Korean seafood market in 2024, prepared by the Agricultural Trade Office in Seoul, Republic of Korea, dated November 25, 2025.

**Key Market Overview:**
- The Republic of Korea's (ROK) total seafood imports reached $5.52 billion in 2024, a 6.9% decrease from 2023.
- Imports from the United States totaled $182 million, down 10.1% year-over-year. The U.S. ranked as Korea's sixth-largest seafood supplier with a 3.3% market share.
- Korean consumers continue to associate U.S. fishery products with high quality, but elevated prices of preferred U.S. species and slowed foodservice demand during the economic downturn caused overall imports to fall.

**Production:**
- Korean seafood production fell to 3.61 million metric tons in 2024, a 2% decline from 2023. Shallow sea aquaculture (including seaweed) accounted for the largest share (2,249,000 MT), followed by adjacent waters (841,000 MT), distant waters (479,000 MT), and inland waters (41,000 MT).
- Aquaculture contributed over 62% of total seafood output in 2024, up from 47% in 2014. Major aquaculture products included sea mustard (572,000 MT), laver (552,000 MT), oyster (310,000 MT), flounder (40,000 MT), and abalone (23,000 MT).
- Seaweed production overtook fish production by weight in 2016 due to growth in exports and consumption of dried seaweed products driven by K-Wave and K-Food expansion.
- Global warming is shifting fish distribution northward and altering traditional fishing grounds, constraining production growth.
- Korean seafood processors produced 1.1 million MT of processed seafood in 2024, down 8.7% from the prior year, though production value increased 5.8%, indicating rising prices.

**Consumption:**
- Korean annual per capita seafood consumption (fish and shellfish) fell from 42.0 kg in 2019 to an estimated 34.8 kg in 2024; total (including seaweed) was 60.0 kg in 2024, still well above the world average of ~20 kg.
- Consumption declined across all age groups except those 60 and older between 2020 and 2023.
- Meat consumption surpassed seafood annual per capita volume for the first time in 2022. Meat CAGR (2017–2023) was 2.1%, while seafood was -1.4%.
- Consumer purchasing is shifting toward convenience: raw seafood purchases are declining while processed seafood and home meal replacement (HMR) products grow.
- Korea's self-sufficiency rate for fish and shellfish was 57% in 2023, making it a net importer.

**Trade:**
- Korea's largest seafood exports are seaweed. Korea imported $3.7 billion more in seafood than it exported in 2024.
- Major seafood suppliers to Korea in 2024: China ($1,367M, +5.5%), Russia ($898M, -18%), Vietnam ($811M), Norway ($552M), Japan ($185M), United States ($182M), Peru ($165M), Thailand ($142M), Canada ($113M), and Chile ($108M).
- Top U.S. seafood exports to Korea in 2024 by value: Alaska pollack surimi ($45.3M, 65.5% market share), other fish frozen, fillet of plaice (70.9% market share), frozen Atka mackerel, other Pacific salmon, other flatfish, roes/milt, cod, fish offals, and fillet of other fish. These ten products accounted for 60% of U.S. seafood imports.
- Vietnam and China currently rank as top suppliers of surimi to Korea, ahead of Alaskan sources.

**Tariffs and Regulations:**
- U.S. seafood benefits from duty elimination under the KORUS FTA since 2012; prior tariffs ranged from 5–20%.
- Korea imposes adjustment tariffs of 22–50% on seven fish species not covered by WTO-bound rates. Frozen Alaska pollack (HS 0303670000, 0303699000) is the only U.S. export affected.
- Under KORUS FTA, the first 12,263 MT of U.S. Alaska pollack enters duty-free (2025 TRQ), with 6% tariff above that threshold. TRQs are being phased out: flatfish became unlimited in 2023, croaker became unlimited, and Alaska pollack will be unrestricted in 2026.

**Marketing and Distribution:**
- Seafood enters through major ports (Busan, Incheon, Yeosu) with customs clearance and quarantine by MOF and Korea Customs Service.
- Distribution channels include wholesale markets (Noryangjin in Seoul, regional Agriculture and Fishery Wholesale Markets), hypermarkets (E-Mart, Lotte Mart, Homeplus), online marketplaces (Coupang, Market Kurly), and traditional wet markets.
- Thirty species represented 92% of seafood imports from the United States in 2024.
- Two major seafood trade shows: Korea Seafood Show (formerly Seoul International Seafood Show, at COEX Seoul; 2026 show May 19–21) and Busan International Seafood & Fisheries Expo (BIFSE, held annually in early November).
- Korean importers prioritize price competitiveness, product quality, and logistical efficiency. U.S. seafood's higher cost relative to regional alternatives limits market penetration.
- FAS/Seoul forecasts Korean seafood imports to remain stable in 2025, holding opportunities for U.S. seafood exporters.

The report includes extensive appendices with detailed trade statistics tables covering imports by country, top 30 U.S. fish products by value and volume, and detailed tariff schedules for fishery products under the KORUS FTA.

URL: https://www.sprfmo.int/assets/Meetings/02-SC/12th-SC-2024/Habitat-Monitoring/SC12-HM02-PER-SPRFMO-Abundance-of-Jack-and-chub-mackerel-Peru-2022-2024.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a scientific report presented to the 12th Meeting of the Scientific Committee of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organization (SPRFMO), held in Lima, Peru (30 September – 5 October 2024). The report, authored by Mariano Gutiérrez (IHMA), Salvador Peraltilla (SNP), Cristian Vasquez (TASA), Naldi Herrera and Carlos Valdez (IMARPE), assesses the abundance of Jack mackerel (Trachurus murphyi) and Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Peruvian Current in the Humboldt System between 2020 and 2024. Notably, Peru reiterates that SPRFMO decisions do not apply within Peruvian jurisdictional waters and provides this data voluntarily.

Key findings on Jack mackerel:
- Two biomass regimes observed between 1983 and 2024: medium-high levels from 1983-2002, and medium-low levels after 2002, with a recent positive trend toward medium abundance.
- Acoustic abundance estimates for summer 2024 range from 22 to 458 thousand tons (using various stratification methods) in areas prospected by fishing vessels.
- Geostatistical analysis of 1,539 fishing sets (January 2023–February 2024) showed average catch of 77.68 tons/set, with 118,604 tons caught; sets distributed between 20 and 200+ nautical miles offshore, latitudes 11°30'S to 21°00'S.
- Highest geostatistical abundance was 1.2 million tons in July 2023; highest inertia (distribution area indicator) was 17,120 mn².
- Vertical distribution during 2024 ranged from surface to 94m depth (average 14.06m).
- 629 schools detected; average size 31 cm, range 21-54 cm.

Key findings on Chub mackerel:
- Three biomass regimes observed (1983-1992 uniform medium abundance; 1992-2002 medium-high; after 2002 medium-low), with recent positive trend.
- Acoustic abundance estimated at 55-60 thousand tons for the fourth fortnight analyzed (January 2024 only).
- Geostatistical analysis of 1,067 hauls (January 2023–January 2024) showed average catch of 47.58 tons/set, with 67,289 tons caught; sets distributed between 10 and 200+ miles offshore, latitudes 5°00'S to 21°00'S.
- Highest geostatistical abundance was 1 million tons in December 2023; highest inertia was 4,346 mn² in September 2020.

Methodology: Two estimation methods used—(1) acoustic surveys using 120 kHz Simrad ES70 echo sounders on 13 fishing vessels (25,546 nautical miles surveyed, with stratification into 15x15 nm statistical squares), and (2) geostatistical analysis of fishing set data by 8 geographical areas and fortnights. Data were collected from January 2020 to March 2024. The report notes uncertainties from random (non-systematic) fishing trips, and that estimates apply only to fleet-operated areas.

Mesopelagic species (primarily lantern fish/Vinciguerria lucetia): Abundance estimates ranged from 7,000 to 5.8 million tons, but reliable assessments are not possible due to lack of length data/biological sampling; an average size of 6 cm was assumed. A large biomass of mesopelagic fishes exists in the surveyed area.

The report concludes that both Jack and Chub mackerel show positive biomass trends in recent years, with better catches in years of higher biomass, and emphasizes that unreliable mesopelagic estimates stem from insufficient biological sampling. The report was produced following the Eleventh SNP Workshop (June 2024) on habitat conditions of these species in the Humboldt System.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Development of characterization factors for Peruvian fish stocks within the fisheries impact pathway framework ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment (Volume 31, article 69, 2026) as open access, presents the development of characterization factors (CFs) for 10 Peruvian fishing stocks within the Fisheries Impact Pathway (FIP) framework for Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The authors (Rubén Manrique-Muñante, Alejandro Deville, Ramzy Kahhat, and Ian Vázquez-Rowe, all from the same institution) address the gap that biodiversity impacts of Peruvian fisheries—strongly influenced by El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)—are not fully covered by current LCIA models.

Key methodological aspects include: (1) optimization of CMSY++ stock assessment model performance using exhaustive statistical analysis (including retrospective, hindcasting, biological plausibility, and jittering analyses); (2) calculation of CF time series (2007–2023) under an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) approach for anchoveta, jack mackerel, chub mackerel, bonito, hake, common dolphinfish, skipjack tuna, jumbo squid and calico scallop; (3) statistical evaluation of enhanced CFs including uncertainty, sensitivity analyses, and correlation with ENSO indices; and (4) application of CFs in case studies for direct and indirect human consumption fisheries.

Key findings:
- Enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values, usually showing lower values
- CFs exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with typical ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship
- Case studies in the Peruvian EEZ confirmed significant differences in fishing impacts for stocks destined to direct human consumption during El Niño and La Niña years, with additional LCIA impacts ranging from 0.1% to 61% in fishmeal and fish oil production among plants of a major producer during 2019 and 2021

Background context: Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally, with Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens) being the largest fishery worldwide by volume. Approximately 95% of landed anchoveta goes to fishmeal and fish oil (FMFO) production, supplying 15–20% of global FMFO. Other species (jack mackerel, bonito, chub mackerel, hake, jumbo squid, calico scallop) contribute to about 20% of annual landings and generated 2600 million US$ in export revenue in 2023. The historical context includes the fishery collapse in 1972 driven by ENSO and overfishing, after which quota systems (individual quotas for industrial fleet since 2009, artisanal fleet TAC since 2017) have helped maintain stock health.

The authors argue that the enhanced CF time series more accurately represents stock population dynamics under fluctuating climatic stressors and management regimes than the original FIP method, responding to international LCA guidelines calling for regionalized and temporally explicit impact assessment. The study recommends using these CFs for assessing biotic resource depletion in Peruvian seafood and aquaculture systems, and extending the methodology to other EEZs affected by similar ecosystem dynamics and fishing pressure.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values, usually showing lower values. These CFs also exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with typical ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship."
