--- SOURCE 7: A summary report of life history information on Pacific ... ---
URL: https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/52097/noaa_52097_DS1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NOAA Technical Memorandum (NMFS-SWFSC-689, August 2023) provides a detailed summary of life history information collected and analyzed for Pacific mackerel (Scomber japonicus) used in the 2023 benchmark stock assessment. The report was authored by researchers from NOAA Fisheries' Southwest Fisheries Science Center (SWFSC), Lynker Technologies, UC Santa Cruz's Cooperative Institute for Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Systems (CIMEAS), and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

**Purpose and Data Sources:** The report aims to: (1) provide updated age and length data; (2) compute ageing error matrices for the stock assessment model; (3) provide updated estimates of length and age at maturity; and (4) discuss future life history research priorities. Biological samples were collected from spring 2010-2021 and summer 2012-2022 SWFSC trawl surveys (otoliths and ovaries) and from monthly CDFW Port Sampling Program fishery samples from 2008-2022 (otoliths only). Ages were assigned using a July 1 birthdate convention, and ovaries were histologically processed for maturity classification.

**Key Results—Age and Length Data:**
- SWFSC survey fish (2012-2022, n=1,762 aged) ranged from 53-402 mm FL and ages 0-7 years. Age composition was dominated by young fish: age 0 (46%), 1 (29%), 2 (16%), 3 (6%), with ages 4-7 comprising only 2.3% of samples.
- CDFW port sampling (2008-2022, n=9,035 aged) ranged from 84-429 mm FL and ages 0-9 years, with ages 0-3 representing 47%, 30%, 12%, and 7% respectively; ages 4-9 comprised only 4%.
- All-read samples from 2008-2017 (n=1,614 otoliths) showed high agreement for ages 0-1 (94% and 78%), moderate for ages 2-3 (52% and 41%), and low for ages 4-6 (22-30%). Survey data (n=643) showed 100% agreement for ages 0-2, 94% at age 3, 75% at age 4, and 70% at age 5.
- Model C (unbiased readers with equal SDs) was selected via AICc for both datasets. Survey SDs-at-age ranged from 0.001-0.319; fishery CVs-at-age were below 32% across all age classes.
- Age validation: Annual periodicity of annuli was confirmed for fish up to ~2 years old via captive growth experiments (consistent with Shiraishi et al. 2008 from Japan), but no full age validation exists for the eastern North Pacific.

**Key Results—Maturity:**
- A total of 911 female gonad samples (174-402 mm FL, ages 0-7) were histologically examined using standardized terminology (Brown-Peterson et al. 2011). Age data were available for 494 females.
- Length at maturity (L50) was estimated at 274 ± 1.26 mm FL, with all females (L95) at 309 ± 2.60 mm FL predicted mature.
- Age at maturity (A50) was 1.01 ± 0.06 years, with all females older than 2.52 ± 0.15 years predicted mature. The L50 is nearly identical to previous estimates, but A50 is lower than the previous estimate of 2.2 years, attributed to improved ageing precision and greater availability of small age classes in surveys. Results indicate maturity schedules have remained constant over recent decades.

**Future Research Priorities:** (1) Collect data from Mexican waters (where a significant proportion of commercial catch occurs) through collaboration or surveys to cover the full population range; (2) improve age estimation by coordinating between ageing labs, standardizing age reads, refining age-reading error quantification, and developing a fecundity-weight relationship.

**Context:** Pacific mackerel is one of five coastal pelagic species under the PFMC's CPS Fishery Management Plan. The 2023 benchmark assessment estimated total biomass of 93,823 metric tons for 2021 (86.9% from ages 0-2), with projected spawning stock biomass of 46,167 mt (2023) and 50,372 mt (2024). The species is managed as a single unit by the PFMC under a quota system, with the fishery reopening in 1977 after a moratorium following a mid-1960s population decline.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Development of characterization factors for Peruvian fish ... ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment (Volume 31, article 69, 2026) as open access, presents the development of characterization factors (CFs) for 10 Peruvian fishing stocks within the Fisheries Impact Pathway (FIP) framework for Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). The authors (Rubén Manrique-Muñante, Alejandro Deville, Ramzy Kahhat, and Ian Vázquez-Rowe, all from the same institution) address the gap that biodiversity impacts of Peruvian fisheries—strongly influenced by El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)—are not fully covered by current LCIA models.

Key methodological aspects include: (1) optimization of CMSY++ stock assessment model performance using exhaustive statistical analysis (including retrospective, hindcasting, biological plausibility, and jittering analyses); (2) calculation of CF time series (2007–2023) under an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) approach for anchoveta, jack mackerel, chub mackerel, bonito, hake, common dolphinfish, skipjack tuna, jumbo squid and calico scallop; (3) statistical evaluation of enhanced CFs including uncertainty, sensitivity analyses, and correlation with ENSO indices; and (4) application of CFs in case studies for direct and indirect human consumption fisheries.

Key findings:
- Enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values, usually showing lower values
- CFs exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with typical ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship
- Case studies in the Peruvian EEZ confirmed significant differences in fishing impacts for stocks destined to direct human consumption during El Niño and La Niña years, with additional LCIA impacts ranging from 0.1% to 61% in fishmeal and fish oil production among plants of a major producer during 2019 and 2021

Background context: Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally, with Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens) being the largest fishery worldwide by volume. Approximately 95% of landed anchoveta goes to fishmeal and fish oil (FMFO) production, supplying 15–20% of global FMFO. Other species (jack mackerel, bonito, chub mackerel, hake, jumbo squid, calico scallop) contribute to about 20% of annual landings and generated 2600 million US$ in export revenue in 2023. The historical context includes the fishery collapse in 1972 driven by ENSO and overfishing, after which quota systems (individual quotas for industrial fleet since 2009, artisanal fleet TAC since 2017) have helped maintain stock health.

The authors argue that the enhanced CF time series more accurately represents stock population dynamics under fluctuating climatic stressors and management regimes than the original FIP method, responding to international LCA guidelines calling for regionalized and temporally explicit impact assessment. The study recommends using these CFs for assessing biotic resource depletion in Peruvian seafood and aquaculture systems, and extending the methodology to other EEZs affected by similar ecosystem dynamics and fishing pressure.
</summary>

**Purpose and Context:** The chub mackerel has been managed under Korea's Total Allowable Catch (TAC) system since 1999, but prior stock assessments have yielded conflicting results regarding whether the stock has recovered or remains overfished, complicating management decisions. Crucially, the BSS model incorporated a 2% annual technical creep correction to CPUE data—a factor frequently overlooked in previous research. The analysis used 55 years of catch data (1970–2024) from Korea, China, and Japan (Tsushima Current stock), plus 27 years of CPUE data (1997–2023) from Korea. - BSS estimated: r=0.310, k=1,802,382 tons, MSY=139,902 tons, B2024=549,884 tons.
- Kobe plot analysis revealed sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s has impeded recovery, with 87.6% (CMSY++) and 95.3% (BSS) posterior probability of the stock remaining in the "overfished and overfishing" red quadrant.

**Conclusions:** The study demonstrates CMSY++ as an effective tool for reconciling discrepancies in data-limited stock assessments and underscores the necessity of correcting for technical creep. Landing data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market shows an increasing proportion of small-sized (≤250g, ~29.7cm TL, below the L50 of 31.4cm) immature individuals in the catch (from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024), providing biological evidence of stock depletion. This is an open-access peer-reviewed review article published in Fisheries Science (Springer/journal 12562) on April 3, 2019, by Akihiko Yatsu (Volume 85, pages 611-639). The article reviews the population dynamics and management of small pelagic fishes (SPF) around the Japanese Archipelago, focusing on four target species: Japanese sardine (Sardinops melanostictus), Japanese anchovy (Engraulis japonicus), chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus), and Pacific saury (Cololabis saira). Key findings:

--- SOURCE 1: The Spatio-Temporal Distribution and Population Dynamics of Chub ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12024016

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Animals (an open-access MDPI journal) in April 2025, examines the spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (NPO). Authors: Guoqing Zhao, Heng Zhang, and Fenghua Tang (corresponding author: f-h-tang@163.com).

**Study Methodology:**
- Study area: High seas of the NPO between 35°N–45°N and 145°E–160°E
- Data: 38,123 fishing operations from Chinese commercial light purse seine vessel logs (2016–2021), plus 4,440 biological samples
- Methods: Length-weight relationships, Von Bertalanffy growth equations (ELEFAN I in FISAT II), mortality estimation (Pauly's equations), and Length-based Bayesian (LBB) stock assessment using the TropFishR package in R

**Key Findings:**
1. **Spatio-temporal distribution**: High catches were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan and Russia's EEZ lines. The gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward from 2016-2021, with a northeast-southwest-northeast pattern. CPUE decreased year by year, with large values dominating 2016-2018 and small values dominating 2019-2021. Strong negative correlation existed between CPUE and year (r = -0.489, p < 0.01).

2. **Biological characteristics**: Sex ratios (female:male) ranged from 1.09 to 2.55 across years (all >1). Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020). Mean lengths varied from 212.07 mm (2016) to 268.28 mm (2018). Growth parameters: asymptotic length (L inf) ranged 36-42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged 0.31-0.65.

3. **Stock assessment (LBB results)**: No overfishing occurred during 2016-2021. F/M ratios were all <0.5, E (exploitation rate) values ranged 0.17-0.32 (all below 0.5), B/B0 were all >0.5, B/Bmsy were all >1, L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt were close to 1, and Lc/Lopt were >1. All years were classified as "healthy" stock status with reasonable body length structure and presence of large individuals.

4. **Concerns**: Although not currently overexploited, the exploitation ratio (E) showed an increasing trend, reaching 0.48 by 2021 (from conventional methods), suggesting it may soon reach critical thresholds. The study emphasizes that climate warming, marine heatwaves (frequent in NPO since 2014), and increased competition with Japanese sardine are important factors affecting chub mackerel population dynamics.

**Explanations for CPUE decline despite healthy stock**: (1) Reasonable resource fluctuation not reaching critical population thresholds; (2) spawning grounds in south-central Pacific coast of Japan may have changed, reducing recruitment via Kuroshio Current transport; (3) increasing food competition with Japanese sardine, which also serves as a food source for adult chub mackerel; (4) interactions among proliferating fishing vessels' fish-attracting light systems.

**Conclusions**: (1) Fishing ground gravity center moved northward with year-by-year CPUE decline; (2) Chub mackerel grew well with no miniaturization and reasonable length structure; (3) Fishing mortality was low, no overfishing occurred; (4) E value increase warrants attention from international management organizations. Managers should consider climate warming impacts on marine ecosystem population composition.

Funding: National Key Research and Development Programme (2019YFD0901405) and Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Polar Science Base Open Subject Fund (SOO2024-15).
</summary>

"From 2016 to 2021, high catches of chub mackerel were concentrated along the outer edge of Japan or Russia's exclusive economic zone line, and the gravity center of the fishing grounds moved to the northwest gradually, with a decrease in the average value of catch per unit effort (CPUE) year by year."
</key_excerpts>

1. **Species identification:** Of 305 Scomber spp. specimens (2017-2019), S. japonicus larvae were dominant (273 vs. 32 S. australasicus). 3. **Feeding habits:** Both morphological and DNA metabarcoding analyses showed copepods (particularly Calanidae, Paracalanidae, Oithonidae, Oncaeidae) and appendicularians (Oikopleuridae) were the primary prey. Appendicularians were more prominent in metabarcoding analysis (%N: 24.9-32.5%, %F: 42.3-54.8%) than morphological analysis (%N: 1.7%), likely due to the difficulty of detecting fragmented appendicularian houses microscopically. Larger larvae (≥6.0 mm) fed on appendicularians more actively (45.4% for %N). 5. **Environmental conditions:** Water temperature and salinity were significantly higher in the Osumi Strait (due to Kuroshio Current influence), while chlorophyll a concentrations were consistently higher in Kagoshima Bay (due to winter-spring upwellings), which may create favorable feeding conditions for S. japonicus larvae.

**Conclusions:** The study strongly supports the northern Satsunan area as a major spawning and nursery ground for the Pacific stock of S. japonicus during high-stock periods. The area provides favorable conditions for sustaining high larval population densities, and findings provide important insights for fisheries management of S. japonicus in the Japanese Pacific coastal area.

## Pacific Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Stock Assessment for USA Management in the 2015-16 Fishing Year

### Document Overview
This is a comprehensive stock assessment report by P.R. Crone and K.T. Hill from the NOAA Fisheries Southwest Fisheries Science Center, submitted to the Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) in May 2015. The assessment provides management advice for Pacific mackerel for the 2015-16 and 2016-17 fishing years (July-June seasons).

### Stock Status
- Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California, with majority distributed from Monterey Bay, California to Cabo San Lucas, Baja California Sur. Three spawning aggregations are hypothesized (Gulf of California, Cabo San Lucas, and Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos extending to southern California/Pacific Northwest).
- The assessment uses a Stock Synthesis (SS) age-structured model, specifically "Model H3," which closely resembles the previously accepted model XA from 2011.
- Model H3 uses data from 1983-2014 including: catch time series, age compositions from the commercial California fishery, and CPFV (commercial passenger fishing vessel) index of abundance with length compositions.
- Key estimated parameters: virgin recruitment (R0) ≈ 0.54 billion age-0 fish; virgin female SSB ≈ 78,425 mt; steepness (h) = 0.48; recruitment variance (σR) = 0.75; natural mortality and growth based on von Bertalanffy equation (W-L parameters a = 2.7E-06, b = 3.4).

### Population Trends
- SSB has continually declined since the mid-1980s, remaining consistently low over the last decade, with some recent increase.
- High recruitment periods last occurred mid-1980s and mid-1990s (1-2.7 billion fish); very low recruitment from mid-1990s to 2012, with somewhat higher levels recently (highly uncertain).
- Since the late 1990s, abundance has remained at historically low levels (<150,000 mt).
- Model H3 estimates: 2014 stock biomass = 97,395 mt; 2015 = 120,435 mt; 2016 = 118,968 mt. Forecasted SSB for 2016 = 47,178 mt.
- Recent fishing mortality (F) generally <0.2 over the last decade; exploitation rates ranged from <5% to 20% in recent years.

### Harvest Control Rules
The FMP harvest rule is: **Harvest = (Biomass - Cutoff) × EMSY × Distribution**, where:
- Cutoff = 18,200 mt (lowest biomass above which harvest allowed)
- EMSY = 30% (fraction of biomass above cutoff harvestable)
- Distribution = 70% (assumed proportion of stock in USA waters)

**2015-16 Management Year:** Biomass = 120,435 mt; OFL = 25,291 mt; HG = 21,469 mt
**2016-17 Management Year:** Biomass = 118,968 mt; OFL = 24,983 mt; HG = 21,161 mt

ABC calculations provided using P-star buffers (0.45 to 0.05) for both Tier 1 and Tier 2.

### Management History
- 1970: State of California imposed moratorium after stock decline in mid-1960s.
- 1977: Fishery reopened under quota system.
- 1985: Regulations imposed moratorium when biomass <18,200 mt; fishing year set July 1-June 30.
- 2000: Federal FMP for coastal pelagic species implemented.
- HGs: ~15,000 mt average (2001-06); 40,000 mt (2007-08); reduced to 10,000 mt (2009-2010-11); ~31,000 mt (2011-13); ~39,000 mt (2013-14); ~29,000 mt (2014-15).
- Fishery has not fully utilized HGs recently, with average landings ~5,000 mt over the last decade.

### Methodology and Data
- Catch data from commercial (USA and Mexico) and recreational fisheries (1983-2014) combined into a single fishery.

# Cleaned Research Findings: Interannual Variations in Body Weight and Length Measurements of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Across Pacific Populations

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

**Search queries executed via Tavily Search:**
1. Chub mackerel Scomber japonicus interannual variations body weight fork length Pacific stock Japan stock assessment
2. Tsushima Warm Current stock chub mackerel length weight trends 2010 2020
3. Chub mackerel Pacific stock Japan strong year class 2013 mean length at age
4. Scomber japonicus California Current stock size composition trends
5. Chub mackerel Pacific stock Japan stock assessment 2023 2024 mean body weight length at age decline
6. Scomber japonicus strong 2013 year class Pacific stock effects mean length at age density dependent growth
7. Chub mackerel Peru Humboldt current Scomber japonicus length weight trends 2010 2020
8. Chub mackerel East China Sea stock body size decline sardine competition 2010s
9. Pacific stock chub mackerel Japan body weight decline 2014 2020 strong year class density dependence Kamimura Yukami Nakayama
10. Scomber japonicus Peru IMARPE length at age condition factor 2015 2023 Humboldt current
11. Chub mackerel Tsushima stock body weight mean fork length trend 2010 2024 Japan assessment
12. Japanese chub mackerel Pacific stock stock assessment 2023 2024 biomass recruitment age composition
13. Pacific stock chub mackerel mean body weight decline 2014 2019 "weight at age" Japan purse seine port sampling
14. NPFC chub mackerel stock assessment 2024 total biomass recruitment strong year class 2013 2017
15. Watanabe Yatsu 2004 density dependence length at age chub mackerel Pacific stock 1970s 1990s

**Internal reflection notes recorded** at each stage of the search process (not separately cited).

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Species Background and Global Stock Overview

**Basic biology (FishBase):** *Scomber japonicus* (Houttuyn, 1782) belongs to Scombriformes/Scombridae. It is distributed in the Indo-Pacific, is anti-tropical, and is absent from the Indian Ocean except for South Africa (KZN to Western Cape). Reports from the Atlantic including the Mediterranean are actually *Scomber colias*, and reports from the Red Sea and northern Indian Ocean are *Scomber australasicus*. It is a marine, pelagic-neritic, oceanodromous species with a depth range of 0-300 m (usually 50-200 m), preferring subtropical waters of 10°C–27°C, spanning latitudes 60°N to 48°S. Dorsal spines: 9-11; Dorsal soft rays: 11-12; Anal spines: 1; Anal soft rays: 12-14; Vertebrae: 31. Lm at first maturity is 26.1 cm; max length 64.0 cm TL; common length 30.0 cm FL; max published weight 2.9 kg; max reported age 18 years. This coastal pelagic species schools by size starting at approximately 3 cm and may form schools with *Sarda chiliensis*, *Trachurus symmetricus*, and *Sardinops sagax*. Adults stay near the bottom during the day and rise to open water at night to feed on copepods, other crustaceans, fishes, and squids. They spawn in batches at 15°–20°C, with 250-300 eggs per gram of fish, totaling 100,000-400,000 eggs per female. IUCN status: Least Concern (LC), assessed 01 June 2022. Generation time: 3.6 years; Resilience: Medium; Bayesian length-weight: a=0.00741, b=3.05. Main reference: Collette and Nauen, 1983, FAO Species Catalogue. Vol. 2. Scombrids of the world. [14]

**FAO synopsis (Castro Hernández, 2000):** The chub mackerel is a very important species in commercial and artisanal fisheries throughout the world, with catches reaching over 1.5 million tons annually. Chub mackerel can reach lengths of 50 cm, but the most common size is around 30 cm. Females typically reach sexual maturity at lengths between 22 and 34.5 cm, with fecundity ranging from 101,859 to 1,859,173 eggs. Population structures exhibit significant regional variations, influenced by environmental factors and fishing pressures. The 80-page synopsis contains 503 references covering regions including Chile, South Africa, Japan, the Mediterranean, California, Argentina, Canary Islands, Morocco, and the East China Sea. [13]

**Northwest Pacific management context (FishSource):** Pacific chub mackerel is a transboundary and straddling species identified as a priority by the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC 2019). Japan conducts separate annual assessments for the Pacific coast and Tsushima Current fisheries. Management entities include the Japan Fisheries Agency (MAFF), Korea Fisheries Resources Agency (FIRA), and the North Pacific Fisheries Commission; the assessment entity is the Fisheries Research Agency of Japan (FRAJ). Landings: 538.0 thousand tonnes. While some genetic studies suggest variation between regional fish populations, the most recent comprehensive study (Cheng et al. 2018) found a high degree of genetic homogeneity. [5]

---

### 2. Japanese Tsushima Warm Current Stock

**2019 Stock Assessment (National Research Institute of Fisheries Science and Saikai National Fisheries Research Institute):**
- **Distribution:** Southern East China Sea to northern Japan Sea, Yellow Sea, and Bo Hai.
- **Growth (length at age):** 25-28 cm FL at age 1, 29-32 cm at age 2, 33-35 cm at age 3, 36 cm at age 4, 37 cm at age 5; longevity ~6 years.
- **Spawning:** Main grounds in East China Sea off Chinese coast, Korean Peninsula coastal waters, and Kyusyu/Sanin coastal waters of Japan; season Jan-Apr in south, May-Jun in north.
- **Maturity:** 60% at age 1, 85% at age 2, 100% at age 3+.
- **Natural mortality (M):** 0.4 per year.
- **Biomass history:** Around 1 million tons during 1973-1996, peaked at 1,370,000 tons (1996), decreased to ~500,000 tons after 2000, fell to 370,000 tons (2013, lowest), then recovered to 654,000 tons (2018).
- **SSB history:** Peaked at 470,000 tons (1993-1996), dropped to 120,000 tons (2003), fluctuated 110,000-190,000 until 2014, increased to 240,000 tons (2018). SSB in 2018 estimated at ~238,000-240,000 tons.
- **Recruitment:** Peak 3,300 million (1995), dropped to 800 million (2013), strong year classes 1,500 million (2014) and 2,000 million (2017), 1,329 million (2018).
- **Reference points:** SBmsy = 310,000 tons; MSY = 323,000 tons; SB2018/SBmsy = 0.77 (below SBmsy); F2018/Fmsy = 1.24 (above Fmsy); %SPR(Fmsy) = 20%. Fishing ratio (U) rapidly increased 1996, stayed high at 40-50%, was 45% in 2018. %SPR was lowest in 1996 (8.31%), 16.7% in 2018, and 15.6% for F2016-2018.
- **Catches:** Japanese catch 2018: 150,000 tons (0- and 1-year-old fish dominate); Korean catch 2018: 140,000 tons (age composition unknown); Chinese catch up to 500,000 tons since 2010 (species composition unknown, NOT included in analysis). Total catch 2018 (Japan + Korea): 292,000 tons. Mainly caught by purse seine fisheries in East China Sea, Korean coastal waters, northwest Kyusyu, and western Japan Sea.
- **Stock-recruitment relationship:** Hockey Stick (HS) model, no autocorrelation (parameters: a=0.00755, b=237,192 tons).
- **Management:** Effort control (licensed purse seine vessels) and TAC for "mackerels" (including blue mackerel) since 1997; stock rebuilding plan for western Japan Sea/western Kyusyu (2009-2011) focused on protecting juveniles. Major uncertainty from lack of Chinese catch data; satellite night vision monitoring of Chinese fishing vessels started 2014. [7]

---

### 3. Japanese Pacific Stock

**Historical dynamics (Kawabata et al., presented at J-STAGE):**
- Stock biomass ranged from approximately 4-6 million tons in the early-to-mid 1970s, declining to about 2 million tons in the 1980s and less than 1 million tons in the 1990s.
- Peak catch was 1.5 million tons in 1978; by 1990 the catch had fallen to less than 25,000 tons.
- SSB ranged from 0.45 to 1.60 million tons during 1970-1985, declining to around 0.1 million tons in the late 1990s.
- Dominant year classes appeared in 1992, 1996, and 2000, but intensive fishing on immature fish (age-0 and age-1) prevented stock recovery. The 1990s exhibited recruitment overfishing because dominant 1992 and 1996 year classes did not lead to SSB recovery.
- Two major regime shifts in recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS) occurred in the late 1970s and 1980s, likely corresponding to Kuroshio Path meandering or North Pacific regime shifts.
- The optimal harvest age was determined to be age-3 and older, matching the first age of 100% maturation. A target SSB of 0.45 million tons was established as the rebuilding threshold. [41]

**Recovery and the strong 2013 year class:**
- The Pacific stock declined in the 1990s–early 2000s but dramatically increased after a strong 2013 year class. [23][29]
- The Pacific stock population of S. japonicus grew from 153,000 tons in 2001 to 6,808,000 tons in 2019 (per larval survey context in the northern Satsunan area, southern Japan). [17]
- Review by Yatsu (2019): Overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, but both have been recovering since the mid-2000s due to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing stemmed from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity following the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF shifted from sardine to anchovy. [27]
- Larval densities increased dramatically from 2016 (10.8 individuals per 1,000 m³) to 2018 (724.0 in Kagoshima Bay, 343.2 in Osumi Strait), corresponding with the increasing Pacific stock population. A significant negative relationship was found between larval density and chlorophyll a concentration. [17]

**Recent quota reduction related to stock decline:** New regulations effective 2025 have reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). [1]

**Northern Satsunan area spawning/nursery ground study (2015-2019):** Of 305 Scomber spp. specimens (2017-2019), S. japonicus larvae were dominant (273 vs. 32 S. australasicus), comprising 96.8% of larvae in Kagoshima Bay and 87.7% in the Osumi Strait. Instantaneous growth rate (G) was 0.072 in 2018 and 0.078 in 2019; daily specific growth rate (K) was 7.5% BL d⁻¹ in 2018 and 8.1% BL d⁻¹ in 2019. Copepods (Calanidae, Paracalanidae, Oithonidae, Oncaeidae) and appendicularians (Oikopleuridae) were the primary prey. [17]

**Larval/juvenile growth and recruitment (Kamimura et al. 2015, Fisheries Science 81(3):505-513, DOI 10.1007/s12562-015-0869-4):** This study examined larval and juvenile growth of chub mackerel in relation to recruitment in the western North Pacific. [22]

**Larval/juvenile recent growth (Taga et al. 2019, Fisheries Science 85(6):931-942, DOI 10.1007/s12562-019-01354-8):** Along the Boso–Kashimanada Pacific coast (March-July 2015 and 2016), temperature positively affected recent growth rate (RGR) of larvae in body length classes <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and 9-11mm. Prey density affected growth in the <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and >11mm classes, with effects being stronger for larger (>11mm) larvae and juveniles. S. japonicus larvae transform into juveniles at around 12mm BL. Otolith increment widths of collected larvae/juveniles were significantly narrower than those of 1-year-old S. japonicus from purse seine fisheries in the Joban or Kashimanada areas, suggesting growth-dependent mortality. [21]

**Long-term maturity changes (Watanabe & Yatsu 2006, Fisheries Research 78(2-3):323-332, DOI 10.1016/J.FISHRES.2006.01.001):** For the Pacific stock (heavily exploited, abundance declining since the 1970s), the researchers analyzed fork length, body weight, and gonad weight of 21,048 individuals (ages 1-4) collected during 1970-1998. A clear trend was found for the proportion of mature females at given ages to increase, and the length and age at 50% maturity to decrease. Changes in maturity were mainly explained by changes in length at a given age (density-dependent growth acceleration). Sea surface temperature (SST) of the spawning ground also affected maturation of young (1-year-old) females. A model incorporating length-at-age, spawning-season biomass, and SST well described changes in mature female proportions over 29 years. The population's total biomass peaked in 1978 and declined rapidly until 1990 due to poor recruitment from 1978-1981 and 1987-1991, plus extensive exploitation. Chub mackerel spawn from April to June around the Izu Islands near central Japan, migrating northeast after spawning to feeding grounds at the Kuroshio-Oyashio transition area and Oyashio Current. [11][12]

**Effects of density-dependence and SST on length-at-age (Watanabe & Yatsu 2004):** Published in the NOAA Fisheries journal (Fishery Bulletin) as "Effects of density-dependence and sea surface temperature on interannual variation in length-at-age of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Kuroshio-Oyashio area during 1970-1997" - this foundational study examined environmental (SST) and biological (density-dependence) factors influencing the body length-at-age of chub mackerel. [42]

---

### 4. Korean Stock / Tsushima-influenced Waters

**2026 assessment by Kwak, Kim & Lee (Frontiers in Marine Science, Vol 13, May 14, 2026):**
- The chub mackerel has been managed under Korea's TAC system since 1999, with prior assessments yielding conflicting results on recovery status.
- Analysis used 55 years of catch data (1970-2024) from Korea, China, and Japan (Tsushima Current stock), plus 27 years of CPUE data (1997-2023) from Korea.
- **In 2024:** B/BMSY estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), classifying the stock as "Overfished." CMSY++ estimated r=0.255, k=2,273,005 tons, MSY=145,462 tons, B2024=779,191 tons. BSS estimated r=0.310, k=1,802,382 tons, MSY=139,902 tons, B2024=549,884 tons.
- Kobe plot: 87.6% (CMSY++) and 95.3% (BSS) posterior probability of the stock remaining in the "overfished and overfishing" red quadrant, due to sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s.
- **Korean catch:** Peaked at 415,003 tons in 1996, reached a historical low of 77,603 tons in 2020, and was 124,928 tons in 2024. Large purse seine fishery accounts for 82.2% of domestic catch (average 91,349 tons, 2020-2024).
- **Body size evidence of depletion:** Landing data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market shows an increasing proportion of small-sized (≤250g, ~29.7cm TL, below the L50 of 31.4cm) immature individuals in the catch — **from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024** — providing biological evidence of stock depletion.
- Fishing effort effectively increased despite fleet reduction: vessels decreased from 342 (1992) to 106 (2024), but GT/vessel rose from 131 to 188 and EHP/vessel from 827 to 1,471.
- Recommendation: more stringent TAC reductions, extended closed seasons, vessel buybacks, and upward revision of minimum legal size limits. [1][2]

**Hong, Kim & Kim 2022 (Sustainability, DOI 10.3390/su15010358):** Stock assessment of chub mackerel in the Northwest Pacific Ocean based on catch and resilience data. Current chub mackerel biomass level is lower than the biomass required to achieve MSY based on median values. Prior studies using CMSY and Bayesian state-space (BSS) models classified Korean chub mackerel as "Grossly overfished" or "Overfished." [30]

---

### 5. Northwest Pacific High Seas (NPFC Area) and Chinese Fisheries

**Zhao, Zhang & Tang 2025 (Animals 15(8):1135, DOI 10.3390/ani15081135; PMC12024016):** Examined spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (35°N–45°N, 145°E–160°E) using 38,123 fishing operations from Chinese light purse seine vessels (2016-2021) and 4,440 biological samples.
- **Biological characteristics:** Sex ratios (female:male) ranged 1.09-2.55 across years (all >1). **Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020). Mean lengths varied from 212.07 mm (2016) to 268.28 mm (2018).** Growth parameters: asymptotic length (Linf) ranged 36-42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged 0.31-0.65.
- **CPUE:** Decreased year by year (strong negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01), with large values dominating 2016-2018 and small values dominating 2019-2021. The gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward, driven largely by climate warming and marine heatwaves since 2014.
- **Stock status (LBB):** Healthy during 2016-2021; F/M values all <0.5, E (exploitation ratio) ranged 0.17-0.32; B/B0 exceeded 0.5; B/Bmsy exceeded 1. L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt close to 1; Lc/Lopt >1. Body length structure was reasonable with no miniaturization and large individuals still present. Total mortality (Z) ranged 1.01 (2016) to 1.64 (2021), natural mortality (M) 0.59-0.85, fishing mortality (F) 0.23-0.79, with natural mortality dominant. However, E showed an increasing year-by-year trend, reaching 0.48 in 2021 by conventional methods.
- **Explanations for CPUE decline despite healthy stock:** (1) reasonable resource fluctuation; (2) spawning grounds in south-central Pacific coast of Japan may have changed, reducing recruitment via Kuroshio Current transport; (3) increasing food competition with Japanese sardine; (4) interactions among proliferating fishing vessels' fish-attracting light systems. [4][6]

**Huang, Zhang, Gao & Li 2026 (Fishes 11(5):276):** Integrated LBB (using 6,061 specimens sampled from light purse seine fisheries, 38°00′N–46°00′N, 147°00′E–162°00′E, April–December 2019–2024) and Catch-MSY (1995-2024 catch data) models.
- **Significant interannual variability in stock status:** Stock within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, but suffered overfishing in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Pooled two-year analysis: B/BMSY dropped to 0.51 during 2023-2024, reflecting marked stock deterioration.
- Catch-MSY: MSY = 278,000 t (95% CI: 162,000-475,000 t); r peaked at 0.2; K peaked at 5,406,100 t.
- Kobe plot: only 23.2% probability of healthy stock state in the final assessment year; probabilities of recruitment-overfished, fishing-overfished, and severely overfished were 37.6%, 14.9%, and 24.3%. Final-year diagnosed as recruitment overfishing.
- Fishing mortality exceeded natural mortality in recent years (F/M > 1.5), making fishing pressure the primary driver.
- Management recommendation: TAC at 60-80% of the baseline TAC (352,100 t) during the medium term (5-10 years), i.e., 211,300-281,700 t.
- Notes that new regulations effective 2025 reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). Contrasts with earlier research (Zhao, 2016-2021 data) suggesting good condition, indicating recent transition to overfished status. [1]

**Cai et al. 2023 (Fishes 8(2):80):** Multi-model stock assessment (CMSY, BSM, SPiCT, JABBA, JABBA-Select) using NPFC catch and CPUE data (1995-2020; CPUE 2010-2020). Purse seine fleets (about 72% of landings) from China, Japan, and Russia provided CPUE.
- Results mixed: CMSY (B2020/BMSY=0.98, F2020/FMSY=1.12), BSM (B2020/BMSY=0.97, F2020/FMSY=1.21), JABBA-Select (SB2020/SBMSY=0.99, H2020/HMSY=0.99) indicated slightly overfished; SPiCT (B2020/BMSY=2.30) and JABBA (B2020/BMSY=1.40) indicated healthy.
- MSY estimates ranged 0.40-0.66 million tons; r from 0.38-0.56. 2020 catch in NPFC area ≈ 460,238 tons (34% of global production). JABBA showed 88.3% probability of healthy status in 2020. [39]

**NPFC 2024 assessments:** (a) "Stock assessment based on age-structured assessment program (ASAP) for chub mackerel in the North Pacific Ocean 2024" — used the latest aggregated dataset and agreed scenarios with the Age-Structured Assessment Program. (b) "Base case stock assessment for chub mackerel in Northwest Pacific Ocean 2024" — used a state-space age-structured assessment model (SAM), presenting model selection, parameter estimates, and diagnostics for two base case scenarios (with different settings of M). Estimated total biomass and spawning [stock biomass reported in the documents]. [35][36]

**Tong et al. 2022 (Frontiers in Marine Science 9:856483):** Target strength study — 18 samples (body length 12.98-22.17 cm, mean 16.08±3.15 cm) from 147°E–165°E, 33°N–44°N collected June-August 2021. Notes chub mackerel global catch was 1.56 million tons in 2018 with biomass declining since 1997. Average TS ranged -48.55 to -49.75 dB at 38-200 kHz. [24]

### 6. East China Sea and Yellow Sea Stock

**Wang et al. 2014 (Journal of Fisheries of China 38(1):56-64, DOI 10.3724/SP.J.1231.2014.48737):** Analyzed chub mackerel catch data from the large lighting-purse seine fishery (1999-2011) using GLM and GAM. "Year" was the foremost factor contributing 53.9% of total deviance reduction. **Chub mackerel abundance showed a declining trend over the 13-year period, especially after 2008, with the abundance index (AI) falling from 1.22 in 2008 to 0.82 in 2011.** AI showed a significantly positive relationship with SST of the spawning ground (AI = -3.5 + 0.23SST, P < 0.05). Decline attributed to the rapidly increasing number of purse seine vessels. [26]

**Cai et al. 2022 (JMSE 10(2):301, DOI 10.3390/jmse10020301) — Growth heterogeneity study (Zhejiang coastal area and high seas near Japan, 2016-2020):**
- 2,686 specimens: fork lengths 40-294 mm (average 181.91 mm), body weights 0.8-311.8 g (average 73.27 g). Dominant fork length group 210-220 mm; dominant weight group 20-30 g.
- **Length-weight relationship: W = (1.41 × 10⁻⁶) × FL³·³⁷.**
- Linear mixed-effects modeling showed year-to-year variation was the largest source of growth heterogeneity: differences in parameter "a" were larger for years (7.66 × 10⁻⁷) than regions (5.57 × 10⁻⁷) or seasons (3.20 × 10⁻⁷). Growth heterogeneity most pronounced for specimens >200 mm FL.
- **Relative condition factors varied among years, seasons, and regions. Only K relative to 2006-16 and 2016 reference periods had mean values higher than 1. The lowest relative condition factor was observed in 2017.** Summer had the highest seasonal condition factors.
- **Fork length was significantly greater in 2020 than other years.** Median fork length in the high seas near Japan (220 mm) was much higher than in the Zhejiang coastal area (150 mm).
- Ages from otoliths ranged 0-5 years (13 age-0, 54 age-1, 60 age-2, 40 age-3, 7 age-4, 1 age-5); von Bertalanffy growth model provided the best fit. Individual chub mackerel exhibited a slower growth rate than observed in previous studies. [8][3]

### 7. California Current / Eastern Pacific (U.S.-Mexico) Stock

**Life history report for the 2023 benchmark (NOAA-TM-NMFS-SWFSC-689, August 2023):**
- SWFSC survey fish (2012-2022, n=1,762 aged): 53-402 mm FL, ages 0-7; age composition dominated by young fish: age 0 (46%), 1 (29%), 2 (16%), 3 (6%), ages 4-7 only 2.3%.
- CDFW port sampling (2008-2022, n=9,035 aged): 84-429 mm FL, ages 0-9; ages 0-3 representing 47%, 30%, 12%, and 7% respectively; ages 4-9 only 4%.
- **Length at maturity L50 = 274 ± 1.26 mm FL; L95 = 309 ± 2.60 mm FL. Age at maturity A50 = 1.01 ± 0.06 years; all females older than 2.52 ± 0.15 years mature.** L50 nearly identical to previous estimates, but A50 lower than the previous estimate of 2.2 years. Maturity schedules have remained constant over recent decades.
- Ageing agreement high for ages 0-1 (94% and 78%), moderate for ages 2-3 (52% and 41%), low for ages 4-6 (22-30%).
- 2023 benchmark assessment: total biomass 93,823 mt for 2021 (86.9% from ages 0-2); projected SSB 46,167 mt (2023) and 50,372 mt (2024). [15][4]

**2023 benchmark assessment (Kuriyama et al., June 2023):**
- Landings 2008-2022 from Mexico (Ensenada and Magdalena Bay) and U.S.; total landings ranged from a low of 3,656 mt in 2009 to a high of 32,060 mt in 2020. Mexico landings reached 31,368 mt in 2020; U.S. total landings peaked at 11,909 mt in 2013.
- **SSB projected: 43,864 mt in 2022, 46,167 mt in 2023, 50,372 mt in 2024.** Stock biomass (age-1+) for PFMC management: 49,977 mt in 2021, projected 46,682 mt in 2022. Initial SSB estimated at 136,664 mt; virgin recruitment 917,938 thousand fish. U.S. exploitation rate peaked at 27% in 2020.
- Harvest control rule: Harvest = (Biomass − Cutoff) × E_MSY × Distribution, with Cutoff = 18,200 mt, E_MSY = 30%, Distribution = 70%. U.S. fishery has not fully utilized HGs since the late 1990s (e.g., 990 mt USA landings in 2022 vs. 4,822 mt HG). [34][37]

**2019 benchmark assessment (Crone, Hill, Zwolinski, Kinney, May 2019):**
- Landings (2008-18): total average annual landings (commercial and recreational, U.S. and Mexico) 9,018.6 mt per year; recreational fishery ~3%; Mexico landings averaged 4,435.3 mt; California commercial 3,900.6 mt; Oregon 363.6 mt; Washington 151.0 mt.
- **SSB declined from 26,676 mt in 2008 to 5,822 mt in 2016, then increased to 7,512 mt in 2018, projected at 11,071 mt (2019) and 13,394 mt (2020).**
- **Stock biomass (age 1+) generally declined from 63,535 mt (2008) to 25,943 mt (2018), with projections of 71,099 mt (July 2019) and 56,058 mt (July 2020).**
- High recruitment success in 2011, 2016, and 2018. Instantaneous F ranged ~0.1-0.9 during 2008-18; annual exploitation rates ~5% to 25%. Age 0-2 fish typically comprise roughly 80% of total population biomass. [18][9]

**2015 assessment (Crone & Hill, May 2015, Model H3):**
- SSB continually declined since the mid-1980s, low over the last decade with some recent increase. High recruitment periods last occurred mid-1980s and mid-1990s (1-2.7 billion fish); very low recruitment from mid-1990s to 2012.
- Model H3: 2014 stock biomass = 97,395 mt; 2015 = 120,435 mt; 2016 = 118,968 mt; forecasted SSB 2016 = 47,178 mt. Virgin recruitment R0 ≈ 0.54 billion age-0 fish; virgin female SSB ≈ 78,425 mt; steepness h = 0.48; W-L parameters a = 2.7E-06, b = 3.4.
- Recent landings (mt): 2004: 7,401; 2005: 8,406; 2006: 10,940; 2007: 9,473; 2008: 5,354; 2009: 3,656; 2010: 4,230; 2011: 4,309; 2012: 12,973; 2013: 14,747; 2014: 10,124. Average 2004-14 = 8,328 mt.
- Management history: 1970 California moratorium; 1977 reopened under quota; 2000 federal FMP. Historical fishery peaked at 66,400 mt in 1935-36; Mexico landings peaked at ~43,000 mt (1998-99) and ~34,000 mt (1991-92). [16]

**2025 catch-only assessment (NOAA-TM-NMFS-SWFSC-718, March 2025):**
- Recruitment relatively high for model years 2011, 2016, and 2018. Stock biomass (age 1+) generally declined between 2008 and 2022.
- **Stock biomass estimated at 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26 and 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for 2026-27.** Estimates for 2023 onward highly uncertain due to missing acoustic-trawl (AT) survey data for 2020 and 2022.
- Total landings ranged from roughly 3,331 mt (2009) to 32,027 mt (2020). F fluctuated ~0.05-0.35 yr⁻¹ between 2008-2023; annual exploitation rates ~1% to 27%.
- Harvest: 2025-26 OFL = 12,965 mt; HG = 9,143 mt; 2026-27 OFL = 14,270 mt; HG = 10,448 mt. Stock remains above the 18,200 mt management cutoff. The 2024 summer AT survey estimated Pacific mackerel biomass at 11,129 mt (preliminary).
- Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California. Three spawning aggregations hypothesized. Assumed long-term average distribution ~70% U.S. waters. Abundance can spike during favorable oceanographic conditions. [2][3]

### 8. Peruvian / Humboldt Current Stock

**SPRFMO SC12 Peruvian report (2024):** Habitat for jack and chub mackerel, 2022-2024.
- Summer 2024 dominated by positive temperature anomalies until early March, when the sea began cooling from north to south; in March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that had begun a year earlier.
- During summer 2024, both jack mackerel and chub mackerel were again found in typical coastal-oceanic front zones, unlike 2020 when they were found in unusual oceanic waters.
- Moderate thermal conditions over the last five years (since 2019, except warm 2023) led to higher concentration of jack mackerel, especially in the southern area. **In 2024, adult chub mackerel unusually predominated in the southern area.**
- Salinity remained within a narrow range (34.9-35.4 ups for chub mackerel) across the study period. Both species were available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll (<4 ug/Lt) and intermediate-to-high sea level anomaly values (positive but not exceeding 10 cm). [25]

**SPRFMO SC13 Peruvian National Report (SC13-ECO05, 2025, prepared by SNP/IHMA/IMARPE):**
- **Mackerel (Scomber japonicus):** Positive recent trend in biomass toward medium levels. Highest abundance (geostatistical) March 2024 at 80,000 tons. **Highest abundance February 2025 (week 13) at 80,000 tons.**
- June 2024-March 2025: 347 sets, average catch 31 tons/set, 10,795 tons caught. Fishing in southern zone, 10-100+ miles offshore, 16°S-21°S. Vertical distribution: surface to 154 meters (average 37.83 m). 1,936 mackerel schools analyzed, classified into 3 clusters.
- **In 2025 season: main mode of 35 cm, juvenile (<29 cm) percentage 0.01%.** Acoustic abundance estimates (2024-2025) for mackerel: 55 to 300 thousand tons (weeks 14-16).
- For jack mackerel 2025 season: sizes 30-60 cm TL, juvenile incidence (<31 cm) only 0.1%; main mode 50 cm. During 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018-2023, high juvenile incidence was observed; lower in 2024-2025.
- Fishing operations within 80 nm of coast in 2025 (vs. >140 nm in 2023). Analysis of 224 mackerel sets for 2025 biometric data (January 27-March 28, 2025) showed fishing focused on adults with very low juvenile participation, except 2021/2024 for mackerel. [33]

**Manrique-Muñante et al. 2026 (Int J Life Cycle Assessment 31:69, DOI 10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z):** Developed characterization factors (CFs) for 10 Peruvian fishing stocks including chub mackerel, within the Fisheries Impact Pathway framework. CF time series (2007-2023) under an EEZ approach; enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values; CFs exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship. Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally; other species (jack mackerel, bonito, chub mackerel, hake, jumbo squid, calico scallop) contribute to about 20% of annual landings and generated 2,600 million US$ in export revenue in 2023. [32]

**Salvatteci et al. 2019 (Progress in Oceanography 176, DOI 10.1016/j.pocean.2019.05.006) — paleoecological context (Humboldt Current):** Reconstructed small pelagic fish populations off Peru over the last 25,000 years from fish debris in sediments off Pisco (~14°S). Anchovy (Engraulis ringens) were predominant throughout (~90% of scales). Productivity appears to be the main factor controlling small pelagic fish abundance; sub-surface oxygenation affects mainly anchovy and likely sardine populations. Chub mackerel was among the species identified in the debris. Dramatic decreases in pelagic fish abundances have occurred in response to past large-scale climate changes larger than those in the instrumental period. [31]

### 9. Density Dependence, Body Condition, and Growth (Kamimura et al.)

**Kamimura, Taga, Yukami, Watanabe & Furuichi (bioRxiv preprint 2021; published in ICES Journal of Marine Science, DOI 10.1093/icesjms/fsab191):**
- **Data:** 18,302 chub mackerel landed in fishing ports on the Pacific coast of northern Japan (2006-2019); 68% from purse seine fisheries. 15,415 fish from 2006-2016 year classes for growth analysis. 8,429 age-1+ fish for relative condition factor (Kn) analysis.
- **Key findings:** Chub mackerel body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific (Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanostictus) abundance. Mean annual growth rates were positively correlated with body condition in all four quarters (Q1: χ²=34.6, p<0.001; Q2: χ²=7.23, p=0.007; Q3: χ²=6.50, p=0.011; Q4: χ²=4.83, p=0.028).
- Structural equation modeling showed conspecific and/or heterospecific abundance had strong negative effects on body condition in all seasons; temperature effects on body condition were weak. **Direct effects (food competition) likely have more impact than indirect effects (habitat temperature changes) on density-dependent body condition and growth.**
- **Abundance ranges:** Age-1+ chub mackerel abundance ranged from 8.5×10⁹ (2007) to 141.2×10⁹ individuals (2017); Japanese sardine abundance ranged from 5.2×10⁹ (2008) to 313.6×10⁹ individuals (2018).
- **Weight-length relationship: W = 1.09 × 10⁻⁶ L³·⁴¹.** von Bertalanffy parameter estimates: Linf ranged 339.9-440.5, K ranged 0.25-0.55, t0 ranged −2.88 to −1.26.
- Context: The Pacific stock declined in the 1990s–early 2000s but dramatically increased after a strong 2013 year class; Japanese sardine has also increased over the past decade. The species has overlapping prey (Copepoda, Eupausiidae, Decapoda, Amphipoda) with sardine. [23][29]

**Lin & Ito (PICES ECCWO5 presentation, ID 16093):** Documented the long-term decline of fish weight in the western North Pacific (WNP), collecting weight-at-age data for fish around Japan from 1978-2018 (17 populations, 13 species) and 1995-2018 (6 populations, 4 species) from the Fisheries Agency and Fisheries Research and Education Agency of Japan (2019).
- **Two distinct periods of weight decline were identified: the 1980s and the 2010s, with the 2010s decline reaching levels similar to the 1980s low.** For 1995-2018 data, decreasing trends in the 2010s were detected across a wide range of juvenile, maturing, and mature time series.
- **Proposed drivers:** (1) Inter- and intra-species competition — the 1980s decline was likely driven by competition from high Japanese sardine biomass (reducing Neocalanus copepod biomass; Tadokoro et al. 2005); the 2010s decline was driven by competition from recovering sardine and chub mackerel populations plus intra-species competition (Kawabata et al. 2011). (2) Bottom-up effects — stronger stratification (temperature difference between 0.5m and 200m depth) and reduced carrying capacity; the 2007-2014 period showed stronger stratification compared to 1982-1989. (3) Temperature-size rule — warmer temperatures generally associated with smaller adult size (debated). [10]

### 10. Environmental Drivers, Regime Shifts, and Climate Projections

**Yatsu 2019 review (Fisheries Science 85:611-639, DOI 10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3):**
- SPF catch and biomass show decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s, driven largely by climatic/oceanic variability and "regime shifts." The 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations.
- Six climatic/oceanic indices affect target stock dynamics: North Pacific Index (NPI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Kuroshio Extension South Area SST (KESA), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), and Monsoon Index (MOI).
- Paleoecological evidence (Beppu Bay scale deposition rates, 2,850 years) shows sardine periodicities ~50, 100, and 300 years; anchovy ~30 and 260 years. During the 20th century, Pacific sardines flourished during warmer global air temperatures and positive PDO phases, while anchovies flourished during negative PDO phases.
- Annual average sea surface temperature around Japan has increased +1.11°C over the last 100 years, exceeding the global ocean (+0.54°C) and North Pacific (+0.51°C) averages. [27]

**Go & Jung 2025 (Frontiers in Marine Science 12:1648650):** Individual-based model (IBM-TCM) coupled with a regional ocean circulation model (ROMS) projecting larval chub mackerel under present (2010s) and future (2050s) conditions under IPCC AR5 RCP 8.5.
- Water temperature projected to increase by 0.29-0.33°C across 1-75 m depths; largest May warming (+0.60°C at 1 m). Tsushima Warm Current projected to intensify.
- **Overall larval biomass from February to July projected to increase by 8.88% in the 2050s; northward shift of 0.72°N in biomass-weighted centroid.** Korea Strait/Yellow Sea biomass proportion increased from 6.99% to 15.96% in May; East China Sea decreased from 77.34% to 71.29%. Post-metamorphosis: ECS declined from 71.24% to 66.80%, Pacific from 17.67% to 12.15%, Korea Strait rose from 7.77% to 14.02%, Japan/East Sea from 3.32% to 7.02%. [9]

**Global Seafood Alliance summary of Go et al. 2025 (Fishes 10(1):20):** Potential spawning grounds projected to shift northward from the 2010s to the 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north and become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current. A subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds (from the Pacific side of Japan and JES toward waters off Jeju Island) is expected. Ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production are expected to increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the JES. The Tsushima Warm Current stock is exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the ECS and Korea Strait (February-June) before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the JES and Yellow Sea. [28]

**Yatsu 2019 (via Semantic Scholar-related literature):** Related studies cited include "Fluctuations in chub mackerel abundance related to climate/oceanic regime shifts in the northwest Pacific since the 1970s" (2021) and "The strong 2013 year class effects on chub mackerel spawning" (2026). [11]

### 11. Related Taxonomic and Reference Notes

- FishBase reference listing documents taxonomic history: *Scomber japonicus peruanus* (Jordan & Hubbs, 1925) is a junior synonym; *Scomber colias* (Gmelin, 1789) appears as accepted name in at least one reference (Diaw, 1976); *Scomber diego* (Ayres, 1856) is a junior synonym. Original description: Houttuyn, M., 1782. [19]
- FishSource notes that blue mackerel (*Scomber australasicus*) is closely related to chub mackerel and is assessed by Japan as two units (Pacific and East China Sea/Tsushima Current); the NPFC planned a 2020 assessment potentially covering both species as a single unit. [38]

--- SOURCE 1: A Study on the Impact of Environmental Factors on Chub Mackerel Scomber japonicus Fishing Grounds Based on a Linear Mixed Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/9/8/323

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the journal Fishes (2024, Volume 9, Issue 8, Article 323; DOI: 10.3390/fishes9080323), examines how marine environmental factors affect Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) fishing grounds in the Northwest Pacific using a linear mixed model (LMM). Authors include Jiasheng Li, Fenghua Tang, Yumei Wu, Shengmao Zhang, Weifeng Zhou, and Xuesen Cui (corresponding author), affiliated with the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute (Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences) and Shanghai Ocean University. The study was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (grant 2023YFD2401303) and received on 14 June 2024, published 14 August 2024.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used fishery data from China's high-sea light-purse seine operations (2014–2020) covering fishing grounds between 140–165°E and 30–50°N, combined with monthly averaged sea surface temperature (SST) and chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL) data from Oregon State University's Ocean Productivity database. Data were aggregated at 0.5° × 0.5° spatial resolution. CPUE was calculated as catch per net-haul (t/net). Square-root transformation of CPUE and natural logarithm of CHL were applied to achieve normal distributions; VIF values of 1.990 confirmed no multicollinearity between SST and logCHL. The LMM included SST and logCHL as fixed effects, with Year, Month, and fishing Zone as random effects, using the lme4 package in R. Among 256 candidate models, the optimal model (scenario 5) was selected based on lowest AIC, BIC, and logLik values.

KEY RESULTS: (1) SST had a significant fixed effect on CPUE with a negative slope (p < 0.001), meaning CPUE increases as SST decreases. (2) logCHL had no fixed effect on CPUE but showed significant random effects by month. (3) logCHL was positively correlated with CPUE during spawning and wintering periods (April–May, November–December) and negatively correlated during the summer feeding period (June–October), consistent with patterns observed in neon flying squid. (4) Annual average CPUE decreased from 2014 to 2020, peaking at 15.501 t/net (2015) and 11.363 t/net (2018), with a low of 8.355 t/net in 2020; monthly CPUE peaked in November (14.426 t/net). (5) Low CPUE areas (<5 t/net) were south of 34°N, while high CPUE areas (>15 t/net) were between 148–159°E. (6) The random intercept for Year showed highest value (0.353) in 2015 and lowest (−0.480) in 2019; a high-random-intercept zone at 150–152°E, 39–41°N corresponded to high catch rates. Residuals approximated a normal distribution (skewness 0.031, kurtosis 3.532).

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS: The negative SST-CPUE relationship aligns with prior studies in the East China Sea and Japan coastal waters. Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019). The optimal SST range for fishing grounds is 14–18°C (~16°C ideal), and optimal chlorophyll-a range is 0.3–0.8 mg/m³. LIMITATIONS: Interpretation complexity with crossed random effects, high parameterization risks (overfitting), and incomplete spatial/temporal data coverage (no data from Japan/Russia EEZs, no January–March data).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SST had a significant fixed effect on the CPUE. In contrast, the natural logarithm of chlorophyll (logCHL) had no fixed effect on the CPUE. Based on the monthly analysis, random fluctuations were observed in the impact of logCHL on the CPUE. LogCHL and CPUE show a positive correlation during spawning and wintering periods and a negative correlation during the feeding period."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Projecting the Shift of Chub Mackerel (Scomber japonicus) Spawning Grounds Driven by Climate Change in the Western North Pacific Ocean ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2410-3888/10/1/20

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the MDPI journal *Fishes* (2025, Volume 10, Issue 1, Article 20) by authors Seonggil Go (Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology), Joon-ho Lee (Underwater Survey Technology 21), and Sukgeun Jung (Jeju National University, corresponding author). The study projects how climate change will shift the spawning grounds of the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock of chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) in the western North Pacific Ocean.

**Methodology:** The researchers developed a spawning ground index (SGI) based on a Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′ E, 20°00′–52°00′ N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers), driven by the IPCC AR5 RCP85 scenario. The model simulated ocean conditions from 2010–2059. SGI was calculated using four parameters: water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m). The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001).

**Key Findings:**
- In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June.
- By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes).
- Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea.
- The study suggests biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea.

**Limitations noted:** The model results did not perfectly align with observations in the same space and time (though trends were similar); the assumed spawning period may shift due to photoperiod changes; only 10 m depth environmental conditions were considered; and chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m depth).

**Funding:** Supported by the Korea Institute of Marine Science and Technology (KIMST), Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries (RS-2023-00256330 and RS-2022-KS221566), and Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST grant PEA0306).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite some uncertainty, our model based on climate change scenarios projected that, by the 2050s, spawning grounds will shift northward due to warming of the ocean surface, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Effects of oceanographic conditions on fishery distribution: A case study of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in northeastern Taiwan ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0141113624004641

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Marine Environmental Research (Volume 202, November 2024, Article 106803) as part of a special issue on "Climate Change and the Oceans," edited by Fangli QIAO of the First Institute of Oceanography. The study examines the effects of oceanographic conditions on chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) distribution in northeastern Taiwan.

**Authors:** Sandipan Mondal, Frank Muller-Karger, Aratrika Ray, Shin-Ichi Ito, Ming-An Lee, and Hsueh-Jung Lu.

**Methodology:** The researchers constructed a habitat ensemble model incorporating chub mackerel fishery data, climatic oscillation data, and oceanography data. Fishery and oceanographic data were rescaled using MATLAB (2022a) to a consistent spatial and temporal grid, then standardized using a generalized linear model (GLM). Five single-algorithm models were used: GLM, generalized additive model (GAM), gradient boosting method (GBM), random forest (RF), and classification models, combined into an ensemble approach.

**Key Findings:**
- Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO), which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792).
- NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level.
- Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect.
- Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m.
- Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E.

**Background Context:** Global climate change is significantly affecting marine ecosystems, with ocean warming causing coral bleaching, marine food web disruption, ocean acidification, and sea-level rise. Under RCP 8.5 scenario, a predicted 40% decline in tropical fish catch by the 2050s in some economic zones (Lam et al., 2020) highlights the urgency of this research. Chub mackerel is economically crucial to Taiwan, with Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries accounting for 98.66% of captures. The study addresses a research gap by using multiple algorithms to confirm oceanographic significance, unlike previous studies that relied on single models.

**Funding:** National Science & Technology Council of Taiwan (NSTC) grant 112-2811-M-019-004 and Fisheries Agency, Council of Agriculture, Taiwan grant 112-FM-2.31-A-03.

**Applications:** Findings can be used to develop critical adaptation plans for managing chub mackerel fisheries in northeastern Taiwan waters and may aid decision-makers in protecting other ocean fisheries and dependent communities under changing climate conditions. The article has been cited by 5 subsequent publications (as of the page retrieval date).
</summary>

"Our results indicated that the chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the Western Pacific Oscillation. Moreover, sea-surface height and mixed-layer depth exerted the most and least significant effects on chub mackerel distribution, respectively."

--- SOURCE 4: Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304380014001604

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Ecological Modelling (Volume 283, 10 July 2014, Pages 70-84) titled "Dispersal and survival of chub mackerel (Scomber Japonicus) larvae in the East China Sea" by Yuesong Li, Xinjun Chen, Changsheng Chen, Jianzhong Ge, Rubao Ji, Rucheng Tian, Pengfei Xue, and Liuxiong Xu. DOI: 10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2014.03.016.

The study developed an early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the East China Sea (ECS) unstructured grid Finite-Volume Community Ocean Model (FVCOM). The researchers examined how regional physical processes affect larval dispersal and survival under climatological spring-summer conditions, both with and without short-time fluctuations from a typhoon.

Key findings include:
- Seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages.
- Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location.
- Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing. Comparison of cases with and without Typhoon Alice showed that cancellation of tidally-induced anti-cyclonic and typhoon-driven cyclonic currents limits typhoon influence on low-frequency flow and larval dispersion, but typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds.
- Temperature and food play significant roles in early larval development; water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March-July.
- Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June).
- Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion.

The article provides background on the ECS physical oceanography, including the Kuroshio Current (which acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf), the Taiwan Warm Current, and the Changjiang Coastal Current (which tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East Strait). Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. The study is the first IBM developed to examine chub mackerel recruitment in the ECS.

The paper has 41 references and has been cited 27 times. It was supported by multiple Chinese national research projects including the National 863 project, Shanghai Education Committee, and Shanghai Ocean University programs.
</summary>

"The model results show that the seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during the early life stages."

URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/stock-assessment-of-chub-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-in-the-central-east-china-sea-based-on-length-data/9AC92B324DD34E8BA019F5462A821E73

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Cambridge University Press journal article (published online October 30, 2013, in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom) titled "Stock assessment of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the central East China Sea based on length data." The study addresses the chub mackerel, an important commercial pelagic species in the East China Sea that rose to prominence after the decline of traditional demersal economic species. The research methodology involved separating sample catches from 2009-2010 into three age groups based on an age–fork length key, estimating maximum sustainable yield (MSY), and building a spawner–recruitment relationship using fishery statistics from purse seine vessels, lighting purse seine vessels, and deep-water purse seine vessels from 2006 to 2012. Key findings: (1) The MSY of chub mackerel is approximately 18.8 × 10⁴ tonnes; (2) The fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels (with lighting and deep-water purse seine vessels standardized to purse seine vessels), equivalent to a fishing mortality rate (F) of 0.4; (3) If fishing mortality remains at the current level (F = 0.7), the biomass will remain at 45.3 × 10⁴ tonnes; (4) At current fishing intensity, more than 40% of catches will consist of individuals smaller than 200mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300mm. The study concludes there is little potential for further exploitation of chub mackerel resources in the central East China Sea, and recommends reducing fishing mortality (F) to less than 0.4 for sustainable utilization. The chub mackerel resources are suffering over-exploitation due to increased fishing effort, and this paper represents the first analysis of their response to fishing because of previous data shortages.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Ocean University of China (Volume 20, pages 1483–1494, 2021) titled "Effects of Climate Variability on Habitat Range and Distribution of Chub Mackerel in the East China Sea." Published on November 21, 2021, the study was conducted by authors Wei Yu, Jian Wen, Xinjun Chen, Gang Li, Yuesong Li, and Zhong Zhang, affiliated with Shanghai Ocean University and the Qingdao National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology.

The study investigated how the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) impacts the habitat range and distribution of the chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the East China Sea (ECS). A weighting-based Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) model was established using vertical water temperature data at depths of 2.5 m, 25 m, and 50 m. From ten weighting scenarios tested, the optimal HSI model yielded reliable predictions.

Key findings include:
- A significant negative relationship was found between the PDO index and water temperature anomaly at different depths.
- Water temperatures at three different layers on the fishing ground tended to be LOW during the warm PDO phase and HIGH during the cold PDO phase.
- During a warm PDO phase: vertical water temperature cooled, the monthly preferred water temperature shifted southeastward, habitat quality dramatically decreased, and suitable habitat ranges reduced and moved southeastward.
- During a cool PDO phase: warmer vertical water temperatures occurred, preferred water temperature shifted northwestward, and suitable habitats enlarged and migrated in the same direction.

The study concludes that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of S. japonicus in the East China Sea. The article received 279 accesses, 7 citations, and 1 Altmetric score. The research was funded by the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2018YFD0900906), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 41906073), the Natural Science Foundation of Shanghai (No. 19ZR1423000), and the Shanghai Universities First-Class Disciplines Project (Fisheries A).

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index of chub mackerel in the spawning season and its effect on the abundance ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Marine Science (25 November 2022) examining climate-induced variation in a temperature suitability index (TSI) of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and its effect on stock abundance.

**Study Context and Species:**
- Chub mackerel is widely distributed in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and is fished by China, Korea, and Japan in different seasons and areas.
- The species is divided into two stocks: the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock (distributed in the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and Sea of Japan) and the Pacific stock (inhabiting the Pacific coast of Japan and high seas of the northwestern Pacific).
- Main spawning period is March to June, with suitable spawning SST ranging from 15°C to 22°C and optimal at 18°C.

**Methods:**
- The authors estimated average TSI for chub mackerel in main spawning areas using the relationship between spawning probability and SST, assuming a Gaussian distribution with mean 18°C and variance 2.0°C.
- Data sources included FAO catch data (1950-2017), Japanese Fisheries Agency stock assessments (TWC and Pacific stock data, 1970-2017), and SST data from Japan Meteorological Agency (1970-2011), AVHRR (2012-2015), and GOES (2016-2017).
- Analytical techniques included Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis, sequential t-test analysis of regime shifts (STARS), Gradient Forest (GF) analysis, Generalized Additive Models (GAM), and Threshold GAMs (TGAM) to detect stationary vs. non-stationary relationships.
- Three main spawning areas were defined: coastal waters of China seas (24°N-36°N/118°E-124°E), southern Sea of Japan/Tsushima Strait (31°N-36°N/126°E-132°E), and Pacific coast of Japan (30°N-38°N/129°E-147°E).

**Key Results:**
- TSI in the shelf waters of China seas and Tsushima Strait showed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock.
- TSI on the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock.
- Chinese catch showed an increasing trend since the 1970s with step changes in 1986/1987, 1993/1994, and 2003/2004; TWC catch by Korea/Japan decreased in the late 1990s (step-change in 1998/1999).

--- SOURCE 9: Pacific decadal oscillation - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_decadal_oscillation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin, detected as warm or cool surface waters in the Pacific north of 20°N. It varies irregularly at interannual-to-interdecadal timescales. The PDO was named by Steven R. Hare in 1997, who noticed it while studying salmon production patterns. The PDO index is the leading empirical orthogonal function (EOF) of monthly sea surface temperature anomalies over the North Pacific, with signals reconstructed back to 1661 (and as far back as 993) through tree-ring chronologies.

**Mechanisms:** The PDO is not a single physical mode of ocean variability but rather the superposition of several processes with different dynamic origins:
- **ENSO teleconnections/atmospheric bridge**: El Niño events generate Rossby waves that propagate poleward, modifying surface fluxes over the North Pacific within 2–6 weeks.
- **SST reemergence**: Winter SST anomalies are sequestered beneath the shallow summer mixed layer and reemerge the following winter when the mixed layer deepens again.
- **Stochastic atmospheric forcing**: Random storm forcings integrated into the ocean mixed layer can contribute up to 1/3 of PDO variability at decadal timescales.
- **Ocean dynamics**: Including advective resonance, Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension variability, and North Pacific gyre circulation adjustments driven by westward-propagating Rossby waves.

**Impacts:** During a positive phase, the Aleutian Low deepens, warming the Pacific Northwest to Alaska while cooling Mexico and the Southeast US. Winter precipitation increases in Alaska's coastal range, Mexico, and the Southwest US but decreases in Canada, Eastern Siberia, and Australia. The PDO also affects the Indian summer monsoon (stronger during negative phase) and, along with the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, strongly influences multidecadal drought patterns in the US.

**Regime shifts:** Documented reversals around 1924/25, 1945/46, and 1976/77, with additional shifts in 1988/89 and 1997/98. A 2014 flip to a warm phase coincided with record-breaking global surface temperatures. The last two major reversals corresponded with dramatic shifts in salmon production regimes in the North Pacific. Reconstructions show a 50–70 year periodicity, with a persistent negative phase during medieval times (993–1300).

**Predictability:** NOAA produces PDO forecasts using linear inverse modeling (LIM), with predictability largely arising from ENSO and limited to approximately 4 seasons (~14 months). ENSO tends to lead PDO cycling. The PDO is related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO), a similar but more global phenomenon covering 50°S to 50°N.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin."
