### 3. Japanese Pacific Stock

**Historical dynamics (Kawabata et al., presented at J-STAGE):**
- Stock biomass ranged from approximately 4-6 million tons in the early-to-mid 1970s, declining to about 2 million tons in the 1980s and less than 1 million tons in the 1990s.
- Peak catch was 1.5 million tons in 1978; by 1990 the catch had fallen to less than 25,000 tons.
- SSB ranged from 0.45 to 1.60 million tons during 1970-1985, declining to around 0.1 million tons in the late 1990s.
- Dominant year classes appeared in 1992, 1996, and 2000, but intensive fishing on immature fish (age-0 and age-1) prevented stock recovery. The 1990s exhibited recruitment overfishing because dominant 1992 and 1996 year classes did not lead to SSB recovery.
- Two major regime shifts in recruitment per spawning stock biomass (RPS) occurred in the late 1970s and 1980s, likely corresponding to Kuroshio Path meandering or North Pacific regime shifts.
- The optimal harvest age was determined to be age-3 and older, matching the first age of 100% maturation. A target SSB of 0.45 million tons was established as the rebuilding threshold. [41]

**Recovery and the strong 2013 year class:**
- The Pacific stock declined in the 1990s–early 2000s but dramatically increased after a strong 2013 year class. [23][29]
- The Pacific stock population of S. japonicus grew from 153,000 tons in 2001 to 6,808,000 tons in 2019 (per larval survey context in the northern Satsunan area, southern Japan). [17]
- Review by Yatsu (2019): Overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, but both have been recovering since the mid-2000s due to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing stemmed from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity following the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF shifted from sardine to anchovy. [27]
- Larval densities increased dramatically from 2016 (10.8 individuals per 1,000 m³) to 2018 (724.0 in Kagoshima Bay, 343.2 in Osumi Strait), corresponding with the increasing Pacific stock population. A significant negative relationship was found between larval density and chlorophyll a concentration. [17]

**Recent quota reduction related to stock decline:** New regulations effective 2025 have reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). [1]

**Northern Satsunan area spawning/nursery ground study (2015-2019):** Of 305 Scomber spp. specimens (2017-2019), S. japonicus larvae were dominant (273 vs. 32 S. australasicus), comprising 96.8% of larvae in Kagoshima Bay and 87.7% in the Osumi Strait. Instantaneous growth rate (G) was 0.072 in 2018 and 0.078 in 2019; daily specific growth rate (K) was 7.5% BL d⁻¹ in 2018 and 8.1% BL d⁻¹ in 2019. Copepods (Calanidae, Paracalanidae, Oithonidae, Oncaeidae) and appendicularians (Oikopleuridae) were the primary prey. [17]

**Larval/juvenile growth and recruitment (Kamimura et al. 2015, Fisheries Science 81(3):505-513, DOI 10.1007/s12562-015-0869-4):** This study examined larval and juvenile growth of chub mackerel in relation to recruitment in the western North Pacific. [22]

**Larval/juvenile recent growth (Taga et al. 2019, Fisheries Science 85(6):931-942, DOI 10.1007/s12562-019-01354-8):** Along the Boso–Kashimanada Pacific coast (March-July 2015 and 2016), temperature positively affected recent growth rate (RGR) of larvae in body length classes <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and 9-11mm. Prey density affected growth in the <5mm, 5-7mm, 7-9mm, and >11mm classes, with effects being stronger for larger (>11mm) larvae and juveniles. S. japonicus larvae transform into juveniles at around 12mm BL. Otolith increment widths of collected larvae/juveniles were significantly narrower than those of 1-year-old S. japonicus from purse seine fisheries in the Joban or Kashimanada areas, suggesting growth-dependent mortality. [21]

**Long-term maturity changes (Watanabe & Yatsu 2006, Fisheries Research 78(2-3):323-332, DOI 10.1016/J.FISHRES.2006.01.001):** For the Pacific stock (heavily exploited, abundance declining since the 1970s), the researchers analyzed fork length, body weight, and gonad weight of 21,048 individuals (ages 1-4) collected during 1970-1998. A clear trend was found for the proportion of mature females at given ages to increase, and the length and age at 50% maturity to decrease. Changes in maturity were mainly explained by changes in length at a given age (density-dependent growth acceleration). Sea surface temperature (SST) of the spawning ground also affected maturation of young (1-year-old) females. A model incorporating length-at-age, spawning-season biomass, and SST well described changes in mature female proportions over 29 years. The population's total biomass peaked in 1978 and declined rapidly until 1990 due to poor recruitment from 1978-1981 and 1987-1991, plus extensive exploitation. Chub mackerel spawn from April to June around the Izu Islands near central Japan, migrating northeast after spawning to feeding grounds at the Kuroshio-Oyashio transition area and Oyashio Current. [11][12]

**Effects of density-dependence and SST on length-at-age (Watanabe & Yatsu 2004):** Published in the NOAA Fisheries journal (Fishery Bulletin) as "Effects of density-dependence and sea surface temperature on interannual variation in length-at-age of chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) in the Kuroshio-Oyashio area during 1970-1997" - this foundational study examined environmental (SST) and biological (density-dependence) factors influencing the body length-at-age of chub mackerel. [42]

### 4. Korean Stock / Tsushima-influenced Waters

**2026 assessment by Kwak, Kim & Lee (Frontiers in Marine Science, Vol 13, May 14, 2026):**
- The chub mackerel has been managed under Korea's TAC system since 1999, with prior assessments yielding conflicting results on recovery status.
- Analysis used 55 years of catch data (1970-2024) from Korea, China, and Japan (Tsushima Current stock), plus 27 years of CPUE data (1997-2023) from Korea.
- **In 2024:** B/BMSY estimated at 0.63 (CMSY++) and 0.59 (BSS), classifying the stock as "Overfished." CMSY++ estimated r=0.255, k=2,273,005 tons, MSY=145,462 tons, B2024=779,191 tons. BSS estimated r=0.310, k=1,802,382 tons, MSY=139,902 tons, B2024=549,884 tons.
- Kobe plot: 87.6% (CMSY++) and 95.3% (BSS) posterior probability of the stock remaining in the "overfished and overfishing" red quadrant, due to sustained high fishing mortality since the early 2000s.
- **Korean catch:** Peaked at 415,003 tons in 1996, reached a historical low of 77,603 tons in 2020, and was 124,928 tons in 2024. Large purse seine fishery accounts for 82.2% of domestic catch (average 91,349 tons, 2020-2024).
- **Body size evidence of depletion:** Landing data from the Busan Cooperative Fish Market shows an increasing proportion of small-sized (≤250g, ~29.7cm TL, below the L50 of 31.4cm) immature individuals in the catch — **from 65% in 2015 to 88% in 2024** — providing biological evidence of stock depletion.
- Fishing effort effectively increased despite fleet reduction: vessels decreased from 342 (1992) to 106 (2024), but GT/vessel rose from 131 to 188 and EHP/vessel from 827 to 1,471.
- Recommendation: more stringent TAC reductions, extended closed seasons, vessel buybacks, and upward revision of minimum legal size limits. [1][2]

**Hong, Kim & Kim 2022 (Sustainability, DOI 10.3390/su15010358):** Stock assessment of chub mackerel in the Northwest Pacific Ocean based on catch and resilience data. Current chub mackerel biomass level is lower than the biomass required to achieve MSY based on median values. Prior studies using CMSY and Bayesian state-space (BSS) models classified Korean chub mackerel as "Grossly overfished" or "Overfished." [30]

### 5. Northwest Pacific High Seas (NPFC Area) and Chinese Fisheries

**Zhao, Zhang & Tang 2025 (Animals 15(8):1135, DOI 10.3390/ani15081135; PMC12024016):** Examined spatio-temporal distribution and population dynamics in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific Ocean (35°N–45°N, 145°E–160°E) using 38,123 fishing operations from Chinese light purse seine vessels (2016-2021) and 4,440 biological samples.
- **Biological characteristics:** Sex ratios (female:male) ranged 1.09-2.55 across years (all >1). **Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020). Mean lengths varied from 212.07 mm (2016) to 268.28 mm (2018).** Growth parameters: asymptotic length (Linf) ranged 36-42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged 0.31-0.65.
- **CPUE:** Decreased year by year (strong negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01), with large values dominating 2016-2018 and small values dominating 2019-2021. The gravity center of fishing grounds moved gradually northwestward, driven largely by climate warming and marine heatwaves since 2014.
- **Stock status (LBB):** Healthy during 2016-2021; F/M values all <0.5, E (exploitation ratio) ranged 0.17-0.32; B/B0 exceeded 0.5; B/Bmsy exceeded 1. L95th/Linf and Lmean/Lopt close to 1; Lc/Lopt >1. Body length structure was reasonable with no miniaturization and large individuals still present. Total mortality (Z) ranged 1.01 (2016) to 1.64 (2021), natural mortality (M) 0.59-0.85, fishing mortality (F) 0.23-0.79, with natural mortality dominant. However, E showed an increasing year-by-year trend, reaching 0.48 in 2021 by conventional methods.
- **Explanations for CPUE decline despite healthy stock:** (1) reasonable resource fluctuation; (2) spawning grounds in south-central Pacific coast of Japan may have changed, reducing recruitment via Kuroshio Current transport; (3) increasing food competition with Japanese sardine; (4) interactions among proliferating fishing vessels' fish-attracting light systems. [4][6]

**Huang, Zhang, Gao & Li 2026 (Fishes 11(5):276):** Integrated LBB (using 6,061 specimens sampled from light purse seine fisheries, 38°00′N–46°00′N, 147°00′E–162°00′E, April–December 2019–2024) and Catch-MSY (1995-2024 catch data) models.
- **Significant interannual variability in stock status:** Stock within sustainable limits (B/BMSY ≥ 1.0) in 2019, 2021, and 2022, but suffered overfishing in 2020, 2023, and 2024. Pooled two-year analysis: B/BMSY dropped to 0.51 during 2023-2024, reflecting marked stock deterioration.
- Catch-MSY: MSY = 278,000 t (95% CI: 162,000-475,000 t); r peaked at 0.2; K peaked at 5,406,100 t.
- Kobe plot: only 23.2% probability of healthy stock state in the final assessment year; probabilities of recruitment-overfished, fishing-overfished, and severely overfished were 37.6%, 14.9%, and 24.3%. Final-year diagnosed as recruitment overfishing.
- Fishing mortality exceeded natural mortality in recent years (F/M > 1.5), making fishing pressure the primary driver.
- Management recommendation: TAC at 60-80% of the baseline TAC (352,100 t) during the medium term (5-10 years), i.e., 211,300-281,700 t.
- Notes that new regulations effective 2025 reduced the Pacific coast mackerel catch quota by 60% (from 350,000 t to 139,000 t). Contrasts with earlier research (Zhao, 2016-2021 data) suggesting good condition, indicating recent transition to overfished status. [1]

**Cai et al. 2023 (Fishes 8(2):80):** Multi-model stock assessment (CMSY, BSM, SPiCT, JABBA, JABBA-Select) using NPFC catch and CPUE data (1995-2020; CPUE 2010-2020). Purse seine fleets (about 72% of landings) from China, Japan, and Russia provided CPUE.
- Results mixed: CMSY (B2020/BMSY=0.98, F2020/FMSY=1.12), BSM (B2020/BMSY=0.97, F2020/FMSY=1.21), JABBA-Select (SB2020/SBMSY=0.99, H2020/HMSY=0.99) indicated slightly overfished; SPiCT (B2020/BMSY=2.30) and JABBA (B2020/BMSY=1.40) indicated healthy.
- MSY estimates ranged 0.40-0.66 million tons; r from 0.38-0.56. 2020 catch in NPFC area ≈ 460,238 tons (34% of global production). JABBA showed 88.3% probability of healthy status in 2020. [39]

**NPFC 2024 assessments:** (a) "Stock assessment based on age-structured assessment program (ASAP) for chub mackerel in the North Pacific Ocean 2024" — used the latest aggregated dataset and agreed scenarios with the Age-Structured Assessment Program. (b) "Base case stock assessment for chub mackerel in Northwest Pacific Ocean 2024" — used a state-space age-structured assessment model (SAM), presenting model selection, parameter estimates, and diagnostics for two base case scenarios (with different settings of M). Estimated total biomass and spawning [stock biomass reported in the documents]. [35][36]

**Tong et al. 2022 (Frontiers in Marine Science 9:856483):** Target strength study — 18 samples (body length 12.98-22.17 cm, mean 16.08±3.15 cm) from 147°E–165°E, 33°N–44°N collected June-August 2021. Notes chub mackerel global catch was 1.56 million tons in 2018 with biomass declining since 1997. Average TS ranged -48.55 to -49.75 dB at 38-200 kHz. [24]

### 6. East China Sea and Yellow Sea Stock

**Wang et al. 2014 (Journal of Fisheries of China 38(1):56-64, DOI 10.3724/SP.J.1231.2014.48737):** Analyzed chub mackerel catch data from the large lighting-purse seine fishery (1999-2011) using GLM and GAM. "Year" was the foremost factor contributing 53.9% of total deviance reduction. **Chub mackerel abundance showed a declining trend over the 13-year period, especially after 2008, with the abundance index (AI) falling from 1.22 in 2008 to 0.82 in 2011.** AI showed a significantly positive relationship with SST of the spawning ground (AI = -3.5 + 0.23SST, P < 0.05). Decline attributed to the rapidly increasing number of purse seine vessels. [26]

**Cai et al. 2022 (JMSE 10(2):301, DOI 10.3390/jmse10020301) — Growth heterogeneity study (Zhejiang coastal area and high seas near Japan, 2016-2020):**
- 2,686 specimens: fork lengths 40-294 mm (average 181.91 mm), body weights 0.8-311.8 g (average 73.27 g). Dominant fork length group 210-220 mm; dominant weight group 20-30 g.
- **Length-weight relationship: W = (1.41 × 10⁻⁶) × FL³·³⁷.**
- Linear mixed-effects modeling showed year-to-year variation was the largest source of growth heterogeneity: differences in parameter "a" were larger for years (7.66 × 10⁻⁷) than regions (5.57 × 10⁻⁷) or seasons (3.20 × 10⁻⁷). Growth heterogeneity most pronounced for specimens >200 mm FL.
- **Relative condition factors varied among years, seasons, and regions. Only K relative to 2006-16 and 2016 reference periods had mean values higher than 1. The lowest relative condition factor was observed in 2017.** Summer had the highest seasonal condition factors.
- **Fork length was significantly greater in 2020 than other years.** Median fork length in the high seas near Japan (220 mm) was much higher than in the Zhejiang coastal area (150 mm).
- Ages from otoliths ranged 0-5 years (13 age-0, 54 age-1, 60 age-2, 40 age-3, 7 age-4, 1 age-5); von Bertalanffy growth model provided the best fit. Individual chub mackerel exhibited a slower growth rate than observed in previous studies. [8][3]

### 7. California Current / Eastern Pacific (U.S.-Mexico) Stock

**Life history report for the 2023 benchmark (NOAA-TM-NMFS-SWFSC-689, August 2023):**
- SWFSC survey fish (2012-2022, n=1,762 aged): 53-402 mm FL, ages 0-7; age composition dominated by young fish: age 0 (46%), 1 (29%), 2 (16%), 3 (6%), ages 4-7 only 2.3%.
- CDFW port sampling (2008-2022, n=9,035 aged): 84-429 mm FL, ages 0-9; ages 0-3 representing 47%, 30%, 12%, and 7% respectively; ages 4-9 only 4%.
- **Length at maturity L50 = 274 ± 1.26 mm FL; L95 = 309 ± 2.60 mm FL. Age at maturity A50 = 1.01 ± 0.06 years; all females older than 2.52 ± 0.15 years mature.** L50 nearly identical to previous estimates, but A50 lower than the previous estimate of 2.2 years. Maturity schedules have remained constant over recent decades.
- Ageing agreement high for ages 0-1 (94% and 78%), moderate for ages 2-3 (52% and 41%), low for ages 4-6 (22-30%).
- 2023 benchmark assessment: total biomass 93,823 mt for 2021 (86.9% from ages 0-2); projected SSB 46,167 mt (2023) and 50,372 mt (2024). [15][4]

**2023 benchmark assessment (Kuriyama et al., June 2023):**
- Landings 2008-2022 from Mexico (Ensenada and Magdalena Bay) and U.S.; total landings ranged from a low of 3,656 mt in 2009 to a high of 32,060 mt in 2020. Mexico landings reached 31,368 mt in 2020; U.S. total landings peaked at 11,909 mt in 2013.
- **SSB projected: 43,864 mt in 2022, 46,167 mt in 2023, 50,372 mt in 2024.** Stock biomass (age-1+) for PFMC management: 49,977 mt in 2021, projected 46,682 mt in 2022. Initial SSB estimated at 136,664 mt; virgin recruitment 917,938 thousand fish. U.S. exploitation rate peaked at 27% in 2020.
- Harvest control rule: Harvest = (Biomass − Cutoff) × E_MSY × Distribution, with Cutoff = 18,200 mt, E_MSY = 30%, Distribution = 70%. U.S. fishery has not fully utilized HGs since the late 1990s (e.g., 990 mt USA landings in 2022 vs. 4,822 mt HG). [34][37]

**2019 benchmark assessment (Crone, Hill, Zwolinski, Kinney, May 2019):**
- Landings (2008-18): total average annual landings (commercial and recreational, U.S. and Mexico) 9,018.6 mt per year; recreational fishery ~3%; Mexico landings averaged 4,435.3 mt; California commercial 3,900.6 mt; Oregon 363.6 mt; Washington 151.0 mt.
- **SSB declined from 26,676 mt in 2008 to 5,822 mt in 2016, then increased to 7,512 mt in 2018, projected at 11,071 mt (2019) and 13,394 mt (2020).**
- **Stock biomass (age 1+) generally declined from 63,535 mt (2008) to 25,943 mt (2018), with projections of 71,099 mt (July 2019) and 56,058 mt (July 2020).**
- High recruitment success in 2011, 2016, and 2018. Instantaneous F ranged ~0.1-0.9 during 2008-18; annual exploitation rates ~5% to 25%. Age 0-2 fish typically comprise roughly 80% of total population biomass. [18][9]

**2015 assessment (Crone & Hill, May 2015, Model H3):**
- SSB continually declined since the mid-1980s, low over the last decade with some recent increase. High recruitment periods last occurred mid-1980s and mid-1990s (1-2.7 billion fish); very low recruitment from mid-1990s to 2012.
- Model H3: 2014 stock biomass = 97,395 mt; 2015 = 120,435 mt; 2016 = 118,968 mt; forecasted SSB 2016 = 47,178 mt. Virgin recruitment R0 ≈ 0.54 billion age-0 fish; virgin female SSB ≈ 78,425 mt; steepness h = 0.48; W-L parameters a = 2.7E-06, b = 3.4.
- Recent landings (mt): 2004: 7,401; 2005: 8,406; 2006: 10,940; 2007: 9,473; 2008: 5,354; 2009: 3,656; 2010: 4,230; 2011: 4,309; 2012: 12,973; 2013: 14,747; 2014: 10,124. Average 2004-14 = 8,328 mt.
- Management history: 1970 California moratorium; 1977 reopened under quota; 2000 federal FMP. Historical fishery peaked at 66,400 mt in 1935-36; Mexico landings peaked at ~43,000 mt (1998-99) and ~34,000 mt (1991-92). [16]

**2025 catch-only assessment (NOAA-TM-NMFS-SWFSC-718, March 2025):**
- Recruitment relatively high for model years 2011, 2016, and 2018. Stock biomass (age 1+) generally declined between 2008 and 2022.
- **Stock biomass estimated at 61,737 mt (SD = 41,422 mt) for fishing year 2025-26 and 67,954 mt (SD = 43,375 mt) for 2026-27.** Estimates for 2023 onward highly uncertain due to missing acoustic-trawl (AT) survey data for 2020 and 2022.
- Total landings ranged from roughly 3,331 mt (2009) to 32,027 mt (2020). F fluctuated ~0.05-0.35 yr⁻¹ between 2008-2023; annual exploitation rates ~1% to 27%.
- Harvest: 2025-26 OFL = 12,965 mt; HG = 9,143 mt; 2026-27 OFL = 14,270 mt; HG = 10,448 mt. Stock remains above the 18,200 mt management cutoff. The 2024 summer AT survey estimated Pacific mackerel biomass at 11,129 mt (preliminary).
- Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California. Three spawning aggregations hypothesized. Assumed long-term average distribution ~70% U.S. waters. Abundance can spike during favorable oceanographic conditions. [2][3]

### 8. Peruvian / Humboldt Current Stock

**SPRFMO SC12 Peruvian report (2024):** Habitat for jack and chub mackerel, 2022-2024.
- Summer 2024 dominated by positive temperature anomalies until early March, when the sea began cooling from north to south; in March 2024, ENFEN announced the end of the Coastal El Niño that had begun a year earlier.
- During summer 2024, both jack mackerel and chub mackerel were again found in typical coastal-oceanic front zones, unlike 2020 when they were found in unusual oceanic waters.
- Moderate thermal conditions over the last five years (since 2019, except warm 2023) led to higher concentration of jack mackerel, especially in the southern area. **In 2024, adult chub mackerel unusually predominated in the southern area.**
- Salinity remained within a narrow range (34.9-35.4 ups for chub mackerel) across the study period. Both species were available for fishing in areas with low chlorophyll (<4 ug/Lt) and intermediate-to-high sea level anomaly values (positive but not exceeding 10 cm). [25]

**SPRFMO SC13 Peruvian National Report (SC13-ECO05, 2025, prepared by SNP/IHMA/IMARPE):**
- **Mackerel (Scomber japonicus):** Positive recent trend in biomass toward medium levels. Highest abundance (geostatistical) March 2024 at 80,000 tons. **Highest abundance February 2025 (week 13) at 80,000 tons.**
- June 2024-March 2025: 347 sets, average catch 31 tons/set, 10,795 tons caught. Fishing in southern zone, 10-100+ miles offshore, 16°S-21°S. Vertical distribution: surface to 154 meters (average 37.83 m). 1,936 mackerel schools analyzed, classified into 3 clusters.
- **In 2025 season: main mode of 35 cm, juvenile (<29 cm) percentage 0.01%.** Acoustic abundance estimates (2024-2025) for mackerel: 55 to 300 thousand tons (weeks 14-16).
- For jack mackerel 2025 season: sizes 30-60 cm TL, juvenile incidence (<31 cm) only 0.1%; main mode 50 cm. During 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018-2023, high juvenile incidence was observed; lower in 2024-2025.
- Fishing operations within 80 nm of coast in 2025 (vs. >140 nm in 2023). Analysis of 224 mackerel sets for 2025 biometric data (January 27-March 28, 2025) showed fishing focused on adults with very low juvenile participation, except 2021/2024 for mackerel. [33]

**Manrique-Muñante et al. 2026 (Int J Life Cycle Assessment 31:69, DOI 10.1007/s11367-026-02626-z):** Developed characterization factors (CFs) for 10 Peruvian fishing stocks including chub mackerel, within the Fisheries Impact Pathway framework. CF time series (2007-2023) under an EEZ approach; enhanced CFs deviate up to 4 orders of magnitude from previously reported values; CFs exhibit weak-moderate statistical correlation with ENSO indices, with sea level anomalies showing the strongest relationship. Peru is one of the most important fishing nations globally; other species (jack mackerel, bonito, chub mackerel, hake, jumbo squid, calico scallop) contribute to about 20% of annual landings and generated 2,600 million US$ in export revenue in 2023. [32]

**Salvatteci et al. 2019 (Progress in Oceanography 176, DOI 10.1016/j.pocean.2019.05.006) — paleoecological context (Humboldt Current):** Reconstructed small pelagic fish populations off Peru over the last 25,000 years from fish debris in sediments off Pisco (~14°S). Anchovy (Engraulis ringens) were predominant throughout (~90% of scales). Productivity appears to be the main factor controlling small pelagic fish abundance; sub-surface oxygenation affects mainly anchovy and likely sardine populations. Chub mackerel was among the species identified in the debris. Dramatic decreases in pelagic fish abundances have occurred in response to past large-scale climate changes larger than those in the instrumental period. [31]

### 9. Density Dependence, Body Condition, and Growth (Kamimura et al.)

**Kamimura, Taga, Yukami, Watanabe & Furuichi (bioRxiv preprint 2021; published in ICES Journal of Marine Science, DOI 10.1093/icesjms/fsab191):**
- **Data:** 18,302 chub mackerel landed in fishing ports on the Pacific coast of northern Japan (2006-2019); 68% from purse seine fisheries. 15,415 fish from 2006-2016 year classes for growth analysis. 8,429 age-1+ fish for relative condition factor (Kn) analysis.
- **Key findings:** Chub mackerel body condition, habitat temperature, and growth all decreased with increasing conspecific and heterospecific (Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanostictus) abundance. Mean annual growth rates were positively correlated with body condition in all four quarters (Q1: χ²=34.6, p<0.001; Q2: χ²=7.23, p=0.007; Q3: χ²=6.50, p=0.011; Q4: χ²=4.83, p=0.028).
- Structural equation modeling showed conspecific and/or heterospecific abundance had strong negative effects on body condition in all seasons; temperature effects on body condition were weak. **Direct effects (food competition) likely have more impact than indirect effects (habitat temperature changes) on density-dependent body condition and growth.**
- **Abundance ranges:** Age-1+ chub mackerel abundance ranged from 8.5×10⁹ (2007) to 141.2×10⁹ individuals (2017); Japanese sardine abundance ranged from 5.2×10⁹ (2008) to 313.6×10⁹ individuals (2018).
- **Weight-length relationship: W = 1.09 × 10⁻⁶ L³·⁴¹.** von Bertalanffy parameter estimates: Linf ranged 339.9-440.5, K ranged 0.25-0.55, t0 ranged −2.88 to −1.26.
- Context: The Pacific stock declined in the 1990s–early 2000s but dramatically increased after a strong 2013 year class; Japanese sardine has also increased over the past decade. The species has overlapping prey (Copepoda, Eupausiidae, Decapoda, Amphipoda) with sardine. [23][29]

**Lin & Ito (PICES ECCWO5 presentation, ID 16093):** Documented the long-term decline of fish weight in the western North Pacific (WNP), collecting weight-at-age data for fish around Japan from 1978-2018 (17 populations, 13 species) and 1995-2018 (6 populations, 4 species) from the Fisheries Agency and Fisheries Research and Education Agency of Japan (2019).
- **Two distinct periods of weight decline were identified: the 1980s and the 2010s, with the 2010s decline reaching levels similar to the 1980s low.** For 1995-2018 data, decreasing trends in the 2010s were detected across a wide range of juvenile, maturing, and mature time series.
- **Proposed drivers:** (1) Inter- and intra-species competition — the 1980s decline was likely driven by competition from high Japanese sardine biomass (reducing Neocalanus copepod biomass; Tadokoro et al. 2005); the 2010s decline was driven by competition from recovering sardine and chub mackerel populations plus intra-species competition (Kawabata et al. 2011). (2) Bottom-up effects — stronger stratification (temperature difference between 0.5m and 200m depth) and reduced carrying capacity; the 2007-2014 period showed stronger stratification compared to 1982-1989. (3) Temperature-size rule — warmer temperatures generally associated with smaller adult size (debated). [10]

### 10. Environmental Drivers, Regime Shifts, and Climate Projections

**Yatsu 2019 review (Fisheries Science 85:611-639, DOI 10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3):**
- SPF catch and biomass show decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s, driven largely by climatic/oceanic variability and "regime shifts." The 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations.
- Six climatic/oceanic indices affect target stock dynamics: North Pacific Index (NPI), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Kuroshio Extension South Area SST (KESA), North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), and Monsoon Index (MOI).
- Paleoecological evidence (Beppu Bay scale deposition rates, 2,850 years) shows sardine periodicities ~50, 100, and 300 years; anchovy ~30 and 260 years. During the 20th century, Pacific sardines flourished during warmer global air temperatures and positive PDO phases, while anchovies flourished during negative PDO phases.
- Annual average sea surface temperature around Japan has increased +1.11°C over the last 100 years, exceeding the global ocean (+0.54°C) and North Pacific (+0.51°C) averages. [27]

**Go & Jung 2025 (Frontiers in Marine Science 12:1648650):** Individual-based model (IBM-TCM) coupled with a regional ocean circulation model (ROMS) projecting larval chub mackerel under present (2010s) and future (2050s) conditions under IPCC AR5 RCP 8.5.
- Water temperature projected to increase by 0.29-0.33°C across 1-75 m depths; largest May warming (+0.60°C at 1 m). Tsushima Warm Current projected to intensify.
- **Overall larval biomass from February to July projected to increase by 8.88% in the 2050s; northward shift of 0.72°N in biomass-weighted centroid.** Korea Strait/Yellow Sea biomass proportion increased from 6.99% to 15.96% in May; East China Sea decreased from 77.34% to 71.29%. Post-metamorphosis: ECS declined from 71.24% to 66.80%, Pacific from 17.67% to 12.15%, Korea Strait rose from 7.77% to 14.02%, Japan/East Sea from 3.32% to 7.02%. [9]

**Global Seafood Alliance summary of Go et al. 2025 (Fishes 10(1):20):** Potential spawning grounds projected to shift northward from the 2010s to the 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north and become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current. A subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds (from the Pacific side of Japan and JES toward waters off Jeju Island) is expected. Ratios of exploitable chub mackerel biomass and production are expected to increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the JES. The Tsushima Warm Current stock is exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the ECS and Korea Strait (February-June) before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the JES and Yellow Sea. [28]

**Yatsu 2019 (via Semantic Scholar-related literature):** Related studies cited include "Fluctuations in chub mackerel abundance related to climate/oceanic regime shifts in the northwest Pacific since the 1970s" (2021) and "The strong 2013 year class effects on chub mackerel spawning" (2026). [11]

### 11. Related Taxonomic and Reference Notes

- FishBase reference listing documents taxonomic history: *Scomber japonicus peruanus* (Jordan & Hubbs, 1925) is a junior synonym; *Scomber colias* (Gmelin, 1789) appears as accepted name in at least one reference (Diaw, 1976); *Scomber diego* (Ayres, 1856) is a junior synonym. Original description: Houttuyn, M., 1782. [19]
- FishSource notes that blue mackerel (*Scomber australasicus*) is closely related to chub mackerel and is assessed by Japan as two units (Pacific and East China Sea/Tsushima Current); the NPFC planned a 2020 assessment potentially covering both species as a single unit. [38]

## 1. BACKGROUND AND STOCK STRUCTURE

**Species and stocks.** Chub mackerel (*Scomber japonicus*) is widely distributed in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and is fished by China, Korea, and Japan in different seasons and areas. The species is divided into two stocks: the **Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) stock** (distributed in the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and Sea of Japan) and the **Pacific stock** (inhabiting the Pacific coast of Japan and high seas of the northwestern Pacific) [7]. The TWC stock is an economically valuable fishery exploited by China, Korea, and Japan, spawning mainly in the East China Sea (ECS) and Korea Strait (KS) from February to June before migrating to northern feeding grounds in the Japan/East Sea (JES) and Yellow Sea (YS) [13]. The main spawning period is March to June, with suitable spawning SST ranging from **15°C to 22°C** and optimal at **18°C** [7].

**Central East China Sea stock assessment.** The MSY of chub mackerel in the central East China Sea is approximately **18.8 × 10⁴ tonnes**, and the fishing effort at MSY (EMSY) is about 72 standard purse seine vessels, equivalent to a fishing mortality rate (F) of 0.4. If fishing mortality remains at the current level (F = 0.7), the biomass will remain at 45.3 × 10⁴ tonnes. At current fishing intensity, more than 40% of catches will consist of individuals smaller than 200 mm, and only about 8% will be larger than 300 mm. The study concludes there is little potential for further exploitation and recommends reducing fishing mortality to less than 0.4 [5].

**Northwest Pacific high seas population (2016–2021).** Analyzing 38,123 commercial light purse seine fishing operations (2016–2021) in the high seas of the Northwest Pacific (35°N–45°N, 145°E–160°E), CPUE decreased year by year (negative correlation with year, r = −0.489, p < 0.01), with high values from 2016–2018 and low values from 2019–2021. The fishing ground gravity center moved northwestward over time, with a northeast-southwest-northeast pattern. Fork lengths ranged from 102 mm (2021) to 400 mm (2020); mean lengths ranged from 212.07 to 268.28 mm. Growth parameters: asymptotic length (Linf) varied from 36–42.35 cm; growth coefficient K ranged from 0.31–0.65; total mortality (Z) ranged from 1.01–1.64; natural mortality (M) from 0.59–0.85; fishing mortality (F) from 0.23–0.79. LBB assessment showed no overfishing during 2016–2021: F/M ratios were all below 0.5, exploitation rates (E) ranged from 0.17–0.32 (all below 0.5), B/B0 values exceeded 0.5, and B/Bmsy exceeded 1, indicating a healthy population. However, the exploitation rate reached 0.48 by 2021, approaching critical thresholds. Possible explanations for the CPUE decline despite a healthy stock include: (1) spawning grounds in south-central Pacific coast of Japan may have changed, reducing recruitment via Kuroshio Current transport; (2) increasing food competition with Japanese sardine (*Sardinops melanostictus*); (3) climate warming and marine heatwaves (frequent in the NPO since 2014) affecting population dynamics [2].

**California Current stock status (Pacific mackerel).** Pacific mackerel range from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California, with the majority distributed from Monterey Bay, California to Cabo San Lucas, Baja California Sur. Three spawning aggregations are hypothesized (Gulf of California, Cabo San Lucas, and Pacific coast north of Punta Abreojos extending to southern California/Pacific Northwest). A Stock Synthesis model ("Model H3," 1983–2014 data) estimated virgin recruitment (R0) ≈ 0.54 billion age-0 fish; virgin female SSB ≈ 78,425 mt; steepness (h) = 0.48; recruitment variance (σR) = 0.75; length-weight parameters a = 2.7E-06, b = 3.4 [3]. SSB has continually declined since the mid-1980s, remaining consistently low over the last decade. High recruitment periods last occurred mid-1980s and mid-1990s (1–2.7 billion fish); very low recruitment from mid-1990s to 2012. Since the late 1990s, abundance has remained at historically low levels (<150,000 mt). Model H3 estimates: 2014 stock biomass = 97,395 mt; 2015 = 120,435 mt; 2016 = 118,968 mt. Forecasted SSB for 2016 = 47,178 mt. Recent fishing mortality (F) generally <0.2 over the last decade [3]. The FMP harvest rule is: **Harvest = (Biomass − Cutoff) × EMSY × Distribution**, where Cutoff = 18,200 mt, EMSY = 30%, and Distribution = 70%. For 2015-16: Biomass = 120,435 mt, OFL = 25,291 mt, HG (harvest guideline) = 21,469 mt; for 2016-17: Biomass = 118,968 mt, OFL = 24,983 mt, HG = 21,161 mt [3]. Management history: 1970 moratorium after mid-1960s stock decline; 1977 fishery reopened under quota; 1985 moratorium when biomass <18,200 mt; 2000 federal FMP for coastal pelagic species implemented. Average landings were ~5,000 mt over the last decade; average 2004–14 landings = 8,328 mt. Historical fishery peaked at 66,400 mt in 1935-36; the last California mackerel cannery closed in 1992. Mexico landings peaked at ~43,000 mt (1998-99) and ~34,000 mt (1991-92) [3].

**California Sea Grant biological details.** Pacific mackerel reach lengths up to 63 cm and weights up to 2.7 kg; live up to 18 years; reproduce by age 4; spawn from late April to September off California, multiple times per year, yielding about 70,000 eggs per event. They typically live within 20 miles offshore in water between 50–72°F. Pacific mackerel reached its catching peak in 1978 with 3,412,602 tons. The stock collapsed in the 1960s, resulting in a moratorium in the 1970s; it recovered in the late 1970s [4].

**Japanese recovery policy.** The Pacific stock of chub mackerel off Japan declined in the 1980s and remained at low levels through the 1990s. There were recruitment successes in 1992 and 1996, but those cohorts were heavily fished before reaching maturity, preventing recovery. Policy 3 (a 55% reduction of the average 1970s–1980s fishing mortality after 1992) was considered the best in terms of final stock abundance and total catch from 1992 to 1999. Using average fishing mortality from 1993–1999, the stock will not recover within the next 20 years. Even under the best policy, the risk that the final stock is not recovered to 3 million tons within the next 10 years is 40% [8].

**Pacific chub mackerel fishery context.** Landings are 538.0 thousand tonnes. The species is transboundary and straddling and identified as a priority by the North Pacific Fisheries Commission (NPFC). The most recent comprehensive genetic study (Cheng et al. 2018) found a high degree of genetic homogeneity. Management entities include Japan Fisheries Agency (MAFF), Korea Fisheries Resources Agency (FIRA), and NPFC; assessment entity is the Fisheries Research Agency of Japan (FRAJ). The LMEs covered include Sea of Okhotsk, Sea of Japan, Oyashio Current, Kuroshio Current, Yellow Sea, East China Sea, Insular Pacific-Hawaiian, South China Sea, and West Bering Sea [9].

## 2. SEA SURFACE TEMPERATURE (SST) EFFECTS ON SPAWNING, RECRUITMENT, AND FISHING GROUNDS

**Northwest Pacific linear mixed model (2014–2020).** A study using fishery data from China's high-sea light-purse seine operations covering fishing grounds between 140–165°E and 30–50°N found that SST had a significant fixed effect on CPUE with a negative slope (p < 0.001), meaning CPUE increases as SST decreases. Chlorophyll-α (logCHL) had no fixed effect on CPUE but showed significant random effects by month; logCHL was positively correlated with CPUE during spawning and wintering periods (April–May, November–December) and negatively correlated during the summer feeding period (June–October). Annual average CPUE decreased from 2014 to 2020, peaking at 15.501 t/net (2015) and 11.363 t/net (2018), with a low of 8.355 t/net in 2020; monthly CPUE peaked in November (14.426 t/net). Low CPUE areas (<5 t/net) were south of 34°N, while high CPUE areas (>15 t/net) were between 148–159°E. The negative SST-CPUE relationship aligns with prior studies in the East China Sea and Japan coastal waters. **Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019). The optimal SST range for fishing grounds is 14–18°C (~16°C ideal), and optimal chlorophyll-a range is 0.3–0.8 mg/m³** [1].

**Taiwan (northeastern Taiwan) habitat ensemble model.** Chub mackerel catch was mainly influenced by the **Western Pacific Oscillation (WPO)**, which was the most significant climatic oscillation at a 0.001 significance level (GCV=0.882, AIC=156.792). NPGO, Niño 3.4 I, and MEI V2 also significantly affected catches at the 0.1 significance level. Sea-surface height (SSH) exerted the most significant effect on chub mackerel distribution, while mixed-layer depth (MLD) had the least significant effect. Chub mackerel catch rates peaked with: **sea-surface temperature of 29°C, sea-surface chlorophyll of 0.25 mg/m³, sea-surface salinity of 33.7 psu, and SSH of 0.575 m**. Chub mackerel was most widely distributed between 25°N, 120.5°E and 26.2°N, 121.5°E. Taiwanese purse-seine fisheries account for 98.66% of captures in that region [3].

**Pacific-cohort recruitment GLM/GAM (1980–2016).** Using recruitment and SSB data from the Pacific-cohort of *S. japonicus* (1980–2016), GLM results showed the order of importance of variables was ln(SSB)×Year, ln(SSB), SSS×Year, and SSS, all significant at P<0.05. For single-factor GLM models, the importance order was SST, SSS, Year, ln(SSB), and SSS. The optimal GAM contained Year, SST, and SSH. Suitable environmental ranges identified: **SSH of 62–65 cm, SSS of 34.72–34.74 and 34.78–34.83, and SST of 20.2–20.6 °C**. When ln(SSB) > 6.0, recruitment was at a high level [6].

**Temperature suitability index (TSI) study.** The authors estimated average TSI for chub mackerel in main spawning areas using the relationship between spawning probability and SST, assuming a **Gaussian distribution with mean 18°C and variance 2.0°C** [7]. TSI in the shelf waters of China seas and Tsushima Strait showed simultaneous abrupt changes in the late 1990s for the TWC stock, whereas TSI on the Pacific coast of Japan had a regime shift in the late 1970s for the Pacific stock. Chinese catch showed an increasing trend since the 1970s with step changes in 1986/1987, 1993/1994, and 2003/2004; TWC catch by Korea/Japan decreased in the late 1990s (step-change in 1998/1999). Pacific catch dramatically decreased in the late 1970s and 1980s but began recovering after the 2000s, with step changes in 1979/1980, 1988/1989, and 2014/2015. EOF analysis showed TSI had opposite loading on either side of the Kuroshio axis; first four EOFs explained 43.10% of total variance in TSI. TWC stock showed non-stationary relationships with TSI with threshold years in 1993/1994 and the late 1990s; Pacific stock showed non-stationary relationships with thresholds in the late 1970s to early 1980s. All relationships between chub mackerel abundance and TSI were better fitted by non-stationary Threshold GAMs (TGAMs) than stationary GAMs. Effects of spawning temperature suitability on abundance had a delayed effect of 1 to 2 years, attributed to the 0–2 year age structure of the main chub mackerel stock [7]. TSI in different areas was affected by Arctic Oscillation Index (AOI), Monsoon Index (MOI), and Southern Oscillation Index (SOI). Non-stationarity in the TWC area was linked to declined variance in the Siberian High, while non-stationarity in the Pacific area was linked to the Aleutian Low. The regime shifts in AOI, MOI, and SHI in the late 1980s caused weakening monsoon and decreasing cold air intrusion, increasing water temperatures. The Pacific stock's late 1970s step change was related to interannual-decadal variability in the Aleutian Low and ENSO. The study follows an "atmosphere-ocean-biology" or "double-integration" process mechanism, demonstrating that climate variability influences biological variability through intermediary environmental variability [7].

**Larval growth temperature dependence (southern Japan upwelling system).** In the northern Satsunan area of southern Japan (where upwellings are generated by the intrusion of the Kuroshio branch current into Kagoshima Bay, occurring once every two weeks in winter and spring), water temperature was the primary factor controlling larval growth; recent growth was positively correlated with water temperature but NOT with prey density, indicating prey abundance was adequate for larvae. Instantaneous daily mortality rates were **0.322 in 2021 (27.5% mortality d⁻¹) and 0.252 in 2022 (22.3% mortality d⁻¹)**. Food requirements of *S. japonicus* larvae and mesozooplankton production were 0.00427 ± 0.00334 and 6.37 ± 3.04 mg DW m⁻³ d⁻¹, respectively. *S. japonicus* larvae had no significant predatory impact on mesozooplankton (0.0869 ± 0.0796%). The area provides a good food environment for larvae [10].

## 3. ENSO, PDO, AND REGIME SHIFTS (SARDINE/MACKEREL ALTERNATION)

**Classic Pacific regime shift literature (Chavez et al.).** In the Pacific Ocean, air and ocean temperatures, atmospheric CO2, landings of anchovies and sardines, and the productivity of coastal and open ocean ecosystems have varied over periods of about 50 years. Cool "anchovy regimes" occurred from ~1900–1925 and ~1950–1975; warm "sardine regimes" from ~1925–1950 and ~1975 to mid-1990s. The mid-1970s shift (the "1976-1977 regime shift") from cool anchovy to warm sardine regimes was widely documented; a shift back to an anchovy regime occurred in the middle to late 1990s. Sardine populations flourish for 20–30 years then practically disappear for similar periods, with anchovies increasing during low sardine periods. These variations show **synchronous patterns across Japan, California, Peru, and Chile**. The variability is linked to large-scale atmospheric/oceanic forcing (changes in the Aleutian Low, thermocline depth, basin-scale sea-level slope, and circulation patterns resembling El Niño/La Niña but on longer timescales). During the cool anchovy regime, the eastern Pacific has a shallower thermocline, enhanced nutrient supply, and higher productivity; the opposite occurs during the sardine regime. Off Japan, during sardine regimes the thermocline shoaled and the Kuroshio Current weakened, but sardine populations expanded across the North Pacific. Peru: sardine catch decreased from 4 million metric tons in late 1980s to 40,000 metric tons in 2001, while anchovy populations recovered. A regime shift in the late 1990s was confirmed by satellite observations of increased basin-wide sea-level slope after the 1997-98 El Niño. The authors suggest the terms "El Viejo" (warm sardine regime) and "La Vieja" (cool anchovy regime) [11].

**Humboldt Current sardine-anchovy regime shift.** The 1972 El Niño caused the Peruvian anchoveta population to collapse (catches had exceeded 12 million tons/year in 1970, accounting for 20% of world catches), while sardine populations increased dramatically over the next 15–20 years in a "regime shift" with sardines and anchovies replacing each other periodically as dominant species [12].

**PDO description and mechanisms.** The PDO is a robust, recurring pattern of ocean-atmosphere climate variability centered over the mid-latitude Pacific basin. The PDO index is the leading EOF of monthly SST anomalies over the North Pacific, with signals reconstructed back to 1661 via tree-ring chronologies. Mechanisms include ENSO teleconnections/atmospheric bridge, SST reemergence, stochastic atmospheric forcing, and ocean dynamics (advective resonance, Kuroshio-Oyashio Extension variability, North Pacific gyre circulation adjustments). During a positive phase, the Aleutian Low deepens, warming the Pacific Northwest to Alaska. Documented reversals around 1924/25, 1945/46, and 1976/77, with additional shifts in 1988/89 and 1997/98; a 2014 flip to a warm phase coincided with record-breaking global surface temperatures. Reconstructions show a 50–70 year periodicity. Predictability is limited to approximately 4 seasons (~14 months) [13].

**PDO effects on chub mackerel habitat in the East China Sea.** A significant negative relationship was found between the PDO index and water temperature anomaly at different depths. Water temperatures at three different layers (2.5 m, 25 m, 50 m) on the fishing ground tended to be LOW during the warm PDO phase and HIGH during the cold PDO phase. During a warm PDO phase: vertical water temperature cooled, the monthly preferred water temperature shifted southeastward, habitat quality dramatically decreased, and suitable habitat ranges reduced and moved southeastward. During a cool PDO phase: warmer vertical water temperatures occurred, preferred water temperature shifted northwestward, and suitable habitats enlarged and migrated in the same direction. The study concludes that the PDO produced significant impacts on habitat range and distribution of *S. japonicus* in the East China Sea [14].

**California Current sardine/anchovy climate dynamics (Lindegren et al., PNAS 2013).** Models combining age-structured cohort models, environmentally sensitive stock-recruitment (S-R) models, and a climate module simulating SST variability accurately reproduced sardine and anchovy population dynamics from A.D. 1661 onward. Correlation coefficients between estimated SSB and observed scale deposition rates (SDRs) were **r = 0.52 (P = 0.004) for sardine and r = 0.85 (P < 0.001) for anchovy**. The S-R models explained **77.2% and 70.9% of recruitment variance** for sardine and anchovy, respectively. Population fluctuations are driven by interacting density-dependent processes and climate forcing (PDO-related SST changes). **Sardine and anchovy exhibit opposite responses to SST: sardine recruitment benefits from warmer temperatures, anchovy from cooler temperatures.** Population cycles have dominant periodicities of ~60 years (anchovy) and ~80 years (sardine). The Pacific sardine collapse of the early 1950s was "largely unavoidable" due to poor recruitment conditions, even at zero fishing (~20% collapse risk at zero catch versus ~100% risk at the extreme catch ratios of ~54% before the collapse). No evidence was found for interspecific competition between sardine and anchovy [15].

**Climate, anchovy, and sardine review (Checkley et al. 2017).** Anchovy and sardine made up 52% of landings of small pelagic fish and 13% of global capture fisheries in 2012. The authors hypothesize anchovy and sardine populations are limited by the supply of nitrogen from outside their habitats, originating from upwelling, mixing, and rivers. Anchovy have coarse gill raker filters; sardine have fine filters. Maximal assessed biomasses: Peruvian anchoveta 22.8 million tons (world's largest single-species fishery), Japanese sardine 19.5 MT, sardines off Peru 11.8 MT and Namibia 11.1 MT, Japanese anchovy 3.8 MT, California Current Pacific sardine 3.6 MT. The Japanese sardine's habitat undergoes deep convective mixing each winter (Kuroshio-Oyashio Transition Area), positively related to sardine survival. Anoxic sediment cores reveal population fluctuations with 50–80 year periods. Anchovy are more constrained by land-based features (coasts, rivers) limiting their ability to shift poleward, while sardine rely more on open-ocean processes [16].

**PDO effects on jack mackerel/squid off Chile.** In the Humboldt Current System off Chile, for *Trachurus murphyi* (Chilean jack mackerel), the key environmental factors were SST, mixed layer depth (MLD), and water temperature at 400 m (Temp_400m); all were significantly related to the PDO. PDO regimes identified: two cold regimes (1950–1976 and 1999–2017) and one warm regime (1977–1998). A significantly negative relationship was found between the HSI of *Dosidicus gigas* and the PDO index, while a significantly positive correlation was observed for *T. murphyi*. In the warm PDO regime: MLD was shallower, SST increased, and SSHA decreased from northeast to southwest off Chile; *T. murphyi* habitat quality enhanced with little distribution change. In the cold PDO regime: SST and SSHA decreased, MLD deepened; *T. murphyi* suitable habitats slightly reduced. The study concluded that **Chilean *T. murphyi* dominated in the warm PDO regime while *D. gigas* dominated in the cold PDO regime** [17].

**Sardine/mackerel/saury in Russian waters (TINRO).** Since 2014, mackerel and sardine have appeared en masse in Russian fishery waters; since 2015, saury concentrations shifted eastward and northward. Both the previous and current periods of high sardine abundance are characterized by **dominance of the positive PDO phase**, with relatively cold conditions in the reproduction zone. A large Kuroshio meander off south Honshu Island is observed in recent years, similar to the previous high sardine abundance period; the first low-abundance sardine generation formed after the meander's sharp decrease in the 1988 spawning season. During June 2014–2018, main sardine and mackerel aggregations were observed on the warmer side of the North Subarctic Front. Mackerel catches spanned SST from **8.6–21.1°C, with highest concentrations at 12–17°C**; the 8°C isothermal surface is the northern and deep habitat limit. Chub mackerel migrate into Russian waters during forage migrations, aggregating south of the Kuril Islands from July–November [18].

**New vs. old PDO.** Climate Impact Company (March 2025) reports that the current negative (cool) PDO phase in the 2020s differs from all previous long-duration -PDO regimes because the Northeast Pacific is only relatively cooler compared to the extremely warm central and western North Pacific, rather than being absolutely cool as in the past. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are strongly linked to upper-level high-pressure ridging, and their increase in presence and intensity has contributed to the warming of the North Pacific [19].

**ENSO general effects on fish distribution (NOAA PMEL).** El Niño events cause shifts in sea-surface temperatures, changes in vertical thermal structure of coastal waters, and altered coastal and upwelling currents. Documented effects: tropical warm-water species extend their range northward; cold-water species move north or into deeper water; surface-oriented schooling fish disperse into deeper waters; reduced growth, reproduction, and survival for fish remaining in affected regions. During the 1997 El Niño, yellowtail, Pacific bonito, and albacore moved into northern waters off California/Washington [20].

## 4. KUROSHIO CURRENT PATH, MEANDERS, AND LARVAL TRANSPORT

**Kuroshio physical characteristics.** The Kuroshio Current is a north-flowing, warm ocean current on the west side of the North Pacific Ocean basin, with an annual average sea-surface temperature of about 24°C, approximately 100 km wide, producing frequent small to meso-scale eddies. It originates from the Pacific North Equatorial Current, splits at Luzon (Philippines), enters the East China Sea via the Yonaguni Depression east of Taiwan, is steered by the Okinawa Trough, re-enters the Pacific through the Tokara Strait, flows along southern Japan, and separates at the Bōsō Peninsula as the Kuroshio Extension. Its branch into the Sea of Japan is the Tsushima Current. Transport is ~25 Sv in the Sea of Japan and reaches 65 Sv southeast of Japan. The Kuroshio is a "nutrient stream" with primary production of 150–300 grams of carbon per square meter per year; maximum chlorophyll occurs around 100 m depth [21].

**Kuroshio large meander review.** The Kuroshio south of Japan exhibits bimodal path variations between large meander (LM) and non-LM (NLM) paths, further classified as offshore NLM (oNLM) and nearshore NLM (nNLM). LM and NLM paths can persist from a year to a decade, while transitions occur over several months. The most recent LM event (LM2017) began in August 2017 and was still ongoing as of March 2025 — exceeding seven years, the longest on record. Six LMs have been observed since 1965. Net volume transport is approximately 42 Sv. The Kuroshio region and adjacent areas are spawning and nursery grounds for various fish species, especially in the coastal Kanto-Tokai area where the Kuroshio approaches the coast during S-shaped curvature phases, causing coastal warming [22].

**Kuroshio path modes and chub mackerel larval transport (coupled ocean–biophysical model).** A coupled CROCO v2.0 ocean model with Ichthyop v3.3 biophysical model (domain 122–152°E, 25–45°N, 1/12° resolution, 32 sigma levels) examined three Kuroshio path modes: offshore non-large-meander (ONLM, 2009), nearshore non-large-meander (NNLM, 2013), and typical large-meander (TLM, 2018). Two transport scenarios were simulated: passive drift (PD) and active swimming (AS, 32 cm/s swimming speed with diel vertical migration after day 3). Four spawning grounds were defined (near the Izu Ridge, south of the Kii Peninsula, south of Shikoku, and south of Kyushu); 200 particles were released daily per spawning ground throughout April (peak spawning month), with a 20-day transport duration. Key results: **Active swimming significantly reduced transport distances and shifted larval distributions northward, allowing larvae to reach areas with higher zooplankton aggregation, particularly the Kuroshio–Oyashio transition zone. The largest latitudinal shift (473.2 km northward) between AS and PD scenarios occurred during the TLM period between 142°E–144°E.** In PD scenarios, mid-distance transport (400–600 km) dominated (30–35%); in AS scenarios, short-distance transport (0–400 km) increased to over 25% with long-distance transport dropping substantially. Larvae from southern Kyushu–Shikoku spawning grounds were primarily transported to nursery area 2 (132.5°E–140°E), while those from the Kii Peninsula and Izu Ridge areas were distributed mainly in nursery area 3 (east of 140°E). **The TLM period produced the widest larval distribution due to pronounced meandering flow and eddy activity, while the NNLM produced a narrower distribution** [23].

**Kuroshio as larval transport for jack mackerel (analogous evidence).** Research on Japanese jack mackerel (*Trachurus japonicus*) — a congeneric relative in the same complex — found that recruitment has been decreasing continuously since 2000 in the Pacific coastal waters of Japan. *T. japonicus* were transported from the southern East China Sea to Pacific waters around western Japan through the Tokara Strait; the number of particles transported to the Pacific decreased from 2000 to 2017. Particles passing through the northwest Tokara Strait were transported to the Pacific side during 2000–2005, but to the Sea of Japan during 2006–2017. This bifurcation was caused by an amplification of the northward current where the Tsushima Warm Current originates (west of Kyushu), induced by a **rising sea level west of Kyushu due to the Kuroshio's northward shift along the western Pacific coast of Japan**, which strengthened the Tsushima Strait throughflow. The decrease in larval transportation due to this current system change is identified as one of the causes for the recruitment decline [24].

**Kuroshio, Oyashio, and SST anomaly effects on chub mackerel abundance (ARDL-ECM model).** An ARDL-ECM model using four environmental predictors — Kuroshio volume transport (summer and winter), Oyashio area, Oyashio southern limit, and Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly (SSTA) — applied to 3 age groups of chub mackerel found: **Short-term: positive correlation between Kuroshio intensity and chub mackerel abundance in winter, but negative correlation in summer. Oyashio area significantly impacts fish under 2 years old (p < 0.001). Changes in Oyashio southern limit only significantly impact 0-age fish (p < 0.001). Long-term: Kuroshio significantly influences fish aged 3 years and older (p < 0.001). SSTA had a significant impact on all 3 age groups (p < 0.05) in both short-term (p < 0.001) and long-term (p < 0.001), increasing abundance.** Oyashio area influences fish abundance under 2 years old in long-term relationships (p < 0.05); Oyashio southern limit affects fish aged over 1 year (p < 0.01) in long-term [25].

**Kuroshio/Oyashio background for larval retention.** In the East China Sea, the Kuroshio Current acts as a retention mechanism keeping larvae over the continental shelf; the Taiwan Warm Current and Changjiang Coastal Current tend to advect larvae eastward toward the Tsushima/East China Sea Strait. Chub mackerel in the region are classified into the Tsushima Current stock and the ECS stock. Water temperatures over the ECS continental shelf ranged from 16° to 28°C during March–July [26].

**East China Sea larval dispersal IBM (2014).** An early life stage individual-based model of chub mackerel (IBM-CM) coupled with the ECS unstructured grid FVCOM found that seasonal variability of regional circulation, vertical stratification, and mixing play critical roles in larval dispersal and abundance distributions during early life stages. Under the same physical environment, larval dispersal distributions and survival rates are significantly influenced by spawning ground location. Typhoon impact on larval transport depends on path, intensity, speed, and timing; typhoon-enhanced vertical mixing significantly increases larval mortality and decreases surviving larvae abundance in nursery grounds. Larvae generally advected southeastward and then northeastward over the continental shelf after spawning in the northern shelf region of Taiwan (spawning period February to June). Transport of larvae was mainly controlled by horizontal advection, lateral dispersion, and vertical diffusion [26].

**Kuroshio as food-poor but abundant-larvae habitat.** The Kuroshio has traditionally been considered disadvantageous as a nursery ground for larval fishes due to low plankton standing stocks under oligotrophic conditions, yet early life stages of various fishes appear abundantly in these waters. A study found 16 orders and 78 families of fish larvae; mesopelagic fishes (Gonostomatidae, Myctophidae, Notosudidae) appeared more abundantly in Kuroshio waters while Callionymidae, Bothidae, Labridae, and Bregmacerotidae were representative of continental shelf waters. Significant positive correlations were found between larval fish abundance and ambient salinity for Gonostomatidae, *Sigmops gracilis*, and *Myctophum orientale* [27].

## 5. HUMBOLDT CURRENT AND UPWELLING (PERU/CHILE JACK MACKEREL/CHUB MACKEREL COMPLEX)

**Humboldt Current physical oceanography.** The Humboldt Current (Peru Current) is a cold, low-salinity eastern boundary current flowing north along the western coast of South America, extending 500–1,000 km offshore, from southern Chile (~45°S) to northern Peru (~4°S). Sea surface temperatures off Peru reach as low as 16°C, unusually cold for tropical waters. It is the most productive eastern boundary current system in the world, accounting for roughly 18–20% of the total worldwide marine fish catch. Species are mostly pelagic: sardines, anchovies, and jack mackerel. Three notable upwelling subsystems: seasonal upwelling in Chile (spring/summer), a less-productive upwelling "shadow" in northern Chile and southern Peru, and highly productive year-round upwelling in Peru. A major oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) occupies ~2.18 ± 0.66 million km³ with a core centered off Peru extending from ~100 m to 600 m depth, forcing organisms near the surface. Productivity is strongly affected by El Niño and La Niña events; during El Niño, the thermocline and upper OMZ deepen beyond 600 m. Jack mackerel (jurel) is the second largest fishery; restrictions imposed in 1998 led to population regrowth [12]. The GEF reports the Humboldt provides six percent of the global fish catch (down from 20 percent in 2010), generates goods and services valued at approximately US$20 billion annually, and is particularly vulnerable to El Niño events which prevent upwelling and cause fish stock collapses [28]. The Nature Conservancy reports the current provides up to 15% of the world's fish catch despite covering only 0.1% of the global ocean surface, and is responsible for 50% of global fishmeal production [29].

**Peruvian chub/jack mackerel habitat (2011–2020 synthesis).** Years 2011–2014 had cold-to-normal SST conditions favorable to jack mackerel. Years 2015–2017 were warm with El Niño-like events (weak in 2015–2016, moderate in 2017), which reduced jack mackerel availability but **increased chub mackerel availability (which prefers warmer equatorial waters and distributes further north)**. Years 2018–2020 returned to normal/cold conditions with recovery of both species. Jack mackerel catches peaked at 208,000 tons (2011), declining sharply to ~10,505 tons (2017), then recovering to 86,981 tons (2019) and 76,000 tons (2020). **Chub mackerel catches showed the opposite pattern, peaking at 140,000 tons (2016), with strong catches during 2015–2017 El Niño years**, declining to ~30,000–49,000 tons in 2018–2020. Jack mackerel geostatistical abundance peaked at 639,000 tons (2011) and over 500,000 tons (February 2019), with acoustic abundance high in 2011 (788,764 tons). Chub mackerel geostatistical abundance peaked at over 800,000 tons (August 2016) and over 700,000 tons (March 2017). Jack mackerel sizes fluctuated between 22–52 cm total length (modes typically 24–38 cm); chub mackerel sizes ranged 20–43 cm (modes 15–33 cm). Jack mackerel are predominantly found along thermal fronts between subtropical surface waters and cold coastal waters, generally south of the continental shelf edge; chub mackerel can also distribute over the continental shelf. During El Niño years, jack mackerel were scarce and concentrated centrally/north while chub mackerel dominated [30].

**Peruvian chub/jack mackerel habitat (2021–2024 update).** The summer of 2024 was dominated by positive temperature anomalies until March, when the Coastal El Niño (announced as ended by ENFEN in March 2024) subsided. Jack mackerel and chub mackerel returned to typical habitat patterns along fronts between oceanic and coastal waters during summer 2024, unlike 2020 when they occurred in oceanic waters. Salinity was the only parameter that remained in a narrow range across recent years. Variability analysis of fishing sets from 2019–2024 shows: **for both species, sea surface temperatures ranged 18–25°C (jack mackerel) and 18–24°C (chub mackerel), preferring warmer conditions in 2019, 2020, 2023, and 2024; salinity remained between 34.9–35.4 UPS; chlorophyll was below 4 ug/Lt except in 2021; sea level anomaly and altimetry were mostly positive but not exceeding 10 cm; and distances from coast averaged ~50 nautical miles.** Fishing was generally limited to summer months except in 2023. The last five years' thermal conditions increased jack mackerel availability in the south despite the warm 2023; chub mackerel distributed northward but shared southern areas with jack mackerel; latitudes 13–14°S concentrated the largest catches in the last two years along the front between coastal cold and subtropical waters [31].

**Peru El Niño 2026 impacts.** A July 2026 Grist article reports that a "super" El Niño has disrupted Pacific fisheries: Peru has effectively canceled its anchovy fishing season for April–July due to coastal El Niño conditions (anchovies located over 100 m below the sea surface, twice the depth reachable by purse seine nets); jack mackerel and corvina prices have reportedly doubled in Peruvian markets. El Niño weakens trade winds that normally cause upwelling of cold, nutrient-dense water, reducing algae growth at the surface [32].

**ENSO effects on northern Humboldt pelagic community.** A ResearchGate publication titled "The impacts of El Niño Southern Oscillation on the pelagic fish community structure of the northern Humboldt Current System" addresses this topic [33].

**Humboldt OMZ and anchovy.** The Humboldt Tipping project video explains that if the OMZ expands closer to the surface due to rising water temperatures and reduced coastal winds, anchovies would need to migrate further south, impacting marine mammals, seabirds, larger fish, and artisanal fishers; alternative warm-water species like bonito, tuna, and mahi-mahi could potentially be caught instead [34].

## 6. MARINE HEATWAVES (THE BLOB AND LATER EVENTS)

**2014–2016 Northeast Pacific "Blob" overview.** From December 2013 to August 2016, the northeast Pacific Ocean experienced a severe marine heatwave known as the Blob, lasting 711 days — one of the longest marine heatwaves ever recorded. It spanned from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California, reaching peak intensity in July 2015 with sea surface temperatures 2.6°C (4.8°F) above the interannual mean. On the Oregon Coast, severe temperatures extended to depths of 140 m. The heatwave was caused by a ridge of high pressure that dampened normal winter winds across the eastern Pacific, allowing the sun to warm the sea surface; this was followed by an El Niño event [35]. By fall 2014, the Blob had spread from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California, pushing sea surface temperatures up to 7 degrees Fahrenheit above average. The Blob caused a fundamental shift in the marine food web, from nutrition-rich shelled crustaceans (krill) to gelatinous organisms like jellyfish and pyrosomes [36]. Global marine heatwave frequency increased 34% and duration increased 17% from 1925 to 2016 [35].

**Blob ecological impacts (NOAA).** Krill populations collapsed off Oregon ("You could have fit all the krill from the trip into a little plastic bag" — Ric Brodeur); fish spawning patterns shifted from summer to winter; salmon migration routes changed; subtropical species like tuna and swordfish appeared hundreds of miles beyond their usual range; more than 70,000 endangered young loggerhead turtles were estimated in Southern California waters in 2015, leading to closure of drift gillnet fishing in the Southern California Bight; a record toxic algae outbreak in 2015 shut down West Coast Dungeness crab fisheries; there were seabird die-offs, record whale entanglements, crashing salmon returns, and starving California sea lion pups. Approximately 62,000 dead or dying Common Murres washed ashore between summer 2015 and spring 2016 [36]. The 2014-2016 northeast Pacific marine heatwave was the longest-lasting heatwave globally over the past decade [37].

**California marine heatwave specifics (Scripps).** Off the California coast, an anomaly of 1°C can indicate a marine heatwave, while 2–3°C characterizes a more extreme event. These warm periods can stretch from 500 to 2,000 km across the Pacific. Major recent events: the 2014–2016 "Blob" (combined with the 2015–2016 El Niño, it produced the largest marine heatwave on record for the North Pacific); the 2018 summer marine heatwave localized around the Southern California Bight extending into Baja, Mexico; and the 2019 "Blob 2.0." Impacts included shifts in species' geographic ranges (hammerhead sharks, bluefin tuna, pelagic red crabs moving north), and **surprising fluctuations in anchovy and sardine populations (anchovies skyrocketed while sardines remained low during 2014–2016)** [38].

**Marine heatwave effects on Japanese chub mackerel in the Northwest Pacific (2014–2021).** A dedicated study examined MHWs (defined per Hobday et al.: SST exceeding the 90th percentile of a 30-year (1982–2011) climatology for at least five consecutive days) from June to November 2014–2021 across 135–170°E, 30–50°N. Key results: (1) CPUE concentrated within 145–160°E and 35–45°N, declining overall from 2014 to 2021, peaking at 20 t/d in 2014–2015 and dropping below 10 t/d after 2018, with lowest values in 2019 and 2021; monthly CPUE peaked in October. (2) MHW intensity peaked at 3.5–4.5 °C in 2016; durations exceeded 90 days in the central region from 2020–2021 (up from 10–25 days in earlier years); duration surpassed 50 days in 2016 and 2018, and reached 80 days locally in 2019. Mann–Kendall test confirmed significant upward trend in MHW frequency (p<0.001). Autumn MHWs exhibited stronger intensity and longer durations than summer ones. (3) **CPUE was significantly lower during MHWs (p<0.001, Welch two-sample t-test); Pearson correlation between MHW frequency and CPUE was strongly negative (r = −0.72, p < 0.001).** (4) The CPUE geographic centroid shifted eastward (mean longitude from ~151°E to ~153°E) and latitudinal distributions shifted northward in summer, consistent with the thermal displacement hypothesis (species moving poleward/cooler waters to avoid thermal stress). (5) GAM analysis showed MHW intensity exerted a significant non-linear effect on CPUE (edf = 6.49, F = 15.74), explaining 33.9% of deviance (adjusted R² = 0.336); the partial effect dropped rapidly at low intensity levels (~1.5–2.3 °C), flattened at intermediate levels (~3–4.8 °C), and decreased sharply at higher intensities (>5 °C). (6) Before-during-after MHW case studies (2016, 2018, 2021): paired t-tests showed significant differences between MHW vs. pre-MHW (t = 2.41, p = 0.0511) and MHW vs. post-MHW (t = −2.76, p = 0.0398) [39].

**Northwest Pacific warming and fishing ground shift.** Ocean warming has shifted chub mackerel migration timing earlier and moved fishing grounds northeastward (0.92° east and 1.57° north from 2014–2019) per the LMM study [1].

## 7. CLIMATE CHANGE PROJECTIONS, SPAWNING GROUND SHIFTS, AND NURSERY GROUND CONNECTIVITY

**Spawning ground index projection (Go, Lee & Jung 2025).** A spawning ground index (SGI) was developed based on a ROMS model for the western North Pacific (118°00′–143°00′E, 20°00′–52°00′N, 1/12° horizontal resolution, 30 sigma layers) driven by IPCC AR5 RCP85, simulated 2010–2059. SGI used four parameters: **water temperature (suitable range 15–22°C, normal distribution with mean 18.5°C), salinity (suitable range 33–35, binary function), habitat area (East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Japan/East Sea), and bottom depth (50–300 m)**. The model was validated against KODC observational data from 2010–2019 (r² = 0.967, p < 0.0001). In the 2010s, the main spawning ground (SGI > 0.7) extended from northern Taiwan waters in February, shifting northward through the Korea Strait to the Japan/East Sea and Yellow Sea by June. By the 2050s, projected water temperatures will increase by 0.90–1.42°C across the habitat range, with salinity increasing by 0.112–0.324 (largest changes between 35–40°N latitudes). **Under climate change scenarios, spawning grounds are projected to shift northward due to ocean surface warming, resulting in a subsequent westward shift of nursery grounds from the Japan/East Sea to the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea. Biomass and production ratios of exploitable chub mackerel will increase in the Korea Strait and Yellow Sea relative to the Japan/East Sea** [40].

**Northward spawning shift and reduced Kuroshio influence.** Potential spawning grounds were projected to shift northward from the 2010s to 2050s, meaning chub mackerel will spawn further north in the 2050s and become less strongly influenced by the Kuroshio Current (consistent with earlier work by Li et al.). Chub mackerel may also spawn in shallow coastal areas (<50 m), including Kagoshima Bay and Osumi Strait. Spawning grounds were assumed limited to continental shelf areas (50–300 m depth) [13].

**Larval chub mackerel IBM projection (Go & Jung 2025).** An individual-based model (IBM-TCM) coupled with ROMS simulated early-life stage processes (growth, mortality, dispersal) under present (2010s) and future (2050s) conditions (RCP 8.5). Eggs were distributed at 1–10 m depth, with spawning following a normal distribution centered on April 16 with ~99% of spawning between February and June. Larval growth used a temperature-dependent Gompertz-Laird equation; mortality was size-specific (Z = 0.1097/L). Key results: **water temperature projected to increase by 0.29–0.33°C across all depths (1–75 m) from 2010s to 2050s, with the largest monthly warming in May (+0.60°C at 1 m depth); the Tsushima Warm Current projected to intensify. Larval biomass peaked in May in both decades, concentrated in the East China Sea. Overall larval biomass from February to July projected to increase by 8.88% in the 2050s; monthly biomass increases ranged from 5.4% to 18.38%. Northward shift of 0.72°N in biomass-weighted centroid by the 2050s.** Korea Strait/Yellow Sea biomass proportion increased from 6.99% to 15.96% in May; East China Sea decreased from 77.34% to 71.29%. Post-metamorphosis biomass proportions: ECS declined from 71.24% to 66.80%, Pacific from 17.67% to 12.15%, while Korea Strait rose from 7.77% to 14.02% and Japan/East Sea from 3.32% to 7.02%. Stage duration and mortality remained relatively stable (21.77 vs. 21.52 days; daily mortality 0.1684 vs. 0.1681). Sensitivity analyses: ±20% changes in mortality produced large biomass changes (±184–188% for reduced mortality, −63% for increased mortality); ±20% changes in growth coefficient produced ~28% biomass changes; ±2 week shifts in spawning period caused 31–67% biomass reductions with moderate centroid shifts. Model validation yielded Pearson r = 0.256 with digitized observational data [41].

**Sardine distribution projections (California Current analog).** End-to-end projections for 21st-century sardine in the California Current System (ROMS-NPZ-IBM-fleet model, 1983–2100, RCP8.5) showed simulated sardine biomass exhibits low-frequency (decadal) variability, with a ~40% decrease between historical (2000–2020) and mid-century (2040–2060) values, followed by a 2.5–3 times increase by end of century. **A progressive poleward shift of sardine distribution is driven primarily by thermal habitat preference (temperature), not prey availability; the magnitude of poleward displacement is ~500 km under lower warming (~2°C) and ~800 km under higher warming (~3–4°C). By end of century, suitable thermal habitat becomes virtually absent equatorward of 40°N under the highest warming scenario. Catch is projected to increase by 50–70% in the northern CCS and decrease by 30–70% in the southern and central CCS by end of century** [42].

**Seasonal potential distribution in Korean waters.** A 2024 study hosted by NOAA examines "Projected changes in seasonal potential distribution of chub mackerel Scomber japonicus under continued ocean warming in Korean waters" [43]. Related work notes climate change is shifting chub mackerel spawning grounds northward and extending the spawning period (Kanamori et al., 2019, cited in Go et al. 2025) [44].
